Step six: price fungibility honestly. Rautela's instinct was to move cloud engineers onto connector work. Possible, but not at par. Pratyaksh's history showed a cloud engineer delivering about one week of connector progress per 1.4 weeks spent, and costing the lending pool a further half-week per loan in context transfer. Twenty-two stranded cloud weeks therefore buy roughly 22 ÷ 1.4 ≈ 15.7 integration-weeks, enough to cover the nine-week gap. They buy nothing in machine learning, where the scarce input was two people who understood the labelling pipeline. An exchange rate never written down is always assumed to be 1.0, and it never is.

Step seven: separate effort from duration. The camera rev-C item consumed 38 firmware engineer-weeks, but its critical path also held a six-week PCB fabrication and a four-week safety test, which consume calendar and no engineer time. A plan feasible in effort can be infeasible in time.

Step eight: choose a loading level deliberately. Firmware at 50 against 50 is not "exactly right"; it is full utilisation, the worst place to stand. For an approximately M/M/1 system, expected queue time scales with ρ/(1−ρ).

Figure 2. Moving from 80 to 95 per cent loading adds nineteen per cent to nominal output and multiplies expected waiting by nearly five. Mallya planned firmware at 1.00, where the expression has no finite value.

The consequence is a rule most planners find counter-intuitive: load the critical pool to roughly 0.75–0.80 of net capacity and leave the rest unassigned. That reserve is the price of the plan finishing on the date it claims.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Three testable conditions govern whether bottom-up accounting is the right instrument. First, the work must be estimable within roughly a factor of two. Pratyaksh passes for four of five items and fails for the weld-seam model, whose honest ML range was 22 to 60 engineer-weeks depending on whether Qudrat's line imagery was usable. Rozana fails globally, which is why Nair abolished estimates. Second, team composition must be stable over the horizon — Pratyaksh passes for a quarter, fails for a year. Third, the constraint must be person-time. Rozana's real Q1 constraint was one compliance reviewer who signed every screen touching investment advice: a queue of one, unaffected by hiring engineers.

The method actively misleads in two situations. When work is genuinely exploratory, a person-week total converts a range into a number and hands leadership a false precision they will quote back. And when a capacity plan is used as a performance instrument, its estimates stop being estimates and become negotiating positions — arithmetic on fiction, executed with great care.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product companies find the binding pool is almost always a shared platform team. At Rivaaj Apparel Cloud, which ran four products on one identity-and-billing core, the nine-person platform group was claimed by all four roadmaps at once, each claim individually modest. Rivaaj's answer was an internal market: each line got a quarterly allocation of platform weeks proportional to revenue, could trade it, and unclaimed weeks reverted to platform's debt backlog. It is clumsy and it works, because contention becomes visible in advance rather than as an escalation in week seven.

Two-sided marketplaces have a subtler problem. At Panghat Marketplace, an agricultural trading platform, supply-side and demand-side squads planned independently, but a feature improving buyer conversion is worthless if seller listing quality has not kept pace. Capacity must be planned for the coupled pair: the demand-side item alone is not half the value, it is close to none.

In regulated products, part of capacity is claimed before planning starts. Rozana's obligations under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, plus its bank partner's audit remediations, took twelve to twenty per cent of engineering each quarter, timed by someone else's calendar. Treating that as a surprise is a choice, not a fact.

Hardware-plus-software is where effort and duration decouple most violently; the planning unit must be a schedule with lead times, not a pool of weeks. AI-native work adds a third currency: the model team's real constraint in January was 2,400 labelled weld images Qudrat had not yet produced, plus GPU quota under a fixed monthly commitment. Engineer-weeks were abundant; the inputs were not. Mature companies say they handle these seams with a quarterly process. What they do is keep a few senior people whose job is to notice in week three which pool is drowning, and move scope before anyone writes a status report.

6. Eight distinctions that separate expert from competent

Aggregate sufficiency is not pool sufficiency

The tell-tale sign is a plan reporting capacity as one number. An expert reads a single total as evidence that nobody checked, because above roughly fifteen people the skills have specialised enough that the total is a fiction. The obvious reading — a surplus means comfort — is wrong: surpluses strand off the critical path and deficits concentrate on it.

The productive fraction is endogenous, not a property of the team

Planners treat the fraction as a measurement, like a team's height. It is closer to a thermostat reading: load a pool to ninety-five per cent and the fraction falls, because expedites, context-switching and queue management eat the margin. The tell-tale sign is a team whose efficiency degrades in exactly the quarters it was loaded hardest, and is then given a productivity intervention rather than a lighter plan.

Effort and duration are different quantities

A fabrication run, a penetration test, a bank's sign-off and an external audit consume calendar and almost no engineer-weeks. The tell-tale sign is a schedule where every bar's length equals its effort estimate. Experts keep a second list — the lead-time items — and start those first regardless of priority, because they are the only things that cannot be compressed by working harder.

Buffers aggregate as the square root, not the sum

If five independent items each carry safety to reach ninety per cent confidence, the pooled buffer is roughly the root of the sum of squares: five items padded four weeks each need about nine weeks pooled, not twenty. The tell-tale sign is estimates ending in round numbers about 1.5 times the engineer's private guess. Goldratt's point holds — individual padding is wasteful and, through Student syndrome, gets consumed anyway.

New headcount is negative capacity first

Adding four engineers to a drowning pool removes senior capacity from that pool for eight to ten weeks. The tell-tale sign is a plan in which a January joiner contributes a full quarter of output. Hiring relieves pressure eventually, and fails to exactly when the pressure is acute — which is when it gets approved.

Fungibility has an exchange rate, and the lender pays too

"We'll borrow two cloud engineers" hides three numbers: the borrowed engineer's inefficiency factor, the supervision cost to the receiver, and the ramp-down cost to the lender's throughput. Pratyaksh's honest figures were 1.4, about a week, and half a week per loan. The tell-tale sign is a reallocation drawn as a clean transfer of weeks between two columns.

Unplanned work has a distribution, not an average

A line reading "20% for support" states a mean, the wrong statistic for a commitment. If support takes eighteen per cent in a median quarter and thirty-four in a bad one, planning at eighteen means being wrong half the time in the direction that costs a renewal. The tell-tale sign is an overhead allowance quoted without a range or a worst observed value.

The plan's second-order effect is on next quarter's ask

A capacity plan is a negotiation artefact as much as a forecast. Teams that under-promise and over-deliver teach stakeholders to inflate the next request; teams punished for a shortfall learn to pad, then to spend the padding. The tell-tale sign is quarter-on-quarter oscillation in requested scope correlating with nothing in the market. Experts make the arithmetic public, because a visible subtraction is harder to game.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products, capacity is contested by many small bets rather than a few large ones, so the useful unit is a percentage allocation to squads plus a throughput forecast — Rozana's shape. In business software sold on contract, commitments attach to dates with financial consequences, which makes bottom-up costing worth its price. In platform and marketplace businesses the important number is the shared team's, and planning becomes arbitration. In hardware, lead time dominates and capacity planning becomes scheduling. In AI-native products the constraint migrates to data, labelling and evaluation throughput, and anyone planning in engineer-weeks alone will be confidently wrong.

Stage matters less than people claim. Below roughly twenty engineers one person holds the whole picture and formal planning adds little; above fifty no one does and it becomes mandatory. The gap between a Series B company and a listed one is consequence, not method: the same mistake costs a delayed launch in one and restated guidance in the other. Early-stage companies still need the arithmetic for hiring decisions with a six-month lag, the one place it cannot be improvised.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Rozana Money: forecasting instead of adding

Nair's twelve throughput observations had a mean of 11.33 items per sprint and a standard deviation of 2.90. Six independent draws therefore have an expected sum of 68 and a standard deviation of 2.90 × √6 ≈ 7.1, which converts into commitments at stated confidence: about 68 items at even odds, 61 at eighty-five per cent, 56 at ninety-five. The slide promised 78 — 1.41 standard deviations above the mean, roughly an eight per cent chance. Ramaswamy's contribution was not to lower the number but to attach a probability, turning an argument about optimism into arithmetic about risk appetite.

Figure 3. The same backlog as a forecast rather than a promise. The slide sat well up the tail, and the discussion that followed was about which items to move, not about whether the team was trying hard enough.

A second intervention needed no arithmetic about people. Rozana carried 34 items in progress. By Little's Law, cycle time equals work in progress over throughput: 34 ÷ 11.33 ≈ 3.0 sprints, or six weeks. Halving work in progress to 17 halves cycle time to three. No one was hired; capacity in the sense customers felt doubled.

Pratyaksh Vision Systems: the reallocation

Rautela's proposal moved the drift-monitoring service out of the quarter, removing 22 ML and 24 cloud weeks. Machine learning went from a deficit of 8 to a surplus of 14, enough to absorb the weld-seam model's bad case. Cloud's surplus rose to 46, of which about 13 weeks went to integrations at the 1.4 exchange rate, closing that gap and leaving firmware as the only fully loaded pool — which Mallya relieved by sending rev-C sensor qualification to an external lab at ₹18 lakh, converting 9 engineer-weeks into cash.

Rachna Build Systems: a textbook plan that failed

Rachna Build Systems, an Ahmedabad firm selling project-controls software to construction companies, did everything the accounting school recommends for the first half of 2026 and missed badly. Fifty-four engineers over twenty-six weeks gave 1,404 gross engineer-weeks; losses of 190 left 1,214 nominal. Rachna had just carved out a six-person support team to raise its productive fraction, so planned at 0.82 rather than its historical 0.68 — 995 net against 900 demand, a comfortable-looking buffer across nine commitments.

Table 2. Rachna's H1 2026 plan against its after-the-fact reconstruction. Every line was defensible in January; one was true.
QuantityPlannedActual

Two things went wrong and only one was arithmetic. The new support team lacked the domain depth to close escalations, so roughly a day a week of feature-engineer time kept flowing into support and the fraction never moved. Separately, a multi-tenant database migration that appeared in no estimate slipped five weeks and blocked three of the nine items. By week eighteen Rachna had shipped four. The recovery was unglamorous: they stopped asserting a fraction and measured it, mapping merged pull requests to ticket type over two quarters to get 0.69; replanned the second half at that figure with the critical pool at 0.75 loading; committed to six items and delivered six. Catching it in May rather than January cost a ₹3.1 crore renewal cut from three years to one, and two senior engineers who resigned after five months of being told the plan was fine.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

The dominant failure is planning the average and committing the tail. Its early sign is an overhead line with no range. The diagnostic — "what was the worst quarter for unplanned work in two years, and does the plan survive it?" — takes thirty seconds and is rarely asked. Caught in week two it costs a scope conversation; in week ten it costs the quarter.

The second is improving the fraction by decree, Rachna's error: raising the assumed fraction because a structural change is expected to help, before evidence that it has. The sign is a fraction that improved with no measurement behind it. The diagnostic: "which quarter's data produced this number?"

The third is the invisible dependency. Aggregate capacity is sufficient, pool capacity is sufficient, and the plan still fails because several items sit behind one migration or one specialist. The sign is that no one can name, per commitment, the one or two people without whom it stops. Late detection is expensive because resequencing is cheap in January and impossible in April.

The fourth is closing the gap with hours. A plan that reconciles without a scope cut, a date move, added people or a deliberate quality trade has not reconciled. It has borrowed against next quarter's estimates and against attrition.

10. Where competent people genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether bottom-up accounting should exist at all. The flow school's argument is empirical: where item sizes vary widely, throughput forecasts have repeatedly beaten estimate sums, and estimating itself consumes capacity — Rozana put story-point sessions at about 4 per cent of engineering time. It would be wrong if item sizes carried a fat tail historical throughput has not yet sampled, exactly the condition at a company shipping its first hardware revision. The accounting rejoinder is that percentile forecasts are silent about skills: one number cannot tell you to hire a firmware engineer.

The second is slack. The utilisation school rests on Kingman's formula and much operational experience; opponents note that a business with sixty per cent of cost in salaries cannot carry twenty per cent idle time through a downturn, and that the queueing model assumes an arrival randomness that disciplined intake removes. Both are right about different companies; the correct slack level depends on how much of your arrival process you control.

The third is allocation versus commitment. The allocation school would have Pratyaksh fund a durable inspection-platform team against an outcome and stop making dated feature promises. Its opponents observe that Qudrat's ₹6.2 crore contract turns on a date in March. For the allocation position to win here, Pratyaksh's customers would have to buy capability rather than dated deliverables — true of Rozana's users, false of Qudrat.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied capacity planning produces a spreadsheet before the quarter and defends it during. Someone who has internalised it does three things differently. They ask which pool binds before asking what the total is, and will not discuss a plan until it is disaggregated. They quote every commitment with a range, and notice when someone else's number has quietly lost one. And they treat the plan as a live instrument, knowing that by week three the actuals have falsified something, and going to find it while remedies are cheap. The tell is that they are relaxed about being wrong and inflexible about being vague.

12. What each decided

Rautela and Mallya deferred the drift-monitoring service, outsourced sensor qualification, lent thirteen cloud weeks to integrations at a stated exchange rate, and held firmware at 0.78 loading. They told Qudrat in October that March was achievable at roughly eighty-five per cent confidence, and named the two conditions: labelled imagery by 20 January, and no second sensor revision. Ramaswamy took the harder path — she replaced "78 items" with "56 committed, 68 expected", absorbed one uncomfortable meeting, and cut work in progress from 34 to 18, which shortened cycle time enough that the quarter delivered 71.

Three questions for discussion:

  1. Mallya's arithmetic was correct and her conclusion was wrong. At what team size does a single capacity total stop being informative, and what would you require in its place?
  2. Ramaswamy lowered a public commitment while raising actual output. Under what governance conditions is that career-safe, and what does your answer imply about where capacity planning really fails?
  3. Rachna raised its fraction because of a structural change. What evidence should have been required before that number entered a plan, and who should have been empowered to demand it?

13. Going deeper

  • Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing — the input this exercise consumes; its optimism is the largest single source of error in any capacity plan.
  • Dependency management — capacity says whether there is enough time; dependencies say whether it can be spent in the order the roadmap assumes.
  • Strategy vs roadmap vs plan — why capacity constrains the plan and must never be allowed to set the strategy.
  • Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later — the format that survives an honest capacity forecast, because it promises no date it cannot price.
  • The roadmap as communication — saying "eighty-five per cent confident" to a customer without sounding evasive.
  • OKRs and goal setting — the allocation school's vehicle: outcomes funded with capacity percentages, not features costed in weeks.
  • Annual and quarterly planning — the cadence question, including whether an annual capacity plan is useful at all.
  • Milestones and release planning — where effort and duration are reconciled and lead-time items become visible.
exp20v2-plan.capacity:
Capacity Planning

Roadmapping, Planning & OKRs — does our ambition match the people and calendar we have?

1. A Tuesday in Bengaluru

On the morning of 14 September 2026, Meera Krishnan, director of product at Ganana Systems — a Bengaluru-based maker of resourcing and delivery software used by mid-sized IT services firms — sat with a roadmap slide she had presented to the CEO three weeks earlier. It listed six commitments for Q4: a redesigned utilisation dashboard, two new integrations, a mobile approvals flow, a billing-rules engine, and a long-requested audit trail. Each item had a one-line justification and a target ship date of 18 December, the week before Ganana's largest customer, a 4,200-person IT services firm, renewed its annual contract.

What the slide did not show was capacity. Ganana's engineering group supporting this roadmap had eleven engineers and two designers, and October carried nine public holidays and planned leave across Dussehra and Diwali. Meera's engineering counterpart, Rahul Bose, had said only "we'll try" when asked if six items were feasible. Nobody had converted the roadmap into person-weeks and set it against the weeks actually available. If the mismatch surfaced in November, Ganana would ship several things badly or renegotiate two weeks before a contract renewal — the worst possible moment to admit the plan had never been real.

2. The idea

Capacity planning is the exercise of comparing the work a team intends to do against the working time the team actually has, expressed in the same unit — typically person-weeks or story points per sprint — so that a roadmap is a commitment the team can keep rather than a wish list. It answers one question: does our ambition match the people and calendar we have? The term entered product and engineering management from operations research and manufacturing scheduling, where "capacity" long meant machine-hours available against machine-hours demanded; software teams borrowed the logic in the 2000s as agile planning matured, largely through the practice of tracking sprint velocity and then extrapolating it across a quarter.

The sentence Meera could say in the CEO's office without sounding glib: "A roadmap is a set of promises, and capacity planning is the arithmetic that tells you which of those promises you can actually keep." It is deliberately unglamorous — no model, just addition and subtraction done honestly and in public, before the quarter starts rather than after it has gone wrong.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in five steps, and practitioners usually skip three, four and five — teams are good at listing engineers and bad at subtracting from them.

Step one: establish gross capacity. Count the people who will actually write code or design screens for this roadmap — not the org chart, the working roster — and multiply by the calendar weeks in the planning period. Eleven engineers over a thirteen-week quarter is 143 engineer-weeks.

Step two: subtract known-in-advance losses. Public holidays, approved leave, onboarding for new hires who won't be productive from day one, and any fixed commitment to on-call or support rotation. This is the step most roadmap slides never show, because it makes the number smaller than the team's self-image.

Step three: apply a realistic productive fraction. Even a fully staffed, fully present team does not spend 100% of its time on roadmap features — code review, incident response, sprint ceremonies, cross-team dependencies and plain friction consume real hours. Mature teams use a historical figure, usually 70–85% of nominal time, derived from past sprints rather than asserted from optimism.

Step four: convert roadmap items into the same unit. Each roadmap commitment gets an estimate in engineer-weeks (ideally from the engineers who will build it, using the estimating discipline — T-shirt sizing or planning poker — that capacity planning takes as its input, not something it generates itself).

Step five: net the two totals and decide what happens to the gap. If demand exceeds available capacity, something must change: scope shrinks, the date moves, headcount grows, or a lower-priority item is explicitly cut and named as cut, not quietly slipped. Capacity planning does not resolve the gap; it makes the gap visible early enough that a leader can choose how to close it.

Figure 1. Gross capacity of 143 engineer-weeks falls to 98 net of holidays, leave and a 70% productive fraction; the six-item roadmap demands 141 engineer-weeks — a shortfall of 43, or roughly four and a half engineers' worth of work.

4. The worked example, line by line

Meera and Rahul built the numbers together on a whiteboard. Eleven engineers, thirteen weeks: 11 × 13 = 143 engineer-weeks of gross capacity. Known losses: nine public holidays plus an estimated four days of festival leave per engineer averaged 2.6 weeks per person, or 28.6 engineer-weeks; one new hire joining in November would contribute only half his nominal six weeks, a further loss of 3. Gross minus losses: 143 − 28.6 − 3 = 111.4 engineer-weeks of nominal available time. Applying Ganana's historical productive fraction of 70% — drawn from two quarters of sprint retrospectives, where roughly 30% of hours went to support tickets, code review and incidents — yields net capacity of 111.4 × 0.70 ≈ 78 engineer-weeks, below the 98 in the illustrative chart above, because the team's real support load that quarter ran heavier than the model figure.

Roadmap itemEngineer-weeks
Utilisation dashboard redesign22
Two integrations (payroll, HRIS)34
Mobile approvals flow18
Billing-rules engine41
Audit trail26
Total demand141

Against 78 net engineer-weeks of supply, demand of 141 is nearly double — a gap of 63 engineer-weeks, worse than the round figure the CEO had been shown. Rahul then ran a second pass, changing one input: hire two contract engineers, adding roughly 20 engineer-weeks net of ramp-up, and cut the audit trail entirely, removing 26 engineer-weeks of demand. Supply rises to 98; demand falls to 115. The gap narrows to 17 engineer-weeks — still not zero, but small enough that trimming the billing-rules engine's scope by a third, to about 27 engineer-weeks, could close it without touching the integrations the renewal depended on. The exercise took ninety minutes and changed the plan the CEO would see the following week.

5. The nuances a learner must become aware of

Capacity is not the same as velocity

Velocity is an empirical output — points a team actually completed last sprint. Capacity is a forward-looking input built from headcount and calendar. Teams that use last sprint's velocity as this sprint's capacity implicitly assume nothing changes — no leave, no new hire, no shift in support load — which is rarely true across a full quarter.

The productive fraction is a habit, not a constant

A team's 70% today reflects its current support burden; it drifts. Planners who inherit a "standard" 80% figure from a template without checking recent retrospectives are planning against a number that describes a different team.

Capacity planning presumes good estimates

It is arithmetic performed on numbers someone else supplied. If the engineer-week estimates in step four are systematically optimistic — a chronic pattern in software — capacity planning will faithfully compute a gap that is too small, and the team will discover the real gap mid-quarter instead of before it.

It tells you about time, not about the right work

A team can be perfectly within capacity while building the wrong five features. Capacity planning answers "can we do this," never "should we." Confusing the two lets a feasible plan stand in for a wise one.

Dependencies do not show up in a person-weeks total

Two items can each fit comfortably within capacity yet be impossible to do simultaneously if they require the same specialist — Ganana's billing-rules engine and its audit trail both needed its one engineer with deep knowledge of the invoicing schema. Aggregate capacity hides this; only a named-person allocation reveals it.

Buffers are not padding, they are honesty about variance

Teams that plan to 100% of net capacity are planning for a quarter with no incidents, no unplanned leave, no re-estimation. Experienced planners reserve 10–15% unassigned — not slack wasted, but variance priced in.

The unit of capacity should match the unit of estimate

Mixing story points from one team with engineer-weeks from another, or comparing a designer's capacity against an engineering estimate, produces numbers that look precise and mean nothing. Capacity and demand must be measured in the same currency for the same population.

A capacity model is a forecast, and forecasts should be revisited

Treating the Q4 numbers as fixed on 14 September, then never updating them as the new hire's start date slips, converts a living forecast into a stale artefact that misleads everyone who still trusts it in November.

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

In a consumer product, capacity is usually contested across many small experiments rather than a handful of large features, so planning often works as a shared pool of engineer-weeks allocated weekly to whichever experiment is winning. In B2B software like Ganana's, capacity planning tends to be more formal and calendar-anchored, because commitments are tied to specific customer renewal dates, and a missed date has a named financial consequence. In marketplace products, capacity planning must additionally account for two-sided demands — supply-side and demand-side teams drawing on shared platform engineering — which makes dependency mapping especially important, since one checkout change touches both sides at once.

At an early-stage company, capacity planning is often informal and verbal, done in a weekly stand-up by a founder who holds the whole roadmap and team in her head; formalising it too early can feel like bureaucracy for a six-person team. At a larger company like Ganana at 60 engineers, informal capacity planning breaks down because no one person holds the full picture, dependencies cross team boundaries, and the cost of a missed commitment is large enough to justify the ninety minutes of arithmetic Meera and Rahul spent on it.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake one: counting gross headcount as capacity. Symptom: a roadmap that looked achievable in the planning meeting falls behind within three weeks. Underlying error: no subtraction for holidays, leave or ramp-up. Cheap diagnostic: ask what fraction of the quarter's calendar weeks are actually holiday-free working weeks, and whether that number appeared anywhere in the plan.

Mistake two: never revisiting the plan. Symptom: the November status update is the first moment anyone admits the quarter is off track. Underlying error: capacity treated as a one-time September exercise rather than a forecast checked against actuals. Cheap diagnostic: ask when capacity was last compared against real burn-down.

Mistake three: closing a capacity gap only by adding hours. Symptom: a plan that "closes the gap" purely through unpaid overtime or weekend work. Underlying error: treating capacity as elastic rather than fixed, which borrows against burnout and inflates next quarter's optimistic estimating. Cheap diagnostic: ask whether the gap closed through a scope cut, a date move, or added headcount — if none of the three, it was not actually closed.

Mistake four: ignoring named-person dependencies. Symptom: two roadmap items each individually "fit" but both stall the same week. Underlying error: planning against an aggregate pool instead of specific people with specific skills. Cheap diagnostic: for each roadmap item, name the one or two people without whom it cannot proceed, and check for overlap.

8. What good looks like

Three weeks after her whiteboard session, Meera returned to the CEO with a revised plan: four roadmap items instead of six, two contract engineers approved for the quarter, the audit trail explicitly deferred to Q1 in writing, and a 12% buffer left unassigned. The renewal depended on the two integrations and the mobile approvals flow, all three of which now had realistic paths to 18 December because the numbers behind them had been stress-tested rather than assumed. Rahul's team hit every date; the audit trail shipped in February, later than the original wish-list date but with no surprise and no late-quarter scramble. Nobody mistook the plan for a guarantee — capacity planning does not remove risk — but everyone had seen the arithmetic, which meant the risk that remained was chosen, not discovered.

9. What Meera decided, and what to learn next

Meera cut the audit trail and the scope of the billing-rules engine, added two contract engineers, and told the CEO the truth in September instead of November. Her reasoning was simple: a roadmap the team cannot deliver is not more ambitious than a smaller one it can — it is only a promise made now that becomes a disappointment made later, at a worse time, with less room to fix it. The next idea worth studying is dependency management, mapping which roadmap items share people, systems or sequencing constraints — because capacity planning tells you whether you have enough total time, and dependency management tells you whether that time can be applied in the order the roadmap assumes.

Where in your own team's last quarterly plan did "capacity" mean gross headcount rather than net, working time — and what did that quiet substitution cost you?
If your roadmap depends on one specialist who also has three other obligations, does your capacity total show that dependency, or only hide it inside a healthy-looking aggregate number?

Gunvatta Factory Cloud: Four Promises, One Quarter

Pune, Sunday, 15 November 2026, 10:20 p.m.

The rain had come back to Baner after a dry fortnight, and Sharvari Deshpande could hear it on the balcony grille behind her. On the dining table were three printouts she had brought home on Friday and not opened: the planning office's capacity sheet, her VP of Engineering's re-estimate, and a one-page letter of intent from a Dubai industrial group that her sales head had twice called "the deal that changes the story we tell investors."

At eleven the next morning she would sit on the fourth floor of Gunvatta Factory Cloud's office off Baner Road and table the company's commitment for the January–March quarter. Four things were being asked of the same twenty-four engineers, and Sharvari had spent the weekend discovering that every number she had been given was true in its own terms and that no two could be added together.

Her phone showed an unanswered message from Sameer Kulkarni in Bengaluru, sent at 7:40 p.m.: "Didi, before Monday — can we talk about what happens to the firmware if I am the only one left?" She had read it four times without deciding what an honest reply would be.

1. The company, and a decision made in 2023

Gunvatta Factory Cloud was founded in Pune in 2019 by Abhay Sathe, a former controls engineer at an auto-component maker in Ranjangaon, and Nandini Kulkarni, now its CFO. Their observation was mundane and valuable: Indian tier-one and tier-two plants generated enormous quantities of machine data and threw almost all of it away, because the software that could use it — Siemens Opcenter, SAP's manufacturing suite, Rockwell's stack — was priced for Stuttgart and Detroit, not for Chakan and Hosur.

Gunvatta's product was a manufacturing-quality and downtime-analytics platform: an edge gateway that spoke to programmable logic controllers, energy meters and cameras, a cloud layer that turned the stream into first-pass yield, scrap cost and downtime reporting, and an application most plant managers opened on a phone. By November 2026 it was in 148 plants — component makers supplying Tata Motors, Bajaj Auto and Bosch, two appliance manufacturers, a pharmaceutical packaging group in Sanand, forging units around Pithampur. Revenue was ₹96 crore of ARR, growing at 40 per cent, on 210 people and a ₹180-crore Series B.

The decision that shaped everything Sharvari now faced was made in late 2023. Gunvatta was losing deals on hardware cost: the gateways it resold landed at about ₹68,000 per line, and plants on thin margins would not sign. Abhay's answer was to build the gateway in-house on a low-cost ARM module from a Shenzhen supplier, with Gunvatta's own real-time layer handling protocol translation and the store-and-forward buffering Indian plant connectivity demanded. Landed cost fell to ₹19,400 per line, win rates against the global vendors went from one in nine to one in three, and the growth that impressed the board was built on it.

It also concentrated something. Three engineers in Bengaluru maintained that firmware, and only two — Sameer Kulkarni and Arjun Dhar — could work below the driver layer. The board had been told, correctly, that the stack saved ₹1.9 crore a year. Nobody priced what it cost in optionality.

2. The industry around them

Three forces pressed on Gunvatta's customers, and so on Gunvatta.

The first was carbon accounting. The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism had entered its definitive phase in January 2026, and Indian exporters of steel, aluminium and a widening list of downstream goods now had to supply verified embedded-emissions data to their EU importers or accept default values that priced them out. For a Pithampur forging unit exporting crankshafts this was a commercial condition, not an ESG nicety. Roughly a third of Gunvatta's installed base had material EU exposure, and those plants had begun asking whether the platform that already read their energy meters could produce the figure their importer's declarant needed.

The second was domestic policy tailwind. The production-linked incentive schemes for auto components and white goods had pushed capital into new lines, and the Bureau of Indian Standards had tightened quality-control orders. New lines meant installs, and installs meant gateways. Meanwhile the Digital Personal Data Protection Act had reached the shop floor: two customers asked Gunvatta to stop associating defect events with operator identity, forcing an unplanned data-model change in Q2.

The third was competitive. Siemens, SAP, PTC and Rockwell sat above Gunvatta and were rarely met below a certain deal size. The nearer threats were Indian engineering-services firms — Tata Technologies, L&T Technology Services, Cyient — who could win a plant by staffing it and were packaging their own analytics layers. Below them sat integrators offering an on-premise dashboard for ₹12 lakh flat. Gunvatta's position had been that it was cheaper than the first group, more capable than the third, and that its gateway ran where connectivity did not. Exposure beyond India was newer: Wei Ling Tan, hired in Singapore in 2025, had opened three accounts in Malaysia and Thailand, and the Gulf was Doug Alvarez's project, run from New Jersey on a schedule that suited nobody's sleep.

3. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

In March 2026 Sharvari scoped an emissions-reporting module. Her assumption, taken from a slide in a customer-success deck, was that Gunvatta already collected sub-meter-level energy data at most sites, making the module a calculation exercise. She sized it Large — 48 engineer-weeks — and put it in the Q4 slot. That assumption came apart first. In October, Ritika Bansal's team sampled 40 sites and found only 40 per cent had sub-meter instrumentation wired through the gateway; the rest needed a firmware change and sometimes a physical meter. The deployment install log, which Sharvari queried on Friday, put it at 68 per cent. Neither number had been reconciled; both were in circulation.

In June, Doug demonstrated a vision-based surface-defect prototype at a manufacturing show in New Jersey, built in six weeks by Marc-André Tremblay on one customer's data. Eleven opportunities entered the pipeline behind it. None had been told the prototype worked on one line, one part family and one lighting rig.

In August, Gunvatta moved its engineering tracking to a new Jira instance; historical data was recomputed by a script, and the deployment engineers, who had never logged in Jira, stayed invisible.

In September, product and engineering agreed T-shirt sizes for Q4. In October, Doug and Abhay returned from Dubai with a letter of intent from Ghadeer Industrial Group covering nine plants in the UAE and Oman: ₹22 crore of contract value over four years, conditional on a proof of value at Ghadeer's board on 18 February 2027.

On 28 October the supplier issued an end-of-life notice for the ARM module, with last-time-buy on 30 June 2027. The successor part was pin-incompatible and needed a different real-time kernel.

On 6 November, Jayant Rao completed a bottom-up re-estimate of the quarter. On 9 November, Arjun Dhar resigned to join a Bengaluru semiconductor company; last working day, 9 January. On 12 November the planning office circulated the sheet reproduced as Exhibit 2, showing 98 engineer-weeks of headroom. On 13 November, Wei Ling forwarded two customer emails asking for a written CBAM commitment before their April renewals.

4. The people

Sharvari Deshpande — VP Product, Pune. Joined from a Bengaluru SaaS company in 2024. Believes the growth has outrun the planning discipline and that she will be blamed for the gap. Has not said she thinks the Ghadeer timeline was agreed without her.
Abhay Sathe — Co-founder and CEO, Pune. Wants a Gulf reference account before the Series C conversation opens in mid-2027. Says he will back whatever Sharvari commits to; has separately told Doug the Ghadeer proof of value "cannot slip."
Jayant Rao — VP Engineering, Pune. Produced the re-estimate in Exhibit 4 and regards it as conservative. Believes the firmware migration is the only existential item and resents that it has no revenue line to defend it. Does not say that the support load is partly self-inflicted, from a 2025 multi-tenant change shipped without a migration path.
Ritika Bansal — Engineering Manager, Edge and Firmware, Bengaluru. Three reports, shortly two. Asked for two backfills in August, was given one. Says the migration needs eleven weeks of Sameer alone. Has not said that Sameer has been interviewing.
Doug Alvarez — SVP Global Sales, New Jersey. Carries a ₹46-crore new-business number for FY27 and is ₹11 crore behind. Argues CBAM is "a compliance report, not a product" and the vision pipeline is the only real growth story. Does not mention that four of the eleven vision opportunities have asked for a Q4 pilot.
Wei Ling Tan — Director of Customer Success, Singapore. Owns renewals worth ₹62 crore, ₹19.4 crore of it with export-exposed accounts. Has told those customers the emissions module is "on the Q4 roadmap." Is quietly relieved that Ghadeer is not hers to support.
Katharina Weiss — Principal Designer, Berlin, 60 per cent allocated. Has done right-to-left localisation before and thinks the Arabic work is small. Frustrated that every review costs a day to the time difference. Does not know the Ghadeer scope includes a plant-floor interface for operators, not only managers.
Marc-André Tremblay — Staff ML Engineer, Toronto. Built the vision prototype and wants to productionise it. Has an undisclosed offer from a Montreal company. Says the model work is forty weeks; says less loudly that it cannot start without an image pipeline from the platform team.

6. Voices

"I am not disputing the sheet. I am saying it measures the wrong thing. Ninety-eight weeks of headroom, and I cannot find one week of Sameer." Jayant Rao, engineering review, 10 November

"They could produce it in Excel, and then ask why they pay us ₹1.4 crore a year. Two want it in writing before they sign. I have said it is on the Q4 roadmap. I would like to know whether that was true." Wei Ling Tan, reply on the same thread, 11 November

"The model is forty weeks. But I cannot start until somebody builds a pipeline that moves images off the gateways, and that is on nobody's list. So the honest number is forty weeks, starting whenever the platform team gets to it." Marc-André Tremblay, Toronto, written comment on the roadmap document, 14 November

7. The options as Sharvari sees them

Option A — Take the revenue. Commit the quarter to CBAM and Ghadeer, defer firmware v4 to April–June. This fits the planning sheet and looks disciplined: one compliance obligation, one growth account, nothing speculative. It assumes the migration fits one quarter after Arjun has gone, with Sameer coming off three months of Ghadeer work.
Option B — Protect the hardware. Commit firmware v4 and CBAM, and tell Ghadeer that 18 February becomes an architecture review rather than a working proof of value. The LOI lapses on 28 February without one, and Doug's position is that the account then goes to a competing bid on the table.
Option C — Take the growth story. Ghadeer plus the vision pilot, buying CBAM time by having a Pune services partner build the emissions module against Gunvatta's public API for ₹2.6 crore. Nandini will not fund it until the renewals are signed, and the renewals are conditional on the module existing.
Option D — Buy firmware capacity. Contract four embedded engineers from a Bengaluru design house at ₹1.9 crore for the quarter. Ritika estimates eight to ten weeks of onboarding to the real-time layer, taught by Sameer — spending the scarcest person in the company on teaching.

Each option chooses which of the four things not to do. None asks whether the four are the right four, whether the emissions figure must be a product feature rather than a quarterly service the deployment team performs, whether Ghadeer's 18 February date is a board date or a procurement date, or what the 40 per cent support load in Exhibit 3 is made of. Sharvari had written that question on a sticky note and never pulled the data.

8. The hard constraints

The planning review is at eleven on Monday 16 November; the pre-read closes Wednesday; the board sits on 27 November. Nandini's freeze allows two backfills, one of them Ritika's, against ₹112 crore of cash, ₹4.1 crore of monthly burn and a breakeven promise for March 2028. The Ghadeer LOI lapses without a proof of value by 28 February 2027. Export customers need verified 2026 emissions data by 31 March 2027, and ₹19.4 crore of their ARR renews from April. An SLA schedule with the largest appliance customer carries a credit of 4 per cent of annual fee per Severity-1 incident, which is why nobody proposes cutting the support reserve. Last-time-buy is 30 June 2027, after which Gunvatta can sell software to plants it cannot instrument.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 2 shows 98 engineer-weeks of headroom; Exhibit 4 shows demand of 312 against 246. Reconstruct how both come from one roster, and name the assumption in each that does the work.
  2. Exhibit 3 implies about 149 engineer-weeks of realised roadmap output. What would you need to know before using it as a planning input rather than a historical accident?
  3. Ritika's 40 per cent and the deployment log's 68 per cent both bear on the CBAM estimate. How should Sharvari handle a disputed number on Monday with no time to resolve it?
  4. Exhibit 5 sets ₹19.4 crore of contracted ARR beside a ₹31 crore weighted pipeline and a ₹0 firmware line. What would each stakeholder decide on this exhibit alone, and what does that say about how it was built?
  5. Sameer Kulkarni is the single point of failure in three of four workstreams. Is that a staffing problem, an architecture problem, or a consequence of the 2023 hardware decision — and does the answer change what Sharvari can do this quarter?
  6. What should Sharvari commit to on Monday morning, what should the board pre-read say on Wednesday, and what will she say when Doug asks her, in front of Abhay, whether she is choosing to lose the Gulf?

10. Sunday night

She reopened the sheet, deleted the headroom row, and typed underneath: capacity available to the firmware layer: one person, eleven weeks, committed elsewhere. It was the truest line in the document, and she could not see how to say it aloud on Monday without conceding something — to Doug, to Nandini, to the board — that she was not ready to concede.

The rain had thinned. Sameer's message was still unanswered, and it was already past midnight in Bengaluru.

Vidyut Mobility Cloud: The Capacity Question

Bengaluru, Tuesday, 6 October 2026, 9:40 a.m.

Ananya Krishnan, VP of Product at Vidyut Mobility Cloud, read the same email a third time before closing her laptop. Marco Villanueva, the company's sales head, had written from New Jersey overnight: Dubai-based Aramex wanted a working demonstration of "predictive charge-slot allocation" at its January operations review, or the three-year, ₹18-crore Gulf fleet contract would go to a rival bidder. In eleven days, on 17 October, Ananya was due in front of Vidyut's leadership team with a Q1 (January–March 2027) roadmap commitment for the twelve-engineer Fleet Intelligence pod — the same pod that also had to ship a government-mandated telematics upgrade by 31 March. She had estimates from both work-streams. What she did not yet have was a plan that reconciled them with the calendar, the holidays, and the two engineers only a handful of people could replace.

1. Company background

Vidyut Mobility Cloud was founded in 2019 in Bengaluru to solve a narrow problem: helping commercial electric-vehicle fleets in India route, charge, and track their vehicles without stitching together five vendors. Its software sat between a fleet operator's vehicles and India's fragmented charging network — public chargers from Tata Power EZ Charge and Statiq, private depots, and battery-swap stations — recommending routes, booking charging slots, and monitoring battery health. A separate module handled compliance with AIS-140, the government's mandatory GPS-and-panic-button telematics standard for commercial vehicles, which every India customer needed to keep its permits current. By late 2026 the company managed roughly 3,200 vehicles for last-mile fleets serving Flipkart, Amazon, and BigBasket dark stores, plus several EV-cab aggregators, and had begun a cautious Gulf expansion, where Aramex was its first major account. Annual recurring revenue stood at ₹64 crore. Vidyut competed on fleet software with LogiNext and Locus, and watched charging-network players like Ather Grid and Statiq push upward into software; none had yet undercut Vidyut on reliability, the reputation Ananya guarded most closely.

2. The situation

Two demands had landed on the same team in the same quarter. First, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways had notified an updated AIS-140 specification, effective 31 March 2027, tightening data reporting frequency and adding a mandatory battery-temperature alert. Every one of Vidyut's roughly 1,400 India vehicles needed the upgrade before that date or their fleets risked losing permit renewals — a base worth close to ₹40 crore of ARR, mostly up for renewal through the spring. Farah Haddad, Vidyut's customer-success lead in Singapore, had already fielded two anxious calls from BigBasket's fleet manager wanting written assurance the upgrade would land on time.

Second, Aramex's regional operations head wanted proof, not a slide deck, that Vidyut's charging-slot allocation could handle the density of Dubai's public charging network before committing to the expansion. Lena Fischer, the product designer in Berlin sketching the allocation dashboard, felt the brief had crept: what began as a slot-ranking view was now expected to explain its recommendations, a harder modelling problem. That model depended almost entirely on Noah Reyes, Vidyut's Toronto-based data scientist and the only person who could train and tune it — and Noah was due to begin four weeks of parental leave in mid-November, squarely inside the build window. Rohit Malhotra, the Bengaluru engineering lead running the pod day to day, kept arriving at the same conclusion from his estimates: on paper the hours fit; in practice, the two people the plan leaned on were not free when the deadlines needed them.

3. The people

Rohit Malhotra — Engineering Lead, Fleet Intelligence pod, Bengaluru. Wants a plan that survives October's holidays and Noah's leave, not twelve interchangeable engineer-months. Distrusts any commitment made before dependencies are mapped.
Marco Villanueva — Head of Global Sales, New Jersey. Needs the Aramex demo ready for January; his FY27 number and the company's first Gulf reference account depend on it. Calls India compliance "table stakes, not a growth story."
Farah Haddad — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Owns renewal conversations with the India base and has informally promised customers AIS-140 v2 ships on time. Worried a slip becomes a churn conversation in January and February.
Lena Fischer — Product Designer, Berlin. Wants the Aramex feature scoped honestly before more design hours go into a dashboard whose model may not be ready. Notes a nine-hour timezone gap already slows every review by a day.

4. Exhibits

5. The options

Option A — Prioritise the Aramex feature. Put both senior backend engineers and all of Noah's pre-leave weeks against predictive charge-slot allocation; push AIS-140 v2 into Q2 FY27. Upside: protects the ₹18-crore Gulf contract and gives Marco a defensible board story. Cost: roughly 1,400 India vehicles miss the 31 March compliance date, risking permits and, per Farah, renewal conversations from a position of weakness.
Option B — Prioritise AIS-140 v2. Staff it fully with the senior backend pair and the Bengaluru/Pune bench; tell Aramex the demo waits until Q2. Upside: protects the ₹40-crore renewal base and Farah's commitments; regulatory risk disappears. Cost: Aramex's operations head has said plainly that a delayed demo likely loses the deal to a rival Gulf bidder, foreclosing Vidyut's first reference account outside India.
Option C — Resequence and re-scope, rather than reallocate. Commit the senior backend pair and the India/Pune bench to AIS-140 v2 on its existing timeline, untouched by Noah's leave since it needs no ML work. For Aramex, replace the full predictive model with a simpler rules-based ranking of charging slots — built from Lena's existing design and one backend engineer's spare time, not from Noah — sufficient for a credible January demonstration, with the full model following in Q2 once Noah returns. Upside: both deadlines are met by people actually available when the work needs them. Cost: the January demo is visibly less sophisticated than Aramex first asked for, and Marco must manage that expectation directly.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 2 shows the combined ask (23 engineer-months) comfortably inside usable capacity (27.4). Why is that comparison misleading on its own, and what does Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 3 add that a simple sum does not?
  2. Whose risk is larger if nothing changes: Farah's renewal base or Marco's Gulf deal — and how would you weigh a regulatory deadline against a discretionary but revenue-bearing one?
  3. What would you say to Aramex's operations head if Vidyut chose Option C, and how would you decide whether a "rules-based" demo is honest, or a promise Vidyut cannot keep in Q2?
  4. If you were Ananya, what would you tell Vidyut's leadership team on 17 October, and what single dependency in Exhibit 3 would you flag as the one that could break your plan?

7. A note for the learner

Capacity planning answers one question: does our ambition match the people and calendar we actually have? It is easy to answer that badly by summing estimates against headcount, as Exhibit 2 does — 23 engineer-months fits inside 27.4, so the plan looks safe. Vidyut's case shows why that arithmetic fails. Capacity is not a fungible pool of hours; it is a small number of specific people, each with a calendar of their own, and two of them — the senior backend pair and Noah Reyes — are load-bearing for both commitments at once. Good capacity planning takes engineering estimates and T-shirt sizes as an input, then sums them against named people and a real calendar, including holidays, leave, and other teams' review dates, before deciding what ambition is realistic. That is what unlocks the next discipline in this sequence, dependency management: once you know where the plan actually breaks, you can decide what to resequence rather than discovering the break in March.

A well-reasoned answer does not simply rank the two deadlines by revenue; it asks whether either work-stream's ambition can shrink without being abandoned, so the calendar and the people line up. Options A and B both accept the estimates as fixed and choose which deadline to miss. Option C is the defensible path: it keeps the regulatory deadline untouched, because permits and renewals are not negotiable, and it protects the Gulf relationship by reducing what "done" means for January — a rules-based ranking Aramex can see and react to — rather than betting the deal on a data scientist's leave colliding with a fixed board date. The reasoning is not that compliance matters more; it is that Option C is the only one actually planned against who is free when, instead of how many hours are notionally left in the quarter.

Fifteen Days to the Freeze: Release Planning at Shamiana Screen Systems

An Indian-context teaching case on milestones and release planning

1. The night before

It was past ten on Friday, 25 September 2026, and the third floor of Shamiana Screen Systems' office off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru had emptied except for the guard and Nandita Iyer, Head of Product. On the glass wall she had written, in four colours of marker, every dated promise the company carried into the festival quarter. There were eleven: four set by customers, three by sales, two by the board, one by a film studio that had never spoken to anyone at Shamiana, and one — the oldest and most dangerous — by Shamiana itself.

That last was the Festival Freeze. From 10 October to 20 November, nothing reached production but security patches and incident fixes. Written after the Dussehra outage of 2023, it had never been broken, and it was why the company could tell every prospect it had gone three festival seasons without a customer-visible failure — the sentence Ramnath Varma, the founder, used in the first two minutes of every investor meeting.

On Monday at 8.30 a.m. she would face the steering committee — Varma, the VP of Engineering, the head of sales dialling in from New Jersey — and table a release plan; on Thursday it went to the board. Fifteen days remained before the freeze closed the gate, and behind it sat a feature her largest Indian customer now expected before Diwali, a Dubai go-live inside the frozen window, a compliance workstream nobody could date, and two internal reports that could not both be true.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Shamiana was founded in 2015 by Varma and two colleagues from a Chennai payments firm, to sell box-office software to exhibitors who could not afford what PVR INOX or Cinepolis ran. By 2019 it had added seat inventory and a white-label booking engine. By FY26 it ran the box office for about 2,180 screens across 310 properties in India, plus 74 in the Gulf, on annual recurring revenue of roughly ₹96 crore, about half of it per-screen fees and the rest convenience-fee share on some twelve crore tickets a year.

What shaped everything Nandita could now do was decided in October 2023. On the Saturday of the Dussehra weekend, during the opening shows of a heavily pre-sold release, Shamiana's seat-lock service — the component that holds a seat for the ninety seconds between selection and payment — began releasing locks it should have held. For ninety minutes, roughly 41,000 bookings across four chains failed at payment or produced double-sold seats. Shamiana paid ₹1.9 crore in refunds and credits and lost a 60-screen chain in Kerala.

The board's response was structural. It mandated the Festival Freeze, on the reasoning that revenue and reputation were concentrated in a handful of weekends and nothing shipped in them could earn enough to justify the risk. It also mandated the Gate system: every item in a release train had to pass G0 (scoped, with an owner), G1 (design and data contract agreed), G2 (built, tested, load-profiled) and G3 (validated in a customer-like environment) before scheduling. Gate dates were published, compliance went to the board quarterly, and Sreenath Pillai, the VP of Engineering who wrote the policy, had part of his bonus tied to it. Three seasons passed without incident, and nobody asked whether the freeze had stopped being a risk control and become a calendar.

3. The industry

Indian exhibition was a business of extreme concentration in time. About a quarter of the annual box office arrived in three windows — Dussehra, Diwali, the Republic Day-to-Pongal run — and within them the first three days of a major release could account for most of a property's quarterly profit. Exhibitors ran pricing and staffing around single dates set by studios, who moved them for reasons of their own.

Ticketing had consolidated around aggregators — BookMyShow most visibly, District by Zomato pushing in — which gave reach but kept the customer data. Shamiana's pitch, and the reason chains such as Suroor Cineplex Group in Mumbai had moved to it, was the opposite: own your audience, run your own loyalty and F&B upsell, pay a platform fee rather than a per-ticket cut. That depended on the booking engine matching an aggregator's on the one night a year when a hundred thousand people wanted the same three hundred seats.

Two other forces pressed on the product. UPI carried most ticket transactions, leaving the company dependent, in peak minutes, on bank-side success rates it did not control and NPCI norms it designed around. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, phasing in through 2026, had turned eight years of booking history into a compliance surface: consent notices, purpose limitation, a deletion path touching fourteen services. And the Gulf had become material — Indian-language releases opened there the same day, at higher per-screen revenue — which was why Fanoos Cinemas LLC, a 74-screen Dubai exhibitor, was Shamiana's first international implementation and its reference account.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The Q4 release train was signed off in August. Its headline item was Instant Row Release: a mechanism that detects abandoned seat holds during a house-full show and returns them to sale through a managed queue instead of letting them expire silently — 3 to 6 per cent of inventory, by Priyanka Sequeira's estimate in Toronto. It passed G0 in August and G1 on 4 September, and was scheduled for 3 December — after the freeze, in time for Republic Day.

On 18 September, Falak Pictures moved its tentpole Kashmakash from Republic Day 2027 to Friday 6 November, the Diwali weekend. Within a day Devangi Shah, Chief Operating Officer of Suroor Cineplex Group — 418 of Shamiana's screens, about ₹11 crore of ARR — asked whether Instant Row Release could be live for it. Her reasoning was concrete: on the last comparable release her Andheri and Pune properties showed house-full for shows that ran at 94 per cent occupancy, and she blamed seats dying in hold.

Nandita first took this for a scoping question. Harmeet Kaur Bhatia's team in Pune, which owned payments and seat-lock, had told the July planning session that the feature was "about seven weeks of work". Seven weeks from 19 September was 7 November: one day late, and so, in principle, negotiable.

Three things had since turned out to be wrong. First, the estimate assumed the seat-lock rewrite would be done by September. On 22 September Harmeet confirmed it stood at "sixty, maybe sixty-five per cent", and that the two engineers who best understood the old lock semantics had resigned, their notice ending 17 October. The feature could be built on the old service; nobody in Pune wanted to write new concurrency logic into the component that failed in 2023.

Second, Grace Tan, the customer-success lead in Singapore, circulated her commitments register on 23 September. Against Sreenath's gate-compliance report for the same quarter it described a different company: 94 per cent of gates passed on time, against 58 per cent of dated customer commitments met when promised. Both had gone to the board in one pack, on consecutive pages, for four quarters (Exhibits 3, 4).

Third, Fanoos was less protected by the calendar than assumed. The contract set go-live "on or before 30 November 2026", with 30 per cent of the ₹3.6 crore implementation fee — ₹1.08 crore — payable at that gate and ₹6 lakh per week in credits thereafter. But Omar Hashmi, Fanoos's COO, had built his launch around a UAE holiday weekend beginning Thursday 19 November, and said so on a 15 September call that Grace minuted and nobody else read. The 19th sat inside the freeze.

Underneath ran the DPDP workstream: no customer asking, no revenue attached, and a deadline resting on what counsel in Delhi called "the prudent interpretation" of the phased rules. It had passed G0 in June and had not moved.

5. The people

Nandita Iyer — Head of Product, Bengaluru
Joined from a Chennai fintech in 2023, months before the outage. Owns the release train and the roadmap the board sees. Believes the freeze saved the company once and is now doing something else; has not said so aloud.
Sreenath Pillai — VP Engineering, Bengaluru
Wrote the freeze and the Gate system. Position: no exception, ever. His variable pay tracks P1 incidents and gate compliance, both protected by the freeze. Not saying: the rewrite has slipped twice under him, and a frozen November is why that is not yet visible to the board.
Harmeet Kaur Bhatia — Engineering Manager, Pune
Owns payments and seat-lock. Position: it can reach Diwali only on the old service, which she will not recommend. Not saying: her July estimate carried two weeks of padding she cannot admit without inviting the crunch she is resisting.
Priyanka Sequeira — Senior Data Scientist, Toronto
Built the demand and abandonment models. Position: the uplift is real, the estimate weak. Not saying: asked for "a number", she gave a wide band's midpoint without the band (Exhibit 5).
Tobias Wenzel — Product Designer, Berlin
Owns the booking flow. Position: a queue handing a released seat to a waiting customer must be designed before it is built, or it will be worse than the expiry it replaces. Not saying: his research is nine sessions, all urban, in English.
Grace Tan — Customer Success Lead, Singapore
Carries the Gulf accounts and keeps the commitments register. Position: the company promises dates it does not track, and tracks gates nobody outside engineering reads. Not saying: she has told Omar that mid-November "should be fine".
Vikram Sahni — Head of Sales, New Jersey
Sells to North American exhibitors programming Indian-language releases. Position: the feature is the differentiator against aggregators, and three Q4 deals reference it. Not saying: in two demos a staging prototype was shown without the word "prototype".
Omar Hashmi — Chief Operating Officer, Fanoos Cinemas LLC, Dubai
The reference customer; he championed Shamiana over a regional incumbent. Position: 19 November, as discussed. Not saying: his board reviews the vendor decision in January, when a late launch meets a colder room.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Dates in the festival quarter, by who set them. Green: Shamiana's plan. Brown and red: the market and the freeze. Blue: the Fanoos contract and its customer's preference, eleven days apart. Purple: an interpretation, not a notification. Product team reconstruction.

Exhibit 3. As reported to the board: a Jira filter counting "Gate" items resolved by their published date, over "Gate" items scheduled in the train. Items descoped or moved to a later train before their gate date leave the denominator; in Q3 FY26, 61 of 214 were moved. The red bar is Exhibit 4, set beside it for the first time.

7. Voices

"The freeze isn't a process. It is the only thing between us and a repeat, and it works because it has no exceptions. The day we grant one for a customer important enough, we can never refuse one again."

Sreenath Pillai, engineering leadership call, 22 September

"Six weeks on the new lock service, three on the old. The three-week version puts new concurrency code into the component that failed in 2023, two weeks after the only two people who understand it walk out. I'll do it if you decide it. I won't recommend it."

Harmeet Kaur Bhatia, message to Nandita Iyer, 23 September

"Three chains in my pipeline have seen the queue demo. I promised nobody November — I did say 'this season'. I'd rather not discover mid term-sheet that our board hears 94 per cent while my customers count 58."

Vikram Sahni, email to Nandita Iyer and Ramnath Varma, 24 September

"Please note the band: the central estimate assumes we recover 45 per cent of abandoned holds, never measured on this flow. If the queue confuses people, recovery could be negative."

Priyanka Sequeira, comment on the sales deck, 21 September

"We are holding the 19th. Marketing is booked, the roster built, my chairman at the first show. I have told him this is the weekend we stop running two systems."

Omar Hashmi, Fanoos Cinemas, email to Grace Tan, 23 September

8. The options, as Nandita currently frames them

A. Hold the line. No exception; the feature ships 3 December on the new lock service; Fanoos goes live 23 November, four days after Omar's weekend; Devangi is told plainly that nothing new will be live for Kashmakash. This costs nothing that appears in Exhibit 6, and everything that does not.

B. One surgical exception. Ship on the old lock service by 5 November, behind a flag, enabled first at two Suroor properties, with Harmeet's team on standby and a documented rollback. Cost ₹34–41 lakh, plus the precedent Sreenath fears; the exposure is Exhibit 6's last row.

C. Move the freeze, not the release. Redraw it around the actual risk windows — 3–10 and 19–23 November — and release in the gaps. This means arguing against the board's own artefact, in a quarter when the founder is raising money, on a risk estimate (Exhibit 6, row 6) finance has not reviewed.

Each option assumes the question is when to ship Instant Row Release — a sentence Nandita had written at the top of Monday's deck and then circled rather than deleted. The Suroor commitment, the only one driving the crunch, has no contract, no definition of done and no agreed test (Exhibit 2, row 1). The commitment that is contractual, carries ₹1.08 crore and a weekly credit, and belongs to a customer whose board reviews the relationship in January, has never reached a steering committee. And the two numbers the board has read for a year, 94 and 58, do not describe the same thing in the same units — which may mean the company reports a milestone system rather than operating one.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Monday, 28 September, 8.30 a.m. IST: the steering committee expects a plan; Thursday, 1 October, the board pack closes. The freeze opens on 10 October, and Sreenath controls the pipeline. The two engineers who know the old lock service leave on 17 October; the hiring freeze means contractors replace them. The Fanoos contract fixes 30 November and ₹1.08 crore; Omar's plan fixes the 19th and is written nowhere Shamiana can cite. Suroor's ₹11.2 crore renews in March, with no clause either side can invoke. Counsel's DPDP reading carries no enforcement date, making it the easiest to defer and the only one whose consequence is not measured in a quarter. And every pipeline meeting ends with the same unspoken figure: a Series C in which three clean festival seasons is the headline.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Of the five commitments in Exhibit 2, which are milestones in any useful sense — an owner, a date, an observation that settles whether they were met — and which are only dates?
  2. Exhibits 3 and 4 have gone to the same board for four quarters. What does each measure, why do they diverge, and what would it take to make one of them the number the company manages by?
  3. Exhibit 5's central column is already in the market without its band. What should a product leader do about that, and what does it imply about how estimates enter a plan at all?
  4. The freeze solved a real problem in 2023. What is it solving in 2026, for whom, and what is it concealing? On what evidence should such a control be retired?
  5. Suppose Option B is chosen and goes well. What has the organisation learned, and what has it learned wrongly? Answer the same for Option A ending in a quiet December.
  6. It is Monday morning. What should she table at 8.30, in what order, with which exhibit on screen? What will she tell the board on Thursday about four quarters of milestone reporting — and what will she not say?

11. Bannerghatta Road, near midnight

Nandita photographed the glass wall before leaving. In the photograph the eleven dates looked orderly, which was the problem: the same certainty whether a contract stood behind them or a phone call did. She thought about writing to Devangi Shah that night — offering a decision by Monday evening rather than a date — and did not, unable to tell whether that was candour or a way of borrowing seventy-two hours.

Harmeet's message was still unanswered on her phone; Omar's still unanswered in Grace's inbox; and in a Toronto afternoon Priyanka's comment sat open on slide nine of a deck already shown to three prospects. In fifteen days the freeze would shut behind all of it, and the only question Nandita was sure of, waiting for the lift, was whether what she carried into Monday would be checkpoints the company could miss honestly, or another year of numbers agreeing with each other and with nothing else.

This case is fictional, written for classroom discussion. Shamiana Screen Systems, Suroor Cineplex Group, Fanoos Cinemas LLC and Falak Pictures are invented, as are all individuals named. PVR INOX, Cinepolis, BookMyShow, District by Zomato, UPI, NPCI and the DPDP Act appear only as market and regulatory context; no real organisation is a party to these events.
