The Ten-Minute Promise: Milestones at Yaqeen Logistics Cloud

A teaching case on milestones and release planning

Bengaluru, 24 September 2026. Past nine at night, the product floor of Yaqeen Logistics Cloud on Outer Ring Road was still lit. Ananya Rao, the company's VP of Product, sat before a whiteboard covered in a milestone chart she had redrawn twice that week. In forty-eight hours she was due on a joint steering call with the Dubai-based supply-chain leadership of Yashasvi Quick Commerce, Yaqeen's largest client, and her own sales head dialling in from New Jersey. She had to arrive with one recommendation: hold, split, or slip the release of the ten-minute slot-allocation engine Yashasvi was counting on before the Navratri-to-Diwali surge began in mid-October. Whatever she proposed would keep a ₹14-crore, two-year contract on track, or put it — and her team's credibility — at real risk.

Company background

Yaqeen Logistics Cloud was founded in Bengaluru in 2016 by two engineers who had built route-optimisation tools for kirana delivery fleets. By 2021, as quick-commerce platforms such as Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart raced to shrink delivery windows, Yaqeen pivoted toward dark-store operations: inventory sync, picker routing, and — its newest product — a slot-allocation engine promising a defensible ten-minute window instead of a hopeful one. The company now earned about ₹180 crore in annual recurring revenue from roughly forty clients, competing against LogiNext, FarEye, Shipsy and Locus, and increasingly against in-house platforms larger players like Delhivery and Shadowfax had built themselves. Its edge, sold hard in every pitch, was reliability: a slot promise Yaqeen's software made was one that held, even in monsoon traffic or a festive-season spike. That promise was about to be tested.

The situation

In March 2026, Yaqeen had signed Yashasvi Quick Commerce, a fast-growing grocery-and-essentials platform expanding from twelve Indian metros into a pilot in the UAE, to a ₹14-crore, two-year contract anchored on three milestones: M1, dark-store inventory sync across 220 stores; M2, the real-time slot-allocation model itself; and M3, a redesigned dispatch-agent interface built around the new model's output. The contract fixed 5 October as the go-live date for the full engine, timed deliberately to land before the Navratri-Diwali order surge, India's largest online shopping season and the one quarter in which Yashasvi's own marketing calendar and investor narrative depended on visibly beating Zepto and Blinkit on speed.

M1 shipped on schedule in July. M2 was where the plan cracked. Devika Menon, Yaqeen's lead data scientist in Toronto, had trained the allocation model on eight months of delivery data — but a re-validation in September, prompted by the first heavy monsoon week in Mumbai and Pune, showed the model's confidence intervals widening sharply whenever traffic and cancellations spiked together, precisely the condition a festive surge would create. Shipping now risked slot promises the model could not keep, the very failure mode Yaqeen had sold against. Devika needed three more weeks to retrain and validate against monsoon-disrupted data. That slip cascaded into M3: Lukas Berger, the designer in Berlin who owned the dispatch-agent UI, had built his screens around the model's expected output, and a changed model meant reworking parts of that interface too. Rahul Deshmukh, the engineering lead in Pune who owned integration, warned Ananya that stacking all three milestones onto one go-live date meant a slip in any one workstream now read as a slip in the whole release, when only one piece was actually broken.

Compounding the pressure, the contract carried a penalty clause: ₹15 lakh for every week the full engine ran late past 5 October, capped at ₹90 lakh, with a termination right past 25 October. Brian Kessler, Yaqeen's New Jersey-based head of sales, who had closed the deal, was blunt on a call that afternoon: the account underpinned a large share of Q3 bookings, and a public slip risked the November renewal, not just the penalty. From Dubai, Naina Kapoor, Yashasvi's VP of international supply chain, was equally direct: her festive-season marketing was already booked around a ten-minute promise, and she needed a date she could repeat to her own leadership, not a range.

Exhibit 1. The original plan compressed all three milestones onto one contract date, so M2's three-week slip now reads publicly as a whole-release slip, though M1 shipped on time and M3 is blocked, not broken.

The people

Devika Menon — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto
Must retrain the slot-allocation model. Wants three honest weeks to validate against monsoon data rather than ship a model she cannot stand behind.
Lukas Berger — Product Designer, Berlin
Owns the dispatch-agent interface built around M2's output. Wants the two milestones formally decoupled so his workstream is judged on its own readiness.
Naina Kapoor — VP Supply Chain (International), Yashasvi Quick Commerce, Dubai
The client sponsor. Wants one firm, bankable date for her own leadership and marketing calendar, not a probability range.
Brian Kessler — Head of Sales, New Jersey
Closed the ₹14-crore deal and owns the November renewal. Wants the original date held, or at minimum a message that protects the account and this quarter's bookings.

Exhibits

Exhibit 2. Milestone readiness scorecard, 24 September 2026
MilestoneOwner / locationContract dateStatusConfidence at contract date
M1 — Inventory sync, 220 storesRahul Deshmukh, Pune15 JulShipped, stableHigh
M2 — Slot-allocation modelDevika Menon, Toronto5 OctRetraining on monsoon dataLow if forced to 5 Oct; high if given to ~25 Oct
M3 — Dispatch-agent UILukas Berger, Berlin5 OctBlocked on M2 output shapeDepends entirely on M2
Exhibit 3. Financial exposure under the Yashasvi contract
ItemAmountTrigger
Total contract value (2 years)₹14 crore—
Penalty for delay past 5 Oct₹15 lakh / week, capped ₹90 lakhFull-engine go-live after 5 Oct
Termination rightFull contract at riskGo-live still not achieved by 25 Oct
Estimated crunch cost to hold 5 Oct~₹22 lakh (overtime, contract QA) plus unquantified accuracy riskCompressing M2 validation to meet the original date
Estimated cost of a clean 25 Oct release₹60 lakh penalty (4 weeks)Full transparency, no compression

Exhibit 1 shows why three milestones planned as one block now read as one block, though only M2 is at risk. Exhibit 2 shows what is actually ready versus assumed ready. Exhibit 3 shows the penalty is smaller and more bounded than the cost of a slot promise failing publicly during Diwali week — the failure the client is paying Yaqeen to prevent.

The options

  1. Hold the 5 October date for the full engine. Compress Devika's validation window and ship the current model, leaning on Rahul's team to patch issues live. Upside: no penalty, no visible slip, Brian's renewal stays clean. Cost: the model's weakness is exactly the monsoon-and-surge condition Diwali week guarantees, risking the promise breaking in front of the client at the worst moment — a larger, less bounded loss than any penalty.
  2. Split the release: ship a rule-based fallback slot engine by 5 October, defer the full ML model to around 25 October. M1 stays as is; M3's UI ships against the simpler, already-reliable rule-based logic Yaqeen used before the ML model, giving Yashasvi a working, bounded ten-minute window while Devika retrains without compression. Upside: a testable checkpoint at each date, no penalty, a second milestone the client can see coming. Cost: less differentiated than the ML version, so the speed claim against Zepto and Blinkit is modestly weaker, and it needs Naina's sign-off on reduced scope.
  3. Slip the whole release to 25 October and renegotiate now. Tell the client immediately, ship the full engine only when Devika is confident, and pay the penalty. Upside: the product that ships is the one Yaqeen actually promised, with no compromise on accuracy. Cost: a guaranteed ₹60 lakh penalty, the Diwali window passes with no engine live, and Brian believes the account risks walking to a competitor mid-negotiation.

Questions for discussion

  1. What made the original milestone plan optimistic in a way that only became visible in September, and could that have been surfaced earlier?
  2. How should Ananya weigh Devika's technical judgment, Lukas's dependency, Naina's need for a firm date, and Brian's commercial pressure?
  3. Using Exhibits 1–3, which risks in each option are visible in the contract, and which stay hidden until the surge begins?
  4. Which option would you choose, and what checkpoint would you set so a further slip can be called honestly rather than discovered late?

A note for the learner

The lens here is simple to state and easy to violate under pressure: a milestone is only useful if tied to something you can actually observe — a model's validated accuracy, an inventory sync's completion — rather than to a date chosen to please a stakeholder. Yaqeen's plan collapsed three kinds of readiness (data-sync, model accuracy, interface build) onto a single date, turning one team's honest three-week slip into what looked, from Dubai and New Jersey, like the whole release failing. A milestone that can slip honestly is one where the owner, the dependency, and the test for "done" were stated clearly enough in advance that a slip is a data point, not a surprise.

A well-reasoned answer does not simply pick the option that avoids the penalty, or the one that avoids conflict with sales. It separates what is genuinely ready (M1, a fallback slot engine) from what is not (the ML model under surge conditions), and asks which sequencing lets the client see progress while Yaqeen keeps its core promise — reliability — intact. Option 1 gambles that claim on exactly the condition most likely to break it. Option 3 is honest but forfeits the festive window the contract exists to serve, a cost larger than Exhibit 3's penalty line suggests. Option 2 is the defensible path: a real, tested milestone at 5 October, the three weeks Devika's validation genuinely requires, and a second, checkable milestone on 25 October rather than a hidden dependency inside the first. Ananya should propose Option 2, with Exhibit 2's scorecard as the shared checkpoint for judging the second milestone honestly when it arrives.

This case is fictional, written for classroom discussion. Yaqeen Logistics Cloud and Yashasvi Quick Commerce are invented companies; references to Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart, Delhivery, Shadowfax, LogiNext, FarEye, Shipsy and Locus describe the real competitive landscape and are not depicted as party to events in this case.
exp20v2-plan.milestones:
Milestones and Release Planning

Delivery & Technology — Roadmapping, Planning & OKRs

1. A date that is really a claim

On the second Monday of June 2026, Ananya Rao, VP of Product at Falak Platform Systems, a 340-person Pune-based maker of warehouse allocation software, sat across from her engineering director with a single number between them: September 25. That was the date by which Project Saptarishi — a rebuilt engine deciding, in real time, which distribution centre ships which order — had to be live across all 46 warehouses of Falak’s largest client, a national retail chain. The reason was not preference: the client’s Diwali inventory push begins the first week of October, when order volumes triple overnight, and the contract carried a penalty of ₹40 lakh per week late, capped at ₹2 crore. Ananya had fourteen weeks, three engineering pods, and one sentence from her director: “We’ll have it done by the 25th.”

That sentence was the problem, not the answer. A single date, held for fourteen weeks, tells Ananya nothing about whether week six is going well; it only tells her, on September 25, whether she was right to trust it. If the team discovers in week eleven that the data-migration layer cannot handle the client’s legacy SKU codes, there will be three weeks left to fix a problem that needed six. Ananya’s real decision that Monday was not whether September 25 was achievable, but whether to replace one distant date with checkpoints specific enough that she could tell, in week four, whether week fourteen was still true — and honest enough that a slip would surface immediately rather than three weeks later.

2. The idea

A milestone is a checkpoint on a roadmap that names a verifiable state the product or market will be in by a given date — not the date itself, but a falsifiable claim about what will be true when it arrives. “Integration environment accepts live data from three pilot warehouses without manual reconciliation” is a milestone. “Integration done by July 13” is a hope wearing a milestone’s clothes, because no one can check on July 6 whether it is on track.

The discipline has an old lineage. Critical-path and programme-evaluation scheduling were formalised in 1958 by the US Navy and Booz Allen Hamilton for the Polaris submarine programme, and independently by DuPont, because large projects with interdependent teams needed to see risk before the deadline, not after. Software carried the same logic through staged release planning, and later through frameworks like the Scaled Agile release train and OKR-linked roadmaps, popularised inside Intel by Andy Grove and carried into Silicon Valley by John Doerr, which tie a milestone’s state to a measurable objective rather than a shipped feature. All solve the problem Ananya faced: a distant single commitment hides its own risk until it is too late to act on it.

The sentence Ananya could say in any meeting without sounding glib: “A milestone is a promise about a state of the world on a date, not just a date — and it only earns the name if we can tell three weeks early that it will be missed.”

3. How it actually works

Building milestones that behave this way starts, counter-intuitively, at the end. Ananya did not begin with what the team could plausibly do in fourteen weeks; she began with the one date she could not move — September 25, imposed by the client’s season — and worked backward, asking at each stage what state must be true for the next stage to even be attemptable. That produced a chain of checkpoints rather than tasks, because a task (“build the reconciliation module”) tells you effort was spent, while a state (“module passes on three warehouses’ real data”) tells you the effort worked.

Each checkpoint then needed three things practitioners often skip because they feel like paperwork: a named owner accountable for reporting it, not just doing the work; a pass/fail test decided in advance, in writing, before anyone has an incentive to grade their own homework generously; and an explicit map of what it depends on outside the team’s control — a client sign-off, a vendor API, a security review — because ignoring external dependencies creates false confidence. Slack, the deliberate buffer built into a schedule, is not spread evenly; it sits at whichever checkpoint carries the most genuine uncertainty, here the first, because nobody yet knew how clean the client’s eleven-year-old SKU data actually was. Finally, the team agreed what an honest slip looks like: a milestone may move, but only forward, with a stated reason, the moment the team first believes it will move — not the week it was originally due.

Fig. 1 — Four state-based checkpoints working backward from the fixed external date, with slack concentrated at the point of highest uncertainty (M1), not spread evenly.

4. A worked example

Falak’s three pods had delivered roughly 120 combined story points per two-week sprint across their last three releases — a measured velocity. Project Saptarishi’s scope came to 840 points. Divided by 120 points per sprint, that is exactly seven sprints, or fourteen weeks: the plan fit the window with zero slack in the schedule itself, which is precisely why slack had to live in the sequencing of checkpoints instead.

MilestoneDateCumulative weeksPass/fail test
M1Jul 134Allocation model ≥95% match on 3 years of historical orders
M2Aug 1083 pilot warehouses ingest live feed, zero manual reconciliation
M3Aug 3111All 46 warehouses staged, load test at 2x historical peak passes
M4Sep 2114Production cutover, rollback tested, client sign-off

Now run the second pass, because the value of a milestone is what it does when reality disagrees with the plan. At the M1 review, the accuracy test came back at 91%, not 95% — the legacy SKU codes were messier than expected. Ananya now had two priced options, not a vague sense of being “a bit behind.” Option one: a fourth, contract pod for three weeks to run a data-tuning sprint alongside M2, at roughly ₹18 lakh, keeping all four dates fixed. Option two: drop the multi-warehouse rebalancing feature, estimated at 80 of the 840 points — about 0.67 of a sprint — freeing enough capacity to absorb the tuning work without added cost. Both options were visible only because the checkpoint carried a number, not a feeling; had the plan said “on track” through week four, the same gap would have surfaced as a crisis in week eleven, with no time left for either.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Milestone versus task

A task describes effort spent; a milestone describes a state achieved. “Finish the reconciliation module” is a task a developer can mark complete regardless of whether it reconciles anything correctly. “Module passes on real data from three warehouses” is a milestone, marked true only by a test, not a sense of having worked hard.

Exogenous dates versus internal checkpoints

September 25 was fixed by the client’s season; M1 through M3 were internal checkpoints chosen because they were verifiable earlier. Treating every internal checkpoint as equally immovable as the contract date removes the flexibility that makes milestones useful.

Status theatre

Without a pre-agreed test, “on track” becomes whatever the reporter needs it to mean that week. The fix is deciding the test before anyone has a reason to read it generously.

Where slack belongs

Padding every checkpoint equally feels fair but wastes protection on parts of the plan never in doubt. Slack should sit at the step with the least prior evidence — here, data quality, not rollout, which was well understood from two prior releases.

What a milestone cannot tell you

A milestone can be green while the product is wrong. It verifies the team reached the planned state, not that the state was worth reaching. Falak could hit all four on schedule and still discover warehouse managers hate the new interface; milestones track delivery risk, not desirability risk.

A slip is not a failure

A milestone that moves in week four, with nine weeks left to react, is the system working as designed. One only discovered slipped in the final week has failed at its one job, regardless of whether the work itself was late.

Cadence and the reward for bad news

Checkpoints decay into decoration without a fixed review rhythm and a culture that rewards saying “at risk” early rather than punishing it. Teams that penalise early bad news train people to report good news for as long as they can.

Hidden dependencies

A milestone written only in terms of what engineering controls, with no line for a client’s security review or a vendor’s API changelog, looks achievable until an outside party misses a date nobody was tracking.

6. Where this looks different

In a consumer product, milestones orbit external calendars the company does not control either: app-store review windows, a festive shopping peak, a marketing campaign already booked. In a B2B company like Falak, the critical path often runs through the client’s own organisation — procurement, a security audit, a data-mapping sign-off — so a well-built milestone set includes checkpoints the client must clear, placed early enough that a client delay is visible while there is time to renegotiate scope. In a marketplace, a milestone on one side is close to meaningless without a matched checkpoint on the other: onboarding 500 sellers is not progress without a matching demand-side milestone, because sequencing between the sides matters more than either side’s own pace.

Company stage changes the texture further. An early-stage team facing enormous uncertainty is usually better served by two or three coarse, widely-spaced milestones with generous slack, since an early slip is cheap and over-specifying an unproven plan is not. A large organisation with many interdependent teams and a formal OKR cycle needs more numerous, precisely defined milestones, because more people downstream rely on each one, and a late discovery ripples through committees a ten-person startup does not have.

7. Common mistakes

Date-only milestones. Symptom: status says “on track” for thirteen weeks, then “two weeks late” appears in week fourteen. Underlying error: the checkpoint was never given a pass/fail test, only a date. Diagnostic: ask the owner to name the artifact proving the last milestone true; if they cannot, it was never one.

Percent-complete reporting. Symptom: a milestone sits at “90% done” for three straight reviews. Underlying error: task completion stands in for state achievement, when the riskiest part of most integrations is the last ten percent. Diagnostic: check whether past percent-complete figures have ever correlated with the eventual outcome; usually they have not.

Milestones that never move. Symptom: across several releases, not one date has ever shifted. Underlying error: the political cost of reporting a slip is perceived as higher than quietly absorbing it through unpaid overtime or unnamed scope creep. Diagnostic: count how many milestones moved, and how early, over the last three releases; zero is itself the warning sign.

Milestone fatigue. Symptom: a team tracks a “milestone” every sprint. Underlying error: ordinary sprint reviews relabelled as milestones, diluting the term until none feels consequential. Diagnostic: count milestones per quarter; above six or eight, it is task tracking wearing a grander name.

8. What good looks like

In the version of this story that actually happened, Ananya insisted on the four state-based checkpoints in Figure 1, each with a named owner and a written test, reviewed every Friday with both pods and the client’s IT liaison present. When M1 landed at 91% instead of 95%, the review flagged it “at risk” that same afternoon, not weeks later. By July 20, Ananya chose to drop multi-warehouse rebalancing rather than pay for a fourth pod, told the client with nine weeks of runway left, and kept M2 through M4 unchanged. The client, seeing the decision made early and in writing, agreed to take the feature in a January patch instead. September 25 held, the penalty clause was never triggered, and nobody on either side was surprised after week four.

9. Closing

Ananya’s decision was not to work harder toward September 25; it was to stop treating it as the only thing worth knowing and build four earlier moments at which its truth could be checked. What made those moments milestones, rather than four smaller deadlines repeating the same mistake, was that each carried a test decided in advance, an owner accountable for reporting it honestly, and a place chosen for what it would reveal, not for being evenly spaced. The next ideas worth reading are re-planning and change control, which governs how scope and date get renegotiated without either party feeling ambushed, and pre-mortems and risk registers, which ask what could break a milestone before it is even written down.

Two questions worth sitting with: could the owner of a project you are on state the exact pass/fail test for its next milestone, this minute, without checking a document? And in your current plan, is the slack sitting deliberately at the one step nobody yet has evidence about — or has it simply been spread thin everywhere, which is another way of saying it protects nothing?
exp20v2-plan.dependencies:
Delivery & Technology · Roadmapping, Planning & OKRs

Dependency Management

What am I depending on that I don't control, and how do I de-risk it?

1. A rate card that cannot slip

On the morning of 3 March, Ananya Rao, group product manager at Bandhan Freight Systems in Pune, wrote a single date atop her planning document: 2 June. That was the day her largest prospective client, a listed FMCG distributor moving roughly 40,000 tonnes of goods a month, wanted to switch onto Bandhan's Instant Rate Card — a feature quoting a firm freight price in under three seconds instead of the two days its transport desk spent phoning brokers. The client wanted pricing locked in before renegotiating its own trucking contracts ahead of the monsoon; miss the date and the account would go to a competitor already piloting a similar tool. Won, it was worth close to four crore rupees a year — Bandhan's first FMCG logo of that size.

Ananya's own pod could build the pricing screen, quote logic and checkout flow on a timeline she controlled. But Instant Rate Card could not launch on her team's work alone: it needed a validated GST e-way bill check from the compliance data team, a rebuilt pricing-model API from the data platform team, and a live vehicle-telematics feed from an external vendor, Chalan Sensor Systems. None of those three were hers to schedule; each belonged to a manager with other priorities. The question was not whether her team could hit 2 June, but whether work from people who did not report to her, and did not share her deadline, would land in time to be usable at all.

2. The idea

A dependency, in product and delivery work, is any output your plan requires that is produced by a team, system or organisation you do not control the priorities of. Dependency management is finding those dependencies before they surprise you, working out which actually determine your finish date, and putting a plan — a buffer, a fallback, an escalation, a renegotiated interface — that keeps their risk from becoming yours. It sits inside capacity planning, covered elsewhere in this course: a dependency is capacity you need but do not own, so the arithmetic governing a team's throughput also governs how much slack it deserves.

The vocabulary predates software. Its core method, the critical path, was developed in the mid-1950s by engineers at DuPont and the US Navy's Polaris programme to answer one question on projects with thousands of interlinked tasks: which sequence of activities, if any slips, delays the whole project? Product management inherited it as software stopped being built by single teams and started needing platform, data, compliance and vendor contributions before a feature could ship. The sentence Ananya could say without sounding glib: a dependency is capacity I need but don't control, so my job is to make it visible, place it against my critical path, and insure against it slipping.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics start with translating a feature into deliverables, then asking, honestly, which her pod could produce and which needed someone else's output. This is routinely skipped: teams discover a dependency in week six of an eight-week plan because the plan folded it into one line like "integrate pricing API" — as though integration, not the API's non-existence, were the hard part.

Once named, each dependency needs a direction, a type and an owner. Direction distinguishes upstream ones, where Ananya's team waits on someone else, from downstream ones, where another team waits on her. Type distinguishes technical dependencies (an API) from compliance ones (a filing), vendor ones (an SLA, not shared incentives), and people dependencies (one engineer's scarce expertise). Owner means a named individual — "compliance data team" is not accountable the way "Rajesh Iyer" is.

The step most often skipped is negotiating priority with the owner's manager, not just filing a ticket: a ticket asks someone to fit your work into their plan, while a conversation with their manager asks whether your deadline should change that plan. Dependencies rarely slip because the person doing the work was careless; they slip because nobody with authority to reprioritise agreed the item should move up the queue. The other skip is writing the interface contract down — not "the API will be ready" but the exact schema and what happens on a delayed reading.

4. A worked example

Ananya ran the numbers the way a critical-path plan requires: for each dependency, an optimistic, a most-likely and a pessimistic estimate, combined into an expected duration using the weighting (optimistic + 4×likely + pessimistic) ÷ 6. A single "most likely" guess hides how badly a dependency could blow out; the weighted value keeps a level head about both directions.

DependencyOptimisticLikelyPessimisticExpected
D1 — GST e-way bill API (Compliance)4 wk6 wk10 wk(4+24+10)/6 = 6.3 wk
D2 — Pricing model API v2 (Data platform)3 wk5 wk9 wk(3+20+9)/6 = 5.3 wk
D3 — Telematics feed (Chalan Sensor Systems)2 wk4 wk14 wk(2+16+14)/6 = 5.3 wk

D1 and D2 run in parallel from 3 March, and integration starts only once both land, so the pod waits for the longer one: 6.3 weeks, putting integration's start in the week of 17 April. Integration and build take 5 weeks, finishing around 22 May, provided D3's telematics feed — its own 5.3-week clock — has also landed, which it comfortably has. UAT then takes 2 weeks. Adding it up: 6.3 + 5 + 2 = 13.3 weeks, landing around 5 June — three days past the deadline, on the expected case alone. D3 never enters the critical path; it finishes with weeks to spare, which is exactly why flagging all three as equally "urgent" would have been misleading. Only D1 and D2 set the finish date.

Two weeks later, GSTN, the network administering e-way bills, announced a mid-cycle schema change the compliance team would also have to absorb, and Rajesh Iyer's pessimistic case for D1 rose from 10 weeks to 14. Recomputing: (4 + 24 + 14) / 6 = 7 weeks. The critical path became 7 + 5 + 2 = 14 weeks, roughly 9 June — a full week past deadline, still the expected case, not the worst one. One changed input on one dependency turned a marginal three-day miss into a firm one-week miss, without Ananya's own team's work changing at all — the signature of a dependency on the critical path: it moves your launch date even though you did nothing wrong.

5. The nuances a learner must hold onto

Not every cross-team touchpoint is a dependency. A dependency changes your finish date if it slips; a shared review or a heads-up email does not. Treating every touchpoint as one produces a register nobody reads.

Critical and non-critical dependencies deserve different attention. D3 was real and needed an owner, but did not determine 2 June. Managing every dependency with equal urgency spends political capital on ones that don't matter.

Internal and external dependencies carry different leverage. Inside Bandhan, Ananya could escalate to a peer manager and a shared boss. With Chalan Sensor Systems she had only a contract and an SLA — its business does not depend on Bandhan's launch date, only its invoice.

A slipped dependency is a blocker, and the two need different responses. Dependency management is preventive, done before the date arrives; blocker management is reactive firefighting after.

Sequencing without a clear interface still fails. A dependency can land on schedule and still be useless if the two sides never agreed what "done" meant; the interface contract is what makes it usable.

Some of the most damaging dependencies are on no one's map. GSTN's schema change was not a committed task; it was a regulatory event that changed one's size. A mature register leaves room for these.

What the method cannot tell you, and what to ask instead. The arithmetic says which dependency to worry about, but it cannot force a manager to reprioritise, or tell you whether the client will walk or grant grace — it informs a negotiation, not replaces one. So ask: does the named owner know they own it, is there a written interface contract rather than just a ticket, and is there a fallback if this slips two weeks?

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

ContextWhat dependencies typically look like
ConsumerMostly internal, plus a few unforgiving external ones — app-store review, OS release calendars — that set the pace regardless of your plan.
B2B / enterpriseHeavy on compliance review, procurement, and the customer's own IT team, which your company cannot instruct — the dependency sits outside the organisation.
MarketplaceA liquidity dependency on top of delivery ones: a demand-side feature is useful only once enough supply exists.
Early-stage companyInformal, held in one founder's head — fast when it works, a single-point-of-failure risk otherwise.
Large companyFormally logged on a cadence; friction shifts from lack of visibility to competing OKRs, each locally rational and collectively unworkable.

Bandhan sat in the middle: large enough that a handshake would not do, small enough that a written register was still a novelty — the position where this discipline pays off fastest, before informal habits cause real damage.

7. Common mistakes

SymptomUnderlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
The owning team says, late, the work "isn't on our roadmap this quarter".Mapped once at kickoff, never rechecked against the other team's committed priorities.Ask the owner's manager directly if the item is on their committed OKRs.
The schedule slips by exactly as much as the vendor's SLA was missed.An SLA treated as a guarantee, when missing it costs the vendor less than reprioritising.Check if the penalty clause is large enough to change behaviour; if not, buffer on delivery history.
Every dependency is flagged "urgent" and nobody reacts.No one has worked out which sit on the critical path versus which have slack.Run the expected-duration arithmetic; if a delay wouldn't move the launch date, it isn't critical.
Both sides call it "delivered on time" and it still doesn't work when connected.Tracked as a ticket date, not a written interface contract both sides signed off.Check for a shared schema; if none exists, the date was never really shared.

8. What good looks like

Consider Devika Menon, a group product manager at a larger logistics company who faced a similar three-dependency problem eighteen months earlier and handled it well. She kept a single-page register, reviewed at a fifteen-minute stand-up every Monday, each row carrying an owner's name, a recalculated duration estimate, and a status colour: green on track, amber at risk, red slipping and needing escalation that week. When a vendor's pessimistic estimate widened the way GSTN's change widened Ananya's, Devika did not wait for the date to arrive — she raised it at once, proposed a fallback, and got leadership to agree to it in writing before the slip happened. The distinguishing habit was recalculating and escalating the moment an input changed, not waiting for the deadline to prove the plan wrong.

9. What Ananya decided

With the recalculated path pointing to 9 June, a week past deadline, Ananya did not gamble on compliance recovering the lost week alone. She split D1 in two: a simplified, manually reviewed e-way bill check her pod could build in three weeks, used only at launch, alongside a commitment from Rajesh Iyer's team to deliver the full automated version four weeks after go-live. That fallback took compliance off her critical path entirely, leaving D2's 5.3 weeks as the new long pole and putting launch comfortably inside 2 June. She also asked her manager to raise the Chalan Sensor Systems relationship in writing — not because it was critical today, but because its 14-week pessimistic case made it most likely to become critical if anything else moved.

What she carries forward is the reminder underneath this topic: a dependency is capacity she does not control, and the discipline is making that visible early enough to act on, not eliminating it. The natural next studies are capacity planning, which supplies this topic's arithmetic, and what changes when the same problem multiplies across many teams in scaled delivery. Two questions worth sitting with: which dependency in your plan have you not checked against its owner's committed priorities — and if your most fragile dependency slipped three weeks tomorrow, would your plan survive it, or only your belief that it would?
case20v1-plan.dependencies:
Manzil Payments Cloud: The Diwali Dependency

Monday, 14 September 2026 · Koramangala, Bengaluru

Ananya Deshmukh, Senior Director of Product at Manzil Payments Cloud, read the calendar invite from Rohan Bhatt a second time before replying. Rohan, Manzil's sales head, was dialling in from New Jersey at 11 p.m. his time to lock a commitment he had already made to a client: Credit Line on UPI, live at checkout, in time for Al Manara Retail Group's Diwali campaign, opening 25 October. That gave Ananya six weeks. She had spent the morning with engineering, design, data science and Manzil's compliance counsel, and each had told her a version of the same thing: the hard part of this launch was not anything Manzil's own teams controlled. She had to decide, before Friday, what she would tell Rohan — and what Manzil would promise Al Manara.

1. Manzil Payments Cloud

Manzil Payments Cloud, founded in Pune in 2019, builds the checkout and payment-orchestration layer that mid-size and large online retailers plug into their apps. It sat in the same competitive set as Razorpay, Cashfree Payments, PayU and Juspay in India, with a smaller book processing UPI, card and wallet payments for retailers expanding out of India into the Gulf. By September 2026 Manzil routed roughly ₹38,000 crore in annualised payment volume across 210 merchants, from D2C fashion brands to large omnichannel chains. Its pitch was simple: one integration, every payment method India's shoppers used, and increasingly, credit at the point of sale — EMI, Buy-Now-Pay-Later, and the newer RBI-permitted rails that let a bank extend a pre-approved credit line directly through UPI. Manzil did not itself lend; it built the checkout experience and risk plumbing that let a partner bank do so invisibly, in the three seconds between a shopper tapping "Pay" and the order confirming.

2. The situation

Al Manara Retail Group, a Dubai-headquartered chain selling home, electronics and fashion across the UAE and, since 2025, India, was Manzil's second-largest account: a ₹14 crore annual contract, renewed every October. In July, negotiating that renewal, Rohan had told Al Manara's regional e-commerce head that Credit Line on UPI would be ready for the brand's flagship Diwali sale — a promise worth an estimated ₹6 crore in incremental upsell if it landed, and a strain on the relationship if it did not. Rohan had not consulted engineering before making it.

What Ananya now knew, gathered from three time zones over the preceding week, was that the feature depended on a chain of approvals and builds, most of which Manzil did not own. The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) had to certify Manzil's implementation of the credit-on-UPI specification; sandbox testing had begun on 1 September, with no confirmed certification date, and NPCI's own published guidance cited an eight-to-ten-week review window for a first-time applicant. Kaveri Trust Bank, the underwriting partner whose balance sheet would extend the credit, could not finalise its risk-decisioning API until NPCI's sandbox sign-off came through, and its compliance team had separately flagged that the legal draft of the mandatory borrower disclosures — the copy that would sit on the checkout screen — was still with the bank's external counsel. Manzil's own data science function needed bureau-data access to calibrate a credit-risk model, and that data-sharing agreement was itself awaiting sign-off from Manzil's legal team, learned only that morning. Every one of these was, in Ananya's own phrase, "capacity she did not control."

3. The people

Ananya Deshmukh, Senior Director of Product, Bengaluru
Owns the roadmap decision. Wants a commitment Manzil can actually keep.
Rohan Bhatt, Global Sales Head, New Jersey
Closed the Al Manara renewal on the Diwali promise. Wants the feature live on the date he gave the client, and is wary of going back with bad news twice in one quarter.
Mei Lin Goh, Customer Success Lead, Singapore
Owns the day-to-day Al Manara relationship and hears the client's anxiety first. Wants a date she can defend, more than the earliest possible one.
Devika Rao, Data Scientist, Toronto
Building the credit-risk model. Needs three weeks of clean bureau data before she can even begin calibrating, and cannot compress that by adding people.
Sanjana Patil, Engineering Lead, Pune
Owns the SDK that Al Manara's app team must integrate. Cannot freeze the API contract until Rahul's backend team in Bengaluru, mid-way through an unrelated tokenisation migration, frees capacity.

4. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 lays out the dependency chain Ananya's team had mapped that week: who owned each piece, where they sat, and the earliest date each honestly expected to clear. Read left to right, three of five items sat outside Manzil's walls, and the two internal items — the bureau data agreement and the backend API freeze — were themselves blocked on other teams' priorities before Sanjana or Devika could start their own clocks.

Exhibit 1. Dependency map, as of 14 September 2026
DependencyOwnerLocationManzil controls it?Earliest realistic clear date
NPCI sandbox certificationNPCI reviewerMumbaiNo10–24 Oct (range)
Bank risk-API finalisationKaveri Trust BankChennaiNo2 weeks after NPCI clears
Borrower disclosure copyKaveri Trust legalChennaiNoUnconfirmed
Bureau data-sharing sign-offManzil legalBengaluruPartly~3 weeks
Credit-risk model buildDevika RaoTorontoYes, once data lands3 weeks after data
Backend API freezeRahul MenonBengaluruPartly (shared team)~2 weeks
SDK integrationSanjana PatilPuneYes, once API frozen2 weeks after freeze

Exhibit 3 translates the picture into money that Ananya intended to bring to Rohan.

Exhibit 3. What is at stake (₹ crore)
ItemValueNote
Al Manara base renewal14.0Not contingent on this feature
Feature-linked upsell if on time6.0Rohan's estimate, unconfirmed by client
Estimated cost to expedite (legal, vendor overtime, bank fees)0.7One-time
Ananya's estimate: odds NPCI clears by 10 Oct~35%Judgement, not a published SLA
Cost of a rollback if launched non-compliant2–4Rework, client trust, possible RBI scrutiny

5. The options

A. Commit to the original date and compress the chain

Hold the client to 25 October, pull Devika off her other project, pay Kaveri Trust Bank an expedite fee for the disclosure copy, and fast-track the bureau data agreement this week. This preserves the full ₹20 crore relationship and Rohan's credibility. Its cost: Manzil would be racing a regulator's clock it does not set, risking a compliance-pressured launch, or missing the date anyway after burning goodwill and budget.

B. Launch a limited beta before Diwali, full rollout after

Offer Al Manara a capped version — credit line on a curated set of high-margin SKUs, with a conservative ceiling, in time for Diwali, with the unrestricted version following once NPCI and Kaveri Trust formally clear. This still needs the NPCI sandbox to clear in some form by mid-October, so much of the external risk in Exhibit 1 remains, but it gives Rohan a real feature to show the client rather than nothing.

C. Decouple Diwali from the credit feature

Tell Rohan now that Credit Line on UPI will not be ready for 25 October, that Al Manara's Diwali checkout will run on Manzil's existing, proven payment methods, and that the new feature ships as a named fast-follow once NPCI and the bank clear — using the freed capacity over six weeks to de-risk that fast-follow properly rather than rush it. This protects the ₹14 crore renewal and Manzil's reliability record, at the cost of the ₹6 crore upsell this quarter and an uncomfortable call Rohan does not want to make.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Which items in Exhibit 1 are true dependencies Manzil cannot accelerate, and which are internal prioritisation choices dressed up as external ones?
  2. Rohan made a commitment to Al Manara without consulting engineering. What should Manzil change about how commitments involving external dependencies get made, independent of what Ananya decides now?
  3. How should Ananya weigh the ₹6 crore upsell against the probability, from Exhibit 3, that the regulatory dependency clears in time?
  4. If you were Ananya, which option would you choose, and what would you say to Rohan on Friday's call?

7. A note for the learner

Dependency management asks one disciplined question before any roadmap date is promised: what does this depend on that I don't control, and how do I de-risk it? Exhibit 1 shows why that question matters here — three of five items on the critical path sit with a regulator and a bank partner, neither answering to Ananya's roadmap, and the two "internal" items were themselves waiting on other teams' capacity. A good roadmap does not pretend such dependencies away or simply hope they clear on schedule; it sequences around them, builds visible buffer for the ones it cannot influence, and keeps commercial promises decoupled from dates it cannot control.

Option A treats the regulatory and banking dependencies as compressible. They are not: NPCI's review and a bank's legal sign-off do not move faster because Manzil pays overtime, and a rushed, non-compliant launch on a lending product carries real regulatory and reputational cost, as Exhibit 3's rollback estimate shows. Option B is a reasonable variant of the sound instinct but still stakes the client-facing date on the same regulator's clock. The defensible path is Option C: separate what Manzil can promise with confidence — a reliable Diwali checkout on proven rails — from what it cannot yet date, and say so this week rather than in late October. Ananya should tell Rohan the truth on Friday, give him a credible fast-follow date built from Exhibit 1's own numbers rather than hope, and use the six weeks to convert the amber bars into green ones: press NPCI and Kaveri Trust Bank for firm dates, finish the bureau data agreement, and have Devika's model ready the day the data lands. That is what turns "we don't control this" into a dependency that has been found, sequenced and de-risked, rather than one simply hoped away.
case40v1-plan.dependencies:
Bhugol Geospatial Cloud: What the Map Does Not Show

Sunday, 4 October 2026 · Gachibowli, Hyderabad

1. The night before

The security desk at Bhugol Geospatial Cloud logged Nandita Bhaskar in at 9.40 p.m. on Sunday, her third entry of the weekend. The board met at eleven the next morning, four directors in the Gachibowli boardroom and two dialling in from Mumbai and Singapore, and the second agenda item carried her name: whether Bhugol should countersign a three-year, ₹41 crore contract with Bareeq Infrastructure Holding of Dubai. Its first milestone — a live flood-and-asset exposure platform covering Bareeq's Gulf portfolio and Indian road concessions — stood in the draft as 15 January 2027, with a ₹2.75 crore service credit on slippage beyond 45 days.

On the whiteboard behind her, from Friday's dependency workshop, someone had drawn eleven boxes and eleven arrows, then added a twelfth in a different marker with a question mark inside it. Nandita, forty-one, Vice President of Product since 2021, had spent eight hours over two days working out which of those boxes Bhugol could actually move. The answer she kept reaching was: perhaps three. The rest belonged to a satellite-imagery vendor in Amsterdam, a regulator in New Delhi, a Government of India hydrology dataset, a cloud provider's capacity queue in the Gulf, Bhugol's own counsel, and a nine-person platform team in Pune already the bottleneck for everything else promised that quarter. Harpreet Sahni, who had negotiated the deal, would join from New Jersey at 1.30 a.m. his time. He had sent her one line at eight: "Whatever you say tomorrow, say it as one company."

2. How Bhugol got here

Bhugol Geospatial Cloud was founded in Hyderabad in 2016 by Yusuf Khatri, a remote-sensing engineer, and Devi Prasad Achanta, a civil engineer with a decade on highway projects. Their first product turned drive-through video of state highways into an inventory of road assets — signage, culverts, crash barriers, pavement distress — at a fraction of manual survey cost. By FY2026 Bhugol recorded revenue of ₹178 crore, employed 640 people across Hyderabad, Pune, Bengaluru, Berlin, Toronto, Singapore and a two-person Dubai office, and served highway concessionaires, six state public works departments, two metro rail corporations and, increasingly, general insurers who wanted to know what they were underwriting.

The decision that shaped 2026 was taken in April 2024. Bhugol's rendering and change-detection layer then ran on a licensed foreign platform costing ₹6.2 crore a year, fees indexed to imagery volume. The board, weighing that against a growing preference in Indian public tenders for indigenous stacks, approved building the layer in-house. The programme, Kshetra, was budgeted at eighteen months and ₹9.4 crore. Thirty months and ₹15.1 crore later it was neither finished nor abandoned: half the catalogue ran on Kshetra, half on the licensed platform, and the Pune engineers who understood both sides had become, in Yusuf's phrase, "the only road into the city." Every new capability — flood model, Gulf deployment, DPDP pipeline, insurer API — had to cross that road.

3. The industry

India's geospatial market had been re-made by policy. The February 2021 guidelines and the National Geospatial Policy of 2022 lifted decades of restriction on acquiring and processing map data, while keeping the rule that finer-than-threshold accuracy data of Indian territory be created and held by Indian entities. Bhugol, Indian-owned, grew inside that opening, alongside listed firms such as Genesys International and CE Info Systems, and against global platforms like Esri and Hexagon with deeper toolchains but thinner Indian ground truth. ISRO's Bhuvan portal, Survey of India reference frames and Central Water Commission gauge records were, between them, the substrate of any credible Indian flood model.

Three forces pressed on the product in 2026. First, insurance: after two heavy monsoons, Indian general insurers — ICICI Lombard, Bajaj Allianz, HDFC ERGO, New India Assurance among them — were rebuilding catastrophe models and buying address-level flood scores, and a consortium RFP worth an estimated ₹8.6 crore a year was due on 20 October. Second, aerial data: DGCA drone rules and clearances near defence installations made corridor re-flights a scheduling problem money could not solve. Third, the DPDP Act, 2023: Bhugol's street-level imagery captured faces and number plates, and the blurring pipeline counsel had asked for since January sat on the Kshetra backlog. Abroad, Gulf infrastructure spending and Dubai's municipal geospatial mandates had made the region Bhugol's fastest-growing market — 22 per cent of FY2026 bookings — and Bareeq, a family-controlled holding company with ports, roads and industrial parks in the UAE, Oman and Gujarat, was the largest prospect the company had ever had.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The Bareeq conversation began in February 2026, when Harpreet met their group digital director, Tariq Al Suwaidi, at an infrastructure conference. By May, Bhugol had proposed a two-part platform: asset intelligence for Bareeq's 1,100 km of Gulf and Gujarat concessions, and a flood exposure layer for the group's captive insurer. In June, Harpreet circulated a commercial draft naming 15 January 2027 for the first milestone. The date came from an April roadmap slide that assumed Kshetra complete by 30 September and the flood model validated by November. Nobody then thought the assumption unsafe.

Four things happened afterwards. In July, Northlight Imaging BV, the Amsterdam vendor supplying tasked high-resolution imagery for the Gulf corridors, served renewal terms raising Bhugol's annual licence from ₹11.4 crore to ₹17.2 crore and imposing a first-come tasking queue with a six-week booking window. In August, defence-proximity clearance for a 140 km Gujarat corridor re-flight, in Bareeq's scope, was deferred without a new date. On 2 September, Arvind Pillai reported from Toronto that the flood model's validation needed twelve years of Central Water Commission gauge data, and that for two of three Gujarat basins only seven years were usable, widening confidence intervals beyond what an actuary would accept without independent review. On 18 September, Ganesh Ambekar told Nandita that Kshetra stood at 58 per cent of scope, not the 85 per cent the July dashboard reported; the dashboard counted a workstream complete when its design document was signed off.

Two further items arrived late and cut in opposite directions. On 25 September Cheryl Fernandes learned informally that Bareeq's own identity platform — which Bhugol's dashboards must authenticate against — had slipped to February 2027, so a January delivery might sit idle. On 30 September, outside counsel returned a first opinion on whether sub-metre Indian survey data processed for a foreign-owned client could be hosted in the provider's UAE region. It ran three hedged pages and recommended a clarification taking "four to eight weeks." Nandita could not tell whether that delay was the regulator's, counsel's, or her own company's for asking in September rather than May.

5. The people

Nandita Bhaskar — Vice President, Product. Hyderabad.
Must recommend to the board. Position: the January date is not defensible on current evidence. Incentive: her credibility rests on dates the company keeps, and she signed the April slide that produced this one. Not saying: she believes the real constraint is the 2024 build decision, and has no appetite to reopen it before the board that approved it.
Yusuf Khatri — Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer. Hyderabad.
Position: Kshetra must be finished before anything is layered on it; a Gulf deployment on a half-migrated stack is "two systems and one team." Incentive: Kshetra is his programme and thirty months of his reputation. Not saying: he has quietly priced a restricted-scope extension of the licensed platform at ₹4.8 crore and not circulated the figure.
Ganesh Ambekar — Engineering Manager, Kshetra platform. Pune.
Position: his team can serve the Bareeq milestone or the DPDP pipeline in Q3, not both. Incentive: he has lost two senior engineers to Bengaluru product firms in six months and is protecting the remaining seven. Not saying: one engineer, Suhasini, holds the tile-cache rewrite alone, and if her December leave is granted the January date is arithmetically impossible.
Harpreet Sahni — Head of Sales, Americas and Gulf. New Jersey.
Position: Bareeq is the reference account that unlocks the region; the date got Bhugol to the table and moving it now reads as weakness. Bareeq's board approved its capital plan on 12 October, and Tariq had said the contract needed to be inside it. The Northlight tasking queue closed for the window on 9 October. The insurer RFP was due 20 October with a ₹35 lakh bid bond. Bhugol held ₹62 crore of cash and had told its Series C investor it would not raise before September 2027. The DPDP pipeline had no statutory deadline counsel would put in writing, though counsel had twice said "materially overdue." Ganesh had seven engineers, one holding the tile cache and asking for December leave. And at eleven the next morning, six directors would want one number and one date.

  3. Exhibits 1 and 4 cannot both be right. How should Nandita reconcile them before Monday, and what does the gap reveal about how Bhugol tracks commitments?
  4. The April roadmap slide became a contractual date in June without anyone re-testing its assumptions. What should stand between a roadmap and a signature, and who should own it?
  5. Each stakeholder is withholding something material. Which omission, surfacing on Monday, would most change the decision — and what does that say about where Bhugol's dependency risk actually lives?
  6. What should Nandita do on Monday morning, and what exactly should she say to the board, including to Rukmini Vaidyanathan, who chaired the meeting that approved Kshetra?

Arvind's last message, 1.20 a.m. Toronto, asked whether to freeze the model or wait; Ganesh's, from Pune, asked whether to tell Suhasini her December leave was approved. Harpreet was awake in New Jersey. The Gachibowli car park was empty, the board met in eleven hours, and Nandita had not written a word on the last slide.
