Dependency Management

What am I depending on that I don't control, and how do I de-risk it? The arithmetic, the schools that disagree, and where the standard answer is wrong.

1. Two decisions, two product types, one week apart

On 21 September 2026, outside Nashik, Meera Kulkarni, vice-president of product at Kshetra Farm Robotics, ringed 12 January on the wall calendar. Kshetra built an autonomous spray rig sold to grape and onion growers and to farmer producer organisations financed by NABARD-linked credit. Spray season in the Nashik belt opens in the second week of January; a rig that misses it sits in a shed for eleven months. Meera had sixteen weeks.

Her own team of twenty-two could finish in nine; the other seven weeks were not hers. The new multispectral camera module came from Jaladhi Optics Works in Coimbatore on a ten-week lead time beginning only after design freeze; the certification slot ran in fixed batches; the spray-dosage model needed retraining by a machine-learning group shared with two other product lines; and the tractor-mount variant needed a CAN-bus change from an OEM partner on a quarterly release train.

Nine hundred kilometres south, on 28 September, Rohit Sathe, director of product at Jamuna Payments Network in Bengaluru, met the same problem in another shape. Jamuna wanted to extend its 140,000 small merchants a working-capital line drawn at settlement: ₹18 crore of annual revenue, and a co-lending partner whose window closed on 15 December. Rohit's build was two weeks of engineering. The decisioning lived in a shared Risk Platform team serving nine pods at eighty-five per cent utilisation; credit on UPI rails moves inside windows set by NPCI's release calendar and a bank partner's compliance review; and the risk committee signed off monthly.

Meera's dependencies were physical and external; Rohit's internal, small in work and long in waiting. Neither could move the thing that decided their date.

2. The idea, its history, and the four schools that fight over it

A dependency is any input your plan requires whose priority you do not set. The definition is about priority rather than ownership, because that is where the risk lives: a dependency hurts you not when someone cannot do the work, but when someone quite reasonably does something else first. Dependency management is finding those inputs early, working out which determine your finish date, and insuring those with buffers, fallbacks, renegotiated interfaces or removal.

The machinery predates software. In 1957 James Kelley of Remington Rand and Morgan Walker of DuPont published the Critical Path Method for plant shutdowns; a year later Polaris produced PERT, which added three-point estimation and, crucially, variance. Donald Steward's Design Structure Matrix (1981), developed at MIT by Steven Eppinger, contributed what mattered most for products: a matrix of who-feeds-whom reveals cycles, and cycles mean iteration, not sequence. Melvin Conway had observed in 1968 that systems mirror the structures that build them, making a dependency map also an org chart. Goldratt's Critical Chain (1997) pooled per-task safety; Reinertsen's Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) recast the field as queueing.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Scheduling (CPM/PERT)"Make every hand-off visible, sequence it, buffer the critical path.""A recurring dependency means the boundaries are wrong."
Architectural (Conway; Team Topologies)"A dependency recurring every quarter is a design defect; fix the boundary, not the calendar.""Coordination rituals materially reduce late surprises."
Flow (Goldratt; Reinertsen)"Most slip is queueing: take the shared team from 85% to 70% loaded and it disappears.""Each dependency deserves its own safety margin."
Contracting (platform-as-product)"An internal interface needs a versioned contract, consumer tests and a deprecation policy.""Escalation to a shared executive is dependable."

They prescribe different first moves on the same Monday. On Rohit's problem, the scheduling school books a slot and buffers it; the architectural school asks why a credit product cannot own its decisioning; the flow school cuts intake until the queue drains; the contracting school writes the interface and builds against a stub.

3. Mechanics in depth, worked rather than named

Expert practice runs in five movements: enumerate, classify, compute, insure, renegotiate. Enumeration is harder than it sounds: the common failure is not forgetting a dependency but wording it away — "integrate the camera module" conceals that the module does not exist. The discipline is to force every plan line into the form who produces what by when, rejecting any line whose who is a team rather than a person. Classification then separates the axis most boards omit: whether the dependency is on a specification or a delivery. A specification dependency — schema, contract, semantics — can be satisfied weeks before the thing exists, because you build against a stub and a contract test; a delivery dependency cannot. Converting the second into the first is the highest-leverage move in the discipline, and it is invisible on registers recording dates rather than kinds.

The matrix separates practitioners: a list of dependencies is a set of arrows, a matrix exposes cycles. Kshetra's dosage model needed field-trial data, and the field trial needed a rig with the model in it. Meera's options were the classical three — iterate and accept a weaker first model; cut the loop with an assumption; or break it with a proxy such as a bench rig on recorded spectral data. She chose the assumption, shipping last season's model with a February update, a choice visible only because of the matrix.

Computation is where most product managers stop too early. Three-point estimation gives an expected duration; it also gives σ = (pessimistic − optimistic) ÷ 6, and variance is what adds along a path. Rohit's path ran queue wait, build, risk-committee sign-off and partner UAT: expected durations 6.0, 2.0, 3.0 and 2.0 weeks, or 13.0 in total. The sigmas were 1.50, 0.33, 0.67 and 0.50; squared and summed, 2.25 + 0.11 + 0.45 + 0.25 = 3.06, so the path σ is √3.06 = 1.75 weeks. With twelve weeks available, z = (12 − 13.0) ÷ 1.75 = −0.57: a 28 per cent chance. An eighty per cent date needs 13.0 + (0.84 × 1.75) = 14.5 weeks. That is what an expert takes into the room — not "we think thirteen weeks" but "thirteen is a coin-flip we lose, and the date I can commit to is fourteen and a half."

Two second-order effects follow. Merge bias is the most under-appreciated arithmetic in planning: when several dependencies must all land before you start, your start date is the maximum of their finish dates, and the expectation of a maximum is worse than the maximum of expectations. Meera assessed on-time probabilities of 0.85 for certification, 0.80 for optics, 0.75 for the dosage model and 0.90 for firmware. Each is more likely than not; multiplied, 0.85 × 0.80 × 0.75 × 0.90 = 0.459. A plan every part of which is probably fine is a 46 per cent plan: four greens produce a red.

Buffer aggregation is the second. Safety hidden inside individual estimates is consumed whether needed or not; pooled safety is consumed only by whoever needs it, and the arithmetic is the square root of the sum of squares. Meera's four owners each carried private safety of 2.0, 3.0, 1.5 and 2.5 weeks — nine weeks scattered. Pooled: √(4 + 9 + 2.25 + 6.25) = √21.5 = 4.64 weeks, so under five shared weeks buy the protection of nine distributed ones. The catch is political: a pooled buffer needs an owner with authority to release it.

Jamuna's Risk Platform did two weeks of real work on the credit line. At eighty-five per cent utilisation the single-queue approximation puts expected waiting at ρ ÷ (1 − ρ) = 5.67 times service, or 11.3 weeks; Rohit's quoted six weeks was optimistic. At seventy per cent it falls to 4.7. The intervention that buys him six and a half weeks is not in his plan at all: it is someone else's decision to commit their team to less. At ₹34.6 lakh a week, those 6.6 weeks are worth ₹2.3 crore.

4. When the discipline applies, stated as tests

ClaimKshetra (hardware + software)Jamuna (platform fintech)
The date must have an external consequence.Passes: the season does not negotiate.Passes: the capital window closes 15 December.
Lead time must be long relative to your own work.Passes: ten weeks of optics against nine of build.Passes severely: eleven weeks of waiting against two of work.
The boundary must be unchangeable within the horizon.Passes: a supply chain is not re-architectable in sixteen weeks.Fails partly: decisioning could move into the pod, but not in twelve weeks.
The work must be specifiable.Fails for the dosage model, which is research; passes elsewhere.Passes: the interface is well understood.

Where the fourth test fails the discipline is actively misleading: a research outcome on a board with a date converts an option into a commitment, and teams defend the date by lowering the ambition. The subtler misapplication is the register that becomes the mechanism of accountability, after which nobody does anything not on it: nothing is late because nothing is interesting.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

Marketplaces carry a dependency no board records: liquidity. A demand-side feature depends on supply existing, and supply is not a team you can escalate to. The honest treatment models it as a delivery dependency given the same variance treatment as an engineering estimate.

Regulated products break the escalation model outright. Jamuna's credit line sits behind an NPCI release calendar and a bank partner's compliance review, and no shared executive stands above both, so influence runs only through lead time and submission quality. Hence front-loading: submit the earliest reviewable artefact rather than the best one, because a first submission buys a queue position and a list of objections — information not otherwise purchasable.

Hardware plus software brings lead times in months and cancellation costs in tooling; Meera's purchase order was irreversible in a way no software commitment is. The mature treatment decouples commitment from design freeze by ordering long-lead parts against a tolerance envelope, buying weeks with waste.

AI-native products add three classes that behave unlike code: a model-version dependency, where a supplier's deprecation date arrives on the supplier's calendar and no escalation exists; a data dependency, where a labelling vendor's throughput sets the evaluation cadence; and a policy dependency, where red-team sign-off is a queue with a committee at the end. The common error is treating the first as technical when it is supplier concentration — better answered by an abstraction layer and a second provider, at the cost of the capabilities only one provider has.

At organisational seams, between divisions with separate P&Ls, mature companies do not resolve dependencies through shared mission, whatever they say. They use a funded transfer, an embedded engineer, or a written commitment ratified where both budgets meet. The public ritual is quarterly planning; the mechanism is one of those three.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The dependency that kills you is rarely the one you fear. Attention follows the longest expected duration, but risk follows variance: a twelve-week dependency with a one-week spread is safer than a four-week one with an eight-week spread. The tell is an expert who asks what the worst case is, and how we would know early, before asking how long it will take. Managing the long pole is wrong: a high-variance near-critical path becomes critical the moment it slips, by which time attention is spent.

Four greens make a red. Merge bias is invisible on status boards, because boards report items while risk compounds across them. The tell is an expert who, hearing four confident greens, asks for probabilities rather than colours and multiplies aloud. Many parallel amber-ish items are worse than a single red, because the red is at least visible.

"Planned" and "committed" are different words in the other team's language. When a platform lead says the work is on their roadmap, an expert hears an unfunded intention and asks which objective it sits under. The obvious reading — that agreement has been reached — is wrong: roadmaps absorb items without displacing any, and displacement is the only evidence of commitment.

Escalation is a depleting asset. The first escalation in a quarter moves the work; the third moves the escalator's reputation. Experts spend it early, when the remedy is cheap, not late, when it is merely loud. The tell is a manager escalating in week two on an item not yet late.

A specification dependency is a different animal from a delivery dependency. With schema and semantics agreed, both sides build in parallel against contract tests and integrate in days. The tell is a first ask of a platform team that is not a date but an interface and a stub, in week one. You cannot finish until they finish; you can usually start, and that gap is worth four weeks.

Removing a dependency by duplication relocates it somewhere invisible. Forking a shared service kills a delivery dependency and creates a semantic one: two definitions of the same concept, drifting apart. The tell is an expert who, hearing "we'll just build our own", asks which entity definitions the fork inherits and who owns them in eighteen months. Duplication is paid for later, in reconciliation.

Utilisation predicts slip better than goodwill does. Two platform teams with identical culture differ wildly in reliability at seventy and ninety per cent load. The tell is a first question that is not "can you help?" but "how much are you committed to this quarter, and what did you finish last quarter?" The intuition that a slipping team needs discipline is backwards: it needs less work.

Downstream dependencies are systematically under-reported. Managers track what they wait on and forget who waits on them, which is why the person demanding early warning from a platform gives none to the pods consuming her API. The tell is a register whose downstream column is filled in. The cost is credibility: a team that surprises its consumers finds its own requests quietly deprioritised, and nobody says so.

7. How it differs by product type and by stage

ContextWhat is genuinely different
ConsumerFew internal dependencies; two unmovable external ones, app-store review and OS calendars. Calendar arithmetic, not negotiation.
B2B and enterpriseThe longest dependencies sit outside: customer IT, procurement, security review. Lead time is bought with pre-sales artefacts.
Platform and marketplaceQueueing dominates; the governing number is utilisation, and liquidity is a dependency with a probability, not a date.
Hardware and physical goodsLong lead times, irreversible commitments; buffers are inventory and tolerance, not days.
AI productsModel versions, labelled data, policy sign-off: supplier calendars, no escalation.
Seed to Series AMostly external. A register is overhead; three names on a whiteboard are not.
Series B to CThe crossing point: dependencies appear faster than coordination habits do.
Public-company scaleVisibility is solved; the constraint is competing objectives. Work moves to negotiation and funding.

What does not differ is the arithmetic: merge bias, variance addition and queueing apply identically to a spray rig and a credit line. Only the lever differs. Meera can buy inventory and cannot cut a queue; Rohit can cut a queue and cannot buy a certification slot.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Kshetra: reference-class forecasting beats the quote

Jaladhi Optics Works quoted ten weeks. Meera's operations lead pulled the last nine purchase orders: six arrived on or before the quoted date, three late by three, five and seven weeks. Mean overrun is 15 ÷ 9 = 1.67 weeks and the eightieth percentile sits around five weeks late, so the planning number is fifteen weeks, not ten — the difference being the whole of Kshetra's January. Meera split the order: forty modules at the quoted date, the balance on the reference-class date. The premium was ₹9.4 lakh against a season worth ₹6 crore: insurance at 1.6 per cent of exposure.

Jamuna: attacking the queue instead of the item

Rohit's first instinct was to escalate inside the Risk Platform backlog; his second, better, instinct was to take the queue curve to the platform director and the CFO together. Deferring three lower-value commitments takes the team to seventy per cent load, cutting average waiting from 11.3 weeks to 4.7 for every pod; his own path falls from 13.0 expected weeks to 8.5 and his eighty-per-cent date from 14.5 to 9.8. He did not get his item prioritised; he got the system unclogged, which was cheaper politically and better for eight other people.

Kachnar Apparel Cloud: the method applied correctly, and failed

Kachnar Apparel Cloud, a Tiruppur-headquartered platform for apparel exporters, ran a textbook programme in 2025 to replatform its order-management stack: big-room planning, a dependency board of forty-seven arrows, a named owner on each, weekly review. It missed by eleven weeks. The post-mortem found that three of the forty-seven mattered and that the item causing the slip was on none of them. To remove a delivery dependency on the shared catalogue service, one team had forked it; the fork inherited a definition of "style code" that the parent changed four months later, and a size-curve representation differing over half-sizes. Reconciling 380,000 SKUs consumed eleven weeks and ₹2.6 crore of duplicated engineering.

The instructive part is why the method missed it: a dependency board records intentions to deliver and has no representation for shared meaning. The recovery was architectural rather than procedural — one canonical product-entity schema with a named owning team, consumer-driven contract tests so a change breaking a consumer failed in the producer's own pipeline, and a dependency-debt line funded at eight per cent of capacity. Kachnar's review put it bluntly: "we managed the arrows we drew, and the one that mattered we had deliberately erased."

9. Failure modes, early signs and the cost of catching them late

Failure modeEarliest warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Agreed with an engineer, not their managerFriendly answers, no change to their sprint content"Which committed objective did this displace?"A re-plan in the last third: a quarter
Merge bias ignoredEvery item green, yet the date keeps drifting"Multiply your four confidences — what do you get?"A miss that looks like luck and repeats
Safety hidden inside each estimateDependencies finish exactly on date, never early"Where is our shared buffer, and who releases it?"Weeks consumed invisibly; no reserve
A delivery dependency that should have been a specificationYour team idle-blocked on an API"Do we have the schema and a stub? Why not in week one?"Three to six weeks of idle capacity
Fork used to remove a dependencyTwo teams claiming one entity definition"Who owns this concept's meaning in eighteen months?"Reconciliation in crores
Register as theatreArrow count rises each quarter; slips do not fall"Which three actually move our date?"Coordination cost, no delivery benefit

Each is cheap to catch in the first fortnight and expensive after the midpoint: early a conversation, late a re-plan, an apology and a lost window.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Eliminate or manage. The architectural school holds that a dependency recurring across three consecutive quarters proves a misplaced boundary, and that coordination effort is interest on a debt nobody amortises; its evidence is the association between team autonomy and throughput in large organisations. The scheduling school answers that re-architecture carries its own transition cost, often a year of reduced output, and that most dependencies are consequences of a strategy that will itself change. For the architectural position to be wrong, boundary changes would have to cost more throughput in transition than the dependencies they remove cost over the boundary's remaining life — under a fast-changing strategy, frequently so.

Pooled buffer or per-item safety. Goldratt's arithmetic is not disputed; its organisational feasibility is. Sceptics argue a central buffer removes the accountability that makes owners deliver, and that pooling works under one authority and fails across separate budgets. Defenders answer that hidden safety is consumed regardless, because work expands into whatever margin is private. The dispute is unresolved because firms that adopt pooling rarely run a control group.

Does big-room planning earn its cost? Critics observe that coordination cost scales with the square of the number of teams, and that planning events institutionalise the dependencies they document by making asking easier than decoupling. Defenders answer that two days of forty people's time to surface three real dependencies is cheap against a quarter lost to one. Both describe real organisations; what separates them is the ratio of real to ritual arrows, unmeasured.

Internal SLAs and chargeback. The contracting school treats platform teams as suppliers with published service levels and sometimes internal pricing, on the evidence that unpriced internal demand is over-consumed like any free good. Opponents hold that pricing corrodes the shared mission behind exceptional cross-team effort, and that requests get routed around platforms instead. What would settle it — whether platform quality rises faster than shadow duplication — is not published.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this keeps a register and reviews it. Someone who has internalised it asks for probabilities rather than colours and multiplies them; converts delivery dependencies into specification dependencies in week one, where weeks are free; negotiates with the queue rather than their place in it, framing the argument in money for the whole system; and gives downstream consumers the discipline they demand upstream, because this is a repeated game.

A harder marker still: they can say which dependencies they have deliberately chosen not to manage. A register containing everything has no judgement in it, and judgement — knowing that firmware at ninety per cent confidence with two weeks of slack deserves one email a month — is what the arithmetic is for.

12. What each protagonist decided

Meera Kulkarni split the optics order on reference-class rather than quoted lead times, at ₹9.4 lakh of premium; cut the dosage-model feedback loop with a February over-the-air update; pooled her four owners' private safety into one five-week buffer released only by her; and booked the certification batch at the earliest slot with a reviewable submission. She left the OEM's release train alone, judging two weeks of slack sufficient. The rig shipped on 8 January 2027.

Rohit Sathe did not escalate. He took the queue curve and the ₹34.6-lakh-per-week cost of delay to the platform director and the CFO, and won a one-quarter deferral of three lower-value items, moving his eighty-per-cent date from 14.5 weeks to 9.8. He also insisted on a written decisioning interface in week one, converting his largest remaining dependency into a specification.

Discussion questions

  1. Rohit improved the whole queue rather than his position in it. Under what governance conditions is that move available to a product director?
  2. Kachnar removed a dependency by forking and paid ₹2.6 crore eighteen months later. How should a product leader price a semantic dependency that has no date and no owner?
  3. Meera pooled four managers' private safety into one buffer she controlled. What would have to be true for that to fail, and how would you detect it before the buffer was exhausted?

13. Going deeper

  • Capacity planning — the throughput arithmetic behind queue reasoning.
  • Scaled delivery: multiple teams — when coordination itself becomes the constraint.
  • Requirements across multiple teams — the specification craft behind parallel builds.
  • Planning a replatform or rebuild — where dependency debt and semantic drift bind at once.
  • Roadmapping with model, data and policy dependencies — the AI-native classes.
  • Strategy vs roadmap vs plan — which artefact may carry a date at all.
  • Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later — where high-variance dependencies sit without a date.
  • The roadmap as communication — warning consumers before you break them.
  • OKRs and goal setting — the mechanism by which "planned" becomes "committed".
  • Annual and quarterly planning — where buffers and intake cuts are negotiated.
  • Milestones and release planning — turning a probabilistic path into usable dates.
case20v1-plan.premortem:
Case 20 · Delivery & Technology · Roadmapping, Planning & OKRs

Disha Commerce Cloud: The Diwali Commitment

Pune, 14 September 2026. Ananya Deshpande has until Friday to tell the board whether an eight-week roadmap she does not fully believe in can be delivered — or to explain, with evidence, why it cannot.

1. A Deadline in Pune

Ananya Deshpande, Head of Product at Disha Commerce Cloud, read the calendar invite for the third time before closing her laptop. "Roadmap Lock — Waman Diwali Commitment" was scheduled for Friday, 18 September, ten a.m., with the founder, the VP of Engineering and the sales head all required. By the end of that meeting, Disha would either promise its largest client a working product on 8 November, the Saturday before Diwali, or renegotiate a contract that had taken nine months to close. Ananya had spent the week collecting opinions from four cities and had grown convinced of one thing: nobody had yet asked, out loud, how this plan could fail. She meant to make sure that question was answered before anyone signed off on the date.

2. Disha Commerce Cloud

Founded in Pune in 2019, Disha Commerce Cloud sells order-routing and fulfilment software to Indian D2C brands and quick-commerce dark-store operators, competing with Shiprocket, Unicommerce and WareIQ. Its engine decides, in real time, which warehouse or dark store should fulfil an order, and plugs into couriers such as Delhivery, Ecom Express, Xpressbees and Blue Dart, as well as the ONDC network, which Disha joined as a seller-side technology partner in early 2026. The company had grown to ₹42 crore in annual recurring revenue across 380 customers, raised a Series B in 2024, and employed sixty people, with engineering split across Bengaluru and Pune and smaller functions in Berlin, Toronto, Singapore and New Jersey. Product decisions were still made the way a founder-led company makes them: fast, often on the loudest voice in the room. Ananya had joined a year earlier partly to change that.

3. The Situation

In July 2026, Disha signed its largest contract yet: a ₹6.4 crore annual agreement with Waman Retail Group DMCC, a Dubai-headquartered omni-channel retailer expanding into India through its subsidiary, Waman India Retail. The contract required a new capability, Smart Routing Engine 2.0, combining a machine-learning allocation model with direct ONDC seller-network integration, live in time for Waman's Diwali sale. Derek Osei, Disha's sales head, had promised an eight-week build. Engineering's own estimate, drawn up afterward by Karan Bhatia, was sixteen weeks.

Through September, warning signs accumulated from every part of the global team. Michael Chen, Disha's data scientist in Toronto, reported that the routing model had only eleven weeks of clean training data from two pilot cities, far short of what he considered safe for a national Diwali rollout across nineteen cities. Karan's Bengaluru and Pune engineers were already committed, at roughly forty percent of their time, to hardening infrastructure ahead of the festival traffic surge — work that could not be paused without risking outages for Disha's other customers. In Berlin, senior designer Lena Fischer flagged that the ONDC seller flows had never been tested with Gulf-based sellers listing products in Arabic script. And from Singapore, Farah Haddad relayed that Waman's Dubai team had begun asking whether a loyalty-points integration could be folded into the same release — a feature nobody at Disha had costed.

Ananya had not yet run a formal pre-mortem: imagining the project has already failed and working backward to name the causes, before the plan is locked. She believed Friday needed that discipline, and a risk register the team could see, rather than another round of Slack messages expressing private doubt.

4. The People

Karan Bhatia, VP of Engineering in Bengaluru, wanted the sixteen-week estimate respected. He had watched two roadmaps slip because sales-promised dates were locked before engineering was consulted, and warned that repeating the pattern would cost him senior engineers already fielding recruiter calls.

Michael Chen, the data scientist in Toronto, wanted the ML routing model descoped from the Diwali release. Shipping an undertrained model into the highest-volume week of the Indian retail calendar risked misrouted orders exactly when Waman would be watching most closely.

Farah Haddad, Customer Success Lead in Singapore, owned the Waman relationship and wanted certainty above all — a date Disha would actually hit, rather than a confident date that slipped in October with runway already lost.

Derek Osei, Sales Head in New Jersey, wanted the eight-week date to hold. Waman's Dubai leadership had told him a larger, second contract was contingent on a clean Diwali launch, and he worried any renegotiation now would read as weakness.

5. What the Numbers Show

Ananya asked Karan and Michael to turn scattered warnings into one document before Friday. Exhibit 1 is the first page of the resulting risk register, ranking risks the team could name by likelihood and cost. Exhibit 2 sets the contract's penalty structure against the three timelines under discussion, and the chart shows how far the original promise sat from engineering's own estimate.

Exhibit 2 — Contract terms and timeline gap

The register does not, by itself, tell Ananya what to do. It converts five private worries into a shared list the team can argue about in the same terms — likelihood, cost, and a warning sign someone is actually watching for. Exhibit 2 makes the arithmetic concrete: the gap between sales' promise and engineering's belief is eight weeks, and the penalty clause makes a slip expensive but survivable for roughly a month before Waman can walk away.

6. The Options

Option A — Hold the eight-week date, add contractors

Disha brings in contract engineers and overtime to close the gap between eight and sixteen weeks, keeping the full scope Waman bought, including the ML router and loyalty integration. This preserves Derek's credibility with Waman's Dubai leadership and protects the second contract he is chasing. It costs an estimated ₹38 lakh in contractor fees, stretches engineers already carrying festival hardening, and leaves Michael's model risk unaddressed.

Option B — Renegotiate to sixteen weeks, keep full scope

Ananya asks Waman for the realistic date, arguing a working system in late October beats a fragile one on 8 November. This is the most honest option and protects quality, but it delivers after the Diwali sale Waman cares about, likely triggering the ₹15-lakh-per-week penalty from week one and giving Derek's counterpart reason to slow-walk the second contract.

Option C — Ship a descoped MVP by Diwali, phase the rest

Disha commits to the nine-week, rules-based routing scope Michael proposed as a fallback, launches by 7 November, and moves the ML model, loyalty integration and Gulf-script ONDC support to a Q1 2027 phase two, formalised as a contract amendment rather than a silent cut. This meets the date Waman's business needs and avoids the penalty. Its cost is that Waman must accept less than it originally bought, and Farah must manage that as discipline, not shortfall.

7. Questions for Discussion

  1. What does the risk register in Exhibit 1 add that scattered private worries from Karan, Michael, Lena and Farah did not?
  2. Which risk in Exhibit 1 is most likely to actually determine whether Disha meets its Diwali commitment, and why?
  3. Derek's and Michael's incentives point in different directions. How should Ananya weigh a risk to quality against a risk to a second sale?
  4. If you were Ananya, what would you say in the Friday meeting, and what evidence from the exhibits would you use to support it?

8. A Note for the Learner

A pre-mortem surfaces bad news before it is expensive, by asking a team to imagine the project has already failed and to work backward to the causes, rather than letting causes surface one at a time, in private, as they did here across Bengaluru, Toronto, Berlin and Singapore. Run against a plan's milestones, it turns scattered doubt into one artefact, the risk register, naming each risk, its likelihood, cost, owner and warning sign, so the team can act before the risk becomes the outcome. A well-reasoned answer does not pick the option that merely feels safest; it uses the register to show which risks the chosen option resolves and which it knowingly leaves open.

Read that way, Option A resolves nothing on the register: it spends money to chase the original promise while the model, bandwidth and scope risks all stay live. Option B resolves the technical risks but ignores the one the register also names: a plan announced before Friday is hard to walk back, and Waman's Diwali case will not wait for October. Option C is the most defensible path, because it removes the register's highest-likelihood risks — model immaturity, engineering bandwidth — from the plan, and turns the scope Waman loses into a named, dated amendment rather than a surprise. Ananya's task on Friday is to show, risk by risk, why nine real weeks beat eight promised ones the register says are unlikely to hold.
exp40v2-plan.premortem:
Delivery & Technology · Roadmapping, Planning & OKRs

Pre-mortems and risk registers: the near-expert treatment

If this plan had failed a year from now, why would it have failed — and what is the honest quantitative answer?

1. Two rooms, two plans, two weeks apart

In Chakan, outside Pune, on 14 August 2026, Revathi Iyengar is studying a number she does not trust. She runs product for Ushakaal Diagnostics Devices, maker of the UD-3, a point-of-care haematology analyser sold to rural diagnostic chains. The FY28 plan commits Ushakaal to 2,400 installed analysers by 31 March 2027, up from 640, on an ₹18 crore budget. The device sells near cost; the annuity is cartridges at ₹28 of contribution each. The plan's spine is one assumption: an analyser runs 180 tests a month. At 2,400 units that is ₹14.52 crore of annual contribution, a line the CFO has already shown the bank.

Her discomfort is not the ramp, which Sandeep Barve's plant has done before. It is that nobody has said aloud what happens if the 180 does not hold. Ipsita Mohapatra, her field lead in Bhubaneswar, has emailed about three clinics in coastal Odisha where the optical bench drifts in the monsoon and technicians have gone back to the district lab. Three clinics out of 640 is noise. It is also, possibly, the first two per cent of something.

Two weeks later, on 3 September, Karthik Raghunathan sits in Lower Parel with a migration plan he believes in. Upaay Claims Cloud adjudicates cashless health-insurance claims for fourteen insurer and third-party-administrator tenants, some 6.8 lakh claim lines a month. The plan retires the legacy rules engine by 31 December 2026 for one carrying a machine-learned pre-adjudication layer. The OKR: raise straight-through processing — lines adjudicated with no human touch — from 41% to 62%, and cut median turnaround from 5.2 hours to 90 minutes. A manual line costs ₹62 in analyst and audit time, an automated one ₹3, so the deck says the shift is worth ₹10.1 crore a year. With the regulator pushing cashless settlement and the National Health Claims Exchange standardising claim movement, the timing looks favourable.

Neither deck says how the plan fails. Both leaders are about to ask.

2. The idea, and the camps that argue about it

A pre-mortem tells a team, before work begins, that the plan has already failed by a stated date against a stated number, and asks it to write down why — in the past tense, as explanation rather than speculation. A risk register is what survives: a revisited log in which each failure story becomes a row with an owner, a likelihood, an impact, a numeric trigger, and a response designed in advance.

The halves have separate ancestries, and most confusion comes from conflating them. The register descends from engineering project management — Boehm's 1991 formulation of software risk management, the RAID logs of PRINCE2, and behind them the Failure Modes and Effects Analysis built in aerospace and adopted across the car industry, which scores each failure mode on severity, occurrence and detectability. The pre-mortem descends from psychology: Mitchell, Russo and Pennington showed in 1989 that explaining a future event as though it had already happened — prospective hindsight — raises both the number and the specificity of causes produced. Klein turned that into a ritual in 2007; Kahneman called it his favourite debiasing device. The problem solved is narrow: private doubt is under-reported in groups, because voicing it early reads as disloyalty, and the plan acquires a consensus it never earned.

The camps give opposite advice in one room. Told the UD-3 may underperform in humid districts, the debiasing camp wants more such causes surfaced; the outside-view camp wants the utilisation comparable Indian fleets reached in year two; the reliability camp wants a humidity sensor logging to the cloud; the option-buying camp wants forty analysers in the worst districts; the resilience camp wants the service network over-built, because the real failure will not be listed.

3. Mechanics, including the steps left implicit

The visible procedure is short: state the failure as fact with a date and a number; write privately for six minutes; round-robin, one cause per turn; cluster into themes; convert themes to rows. Four implicit steps carry the rest of the work.

The first is choosing the failure statement. "The programme failed" is useless; so is "we missed our OKR." Revathi writes three and runs a round on each: contribution under ₹11 crore though the fleet reached 2,400 units; the fleet stalled at 1,400; the numbers landed but two state health authorities suspended purchases. The three produce almost disjoint lists, because one statement samples one branch.

The second is picking the room, a design decision rather than a calendar problem, since the exercise cannot surface a cause nobody present can conceive. Revathi invites Ipsita, and Abhijit Sengupta who runs the service network from Kolkata. She also invites a reagent chemist, Dr Anjali Deshpande, whose contribution — cartridge shelf life at 35°C is 90 days, not the 180 on the datasheet, so distributor stocking matters enormously — is the session's most valuable sentence.

The third is translating causes into indicators. A cause is a story; a row is a control. It asks which number moves first if the story is beginning, what value forces the row open, and what the team then does — decided now, while it is cheap.

The fourth step, separating practice from ritual, is scoring. Most registers inherit FMEA's risk priority number: severity times occurrence times detectability, each ordinal. The arithmetic is illegitimate — multiplying ordinal ranks gives a number whose ratios mean nothing — and it mis-ranks, because detectability enters as a penalty, so a catastrophic but invisible risk scores below a moderate, frequent, visible one.

The honest treatment is duller: per row, state the rupee impact, state a probability you will defend, multiply. The probabilities are guesses, but about one thing at a time, arguable, and updatable when pilot data arrives. Summing them gives Upaay ₹12.9 crore of expected shortfall against a ₹10.1 crore promised benefit. That is not a mitigation problem; it is a signal that the target is wrong.

4. When it applies, stated as testable claims

There is a decision that locks. It is worth its cost in proportion to what becomes expensive to change afterwards. Ushakaal passes emphatically: the plan commits tooling, a reagent run and distributor contracts. Upaay's lock is the decommissioning date, after which the fallback is gone.

The failure is causally rich but not yet observable. If the dominant risk can be settled by a cheap test this week, the option-buying camp is right and the meeting is a detour. Revathi's humidity risk is partly testable, so the pre-mortem should commission the test rather than replace it. Upaay's leakage risk cannot be tested in production, because testing it means auto-approving claims; it can only be shadowed, and so must be reasoned about in advance.

Private doubt exists and is unvoiced. The diagnostic is brutal: ask three people separately what they privately think the chance of hitting the number is. Tight clustering means the session will surface little. Revathi's answers ranged from 30% to 80%, so the consensus was an artefact.

Someone will own the rows. Where no owner has standing to halt work, the exercise converts doubt into documentation — worse than none, because the risk is now believed handled.

It is actively misleading in two situations. In genuinely novel undertakings the imaginable causes come from the team's own past, and a confident register crowds out the slack that would have absorbed the surprise. And where planning is political, the register becomes an alibi: rows written so someone can point at them afterwards.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Hardware breaks the technique's tempo. Ushakaal's worst failure modes have lead times in months — a reagent lot, a moulding tool, a filing — so a trigger firing in week nine of twelve is informative and useless at once. Mature hardware teams push triggers upstream onto proxies that move early: incoming-inspection variance rather than field failure rate, the humidity logs the device already collects rather than utilisation. The seam that hurts is between plant and field. Sandeep's team is measured on units shipped, Ipsita's on units working; the humidity row is hers, but its remedy is executed by people who do not report to her. Firms claiming one register usually run two, with the seam-spanning rows unowned in both.

Regulated and multi-tenant settings bend it differently. Some Upaay rows cannot be mitigated by Upaay at all — a schema revision at the claims exchange, a tenant's compliance team refusing a migration window — so the response reads not "fix" but "detect early and renegotiate the date." In two-sided businesses the useful move is one exercise per side, because stories and owners differ. AI-native features need a category most templates lack, because the failure is statistical rather than binary: not "the model broke" but "calibration degraded on a subpopulation, quietly, while aggregate accuracy held." That demands sliced indicators — false-approve rate by tenant, hospital tier, claim band — which is why Farhan's row is weekly and Abhijit's monthly.

6. Eight distinctions between an expert and a competent practitioner

The failure statement is a sampling choice, not a preamble. The tell is one statement and twenty-five causes: thorough-looking, one branch explored. An expert writes two or three that fail in structurally different ways, because causes cluster around whichever failure was described.

The register's job is to change a decision, not record a concern. The tell is a response field reading "monitor closely." An expert treats that as an admission that no decision was made, and asks who may authorise the response without another meeting. Awareness is not protective: the moment of firing is when a firm can least decide calmly.

Probability estimates are more useful wrong than absent. The tell is high/medium/low labels, which hide that two people saying "medium" mean 20% and 60%. Numbers can be argued against, aggregated and updated; labels cannot. False precision costs less than a register that cannot be summed.

Expected shortfall belongs in the same currency as the benefit. The tell is a plan whose upside is in rupees and whose risk is in colours. Until both sit in one unit, nobody sees a ₹10.1 crore benefit carrying ₹12.9 crore of expected shortfall. Quantifying risk is how a product manager argues for a lower target without appearing unambitious.

The most valuable output is sometimes a changed target. The tell is a session ending in mitigations only. An expert holds open that the right answer may be 54% rather than 62%, or 1,800 analysers rather than 2,400 — the hardest output to land, because it looks like retreat before a board meeting.

Detectability is a design variable, not an observation. The tell is an FMEA column filled in as though visibility were a fact of nature. An expert asks what instrumentation moves a risk from detectability four to one, and prices it as a mitigation. A humidity sensor and a sampled claims audit are purchases of detectability.

The register decays by neglect, and neglect is silent. The tell is not a missing row but a review where no row's status changed for six weeks. An expert instruments the register itself — rows closed, triggers fired, rows added — because a register with no new rows two months in is an unread document.

Who speaks first decides what gets written. The tell is a cause list whose themes track the seniority of the room. An expert defends the silent-writing step with disproportionate rigidity, collecting cards before discussion, because private estimates re-anchor on the first confident sentence.

7. Differences by product type and company stage

Across product types the differences are real but narrower than folklore suggests. In consumer products the stories are behavioural and cheap to test, so the output is a list of experiments. In B2B and enterprise software they concentrate on integration, procurement and account concentration, so rows need owners in customer success and legal, and the highest-impact row is often one named customer: Upaay's two largest tenants carry 46% of volume, and no diligence mitigates a tenant's change-freeze calendar. Platforms need the exercise run per side. Hardware shifts triggers upstream. AI products need sliced indicators, because degradation is gradual and aggregates conceal it. Not different: the mechanics, the numeric trigger, and the dominance of neglect.

Stage changes the failure mode of the practice more than the practice. At seed stage it is three founders and a whiteboard, adequate provided the output is written where a later decision will be checked against it; the characteristic failure is that nothing is written. At growth stage, where both protagonists sit, the register exists, is good, and is owned by one enthusiast whose departure kills it. At enterprise scale it becomes a programme-management artefact reviewed quarterly at two removes from the work, and the failure is compliance theatre: rows worded to be defensible, triggers set where they will not fire, a review whose purpose is attendance.

8. Three worked examples

Ushakaal: a risk with a designed answer. Of the 2,400 planned units, 38% sit in high-humidity coastal districts. The baseline assumes 180 tests a month everywhere: ₹14.52 crore a year. Run the pre-mortem's story instead — humid-district units settle at 70 tests a month while the rest, better supported, reach 195. The blend is 0.38 × 70 + 0.62 × 195 = 147.5 tests, worth ₹11.89 crore: a ₹2.63 crore shortfall. Now apply the row's response, humidity-compensated firmware at ₹40 lakh plus a free monthly quality-control cartridge costing ₹10.08 lakh a year. If that lifts humid utilisation to 160, the blend is 181.7 tests, ₹14.55 crore net of the cartridge. The interesting number is the breakeven: the utilisation that just reaches the commitment is 156 tests a month, one falsifiable question a six-week, forty-unit pilot can answer.

Upaay: a risk that changed the target. At 6.8 lakh lines a month, moving from 41% to 62% straight-through processing saves ₹10.1 crore a year. Farhan Sait asked what the incremental 21 points were made of. Shadow-mode data implied a false-approve rate near 1.4% on newly automated lines — lines the old process would have queried. That is 0.21 × 6.8 lakh = 142,800 lines a month, of which 2,000 are wrongly approved at roughly ₹9,600 of avoidable payout each: ₹1.92 crore a month, ₹23 crore a year. Against a ₹10.1 crore saving, the plan destroys ₹12.9 crore. Gate automation at a calibrated confidence of 0.97 and only 13 points survive: 54% STP, a ₹6.2 crore saving, a false-approve rate of 0.3%, leakage of ₹3.05 crore, a net of ₹3.15 crore. The lower target is the better plan by ₹16 crore a year.

Urvi Agri Networks: where the approach failed. In 2024 the Indore-based input-and-advisory platform ran a textbook session before launching a ₹499-a-season crop-advisory subscription, targeting 40,000 subscribers against a ₹2 crore plan. Fourteen rows, numeric triggers, named owners; the launch landed 9,200 subscribers, and every row stayed green. The failure ran through a mechanism nobody had a category for: village-level entrepreneurs paid a flat onboarding fee found it more lucrative to enrol farmers into a competing free scheme and bundle Urvi's app as a sweetener, so activation was reported and usage never happened. The indicators were all product-side; the incentive sat outside the team's map. Prakash Damle changed the generator rather than adding a fifteenth row: every later pre-mortem includes a pass in which someone argues the failure from the point of view of each party whose incentives the plan touches but whose reporting line it excludes.

9. Failure modes, warnings and the cost of lateness

Softened framing. The early sign is a list containing "execution" or "adoption" without a mechanism. Diagnostic: could a stranger reading this row say what to do differently this week? Caught late, the register gives the illusion of coverage while every real cause stays unnamed.

Discussion before writing. The early sign is that the first cause raised becomes the dominant theme. Diagnostic: does seniority predict the order themes appeared in? Unwritten causes cannot be recovered; everyone now remembers agreeing.

Triggers that cannot fire. The early sign is a threshold the metric has never approached. Diagnostic: in the last two quarters, how often would this have fired? Caught late, the team learns its controls only reassured.

Ranking by RPN. The early sign is a register sorted by a three-factor product. Diagnostic: what is each row's expected rupee shortfall? Exhibit 3 is the cost — attention on a ₹41 lakh row while an ₹8 crore row waits.

Orphaned rows at the seam. The early sign is a row whose owner cannot authorise its response. Diagnostic: name the person who can say yes without escalating. Caught late, the owner spends three weeks assembling a meeting one sentence would have replaced.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The sharpest live disagreement is between the outside-view camp and the pre-mortem camp about where marginal effort belongs. Steelmanned, the outside view runs: across large samples the distribution of overrun is stable and largely independent of how carefully a team reasoned about its own risks, because the mechanisms are many and interchangeable while the aggregate is not. On that evidence the honest treatment of Ushakaal's plan is to take the base rate for comparable Indian device rollouts and stop pretending the causes matter. For this to be wrong, the overrun rate for teams running serious pre-mortems would have to differ from the rate for those that do not — a comparison nobody has made.

Against it, the mechanism camp argues that base rates say how much padding to add and nothing about what to build. Revathi cannot act on "device rollouts overrun by 30%"; she can act on "156 tests a month." For this to be wrong, the causes teams name would have to be systematically not the causes that bite — as at Urvi.

The second disagreement is about the register itself. The reliability camp holds that a risk without a detector and an owner is not managed, and that the list is the smaller half. The Safety-II position is that in complex systems the enumerable failure modes are a small, unrepresentative fraction of what happens, and that rupees spent perfecting the register would buy more safety as slack: a longer dual-run window, a deeper service bench, an unallocated 15% of capacity. Its evidence is that serious incidents, reviewed afterwards, were novel combinations. The counter-evidence is Upaay's leakage row, enumerable and catastrophic, which slack would not have caught. No one has a principled rule for the split.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied the technique runs a good session and produces a register. Someone who has internalised it differs in four ways. They write the failure statement before the invite list, and let the list follow. They hold the possibility of a changed target open throughout, and will spend political capital lowering a number before a board meeting. They treat every response field as a decision already taken by a named person, and refuse the phrase "monitor closely." And they revisit on a cadence set by the risk's own clock rather than the company's calendar, counting the rows that changed, because a register nothing happens to is not a plan going well.

12. What each of them decides

Revathi does not lock the plan on 18 August. She commits to the ramp but places forty analysers in three coastal districts for six weeks with humidity logging on, funds the ₹40 lakh firmware work in parallel, and tells the CFO the ₹14.52 crore number carries one named dependency with a date. Paying ₹40 lakh for an option on a ₹2.63 crore shortfall is simple arithmetic.

Karthik does something harder. He asks the executive team to move the OKR from 62% to 54%, with the confidence gate and a sampled medical audit as standing controls, and the two large tenants dual-running past 31 December. The turnaround goal survives; it was never the risky half. Asked whether he is sandbagging, his answer is Exhibit 3: the ambitious target destroyed ₹12.9 crore, the modest one creates ₹3.15 crore. Whether the room accepts that is a question about the organisation, not the analysis.

Discussion questions

  1. Upaay improved its plan by lowering its target. When can a product manager do that without it reading as a loss of nerve?
  2. Urvi ran a correct pre-mortem and was undone by an incentive outside its map. Is the fix a better generator or more slack?
  3. Revathi's plan reduced to one number. Should ordinary sensitivity analysis have surfaced it first?

13. Going deeper

  • Milestones and release planning — a pre-mortem against a vague plan yields vague risks; milestones give it something to interrogate.
  • Surfacing assumptions — every register row is a failed assumption written forward; this is the upstream skill.
  • Strategy vs roadmap vs plan — clarifies which layer a risk threatens, and who owns it.
  • Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later — shows how commitment hardens, and when a pre-mortem is still cheap.
  • The roadmap as communication — a register works only if its triggers are legible outside the team.
  • OKRs and goal setting — Upaay turns on the gap between an ambitious and a valuable target.
  • Annual and quarterly planning — sets the cadence of revisits, where compliance theatre takes hold.
  • Capacity planning — the resilience camp prescribes slack; slack is bought here.
exp20v2-plan.premortem:
Delivery & Technology · Roadmapping, Planning & OKRs

Pre-mortems and risk registers

It is the second week of March 2026, and Meera Anand, VP of Product at Tatva Freight Cloud in Bengaluru, is two days from locking the roadmap she will present to the board. Tatva runs a marketplace that matches shipper loads to independent trucking fleets across 1,400 lanes and roughly 3,200 partner trucks, and the network moves about 50 lakh kilometres a month. Almost a quarter of every kilometre a Tatva truck drives is empty — a truck delivers a load, then returns with nothing on board because no matching backhaul was found in time. This "deadhead" mileage, at 22% of total network kilometres, is the number the board keeps asking about, because every empty kilometre is one nobody pays for. Meera's team has spent eight months building LoadMatch AI, a model that predicts which empty trucks are likely to be near a compatible outbound load and nudges dispatchers toward matching them before the truck starts its empty run. The OKR on the board deck is blunt: cut deadhead from 22% to 18% of total network kilometres by the end of Q3 FY27. That four-point swing is worth roughly ₹3.36 crore a year in recovered contribution margin, and it is the number Tatva's Series C story leans on hardest. Before she locks the plan, Meera has one more meeting scheduled: not a status review, but an exercise where the team is asked to assume, as a stated fact, that the plan has already failed.

The idea

A pre-mortem is a planning exercise in which a team is told, before a project begins, that it has already failed a year from now, and is asked to work backward and write down the most plausible reasons why — not reasons it might fail, but reasons it did. It was named and popularised by the psychologist Gary Klein in a 2007 Harvard Business Review article, building on earlier research into what is called prospective hindsight: people asked to explain a hypothetical future event as though it had definitely happened generate more causes, and more specific ones, than people asked to merely list risks. A risk register is an older artifact from classical project management — a running log, one row per identified risk, each with a likelihood, an impact, an owner, and a plan for what happens if it starts to materialise. The pre-mortem generates candidate entries; the register holds, ranks and tracks them after the meeting ends. The sentence Meera could say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this: before we lock a plan, we assume it has already failed, and we write down why — then we track those reasons like we track anything else that matters.

How it actually works

Meera's session follows a sequence that looks simple on a slide and is easy to run badly. First, someone states the failure as an accomplished fact, with a date and a number: it is 30 September 2026, and Tatva's network deadhead rate is still above 18%. This framing matters more than it looks — asking "what could go wrong" produces polite answers like "execution risk," while asserting the failure already happened forces the mind toward a specific causal story, because a fact needs an explanation and a possibility does not. Second, and this is the step most teams skip under time pressure, every person writes their own reasons alone and in silence for a few minutes before anyone speaks, protecting the exercise from the ordinary dynamics of a meeting where the most senior voice speaking first quietly reorganises everyone else's list. Third, the group goes round-robin, one reason per turn, so a junior analyst's cause gets the same airtime as the CTO's. Fourth, the raw list — Meera's session produced twenty-six reasons — gets clustered into a handful of causal themes rather than left flat. Only in the fifth step does the exercise stop being a brainstorm and start being governance: each theme becomes a register row with an owner, a likelihood, an impact, a number that would trigger action, and a mitigation that exists before the risk does, not after.

A worked example

One theme from Meera's session: LoadMatch AI's confidence score is trained mostly on high-frequency lanes, and on the 460 lanes (33% of Tatva's 1,400 lanes) with fewer than 30 trips a month, its suggestions are noisy enough that dispatchers may simply stop trusting and using it. Those thin lanes are disproportionately long-haul, so although they are a third of lanes by count, they carry 45% of network kilometres; the remaining 55% runs on 940 well-travelled, already-efficient lanes. Assume thin lanes start at a 34% deadhead rate and thick lanes at 12%, blending to almost exactly the observed 22% (0.45×34 + 0.55×12 = 21.9%). Now suppose the pre-mortem's risk comes true: dispatchers abandon LoadMatch AI on thin lanes, which stay stuck at 34%, while the model squeezes thick lanes to a very good 8%. The blend is 0.45×34 + 0.55×8 = 19.7% — a miss against the 18% target, worth roughly ₹1.93 crore a year instead of the ₹3.36 crore promised, a shortfall of about ₹1.4 crore. Change one input: the register's mitigation is a simple rule-based fallback for thin lanes for the first ninety days, transparent logic dispatchers can audit, which the pre-mortem prompts the team to build before launch rather than after the metric disappoints. If that fallback gets thin lanes only to 26% while thick lanes still reach 8%, the blend becomes 0.45×26 + 0.55×8 = 16.1%, beating the 18% target and worth close to ₹4.96 crore a year. The arithmetic does not change because the model got smarter; it changes because a risk that was named in March got a designed answer instead of being discovered by a dispatcher in July.

Nuances a learner must sit with

A pre-mortem is an event; a risk register is an artifact

People say "we did a pre-mortem" and mean they had a good conversation once. The conversation is only valuable if its output survives the meeting as rows someone is accountable for. A team with a lively pre-mortem and no register has produced entertainment, not risk management.

Certainty of framing, not just topic, does the work

The prospective-hindsight research this technique rests on found that stating failure as already-happened, not as a possibility, is what elicits specific causes rather than vague hedges. "What might go wrong with LoadMatch AI" reliably produces weaker answers than "it is 30 September 2026 and LoadMatch AI has failed" — the grammar of certainty forces the mind to explain rather than merely speculate.

It generates causes; it does not rank them

A pre-mortem is a divergent, generative exercise. It tells you nothing about which of twenty-six causes is likely or severe. Teams that treat every surfaced risk as equally urgent are skipping the convergent step — likelihood times impact scoring — that the register exists to do.

Not the same as scenario planning or a SWOT audit

Scenario planning imagines several different futures for the world (say, fuel-price regimes); a pre-mortem imagines one future — failure of this specific plan — and works backward to causes internal to the project. A SWOT weaknesses list is a static inventory, not a causal chain running from an assumption to a consequence.

It is bounded by who is in the room

A pre-mortem cannot surface a risk that nobody present has the domain knowledge or imagination to conceive. If Meera's session had excluded the Hyderabad data-science lead, the thin-lane confidence problem might never have been named, and the exercise would have produced false confidence rather than real coverage.

Ceremony cost must be worth the stakes

For a two-week, low-capital experiment, a full pre-mortem costs more in senior time than the risk it prevents is worth. It earns its place on plans with a lockable decision point, real capital, and consequences that outlast the meeting — which is exactly what an OKR tied to a board number is.

The register's most common failure is neglect, not omission

Most registers are not missing rows; they are missing revisits. A register written once at kickoff and never reopened against real pilot data is a museum piece, not a management tool, and it fails silently because nobody notices a document nobody is reading.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and stage

The causes a pre-mortem surfaces skew with the kind of product. In a consumer app, the dominant failure stories are behavioural — will people trust a recommendation, will they churn after one bad experience — and they are cheap to probe with a small cohort before committing further spend. In enterprise B2B software, causes skew toward integration, procurement cycles and the concentration risk of a few large accounts, so register rows often need a legal or customer-success owner, not only an engineering one. Tatva is a two-sided marketplace, and that shape matters: a risk that erodes trucker trust in LoadMatch AI is a different animal from one that erodes shipper trust in delivery reliability, so Meera runs the exercise once per side rather than pooling both into a single generic list, because the failure stories, and the people who own the fixes, do not overlap. Stage matters too. At an early-stage company the whole exercise might happen informally between three founders over coffee — which is fine, provided it still ends up written down somewhere a decision will later be checked against. At a large organisation the register tends to migrate into a formal PMO artifact reviewed quarterly by people removed from the daily work, and it is exactly there that it decays into compliance theatre unless someone insists it stays owned by the people actually delivering the milestone.

Common mistakes

Softening the framing into "risks," not failure

The symptom is a list of abstractions — "market risk," "execution risk" — that nobody could act on tomorrow. The underlying error is asking what might go wrong instead of declaring that it did. The cheapest check: for each row, ask whether a stranger reading only that sentence could tell what to do differently this week.

Talking before writing

The symptom is a register whose entries suspiciously mirror what the most senior person in the room said first. The error is skipping the silent, independent writing step. The check is simple: look at who raised each theme first, and see whether seniority predicts the order.

Rows with no trigger and no owner

The symptom is a register that gets reviewed on schedule but never changes anything, because a risk described only in prose has no moment at which it forces action. The fix is a number: for every row, name the value a leading indicator must cross before the row is reopened, and the one person accountable for watching it.

What good looks like

Six weeks before the planned GA date, Meera's team reopens the register because the pilot data crosses the trigger they set for the thin-lane row: dispatcher override of AI suggestions on thin lanes has hit 27%, against a threshold of 25%. Because the fallback logic was already designed in March, not improvised in July, engineering ships it inside the existing sprint rather than as an emergency rewrite. The data-science lead in Hyderabad, named as the row's owner from day one, presents the override numbers at the biweekly review alongside the fix, not as a surprise but as the risk register doing exactly what it was built to do. The board deck Meera eventually presents does not claim the plan is risk-free; it names the three causes the team thought hardest about and shows, for each, what would have to be true for it to bite and what already stands in the way if it does.

Closing

Meera locks the roadmap with the phased thin-lane fallback built in from the start, not bolted on after a disappointing quarter, and she walks into the board meeting with a register instead of a promise. What she takes from this into the next planning cycle is that a pre-mortem is cheap insurance against a specific, well-known failure mode of planning: optimism bias compounding silently across everyone's individual estimate until the group total looks safer than any one person's honest guess. The natural next thing to learn is how milestone and dependency mapping — critical paths, RAID logs, the discipline of converting a feature roadmap into an outcome roadmap — gives a pre-mortem something concrete to interrogate in the first place; a pre-mortem run against a vague plan just produces vague risks. Two questions worth sitting with: in your last planning meeting, whose view would have dominated the room if everyone had spoken in the order they usually do, and which one of your current commitments would most repay imagining, right now, as already failed?
case40v1-plan.premortem:
Case 40 · Delivery & Technology · Roadmapping, Planning & OKRs

Chalaan Tax Systems: The Register That Went Green

Hyderabad, Sunday 27 September 2026. Anuradha Sarangi has a register of thirty-one risks, a pilot that half-worked, and twelve hours before she must tell a programme board whether an eighteen-month migration should cut over on 1 January.

1. Sunday Night, Gachibowli

The Gachibowli office was empty except for two engineers on a call with Toronto and Anuradha Sarangi, Chief Product Officer of Chalaan Tax Systems, who had spread four printouts across the long table, unable to hold them side by side on a screen: the pre-mortem risk register for Project Ekjaal, dated March 2026, when the team spent two days imagining the migration had already failed and writing down why; the same register tonight; the August pilot report; and Friday's dashboard, which called Ekjaal green.

The registers did not match each other, and neither matched the pilot. Risk R-03, rated High in March and described in the team's own words as "reconciliation drift across multi-GSTIN groups, the thing that will actually kill us", had been Medium since 14 April. The pilot had just produced a 4.7 per cent mismatch rate in exactly that cohort. The dashboard put schedule confidence at 78 per cent.

At ten the next morning the programme board would meet to confirm or move the cutover date, and Anuradha owed it a recommendation. What she had was a question she did not know how to put to a board: her company had done what the textbooks asked, had imagined the failure in advance and written it down, and the writing-down appeared to have made the team less able to see it.

2. Chalaan Tax Systems

Chalaan was founded in Hyderabad in 2016 by Vikram Menon and two colleagues from an enterprise resource planning practice. As the Goods and Services Tax Network and the National Informatics Centre stood up the invoice registration portals, it moved from filing returns into e-invoicing and e-way bills, reaching ₹138 crore of annual recurring revenue by FY2026 across 620 customer groups and roughly 4,100 registered entities, with 310 employees. Engineering sat in Hyderabad and Pune with a platform team in Bengaluru; design ran from Berlin, data science from Toronto, customer success from Singapore, sales from New Jersey.

One decision from 2023 shaped everything on Anuradha's table. To win Charkha Apparel Mills — a Tiruppur and Ahmedabad manufacturer with 68 registrations across fourteen states and about 47 lakh documents a year — Chalaan had agreed to a single-tenant deployment with bespoke reconciliation logic for inter-branch stock transfers. Internally it was Ledger-C: eleven weeks, four engineers, two-fifths of its behaviour never merged back into the main platform. Charkha now paid ₹9.2 crore a year, was Chalaan's largest account, and could not be migrated without re-deriving logic that lived in one person's head and in a fork nobody else had read end to end.

3. The Industry

Indian compliance software is a market where the calendar belongs to somebody else. Thresholds, schema versions and portal behaviour are set by the Council and notified by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs; ClearTax, Cygnet, IRIS and the Zoho and Tally ecosystems compete on how fast they absorb a change and how little the customer's finance team notices. Integrators — Infosys, TCS, the SAP channel — sit in between, and a vendor who breaks a filing cycle rarely gets a second one.

The event bearing on Ekjaal was a notified reduction of the e-invoicing threshold to ₹1 crore of aggregate turnover from 1 January 2027, bringing several lakh smaller businesses into scope. Sales leadership treated the October-to-March window as the largest new-logo opportunity since 2020 and sized it at roughly ₹26 crore of recurring revenue, if the company could onboard at pace. The old platform could not: provisioning was manual and support cost per small customer exceeded the price charged. Ekjaal — one multi-tenant platform, self-serve provisioning, one reconciliation engine — had been sold to the board on that basis.

Two other forces pressed in. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had made consent and retention records part of what an invoice archive must carry, and Chalaan's archival partner, Raseed Archival Services in Noida, held seven years of documents under a contract renewable on 15 December. And the exposure was not only Indian: Raunaq Trading LLC, a Dubai group whose India arm signed a ₹4.6 crore contract in July, expected export invoicing live in February 2027 on the new platform.

4. What Happened, and What Turned Out To Be Wrong

Ekjaal was approved in February 2025 with an eighteen-month build and a cutover at the start of calendar 2027, when the third quarter closes and the threshold change lands. In March 2026, at Anuradha's insistence, forty people across four offices were asked to assume that on 1 January 2028 Ekjaal was being written up as a failure, and say why. The exercise produced thirty-one named risks, each with a likelihood, a cost, an owner and an early-warning sign.

The register was then circulated. Charkha's audit committee had a contractual right to programme documentation, since its filings depended on Chalaan, and on 14 April the register went to Ahmedabad, to Chinar Growth Partners, and to Chalaan's board. Within a week three ratings changed. R-03, reconciliation drift, moved from High to Medium. R-11, key-person dependency on the fork, moved from Medium to Low with the note "mitigated by documentation sprint, Q2"; the sprint was deferred twice. Nobody recorded who asked. The wiki shows the edits were made by the engineering programme manager on the afternoon of 21 April, forty minutes after a call with Charkha's controller.

Through the summer the programme reported green. The first pilot wave ran from 11 August to 5 September across eighty-six entities in three cohorts, excluding the largest groups. Cohorts A and B were clean. Cohort C — ten to forty registrations — returned a 4.7 per cent mismatch between reference numbers in the old system and those reconstructed in Ekjaal. Ashwin Pillai's team in Toronto, which built the detector, thought the true figure higher: extraction had failed for three of the cohort's largest entities, and those were dropped from the sample rather than counted as failures.

Two further facts arrived in September. Zaheer Qureshi, the Bengaluru architect who wrote most of Ledger-C, told Ipsita Nayak on 16 September that he had an offer and would decide by mid-October. And an engineer preparing the runbook found that the rollback path — back to the old platform if cutover failed at hour six — had been tested only against a 200-entity synthetic dataset, and that restoring seven years of archived documents from Raseed would take, by Raseed's estimate, fourteen to thirty hours. R-14 had carried the sign "rollback not rehearsed at volume by 30 June" since March. Nobody checked whether it tripped: the risk was Medium, and Medium risks were reviewed monthly, by exception.

5. The People

Anuradha Sarangi, Chief Product Officer, Hyderabad, owns Ekjaal's outcome without owning its engineering, introduced the pre-mortem, and has twice told the board that Chalaan plans better than its size suggests. She is not saying that she approved the April circulation without asking what it would do to the ratings, or that she now suspects the register is written for readers.

Vikram Menon, co-founder and Chief Executive, Hyderabad, wants 1 January held: the threshold window is the last reshuffle before consolidation, and rivals will take the small-entity segment if Chalaan is still hand-provisioning in March. He will not run two platforms and onboard nine hundred entities with one support team. He is not saying that Chinar's second tranche turns on Ekjaal being the system of record by 31 March 2027, or that he has told two prospects it is live.

Ipsita Nayak, VP Engineering, Pune, has the best grasp of the technical state and wants a cohort-phased cutover from January to June, both platforms live. She is not saying that her own programme manager made the April edits and that she let them stand, or that she owns two risks she privately believes are Chalaan's largest.

Zaheer Qureshi, Principal Architect, Bengaluru, is the only person who understands Ledger-C in full. Charkha, he says, should not move in the first wave under any date: the logic needs three months of re-derivation with two engineers beside him. He is not saying what he would need to stay, and has not been asked.

Nandita Ghosh, Head of Customer Success, Singapore, carries Charkha and Raunaq and wants a parallel run with no customer-visible change until March. She is not saying that in August she described a dual-run to Charkha's controller as "our plan", which nobody had approved and which the audit committee may treat as a commitment.

Katarina Voss, Design Lead, Berlin, owns the exception queue, where a clerk resolves invoices the engine could not match; it was built for a few hundred items a day and cutover will produce thousands. She is not saying that two of her four designers move to the self-serve onboarding flow in November, the flow the pipeline depends on.

Ashwin Pillai, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto, insists the pilot understates the problem and wants the excluded entities re-run before any date is confirmed. He is not saying that his detector's recall has never been measured, so "probably double" is judgement, not evidence.

Gurmeet Sethi, Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey, wants 1 January because his pipeline of US manufacturers with Indian subsidiaries has been sold a self-serve platform. He is not saying that two of those deals slipped in August for unrelated reasons, leaving his number softer than the board thinks. Outside the company, Meera Krishnan of Chinar Growth Partners has asked for "the register, not the deck" at each of the last three board meetings, calling it the only artefact where she sees people being honest about their own plan — a request Anuradha read as support for the discipline, and which may be the pressure that bent it.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — Project Ekjaal risk register, selected entries, showing rating history

Exhibit 1 is the document the programme believes it is managed by; Exhibit 2 is what the pilot produced. Together they say R-03's sign tripped at twice its threshold, in the only cohort resembling Chalaan's revenue concentration, and that the rating did not move.
