7. Voices

"Why does a programme three-quarters through carry a High on a document going to our audit committee? If it is genuinely High, that is a conversation. If it is a drafting habit, please fix the drafting." Charkha Apparel Mills, Group Controller, email, 21 April 2026
"4.7% in Cohort C — with the three worst entities dropped because extraction timed out. Count those as failures and it is 11-point-something. I don't know the true number. Nobody does. That is my point." Ashwin Pillai, #ekjaal-pilot, 8 September 2026
"I have told their controller we will run in parallel. I did not invent it; it was on the slide in June. If it is now big-bang on 31 December, I am the person who lied to them and the person who sells them the renewal in May." Nandita Ghosh, call with A. Sarangi, 22 September 2026
"Honestly? The register stopped being useful the day it left the room. In March we wrote 'the thing that will actually kill us'. In April we wrote 'Medium'. Same risk, same week, same people." Zaheer Qureshi, one-to-one with A. Sarangi, 24 September 2026

8. The Options as Anuradha Sees Them

Option A — Hold 1 January, harden the runbook

Cut over all cohorts except Charkha on 31 December, rehearse rollback in early December, absorb the exception queue with temporary staff. This keeps the threshold window and Chinar's milestone, and ends the fork for everyone but the account that most needs it gone. It also puts the cutover inside the year-end freeze (Exhibit 6), when a third of the engineers who wrote the code are away, and rests on a rollback never exercised at volume.

Option B — Phase by cohort, dual-run to June

Move cohorts A and B in January, C in March, Charkha in June, both platforms live throughout. It is what Ipsita and Nandita want, it honours what Charkha's controller believes he was promised, and it turns one large risk into six small ones. It costs ₹7.3 crore, keeps Ledger-C alive two more quarters — and with it Zaheer's indispensability — and asks a stretched support team to run two systems through the busiest quarter in years.

Option C — Move the cutover to 1 April

Onboard threshold-driven customers onto the old platform through the window, cutting over at the start of the new financial year after a quarter of rehearsal. Fewest technical risks, most commercial ones: roughly 900 more entities on the backlog, ₹15 crore of judged opportunity forgone, and a conversation with Chinar about a milestone agreed in writing.

Writing the options out, Anuradha noticed that all three varied the same thing: the date, or the order of the dates. None changed who owned the register, or whether a warning sign could trip without a human remembering to look, or whether an engineer could write "High" in a document his largest customer would read. None costed the line in Exhibit 5 that had no number. She was not certain this meant the options were wrong. She was certain the March pre-mortem had produced the right answer eighteen months early, that the company had spent eighteen months negotiating it downwards, and that nothing in the three options would stop that recurring.

9. The Deadline and the Hard Constraints

The programme board meets at ten on Monday 28 September. Charkha's audit committee meets on 6 October and expects a dated cutover plan. Raseed's renewal must be signed by 15 December or seven years of archived documents move to a rate card 40 per cent higher. Chinar's second tranche of ₹95 crore turns on Ekjaal being the system of record by 31 March 2027 and on net revenue retention above 112 per cent; without it Chalaan has eleven months of runway. Charkha's service credits run at ₹18 lakh per day of disruption, and that contract renews in May. Hiring is frozen below director level. The threshold date is not moveable by anyone at Chalaan. And Zaheer decides on his offer by mid-October, whether or not anybody speaks to him first.

10. Questions for Discussion

  1. Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 describe the same programme in the same month and disagree. What does each measure, and which would you trust on whether 1 January is safe?
  2. R-03 moved from High to Medium with no change in the engineering. What should a register record when a rating moves, and who may move it?
  3. Exhibit 4 was compiled by the case writer, not Chalaan. Why do registers built risk-by-risk miss dependencies of this kind, and what would surface them during a pre-mortem rather than after a pilot?
  4. Nandita's email, Gurmeet's soft pipeline and Vikram's undisclosed tranche condition are each rational from where that person sits. How should Anuradha weigh evidence produced by people whose incentives she can name?
  5. Chalaan ran a pre-mortem, and ran it well. If Ekjaal fails in January, is that evidence against the practice, against this company's use of it, or against something else?
  6. It is Monday morning. What is on Anuradha's first slide, what does she ask the board to decide, and what does she say to Meera Krishnan when asked again for the register rather than the deck?

At half past eleven Anuradha put the printouts into one folder, in the order she had read them, which was not the order she would present them in. She had drafted three recommendations and deleted them. Behind her the whiteboard still carried, in March's hand, the sentence the pre-mortem opened with: it is 1 January 2028 and Ekjaal has failed — what did we already know? Someone had written the date of the pilot beneath it, and nothing else.
exp20v2-plan.replatform:
Planning a Replatform or Rebuild

How do we rebuild without a long gap in shipping?

1. A decision due by Friday

On Monday 14 September 2026, Inderdeep Panag, chief product officer of Amaltas Commerce, had a decision due by Friday. The Ludhiana company runs an ordering platform on which 140 distributors take wholesale orders from retailers. It is a monolith (one program in which every function shares a single codebase and database) written in 2012. It had failed twice at peak hours that quarter, and features that once took a fortnight now took ten weeks.

Ishpreet Pandher, the vice-president of engineering, proposed rebuilding everything on a modern foundation. He estimated 320 engineer-weeks (one engineer working for one week) and could give the project eight engineers, net of the rota that kept the old system alive. That meant forty weeks, ending Monday 28 June 2027. “Nothing ships until it all ships,” he said, “and then everything does.”

Indarjit Parhar, the finance head, estimated that the five main functions, once rebuilt, were worth about ₹15 lakh a week, or ₹780 lakh a year. Panag’s worry was what forty weeks meant: nine months in which distributors would see nothing new, ending in one cutover weekend.

2. The idea

A replatform moves a product onto a new technical foundation while keeping its behaviour; a rebuild also redesigns that behaviour. Either way the planning problem is sequencing: in what order does the old system give way, and what does the customer receive meanwhile? In 2000 the engineer Joel Spolsky argued that rewriting from scratch is among the worst strategic mistakes a software company can make, because the old code embodies years of unrecorded fixes while the market waits.

The remedy most teams now borrow is the strangler pattern, which Martin Fowler described in 2004, naming it after the strangler figs he had seen in Australia, which grow around a host tree until the tree is no longer needed. A thin routing layer, the facade, sits in front of the old system and sends each request either to the old code or to its new replacement. Capabilities move across one slice at a time until the old system can be switched off.

Panag could say it in one sentence: “We ship a slice of the new platform every quarter, and we retire a piece of the old one only after the new one has proved itself on real orders.”

3. How it works

The step practitioners leave implicit is finding the seams, the places where a system divides into capabilities that can move independently. Amaltas’s engineers found five slices, shown in Figure 1. Catalogue and pricing (A) feeds order capture (B); credit and invoicing (C) and dispatch (D) both need B; settlements (E) needs C. D and E do not depend on each other.

Second, the team installs the facade before any slice moves; it costs 32 engineer-weeks and shows nothing, so it is often skipped and regretted. Third, it orders slices by value for effort, subject to the arrows. Fourth, it states each slice’s migration gate, the evidence required before traffic moves, in advance. The slices total 56 + 88 + 72 + 64 + 40 = 320 engineer-weeks.

Each slice then passes four steps: build; shadow (the new code processes copies of live requests while the old code still answers, and the results are compared); canary (a small share of real users is switched over); and cutover with the old code retired. The gates Amaltas set for order capture are below. The usually unstated fifth step is deciding, slice by slice, which system is the source of truth for the data.

Gate for slice BTestThreshold
1. ParityBehaviours the usage audit marks essentialAll live in the new code
2. ShadowMismatches over mirrored ordersAt most 0.5% of 150,000
3. CanaryShare of the 140 distributors moved5%, which is 7 distributors
4. RollbackTime to return traffic to the old codeRehearsed, under 15 minutes

Table 1. Migration gate for order capture. The first shadow run produced 2,250 mismatches, 1.5% of 150,000, and failed; after fixes the second produced 600, 0.4%, and passed.

4. A worked example

Figure 2 draws the two plans over a year. The eight engineers supply eight engineer-weeks per calendar week. The big bang takes 320 engineer-weeks, or 40 weeks. The strangler takes the five slices plus the 32 engineer-weeks of facade: 320 + 32 = 352 engineer-weeks, or 44 weeks, and costs 10% more (352 divided by 320 is 1.10). Slices go in the order A, B, C, D, E, one at a time; C precedes D because ₹5 lakh for 72 engineer-weeks beats ₹2 lakh for 64.

The strangler delivers first value at week 11, Monday 7 December 2026, against week 40. Figure 3 plots the weekly run-rate, which steps from 3 to 7, 12, 14 and 15 lakh as slices land, while the big bang stays at zero until week 40.

Table 2 integrates that area: each slice earns its run-rate from going live to week 52, giving ₹382 lakh against ₹180 lakh for the big bang (15 × 12 weeks), a gain of ₹202 lakh in the first year despite finishing four weeks later.

Second pass. Change one input. Sales leaders insist that order capture reproduce every old behaviour, priced at 40 further engineer-weeks, so B grows from 88 to 128. B then takes 16 weeks, not 11, going live at week 27, five weeks later (40 divided by 8), and C, D and E slip five weeks each. The strangler’s year falls from 382 to 322, losing ₹60 lakh. The big bang grows to 360 engineer-weeks, goes live at week 45 and earns 15 × 7 = ₹105 lakh, losing ₹75 lakh. Parity damages both plans; only the strangler lets a gate decide, slice by slice, whether it is worth buying.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Parity means observed behaviour, not all behaviour

A parity trap is the demand that the new system reproduce everything the old one did. An audit of 412,000 orders over 90 days found 61 special behaviours in the order code (Table 3). Twelve fired 104,800 times, 99.6% of 105,170 firings. The other 49 are what the 40 extra engineer-weeks would buy, roughly 0.8 each.

TierBehavioursFirings in 90 daysShare of firings
1: fired often12104,80099.6%

Total61105,170100.0%

Table 3. Order-capture behaviours by usage. Tier 1 is the 12 most-fired behaviours; tier 2 fired at least once; tier 3 did not fire. One order can fire several behaviours. The log retains 180 days; the audit used 90.

“Never used” depends on the window

Four of the 23 tier-3 behaviours are year-end rebate rules that cannot fire in a 90-day window beginning in June. An audit shorter than the business cycle manufactures false confidence; ask the longest cycle and whether the log reaches back that far.

The strangler needs seams

Routing needs separable capabilities. If two functions write the same tables, the facade cannot send one to new code and one to old until the data is split. That refactoring is real work, and a plan that omits it hides its largest cost.

Data is the hard part

Code is easier to rewrite than state. During migration one system must own each record, with copying in one direction at a time; two systems writing the same customer balance sink many cutovers.

The strangler costs more in total

Here 352 against 320 engineer-weeks is a 10% premium for the facade and for running two systems, a cost Pandher could fairly cite. It buys the option to stop, reorder or drop parity. When the old platform has a hard end-of-life date, or the system is small, the big bang can win.

Order by value density, then by dependency

Value per engineer-week favours C over D, but only after A and B are live. Ignoring the arrows gives a plan that cannot run; ignoring value ships plumbing first.

What the plan cannot tell you

Table 2 multiplies estimated run-rates by weeks. It cannot say whether finance’s ₹15 lakh is real or whether adoption follows cutover immediately. Scaling every run-rate up or down never reverses the ranking, because both totals scale together. Timing decides it. The ₹202 lakh lead equals about 13.5 weeks of full run-rate, but D and E have only 13 and 8 live weeks to lose, so the lead is erased only by a uniform slip of 14 weeks in every strangler go-live (3×14 + 4×14 + 5×14 + 26 + 8 = 202), the big bang not slipping.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; small and large

In a B2B product such as Amaltas, parity includes customers’ integrations: a distributor’s accounting software may call an old interface, so changing it is a customer project. In a consumer app, the old client lingers on phones for months, so the old interface cannot be switched off on the plan’s date. In a marketplace, both sides see the same inventory and prices, so migrate the side whose errors are cheaper to repair first and keep one source of truth for listings.

An early-stage company has less state, fewer integrations and a team that remembers the old code, so a rebuild is often cheaper. A large company has more seams, more auditors and several teams sharing one database, so the facade and gates carry more of the work.

7. Common mistakes

Treating parity as a promise

Symptom: the date moves a month each time someone remembers an old report. Misunderstanding: the old system is the specification. Diagnostic: count firings, as in Table 3, and ask who would notice if a behaviour were missing.

Slices that ship nothing

Symptom: milestones such as “database migrated” that only engineers can see, a big bang in instalments. Misunderstanding: that moving a layer moves value. Diagnostic: on the go-live day, what can a distributor do that she could not do yesterday?

Never switching the old code off

Symptom: both systems still bill for hosting a year on. Misunderstanding: that retirement is cleanup, not scope. Diagnostic: put a switch-off date in each gate and list the tables the old slice still writes.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version is visible from outside. The facade is live in the first month. Every slice has a gate set before it starts, like Table 1, and a gate has failed at least once, which shows it is real. Parity is limited to what usage justifies, with an exception route for the rest. The roadmap is outcome-based: each quarter names a distributor-visible change, its dependencies and its risks. Progress is reported as slices retired, not percentage rebuilt.

9. What Panag decided

On Friday 18 September he chose the strangler: facade first, then A, B, C, D, E. The 32 extra engineer-weeks bought a first release on 7 December 2026 and, on Parhar’s figures, ₹202 lakh more in the year. For order capture he accepted the 12 tier-1 behaviours plus the four year-end rebate rules, about 3 further engineer-weeks at roughly 0.8 each, adding about 0.4 week, ignored here, and leaving the other 45 behind an exception route and a review. Slice B would move only when all four gates in Table 1 were green.

Next comes working with legacy systems, because the old code stays alive for months and someone must keep it safe.

Two questions to sit with. First, which number in Table 2 would you most want measured before approving, and what would you do if it came back at half? Second, think of a parity demand in your own product: which usage log would you check, and how long a window would it need?
exp40v2-plan.replatform:
Planning a replatform or rebuild

Sequencing the replacement of a working system so that value ships along the way — strangler patterns, the parity trap, and migration gates that are counts rather than opinions.

1. Two decisions, four days apart

On Thursday 2 July 2026, in Baner, Pune, Jagmeet Raizada put one slide to Bimasetu Technologies' executive committee. Bimasetu sells a claims platform to nine Indian general insurers; Claims Core, first deployed in 2012, carries about 3,100 newly opened claims a day on ₹31.8 crore of ARR across 48 engineers. Three prospects, each worth ₹96 lakh of ARR, wanted the same thing: let our analysts change adjudication rules without a Bimasetu release. Claims Core compiles its rules into the deployment artefact. Jashnoor Rakkar, its owner since 2017, costed a replacement at 1,331 engineer-weeks to parity. Jeevanjot Ratti, the CFO, wanted the date.

Four days later Juhika Ranota faced a narrower version in Bengaluru. Bistara Living sells mattresses and bedroom furniture through 38 stores and an app; FY26 revenue was ₹412 crore on 2.80 lakh orders, an average order value of ₹14,714. Its seven-year-old order-management system holds inventory reservations in a ledger it alone understands. On Sunday 19 October 2025, the last delivery cutoff before Diwali, that ledger drifted for forty minutes: of the 787 orders taken then, 263 were oversold. Jitwant Rajouria, VP of engineering, scoped the replacement at 338 engineer-weeks against fourteen people. Jaskaur Ramoowalia, in retail operations, owned the hard part: a standing freeze from 1 September to 15 November, carrying 41.0 per cent of the year at ₹169 crore.

Both had to replace a working system without going dark. Their right answers differ sharply, and not because of size, maturity or courage.

2. The idea, and the three schools that disagree about it

A replatform replaces the substrate a product runs on while the product keeps its identity, its data and its customers; a rebuild also reopens its behaviour. Planning either means ordering replacement so each increment is independently valuable, independently reversible, and leaves the system consistent. The enemy is the parity trap: reproducing everything the old system does before any new behaviour ships, which turns a product programme into translation.

The lineage predates the vocabulary. Parnas argued in 1972 for drawing modules around information to be hidden — also the argument for drawing them around units of replacement. Lehman's laws added two facts the field keeps rediscovering: a system in use must change or become less useful, and its complexity rises unless effort is spent reducing it. The best-known argument against rewriting, from 2000, held that a codebase's ugliness is mostly accumulated bug fixes. Fowler's 2004 strangler fig gave the incrementalists their image; Feathers' seams gave them a technique.

Three positions are genuinely held. Incrementalists would sign that the old system should retire piece by piece and that no programme should go a quarter without shipping something a customer notices; not that the seam is cheap. The clean-slate school would sign that where new and old share mutable state the adapter keeping them consistent can cost more than what it replaces, so one rehearsed cutover is safer; not that parity is the right target. The encapsulate-and-starve school would sign that most replatforms re-create the same complexity in newer syntax, so wrap the old system and never rebuild the core; not that maintenance cost justifies one.

3. Mechanics: what the work actually consists of

Expert practice begins with a usage census, because the parity trap is a measurement failure before it is a judgement failure. Rakkar counted every invocation of every user-facing operation in Claims Core — screens and API endpoints alike — over the 90 days from 1 April to 29 June 2026: 4,180,000 invocations across 412 operations, 46,444 a day, or 15 per claim-day. The denominator for every share below is that 4,180,000, measured on the old platform in that window.

The census splits the 412 into three tranches, defined so no operation belongs to two: the 96 most-invoked; the remaining operations invoked at least once, 255 of them; and the remaining operations invoked zero times, 61.

Exhibit 2. Bimasetu's parity census and estimate, by tranche.
Tranche (mutually exclusive)OperationsInvocationsShare of invocationsEngineer-weeksShare of effort
The 96 most-invoked963,882,00092.9%61246.0%
Remainder, invoked at least once255298,0007.1%61846.4%
Remainder, invoked zero times6100.0%1017.6%
Total4124,180,000100.0%1,331100.0%

Effort shares are over the 1,331-engineer-week total. Of the 101 engineer-weeks in the zero-invocation tranche, 78 were retired and 23 retained for eleven operations firing outside the window: nine in the March year-end close, two on a three-yearly actuarial extract.

Read the effort column against the invocation column. The tranche carrying 92.9 per cent of invocations takes 46.0 per cent of the effort; the two tail tranches carry 7.1 per cent of invocations and 54.0 per cent of effort. That is the parity trap as a number.

The second move is the routing key. Bimasetu's facade routes by claim identifier, not by operation, so the unit of migration is a piece of state rather than a screen. A migrated claim's unbuilt tail operations — overwhelmingly reads — proxy back to Claims Core against replicated data until wave 2: that is why wave 1 carries 92.9 per cent of invocations rather than all of them, and why the book of record stays one-sided. Routing by operation would have split each claim's state across two stores, which has no answer when a regulator asks which system is the book of record.

The third move is the migration gate: a pre-committed condition that must hold before traffic moves, expressed as a count, not a sign-off. Bimasetu's gate per wave is fourteen consecutive days with no unexplained divergence on that wave's operations. "Unexplained" matters: an intended behaviour change is not a defect, and must be enumerated in advance.

The formal treatment compares schedules, not architectures. Let S be the engineer-weeks of seam and decommission work existing only under the strangler, w the cost per engineer-week, c the weekly carry of dual running and Ts, Tb its weeks in each plan; Δt the days by which the strangler brings forward the date the new platform carries the same traffic share; A the annual revenue contingent on the new capability, p the chance it is lost by waiting, m the gross margin, n the years of gross profit credited to retained revenue; and qb, qs, L the chance of a failed cutover in each plan and its cost. Prefer the strangler when

Sw + c(Ts − Tb) < m(1 − p)A · Δt/365 + mpAn + (qb − qs)L.

The first right-hand term is a timing gain on the (1 − p) share that arrives either way, the second a retention gain on the p share; charging all of A to both double-counts it.

4. When it applies, stated as testable claims

Claim 1: the boundary can be drawn so that little mutable state crosses it. Measure the seam premium — seam plus decommission engineer-weeks over delivered rebuild scope — and treat anything above a quarter as a warning. Bimasetu's is 180 engineer-weeks on a scope of 1,253, or 14.4 per cent, because a claim's state machine lives in one service. Bistara's full strangle would need 142 on a scope of 338, or 42.0 per cent, because inventory reservation is one mutable quantity both systems must agree on under contention.

Claim 2: there is a capability the old platform cannot host, which customers will pay for before parity. Bimasetu passes: configurable rules are worth ₹288 lakh of prospective ARR and are impossible in Claims Core. Bistara fails on the reservation core — a cleaner engine is invisible until it is the only one — and passes on its read surfaces, where a stock-accurate store locator shows at once.

Claim 3: a cutover window of adequate length exists, and dual running need not straddle a peak. Bimasetu passes; claims intake has no seasonal peak, and the March close touches only the eleven retained operations. Bistara fails: a full strangle from 13 July 2026 keeps the dual-write live through the whole 76-day festive window, which is also the freeze.

Claim 4: the old platform can be frozen, or its drift priced. The condition most often assumed rather than tested; section 8 has the company that did not test it.

The idea misleads actively when read as licence to begin without a decommissioning plan: a strangler that never retires the old system is an extra system, carried permanently. It misleads again on schema: teams that strangle services over one shared database are counting a seam premium of zero on a boundary that does not exist.

5. Hard edge cases

In a multi-product company the seam gets drawn where the org chart is, not where the state is, so the adapter encodes a reporting line. In two-sided businesses both sides write the same listing object, so a plan that strangles supply tooling and leaves the demand app alone has not noticed; the clean cut is by tenant or geography. In regulated settings dual running creates two candidate systems of record, and one must be named per entity.

Hardware plus software breaks the pattern hardest: the installed fleet cannot be migrated at the operator's convenience. In AI-native products the harness cannot compare outputs for equality, because the new implementation is not deterministic and is not meant to agree; the gate becomes a regression band on a frozen evaluation set, which is then the parity artefact.

At the organisational seam, practice differs from policy. Companies say the teams share a roadmap; what they do is move the people who know the old system onto the seam and the harness. What fails is that nobody budgets the legacy team's time as programme cost, so it shows up as collapsing maintenance throughput.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The unit of strangling is a piece of mutable state, not a feature. The tell is a migration plan whose waves are named after screens. Screens feel like the natural decomposition, but two writing the same row cannot move separately without an adapter arbitrating between them, and that adapter is where replatforms die.

Parity is measured against a moving target. The tell is a parity scope with no change-control policy on the system being replaced. The obvious reading — the old system is finished, so it sits still — is wrong because it is the one customers use, and so the one receiving escalations. Freeze it or carry a drift allowance.

A usage tail is not dead code; check the calendar, not the log window. Bimasetu's 61 zero-invocation operations looked retirable until someone asked what a window beginning 1 April cannot see. Eleven fire in the March year-end close or a three-yearly actuarial cycle. The tell is a retirement list justified by one log window.

The seam premium is a property of the boundary, not a constant. Experts estimate it bottom-up; everyone else assumes ten per cent. The spread between Bimasetu's 14.4 per cent and Bistara's 42.0 per cent is reads against contended writes.

A gate is a count or it is theatre. The tell is a gate owned by a committee and phrased as readiness. A committee cannot fail a gate in week nine; a counter can. The subtler craft is enumerating the intended behaviour changes in advance.

A temporary adapter's life is set by the slowest thing it serves. The obvious reading is that temporary means short. Brindavan found the rule: its oldest device generation has no over-the-air channel, so the adapter retires only as those units are replaced — at the observed rate, 4.17 years. A four-year adapter is a product.

Dual-run carry is rent, so schedule slip compounds into it. Under a big bang a ten-week slip costs ten weeks of labour: 10 × 23 × ₹0.70 lakh, or ₹161 lakh. Under Bimasetu's strangler it costs that plus ten weeks of carry at ₹4.3 lakh, ₹43 lakh more. The tell is a programme reporting schedule risk without carry exposure.

Probability-weight both sides, or neither. Bimasetu's finance team first divided the ₹346 lakh cost gap by a delay it treated as certain, then compared that with a competitor-loss figure already multiplied by 0.40. The tell is a sentence where one branch carries a probability and the other a date. If the delay is uncertain, use its expected value on both sides.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the constraint is the client: old app versions call the old contract until users update, so the seam lives in the API gateway, with a life set by the update curve. In B2B and enterprise it is contractual — integrations and SLAs named in signed documents — so migration is negotiated per account, which is why routing by tenant is the default. On platforms and marketplaces the shared object is the business, so the seam is wide and the realistic unit is a geography. In hardware the fleet sets the pace, as Brindavan's 4.17 years shows. For AI products only the gate changes: Baadal Learning swapped its grading model against a frozen 1,400-item evaluation set, requiring the new model within 1.0 point of the old on exact match and no more than 0.5 per cent of items — seven of the 1,400 — regressing to incorrect.

By stage, one difference is real and one asserted. The real one: a company with one product line and under about thirty engineers often cannot afford a seam over contended writes, so the honest choice is a short big bang in a quiet window or no replatform. The asserted one is that large companies are better at this; they are better resourced, which is not the same thing.

8. Three worked examples

Baadal Learning, Noida, 2024–25. A video-delivery and assessment monolith, scoped at 790 engineer-weeks to full parity across 274 screens. A 120-day census found 103 screens with fewer than 50 sessions each; dropping them cut scope to 512 engineer-weeks, 35.2 per cent off the 790, leaving 171 screens — 32.0 weeks for sixteen engineers. Work began Monday 8 July 2024; the first wave went live at week nine, on 9 September 2024. Retirement was planned for week 32, 17 February 2025, and came at week 36, on 17 March 2025. Eleven features shipped inside it.

Brindavan Instruments, Coimbatore. 14,200 diagnostic devices across 2,900 clinics on three firmware generations. The device cloud was strangled in three waves without incident; the firmware could not be. The oldest generation, 4,800 units, has no over-the-air channel, so the adapter retires only as those units are replaced: at the FY26 replacement rate of 1,150 a year, 4,800 ÷ 1,150 gives 4.17 years.

Bansi Mobility, Pune — the failure. A fleet-management platform, replatform approved in February 2024 at 416 engineer-weeks against nine of the company's 21 engineers: 46.2 weeks, targeting a January 2025 cutover. Parity was defined against the old system as it stood that February. Over the next twenty months the other twelve engineers made 214 production changes to it, of which 96 — 44.9 per cent — altered customer-visible behaviour. Absorbing them cost 212 engineer-weeks, a shade over two each, plus 74 of rework; scope grew from 416 to 702, up 68.8 per cent, and the cutover slipped to October 2025.

The recovery, from June 2025, froze the old platform to security fixes, removed 71 of 243 report templates — 29.2 per cent of them, worth 113 engineer-weeks, taking scope to 589 — and split the cutover: read path 8 November 2025, write path 31 January 2026, twelve months late. The instructive figure is not the slip. Between February 2024 and January 2026 the programme had 104 weeks at nine engineers — 936 engineer-weeks of capacity — and delivered 589 of scope. The missing 347, 37.1 per cent of capacity, shows in no scope figure at all: the absorbed changes and the rework were booked as scope growth, leaving invisible only the capacity that delivered nothing.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Exhibit 4. Six failure modes and their earliest diagnostics.
Failure modeEarliest signDiagnostic questionCost if caught late
Parity trapNo wave ships anything visibleWhat reaches a customer in 90 days?Bansi lost 37.1% of capacity
Parity driftNo change-control policy on itWho may change it?Bansi: scope up 68.8%
Seam underestimatedSeam costed as a percentageWhich rows are written on both sides?Quarters of ₹4.3 lakh a week

Orphaned adapterNo decommission dateWhat must hold before deletion?Brindavan's 4.17-year adapter
Tail retired too eagerlyList drawn from one log windowIs the window longer than the cycle?An unfilable return

Every one of the six earliest signs sits in the plan rather than in the code: not one needs a quarter of running to detect. Front-load the seam estimate and the change-control policy; both are unrecoverable by month nine.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The incrementalist case. Programmes that go dark lose the feedback that would tell them their scope is wrong: Bansi's error stayed invisible for twenty months. The seam premium is then not a cost but the price of observability — wrong only if a seam introduces more defects than darkness hides.

The clean-slate case. Where two systems must agree continuously on a mutable quantity, the adapter is harder than what it adapts: Bistara's reservation seam was costed at 142 engineer-weeks against a 212-engineer-week core, 67.0 per cent of it, and must hold at a peak hour carrying 1,180 orders. A rehearsed cutover has a bounded blast radius; a peak divergence does not. It would be wrong if tooling made divergence detection near-instant.

The encapsulate-and-starve case. Lehman's second law implies the complexity blamed on the old platform reappears in the new unless effort goes on reduction, and most programmes spend it on translation. Wrap, starve, let the core shrink by attrition. It would be wrong if the old platform's cost of change were rising super-linearly — and nobody measures that well enough to know.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with a diagram of the strangler pattern. Someone who has internalised it arrives with three questions instead: which rows are written on both sides, what number lets traffic move, and who may approve a change to the old system. They cost the seam bottom-up before choosing an approach, and date the decommissioning in the plan. They will say a replatform should be one cutover, which orthodoxy makes expensive. And they treat the census as a product decision, because deciding that 50 operations go unbuilt decides the product.

12. The decisions

Exhibit 6. Bimasetu: cost of the two plans.
LineBig bangStrangler
Build cost₹877 lakh₹1,003 lakh
Carry on duplicated infrastructure₹26 lakh₹246 lakh
Total programme cost₹903 lakh₹1,249 lakh

Build is engineer-weeks at ₹0.70 lakh each (₹36.4 lakh a year fully loaded): 1,253 of rebuild in both plans after retiring 78, plus 180 of seam and decommission under the strangler. Carry is duplicated infrastructure at ₹4.3 lakh a week, over 6.0 weeks of shadow running against 57.1 weeks of dual running. Synchronisation engineering sits inside the 180.

Raizada recommended the strangler on this arithmetic. The cost gap is ₹1,249 lakh less ₹903 lakh, or ₹346 lakh. Against it: the 158 days between 14 February and 22 July 2027, at 70 per cent gross margin on the 60 per cent of the ₹288 lakh ARR that arrives either way — each prospect carries a 0.40 chance of being lost by waiting — worth 0.70 × 0.60 × 288 × 158/365 = ₹52.4 lakh; and the fall in expected cutover-failure cost, (0.25 − 0.06) × ₹548 lakh = ₹104.1 lakh, where ₹548 lakh is ₹140 lakh of remediation (200 engineer-weeks × ₹0.70 lakh), ₹240 lakh of turnaround penalties capped at ₹60 lakh on each of four contracts, and ₹168 lakh of gross profit on one lost account's ₹240 lakh of ARR — margined like the benefit side. Retained ARR is worth 0.70 × 0.40 × 288 = ₹80.6 lakh a year, so break-even is (346 − 52.4 − 104.1) ÷ 80.6 = 2.35 years of it, against a 6.8-year median tenure. Halving both failure probabilities moves it only to 3.00 years.

Ranota chose neither pure option. She split the 338 engineer-weeks at the state boundary: 126 of read and append-only surfaces needing 22 of seam, 6.5 per cent of the 338; and 212 of reservation core needing none, because it moves in one cutover. Returns intake counts as append-only only because the restock instruction stays on the old ledger until January — a design decision, not an observation. Her first act, on 6 July, was to narrow Ramoowalia's freeze from all production changes to the reservation path alone, which let waves two and three ship on 21 September and 26 October inside the festive window. The hybrid's build cost is 360 engineer-weeks, ₹252 lakh, against ₹236.6 lakh for a pure big bang and ₹336 lakh for a full strangle: ₹15.4 lakh over the cheapest build before any carry, and four releases in the eighteen and a half weeks a pure big bang ships nothing.

The full strangle was rejected on exposure, not cost. It would have run a reservation dual-write through the festive window: 41.0 per cent of 2.80 lakh orders at a flat ₹14,714, so 1,14,800 orders over 76 days, 1,511 a day, peaking at 7,420 on 19 October 2025, of which 1,180 fell in one hour — ₹173.6 lakh at ₹14,714 each. A failed January cutover is not obviously smaller: at 572 orders a day across the 289 non-festive days, two days of outage is ₹168.3 lakh. But two days is a bound Bistara can rehearse, while a peak divergence is unbounded and arrives when everyone who could diagnose it is running a sale.

Three questions. First: Bistara made returns intake append-only by leaving the restock instruction on the old ledger. What else could be reclassified that way, and when does reshaping state to fit a migration plan become a product decision by accident? Second: Bimasetu's ₹104.1 lakh term rests on probabilities of 0.25 and 0.06; what evidence would move them, and who should set them? Third: when is cutting parity scope, as Bansi did with 71 of 243 report templates, a product decision rather than an estimating failure rebranded?

13. Going deeper

  1. Migrations and rebuilds — the parent discipline; the cutover mechanics assumed here.
  2. Dependency management — a seam is a deliberate dependency.
  3. Working with legacy systems — when the answer is starve, not rebuild.
  4. Strategy vs roadmap vs plan — a replatform is a plan masquerading as strategy.
  5. Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later — makes wave boundaries visible.
  6. The roadmap as communication — funding a quarter with nothing to show.
  7. OKRs and goal setting — stops a replatform measuring itself in effort.
  8. Annual and quarterly planning — where freeze windows and carry budgets are agreed.
  9. Capacity planning — Bansi's 347 missing engineer-weeks.
exp40v2-plan.hw.calendar:
Hardware and retail calendars

1. Two desks, one week in March

On Monday 2 March 2026, Mingzhou Precision in Dongguan reopened after a sixteen-day Spring Festival closure running from Saturday 14 February to Sunday 1 March. Yahvi Golwala, vice-president of product at Mewar Acoustics in Pune, had counted every one of those sixteen days. A national electronics chain had confirmed her earbud, the Udyat 2, into its audio-bay reset on Monday 7 September 2026: 400 stores, 45 units of opening stock each, a season order of 56,000 units at a net ₹2,450, or ₹13.72 crore. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November 2026, sixty-two days after the reset.

Her acoustics lead wanted three more weeks to swap in a better driver. Yatidev Gorecha, who ran new-product introduction, had done the backward pass: the enclosure design had to reach Mingzhou's tool room on Sunday 5 April, thirty-four days away. It was Mewar's own date, and every other date on the chain had set it.

Two days later, on Wednesday 4 March, Yamir Gadhia, director of product at Modhera Metering Systems in Vadodara, had a version of the same problem with no shelf anywhere in it. A municipal corporation wanted 42,000 ultrasonic water meters — the Nabhik U4 — at ₹4,850 each, ₹20.37 crore. The rate contract had to be signed before the corporation's financial year closed on Tuesday 31 March 2026, and its crews cannot trench in the monsoon, so installation could only run from Thursday 1 October 2026 to Monday 31 May 2027. His engineering head wanted NB-IoT in place of the cellular module, which restarts legal-metrology pattern approval: ninety-six days of laboratory work and thirty of paperwork, 126 days.

Neither manager lacked competence or budget. Both were handed dates by organisations indifferent to their plans. The discipline is sorting which date belongs to whom, then knowing what each costs to buy.

Exhibit 1. The two calendars, drawn to one scale.

Bars are durations; circles and dashed rules are dates. Mewar's chain reads right to left from the 7 September reset; Modhera's left to right from the 31 March signature. The two red closures at 6–21 February 2027 are the same sixteen days at the same Dongguan plant, which supplies both firms.

2. The idea, and who disputes it

A hardware and retail calendar is the set of dates a product plan inherits from other organisations' cycles: factory shutdowns, tooling and component lead times, retailer cut-offs and shelf-reset windows, certification queues and seasonal peaks. The practice treats them as data rather than negotiating positions, and schedules backward.

The arithmetic is not new. Backward scheduling from a due date is the critical path method of James Kelley and Morgan Walker, 1957 to 1959, and the US Navy's PERT of 1958. Exploding a finished-goods date into component order dates is Joseph Orlicky's material requirements planning of 1975; Eliyahu Goldratt's critical chain of 1997 added the claim that safety belongs in one shared buffer, not inside each step. The retail half descends from category management and the planogram reset of the early 1990s.

Three schools disagree about what to do with the dates. The hard-anchor school holds a counterparty's date fixed and scope variable; it will sign "a date owned by an organisation whose bonus does not depend on your launch is not negotiable on terms you will like," and will not sign "anchors never move." The purchased-date school holds that every anchor has a price — air freight, a second mould, an off-reset bay insertion — and that the job is to price the options, not obey the dates; it will sign "a calendar constraint is a budget line," and will not sign "the cheapest plan is the one that hits the date." The cadence school declines both, publishing a fixed annual rhythm aligned to the resets and varying content; it will sign "the calendar should shape the architecture, not one launch plan," and will not sign "a rare opportunity justifies breaking the train."

Exhibit 2. The eleven items on Yahvi's chart, classified
#ItemDate or durationClass
1Chain's audio-bay resetMon 7 Sep 2026A
2Chain's DC receiving cut-offFri 14 Aug 2026A
3Mingzhou's Spring Festival closureSat 6 – Sun 21 Feb 2027A
4Carrier peak-season surcharge15 Aug – 15 Oct, yearlyA
5Mould, samples, pilot84 daysB
6Production, 56,000 units14 daysB
7Ocean, port, inland to DC33 daysB
8DiwaliSun 8 Nov 2026C
9Mewar's financial-year closeTue 31 Mar 2026C
10Enclosure design freezeSun 5 Apr 2026D
11Photography and asset lockMewar's choiceD

Class A: a date set by another organisation's recurring cycle, which it will not move for one supplier. Class B: a duration, not a date; it moves only if speed is bought. Class C: fixed by neither Mewar nor a counterparty — by the lunar calendar or by statute. Class D: Mewar's own, movable within its float. A = 4 (rows 1–4), B = 3 (rows 5–7), C = 2 (rows 8–9), D = 2 (rows 10–11); 4 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 11. Row 2 follows from row 1 by the chain's 24-day rule, so the eleven are items that bind the plan, not independent causes. Row 3 binds next season; row 4 opens the day after the 14 August arrival.

Two of the eleven are Mewar's. Three more are durations money can shorten. The remaining six she cannot move, though a bay insertion can sidestep the reset for a price, so arguing about the dates themselves is wasted breath. The same test on Yamir's chart puts the monsoon and the fiscal close in class C, the Spring Festival closure in class A.

3. Mechanics: the backward pass, and the buffer

Expert practice starts by converting the retailer's stated date into the date it means. The chain says 7 September; its contract says stock must be received and put away in both distribution centres twenty-four days earlier, Friday 14 August 2026 — and 15 August is Independence Day, so there is no working Saturday behind it. Each duration is then subtracted in turn.

Exhibit 3. The backward pass for the Udyat 2, in elapsed days
StepDaysFinishStart = finish − days
Retailer: DC receipt to shelf24Mon 7 Sep 2026Fri 14 Aug 2026
Ocean, port, inland33Fri 14 Aug 2026Sun 12 Jul 2026
Production, 56,000 units14Sun 12 Jul 2026Sun 28 Jun 2026
Mould, two sample rounds, pilot84Sun 28 Jun 2026Sun 5 Apr 2026
Total155Mon 7 Sep 2026Sun 5 Apr 2026

Durations are elapsed calendar days; work occupies the days after the start date. The 84 days are 42 mould, 16 for each of two sample rounds, 10 pilot. The fourteen production days hold twelve working days on a six-day week, so the line runs 56,000 ÷ 12 = 4,667 a day. Three of the four starts land on a Sunday, so the working dates are Friday 3 April, Saturday 27 June and Saturday 11 July: Mingzhou runs a six-day week, Mewar's release desk in Pune does not.

Three steps are usually left implicit. The first is what a quoted lead time starts and ends on: Mingzhou's fourteen production days begin when the last kit line arrives, not when the order is signed. The second is whose calendar a duration is counted in — a tool room treats its closed days as zero and resumes, an ocean carrier charges for every one. The third is the retailer's definition of receipt, which here means put away and scannable, not delivered to the gate.

The formal treatment is buffer aggregation. Yatidev held five estimates, each with a mean and a ninetieth percentile: mould 42 and 52, samples 32 and 40, pilot 10 and 14, production 14 and 17, logistics 33 and 45. The means sum to 131 days, exactly the freeze-to-DC span in Exhibit 3 (84 + 14 + 33); the ninetieth percentiles sum to 168. Padding every step therefore costs 37 days of safety (168 − 131). Pooling it as the square root of the sum of squared safeties — 10² + 8² + 4² + 3² + 12² = 333, √333 = 18.2, taken as 18 — costs 18 days, saving 19 (168 − 149).

The second-order effect is where the expertise sits. The padded start would be 5 April minus 37 days, Friday 27 February 2026 — inside Mingzhou's closure. The mould clock could not start before Monday 2 March, so three of those 37 padded days bought nothing. The pooled buffer puts the freeze at Wednesday 18 March 2026, 149 days before the 14 August cut-off.

4. When the method applies, and when it misleads

The approach is not universal, and its conditions can be written as claims that a manager can test in an afternoon.

Exhibit 4. Four testable conditions, applied to both firms
ClaimMewar AcousticsModhera Metering
1. The anchor recurs on a published cycleYes: 7 Sep 2026 and 18 Jan 2027, 133 days apartYes: the fiscal close, every 31 March
2. Missing it costs more than the float it buysYes: 133 days with no shelfPartly: a year lost, but the order survives
3. Demand is time-indexedYes: Diwali, Sun 8 Nov 2026No: budget- and trench-weather-indexed
4. Irreversible spend commits before the demand signalYes: a ₹38 lakh mould, 155 days before the shelfYes: 126 days of approval before the window

A firm answering yes to 1 and 4 must plan backward whether it wants to or not. One answering no to 3 can often buy its way out of a missed date; Modhera can, Mewar largely cannot.

Where the method actively misleads is the soft anchor. A marketplace listing has no reset; a server-side flag has no mould. A backward pass against a date nobody imposes converts a soft commitment into a hard one and destroys the option value that was the advantage of having no factory. Yamir's team met the mirror image: its software train had planned backward from the 31 March signature for three years, accepting a nine-month freeze on the meter's configuration tool that no counterparty asked for.

5. Edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product portfolios are where the calendar stops being arithmetic. One tool room and one line serve several programmes, so a slipped Udyat 2 freeze consumes the next programme's float. Two-sided businesses inherit the calendar of whichever side carries inventory: a marketplace selling appliances inherits its sellers' Spring Festival, not its own sprint cadence. Regulated goods add a queue nobody owns — Modhera's 126 days are mostly waiting, and waiting cannot be compressed by adding people.

Hardware-plus-software cases produce the subtlest failure. Firmware can ship after the box, so teams treat software as free float — until the retailer's returns policy makes a broken first run a chargeback, and the float turns out to have been collateral. AI-native features are worse: behaviour is tuned on data that only exists after launch, so a calendar promising a tuned model at reset promises what the plan cannot produce.

At the seams, the honest description is this: sourcing holds the factory dates, key accounts the retailer dates, finance the fiscal dates, and nobody holds the joins. Yojanika Gandecha, who ran Mewar's national accounts, knew the 14 August cut-off cold and had never seen the 84-day tooling figure. What such firms do is less elegant than their process documents: one calendar of record, an owner per anchor, and a weekly meeting where each owner says whether the date moved.

Exhibit 5. Four functions hold the dates; the dashed boxes are the unowned joins.

6. Nine distinctions that separate the expert

A stated date is three dates. The chain's 7 September reset is also a 14 August receiving cut-off and a 12 July sailing. The tell is a plan that names a month rather than a document clause. The obvious reading — that the buyer told you the date — is wrong: it told you its own date.

Lead time steps; it does not slope. Modhera's microcontroller takes twenty-two days, so an order on Friday 15 January 2027 ships on 6 February, the first day of the closure. One day later and the clock pauses through the closure: it ships on 23 February, seventeen days worse. The tell is a supplier answering lead-time questions with a number instead of a date.

Buffers die in closed windows. Float placed immediately before a shutdown cannot be spent. An expert looks at where the slack sits, not how much there is.

Weekday and holiday checks are not clerical. Three of Yahvi's four computed starts fell on Sundays, and the 2025 cut-off on Independence Day. The tell is a Gantt chart with no weekday names on it.

Sell-in is not sell-through. Shipping 56,000 units into the channel books the revenue and transfers the forecasting error, not the risk. The expert asks what happens to units that do not move before 31 December.

The retailer's date has a cost structure. A full reset costs the chain about ₹7,600 a store in labour, ₹30.4 lakh across 400 stores, twice a year. It will not repeat that for one supplier, but it will sell a single-bay insertion at ₹1,250 a store. The date is priced, not immovable.

Two purchased dates are rarely substitutes. An insertion fee of ₹5.0 lakh moves the retailer's date; air freight of ₹54.0 lakh moves the factory's. The insertion costs under a tenth of the air freight and solves a different problem; buying the wrong one leaves the shelf set and empty.

Capacity is a date. Modhera's installation window holds 243 calendar days, of which 35 are Sundays, leaving 208 working days before public holidays. At fourteen crews fitting twelve meters each, 168 a day, it absorbs 34,944 meters — 7,056 short of 42,000, or 16.8 per cent of the order. It needs seventeen crews: 42,000 ÷ 2,496 meters a crew (12 × 208) = 16.8, rounded up. The tell is a delivery schedule with no installation rate in it.

Peaks drift; shelves do not. A lunisolar festival such as Diwali moves about eleven days earlier each year, then jumps forward when a leap month intervenes, while the chain's resets stay in the same retail week. An expert tracks the gap, not either date alone.

Exhibit 6. Three prices for a date, and the one nobody chose.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

The difference across types is real but narrower than usually drawn. Consumer hardware through physical retail has the hardest dates, because factory and chain each impose one and the two are 155 days apart. Enterprise hardware swaps the retailer for a procurement cycle and a certification queue: fewer dates, each longer. Pure B2B software has almost no imposed dates and invents them, which is why its planning literature translates badly to hardware. Platforms inherit whichever side holds stock. Physical goods outside electronics look like Mewar, except that the mould becomes a print run, so the commitment is cheaper and later.

AI products differ only in the direction of the dependency. Nothing imposes a date on them, but they impose one on themselves whenever an evaluation set must be built from production traffic. The temptation is to treat a model refresh as a release train with a reset day; there is no shelf to miss.

Stage changes less than founders expect and more than incumbents admit. A seed-stage firm has a worse calendar than a large one: it buys minimum quantities at the back of a factory's queue and has no leverage over a reset. Growth-stage firms gain the leverage to buy dates and buy them badly, one crisis at a time. At scale the calendar inverts, the firm becoming a counterparty others plan backward from, and the discipline becomes publishing its dates early enough to be believed.

Exhibit 7. Which counterparty owns the hardest date, by product type.

8. Three worked cases

Mewar, 2026: buying the factory's date. Yahvi's three options were costed against the same 56,000 units. Hold the reset with the current enclosure: 56,000 × ₹2,450 = ₹13.72 crore. Take the new driver, miss the reset and sell online until 18 January 2027: 19,600 units, 35 per cent of 56,000, at a net ₹2,500, or ₹4.90 crore, the balance waiting for the January reset. Take the new driver and hold the reset by air-freighting the 18,000-unit opening stock (400 stores × 45) at ₹300 a unit, a premium of ₹54.0 lakh, the balance following by sea as the restock: ₹13.72 crore − ₹0.54 crore = ₹13.18 crore. The third beats the second by ₹8.28 crore and costs ₹54.0 lakh against the first. Break-even is ₹54,00,000 ÷ the ₹930 contribution a unit (₹2,450 net less ₹1,520 cost) = 5,806.5, so 5,807 units, 10.37 per cent of 56,000.

Modhera, 2026: the capacity that was not there. Yamir's contribution was not a date. The corporation had written 42,000 meters into a window its own crews could not install, and the shortfall of 7,056 was found before signature rather than in April 2027. The contract was split: 24,000 meters by 1 October 2026 and 18,000 by 1 February 2027, with three crews added.

Mewar, 2025: the failure. The previous season's reset was Monday 8 September 2025, so the receiving cut-off was Friday 15 August — Independence Day, with the centres shut, making the true cut-off Thursday 14 August. Mewar's planners had scheduled to the 15th. The consignment reached the DC on Tuesday 19 August, five days late; of the 48,000-unit order, 25,000 had shipped earlier and made the reset, and 23,000 did not. Those sat with a third-party warehouse from 19 August 2025 to the next reset on Monday 12 January 2026, 146 days. Recovery cost ₹93.58 lakh: a ₹340 markdown on 23,000 units cleared online, ₹78.2 lakh, plus working capital on ₹3.496 crore of goods at cost (23,000 × ₹1,520) for 146 days at 11 per cent, ₹15.38 lakh. What failed was not logistics: one class-A date had a holiday behind it and no owner in front of it.

Exhibit 8. The three options, drawn on one revenue scale.

9. Failure modes and their early signs

Planning to the stated date. The sign is a milestone named after a retailer's marketing event. Diagnostic: which clause defines receipt? Caught late it costs a season — ₹93.58 lakh in 2025.

Negotiating a duration as if it were a date. The sign is a lead time that shortened without anything being bought. Diagnostic: what did we pay, and who agreed? Caught late it surfaces as a missing kit line in production week.

Padding each step. The sign is every estimate ending in a round number. Diagnostic: what is the ninetieth percentile, and what is the mean? Caught late it costs 19 days of float the firm paid for and never held.

Ignoring the second counterparty. The sign is a factory calendar with no retailer dates on it, or the reverse. Diagnostic: name both anchors and the span between them, for Mewar 155 days.

Treating capacity as unlimited. The sign is a delivery schedule stated in units with no rate. Diagnostic: units over working days, against crews times rate. Caught late it becomes 7,056 meters in a yard.

Confusing sell-in with sell-through. The sign is a season declared successful on dispatch. Diagnostic: what were the channel's weeks of cover on 31 December? Caught late it returns as a markdown claim.

10. Where the experts genuinely disagree

The sharpest disagreement is whether hitting the reset at full volume is worth its cost. Yashvardhini Gudhka, who had bought audio for a national chain before turning consultant, put the hard-anchor case at its strongest: shelf absence is not a delay but a competitor's win, and a bay lost at one reset is usually lost at the next, because the chain's space model follows last season's rate of sale. Her evidence is that rule. For her to be wrong, bay space would have to be re-contested from scratch each cycle.

The purchased-date reply is arithmetic. If the plan assumes 39,200 of the 56,000 units — 70 per cent — sell through by 31 December, then 16,800 remain in the channel, and at the ₹340 markdown Mewar conceded in 2025 that exposure is ₹57.12 lakh. That is more than the ₹54.0 lakh of air freight spent to hit the date at all, so the two decisions are the same size and belong together rather than in sequence. For this position to be wrong, the markdown would have to be the retailer's cost, not the vendor's — which depends on the contract.

The cadence school says both arguments are symptoms. Yatidev's version: a firm shipping twice a year on someone else's dates should design for two freeze dates and stop arguing about each. Its evidence is the 19 days of float aggregation recovers on paper; its weakness is that cadence assumes a product family stable enough for a shared enclosure. Nobody here claims the three reconcile; they describe three different firms.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this builds a Gantt chart. Someone who has internalised it builds two lists: the dates that are not theirs, with an owner and a source document against each, and the durations that can be bought, with a price. They print weekday names. They ask where the float sits before asking how much there is, knowing three of Mewar's 37 padded days fell inside a closed factory. And they state a figure's base first: 208 working days, not 243 calendar days; 34,944 meters, not a confident 42,000.

Exhibit 9. The same safety, scattered and pooled: 19 days of difference.

12. What they decided

Yahvi took the third option, buying the factory's date rather than the retailer's: the new driver, and ₹54.0 lakh of air freight reserved against the opening stock. Her reasoning was that ₹54.0 lakh bought both the driver and the reset, against the ₹8.28 crore gap between options three and two. Yamir signed on Tuesday 31 March 2026 with the tranches split and three crews added, deferring NB-IoT a cycle: the 184 days from signature to 1 October, less 126 of approval, left 58 to build and deliver 24,000 meters.

For discussion. First: Yahvi spent ₹54.0 lakh to hold a date while carrying a ₹57.12 lakh markdown exposure on the same units — should the two have been one decision, and whose? Second: Modhera's shortfall of 7,056 meters was the customer's capacity problem, not Modhera's; on what grounds does a product manager raise it before signature? Third: which of the eleven items in Exhibit 2 would move if Mewar were five times its size, and which would not?

13. Going deeper

When dates matter: launches, seasons, contracts is the parent idea; it separates dates that create value from dates that merely exist. Strategy vs roadmap vs plan matters because the calendar belongs to the plan, and importing it into strategy leaves a tooling schedule where a thesis should be. Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later unlocks how to express a hard date in a vague format. The roadmap as communication is where the calendar of record lives. OKRs and goal setting matters because a quarterly objective cannot be met inside a 155-day chain. Annual and quarterly planning reconciles resets with fiscal closes. Capacity planning is the sibling: Modhera's 208 working days at 168 meters a day are a capacity model.

Exhibit 10. What this topic builds on, and what it feeds.
exp20v2-plan.hw.calendar:
Hardware and retail calendars

1. A calendar Vinit could not edit

On Thursday 8 January 2026, Vinit Eranee, head of product at Lumenair, a Bengaluru maker of home air purifiers, opened an email from the Dongguan factory that builds the company's devices. The factory would close for Spring Festival from Saturday 14 February to Monday 2 March, seventeen days, and reopen on Tuesday 3 March. The same morning Lumenair's hardware lead asked to keep the design of the Aero 2 housing open until Tuesday 31 March, to fit a better dust sensor.

Vinit had three facts to weigh. A national electronics chain had agreed to stock the Aero 2 at its Monday 14 September shelf reset, the single day it redraws its air-treatment shelves, and would accept stock only into its distribution centres, at least fourteen days earlier. The order was 36,000 units at a net ₹9,800 each, or ₹35.28 crore. And Lumenair's plan assumed that 70 per cent of those 36,000 units, 25,200, would sell between the reset and 31 December, as northern India's smog season built towards Diwali on Sunday 8 November. That sell-through, valued at the same net price, came to ₹24.70 crore (24.696 exactly). The chain's next reset was Monday 11 January 2027.

The sensor would make a better product. The question was whether it made a better product on a calendar that Vinit could not edit, and which of the dates in front of him were his.

2. The idea

A hardware and retail calendar is the list of dates that other organisations' schedules impose on a product plan: factory closures, component and shipping lead times, retailer delivery and shelf-reset windows, and seasonal demand peaks. It exists because a product team sets dates by asking when the work will be done, while a factory or retailer sets them by asking when its own cycle turns. The two answers rarely agree, so the calendar treats the second kind as fixed anchors and schedules backward from them.

The arithmetic is older than the practice. Backward scheduling from a due date rests on the critical path method, devised by James Kelley and Morgan Walker between 1957 and 1959, and on the US Navy's PERT technique of 1958. The calendars themselves have no single inventor; they accreted as buyers standardised receiving rules and factories settled into the Spring Festival shutdown. Vinit's sentence for the meeting was plain: every date on our plan is either someone else's calendar or inherited from one, and our first job is to sort which.

Exhibit 1. The four calendars on Vinit's desk
Whose calendarDate in 2026Can Lumenair move it?
FactoryClosed Sat 14 Feb to Mon 2 MarNo
RetailerStock in centres Mon 31 Aug; reset Mon 14 SepNo
DemandDiwali Sun 8 Nov; smog from OctoberNo, and it drifts
LumenairDesign freezeYes, within the float

3. How it actually works

The method has five steps. First, collect every counterparty's date in writing, because the factory's notice and the buyer's receiving rule are the dates that bind hardest. Second, convert each duration into the unit its owner uses: a mould shop counts calendar days through its own closure as zero, an ocean carrier counts them as full. Third, start at the immovable anchor, here the 14 September reset, and subtract each step in turn to find its latest start. Fourth, lay the result on a real calendar, with weekdays and holidays printed, so that collisions show. Fifth, find the chain with the least slack and name an owner for it.

Practitioners usually leave two steps implicit. They ask what a quoted lead time starts and ends on, and they separate the date a buyer says from the date the buyer means. The chain's buyer said "14 September", but the binding date for Lumenair was 31 August, when stock had to sit in the centres.

Exhibit 2. The plan on a real calendar. Scale: 2 pixels per day from 1 January 2026; ticks mark month starts. The dashed outline is float.

Read from the right, the figure shows why the hardware lead's request was not an argument about a sensor. The retailer's two dates fix a block of shipping that cannot compress. Production sits before it, the pilot before that, and the two long-lead items, the mould and the fan motors, feed the pilot. The dashed stretch after the mould is the only visible slack.

4. A worked example

Exhibit 3 subtracts backward from the reset. Each row's latest start is its finish minus its duration; Lumenair's stated durations are the ocean 22 days, clearance and trucking 12, factory to quay 4 and inspection 6. Production runs 36,000 units at 1,200 a day, which is 30 production days, and the factory works six-day weeks, so 15 June to 18 July. The mould needs 45 days to a first sample and two 14-day correction loops, 73 days in all. The fan motors take 63.

Exhibit 3. Backward schedule from Monday 14 September 2026
StepDaysMust finishLatest start
Stock in centres14 before resetMon 31 Augn/a
Berth to centres12Mon 31 AugWed 19 Aug
Ocean sailing22Wed 19 AugTue 28 Jul
Factory to quay4Tue 28 JulFri 24 Jul
Inspection, packing6Fri 24 JulSat 18 Jul
Production30 workingSat 18 JulMon 15 Jun

Each step is dated by subtracting its duration from its finish date, so a step begins the day its predecessor ends, except that the pilot's 14 days include idle Sunday 14 June.

The result surprised Lumenair's engineers. The mould shop is shut until 3 March, so a design frozen anywhere from now to Tuesday 3 March starts the mould that day, and 3 March plus 73 days is Friday 15 May: seventeen days before the 1 June pilot, which equals the gap between 3 March and the latest start of 20 March. Freezing on Friday 27 February, fifty days after the email, costs nothing; Friday 20 March is the break-even, and 27 February simply leaves all seventeen days intact. The fan motors, which no one was discussing, have no float at all: ordering on 30 March delivers on 1 June exactly.

Exhibit 4. Second pass: one input changed
FreezeMould startsMould readyFloat to 1 Jun
Fri 27 FebTue 3 MarFri 15 May+17 days
Tue 31 MarTue 31 MarFri 12 Jun-11 days

Now change one input: hold the design open to 31 March, as engineering asked. The mould is ready on 12 June, eleven days after the pilot needs it. Inspection can shrink from six days to one, absorbing five, so about six days reach the chain: stock lands around Sunday 6 September, effectively Monday 7 September, seven days before the reset against the fourteen required. Seventeen days of float became a breach of a retailer rule by changing a date Lumenair owned.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Hard, soft and derived dates

The reset is hard: the chain sets it. 31 August is hard too, because the chain's 14-day receiving rule is hard. The 15 June production start is derived from Lumenair's own rate and inspection, which can move. The 31 March freeze was a soft request, and it breached a hard rule. People blur the three, and defend derived dates as though they were hard.

Calendar days against working days

A quoted "63 days" may mean calendar or working days, and a supplier's own closure counts differently from a shipping line's. The same label, applied wrongly, moves a date by weeks, so ask which one is meant.

Moving holidays, fixed resets

Spring Festival follows the lunar calendar: Chinese New Year fell on 17 February 2026 and falls on 6 February in 2027. Diwali drifts too, nearly three weeks later in the calendar year in 2026 than in 2025 (20 October that year). A retailer's reset is fixed by its own planning cycle. Each year the gap between them changes, so last year's schedule is evidence, not a template.

The closure is longer than the holiday

Seventeen days is the shutdown; the effect can run longer, because workers return gradually and suppliers restart in sequence. Ask the factory how long last year's restart took before relying on 3 March.

Float belongs to someone

Seventeen days of float is a shared asset and vanishes through small, unrecorded uses. Without a named owner, the slack is consumed first by whoever asks first, and the team learns of it when it is gone.

What the calendar cannot tell you

It gives latest dates, not likelihood. It does not say whether the buyer will list the product, whether the pilot will pass, or how many units will sell. It is also not a roadmap: a roadmap orders outcomes; a calendar tells you which dates the roadmap may not touch.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Ask who wrote each date and when, whether it survives a holiday in the counterparty's country, and what the counterparty does if you miss it. A buyer who will simply take the next reset is a different risk from one who will delist.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

Exhibit 5. Where the immovable dates come from
ModelImposed dateTypical trap
Consumer hardwareRetailer reset and receiving ruleCounting from the promotion date
B2BCustomer's budget year (India: ends 31 March) and installation windowOrder lands after the budget closes
MarketplacePlatform's sale dates and inbound slotsStock arrives after listings freeze

Each row changes the question rather than the method: a consumer team asks when stock must be in the retailer's centres, a B2B team asks when the customer's money stops being available, and a marketplace team asks when the platform stops accepting inventory. In an early-stage company the dates come from small orders and minimum quantities, and a missed slot is often repaired by air freight. A large company holds negotiated line slots, which makes its dates firmer for the factory and harder to repair.

7. Common mistakes

Scheduling forward from the launch idea. The symptom is a plan that says "September" but names no ship-by date. The misunderstanding is that launch is a date rather than the end of a chain. The cheapest diagnostic is to write the chain backward from the shelf to today on one page.

Trusting a lead time without its definition. The symptom is a supplier's promise that lands inside a closure. The misunderstanding is treating "45 days" as a universal unit. Ask what starts and stops it, and print the closure dates on the same page.

Spending float silently. The symptom is a plan green at every review that is red the week before delivery. The misunderstanding is that slack is free. Keep a float ledger with one owner.

Confusing promotion with shelf. The symptom is stock arriving on the day the buyer's advertisement runs. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask the buyer which day stock must be in the centres.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Vinit's decision starts with a one-page chain, written from the reset, that every function can read. The immovable dates are marked as such, with their source. Each step has a latest start, a weekday and a named owner, and the float is shown as a number beside the step that holds it, not as a hope. Engineering receives a firm freeze date and the reason for it. The buyer hears about risk before the risk occurs. For Lumenair, good meant a freeze on 27 February, a motor order well ahead of 30 March, and the 17 days of mould float still intact on the day of the pilot.

9. Closing

Vinit allowed the sensor revision and froze the design on Friday 27 February, releasing the mould order that day. He asked Virat Eruchshaw, the supply chain head, to place the fan motor order on Tuesday 3 March rather than 30 March, buying 27 days of float on the item with none. His reasoning was that engineering's freeze was the one date he could spend without breaching a counterparty's rule, and that it should be spent only if the sensor needed it; freezing on 27 February kept all seventeen days of mould float. Learn next how a roadmap turns dependencies and risks into outcome milestones, because the calendar tells you which dates are fixed but not which outcomes deserve them.

Two questions to sit with. Which date in a plan you know is derived, but being defended as though the counterparty had set it? And who today owns the float on your longest chain?
exp40v2-plan.scenario:
Delivery & Technology › Roadmapping, Planning & OKRs

Scenario planning

Plan for more than one future; know your triggers. What is my plan if the future looks different, and what would trigger it?

1. Two planning rooms, eleven days apart

The case opens on Monday 9 November 2026, in Pune, where Lovleen Trehan was being asked for a number. Trehan is chief product officer of Dakhini Freight Cloud, a transport-management platform used by 1,180 mid-market road-freight fleets; FY26 revenue was ₹96 crore. The FY28 plan is due on Friday 4 December, and the item in dispute is Dakhini Settle, an embedded freight-payments module releasing a carrier's money against a verified delivery event. Built in full it costs ₹31 crore and 34 engineers for three quarters, and the chief financial officer, Laveesh Thakral, wanted one revenue line for it. Settle is worth a great deal if a regime linking freight invoices to e-invoice references arrives in FY28 and, in the slowest future, ₹14 crore less than nothing; nobody could say which.

Eleven days later, on Friday 20 November, Latangi Thaper faced a harder version in Ahmedabad. Thaper co-founded Dharti Instruments, which sells soil-moisture and canal-flow sensors to farmer producer organisations with a subscription analytics layer. By Monday 30 November she must order next year's long-lead radio module, non-cancellably. FY28 demand could be 18,000 units, 42,000 or 76,000; Dharti holds ₹14 crore of cash. A software decision unwinds in a sprint, a purchase order does not.

Both were being asked to collapse a distribution into a point. The right objects are not the point estimate but a small set of futures and the triggers that distinguish them, and the discipline is the arithmetic of what knowing them is worth.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree

Scenario planning is the construction of a small set of internally consistent, causally explicit accounts of how a decision's external environment could develop, chosen to span the uncertainties capable of changing it, and used to design commitments and triggers rather than to predict. Internally consistent rules out a future built from contradictory assumptions; causally explicit rules out a mood such as "pessimistic case"; the third rules out building scenarios around the drivers most discussed rather than the decisive ones.

The parentage is military: Herman Kahn, at RAND in the 1950s, borrowed the word from film for disciplined narratives about nuclear exchange. It became management practice at Royal Dutch Shell, where Pierre Wack and Ted Newland spent the early 1970s building futures in which the oil price was not set by Shell's customers. Wack's claim was not that Shell forecast the 1973 shock but that scenarios work only when they change the manager's microcosm, the map against which new facts are judged.

Ron Bradfield and colleagues' taxonomy names intuitive logics, La Prospective and probabilistic modified trends; robust decision making grew up beside them later. Each signs a different proposition. Intuitive logics — Wack, then Peter Schwartz and the Global Business Network, Kees van der Heijden, and Rafael Ramírez and Angela Wilkinson at Oxford — signs that scenarios are instruments for reframing judgement, and refuses probabilities on them: a number on a narrative invites a reader to back the big one. La Prospective, built by Michel Godet, signs the opposite — combinations enumerated morphologically, screened by cross-impact matrices, given elicited and consistent probabilities, as the probabilistic-modified-trends line of Delphi and cross-impact work also does — and refuses that the value lies in the conversation. Robust decision making at RAND — Robert Lempert, Steven Popper, Steve Bankes, Warren Walker — signs that a strategy should be stress-tested across thousands of generated futures to find where it fails, and refuses that four narratives span the space. Underneath sits the decision-analytic tradition of Howard Raiffa and Ronald Howard, which supplies the quantitative apparatus the other three borrow: probabilities, payoffs, expected values, the value of information. Outside stands Philip Tetlock's forecasting programme, whose objection is unanswered — calibrated forecasters beat narrative on accuracy, and scenario work rarely states anything scorable.

3. Mechanics, and the steps left implicit

Expert practice runs backwards from the decision: write down the decision, its deadline and — the step most often skipped — its lead time, how long between committing and having the thing. Only then nominate drivers, and the test is leverage: does this driver, by itself, change which option you pick?

Dakhini nominated two: whether the invoice-linkage mandate arrives inside FY28 ("early") or slips ("late"), and whether consolidation among sub-50-truck fleets runs fast or slow. Lehna Tarar, Trehan's planning lead, then took the step that separates an analysis from a workshop — she built the joint distribution rather than the two marginals, forcing a probability for each combination.

The options were Commit — the whole module now at ₹31 crore — or Stage: the ledger core alone at ₹11 crore, the rail held behind a trigger at ₹24 crore. Staging costs ₹35 crore if triggered, ₹4 crore more, and lands two quarters later: that is what optionality costs.

Exhibit 1. Dakhini payoffs, ₹ crore, three-year NPV net of build spend.
ScenarioPCommitP × CommitStageP × Stage
S1 Forced March0.186211.16447.92
