Probability-weighted standard deviations: ₹28.74 crore Commit, ₹17.53 crore Stage. Commit's ₹31 crore is ₹12.24 crore of engineering (34 engineers × 3 quarters × ₹12 lakh), ₹8.60 crore of licensing and audit, ₹10.16 crore of integration.

The arithmetic now says what the usual presentation hides. The expected values differ by ₹0.72 crore, which is 0.025 of Commit's own standard deviation of ₹28.74 crore. That is not a finding; anyone saying "the numbers favour building it" has read noise, because the gap sits well inside finance's ±15 per cent band on the cells. The spreads are not tied — Commit's worst cell loses ₹14 crore where Stage's loses ₹3 crore — and that asymmetry decides.

The second-order step, almost always omitted, is to price the information. Knowing both axes, Dakhini would take Commit in S1 and S2 and Stage in S3 and S4, for ₹23.07 crore; against the unconditional ₹18.12 crore, perfect foresight is worth ₹4.95 crore, a ceiling no signpost beats.

Exhibit 2. What resolving each axis is worth, by conditioning and re-optimising within each branch of Exhibit 1.

Mandate branch: given early (P = 0.45) the conditional weights are 0.40 and 0.60, so Commit gives 0.40 × 62 + 0.60 × 38 = 47.60 against Stage's 35.00; given late (P = 0.55), Stage gives 0.40 × 12 + 0.60 × (−3) = 3.00 against Commit's −6.00; and 0.45 × 47.60 + 0.55 × 3.00 = 23.07. Consolidation branch: fast (P = 0.40) favours Commit at 31.20, slow (P = 0.60) Stage at 11.40, so 0.40 × 31.20 + 0.60 × 11.40 = 19.32.

Two results fall out, both invisible without the computation. The consolidation axis is worth ₹1.20 crore standing alone — it does flip the choice — and nothing once the mandate is known, because inside each mandate branch the preferred option is the same in both consolidation states. Information values do not add: ₹1.20 crore plus ₹4.95 crore is ₹4.95 crore. And Dakhini's monitoring programme cost ₹1.20 crore a year to watch consolidation. Three years of it, ₹3.60 crore, is three times the one-off ceiling that axis could be worth over the same horizon, and that ceiling assumes perfect resolution. It was aimed at the wrong axis.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

One: the decision's lead time exceeds the notice the environment will give you. Dakhini's rail, the back half of the nine-month module, needs seven months — six of engineering, one of certification — while the policy desk's log of comparable compliance phases shows notice periods of four, five and seven months between notification and effect, with draft rules circulating three months ahead of notification in all three. On the shortest, deciding at notification lands three months late. Dharti's order locks ten weeks before its order book closes.

Two: at least one uncertainty flips the ranking of options rather than scaling the prize. The mandate axis flips Dakhini's ranking; conditional on it, consolidation does not. Dharti's single axis changes its order quantity in every state, not just its payoff.

Three: an intermediate commitment exists that costs much less and keeps most of the upside. Dakhini's ₹11 crore ledger core qualifies, as does Dharti's supplier option. Where none exists, scenario work can only time a binary, and the honest answer is to buy better information.

Four: payoff spread is large relative to the error in the estimates. Dakhini's cells run from −14 to +62, far wider than finance's own ±15 per cent view of them. Had they run from 16 to 20, the exercise would have measured noise.

The method misleads where the uncertainty is cheaply resolvable, so narrative substitutes for an experiment; where the decision is reversible inside the notice period; and where a forecast is owed to a regulator or investor, so plurality becomes a way of never being wrong, and so of never being accountable.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In a multi-product company the decisive drivers differ by product, so a single corporate 2×2 is wrong for everything; mature practice holds one shared set of external drivers and lets each product own its axes beneath them. Two-sided businesses add a trap: the sides' futures are not independent, so crossing supply growth with demand growth prints cells that cannot exist — "many sellers" with "high buyer scarcity" is one its own network effects forbid.

Regulated products invert the relation between scenario and trigger: the scenario is often known in outline years ahead, because the draft rule is public, and the uncertainty is purely timing — which makes lead-time arithmetic the whole exercise. Hardware adds irreversibility, so Dharti's scenarios are priced against committed cash, not an NPV. AI-native products face a driver no 2×2 handles well, because capability improves discontinuously; make capability an axis with explicit thresholds, not a trend.

The seams are where scenario work dies. Finance owns the base case, product owns the roadmap, and the base case is a budget rather than a scenario — one number per line, with an owner whose bonus depends on it. What mature companies do, rather than what their decks say, is run the scenarios in product and reconcile them to the budget through the trigger, which holds the staged option and releases the rest.

6. Eight things an expert sees

The second axis is often conditionally worthless. The tell is a matrix whose preferred option is constant along one axis, as Dakhini's is. Two axes look like two things to watch; once the mandate is known, watching consolidation buys nothing, and ₹1.20 crore a year was going on it.

Information values are not additive. The tell is a monitoring budget built by summing each driver's value. One axis here is worth ₹4.95 crore and the other ₹1.20 crore; resolving both is worth ₹4.95 crore, not ₹6.15 crore. Whoever adds buys the overlap twice.

Independence is a choice, usually made silently. Dakhini's cells are exactly the products of their margins — 0.45 × 0.40 = 0.18 — so the team assumed independence without saying so. The tell is a joint table reconstructible from its margins. It moved the rankings not at all and the axis values a lot: a correlated table with identical margins (0.24, 0.21, 0.16, 0.39) moves Commit to ₹18.36 crore and leaves Stage at ₹17.40 crore, but it doubles consolidation's value to ₹2.40 crore against the mandate axis's ₹5.25 crore, dropping the ratio between the axes from 4.1 to 2.2. Learnt only by computing both.

The trigger is designed around lead time, not the signal. The tell is a trigger whose named event is the announcement. Dakhini's rail needs seven months against a shortest observed notice of four, so notification is three months too late; the signpost is the draft-rule circulation before it.

Plan off the shortest observed notice, not the median. Dakhini's notice periods were four, five and seven months, median five; a trigger on the median lands a month late in the one phase of three where notice was four. Lead-time assumptions are floors, and floors take minima.

An expected value is rarely an orderable quantity. Dharti's expected demand of 43,300 units occurs in none of its three scenarios and is optimal under none. The tell is a headline figure appearing in no scenario: averaging then optimising is not optimising then averaging.

Dispersion often decides where the mean cannot. The tell is a recommendation resting on an expected-value gap under a tenth of the spread, as Dakhini's ₹0.72 crore does at 0.025. The means are tied; the question is which tail the balance sheet can absorb.

A signpost nobody owns is not a signpost. The tell is a monitoring table whose action column says "review". Pre-commit the action and the money, not the meeting: the release of ₹24 crore. Reviews slip in exactly the quarter the signal fires — and a register that has retired no axis in a year monitors history, not futures.

7. Product type and company stage

In consumer products the decisive drivers sit outside the firm's industry — a platform's ranking policy, a partner's pricing — and nobody will sell you an option on them, so staged commitment must be built internally through modular architecture. In B2B and enterprise the drivers are legible, often contractual and often resolvable by asking twelve customers, so an enterprise team should measure first. Platforms and marketplaces must treat their two sides as correlated rather than independent. Hardware is where irreversibility is physical and therefore honest: Dharti's problem is cleaner because the cash leaves on a known date. AI products differ in one real respect and one imagined — capability thresholds need to be axes, while "the pace of change" is a mood, not a driver.

Stage changes the practice more than product type does. A seed-stage company with two quarters of runway has a lead time shorter than any notice period, so scenario work there is displacement activity; one bet with a kill criterion is honest. The method earns its keep when a company first commits for longer than its forecasting horizon — a platform build, a factory, a licence. At scale the risk inverts: large firms run the ritual and attach no triggers, because triggers bind budget holders who outrank the planners.

8. Three worked examples

Dharti Instruments: buying an option instead of a forecast

Each shipped device earns ₹2,350 of contribution after all variable cost including the module — ₹1,100 on the device, ₹1,250 of first-year subscription. Each module ordered and never shipped is worth ₹95 as scrap against the ₹420 paid, a loss of ₹325. The newsvendor fractile is 2,350 ÷ (2,350 + 325) = 0.879. Demand is 18,000 at 0.30, 42,000 at 0.45 and 76,000 at 0.25, cumulating to 0.30, 0.75 and 1.00, so the smallest quantity reaching 0.879 is 76,000 — the high scenario, not the mean of 43,300 units.

Exhibit 3. Dharti expected profit by policy, ₹ crore. Profit in a state = ₹2,350 × units sold − ₹325 × unsold modules, less any fee.
PolicyIf 18,000If 42,000If 76,000Expected
Order 42,000 (base scenario)3.459.879.877.94
Order 43,300 (expected demand)3.419.8310.187.99
Order 76,000 firm (the fractile)2.358.7717.869.11

Option fee ₹38 per unit on 46,000 units = ₹17.48 lakh, paid whether or not exercised and exercisable at the same ₹420 within ten weeks; the figures assume the order book resolves the scenario before that window closes, which is generous. The Expected column weights the states at 0.30, 0.45 and 0.25 and is computed on unrounded profits, so it can sit ₹0.01 crore away from the rounded state columns.

Thaper could not take that answer. A firm order of 76,000 modules commits ₹3.19 crore of cash and, in the low state, destroys 58,000 × ₹325 = ₹1.89 crore of value out of the ₹14 crore on the balance sheet, 13.5 per cent of it. So she bought flexibility: 30,000 firm plus an option on 46,000 more at ₹38, for ₹17.48 lakh. That raises expected profit from ₹9.11 crore to ₹9.88 crore — ₹0.77 crore net of the fee, or 4.4 times it — and lifts the worst state from ₹2.35 crore to ₹3.67 crore. Sold cheaply, optionality improves both.

Dakhini Freight Cloud: the arithmetic that chose the trigger

Tarar then wrote a signpost definition and used it as a test, not a label: a signpost is an observable a named owner reads on a stated cadence, which moves before the decision's lead time runs out, and to which a pre-committed action and its money are attached. Three candidates passed every clause; one failed.

Exhibit 4. Dakhini's signpost register; every accepted row satisfies every clause, named owner and money included, and the three earmarks sum to the ₹24 crore held.

Dhaaru Exchange: a trigger that could not fire

Dhaaru Exchange, a marketplace for industrial surplus, ran a competent exercise in 2024 and attached a trigger to the cell that would force a pivot: listings per active seller per month below 3.0 for two consecutive months. In January 2025 it carried 2,480 listings from 720 active sellers, a ratio of 3.44. By June, listings had fallen to 1,538 and sellers to 452 — a 38.0 per cent collapse in listings — yet the ratio stood at 3.40, down 1.2 per cent. The trigger never fired: its denominator fell almost as fast as its numerator.

The recovery, once the board forced it in August, was to re-cut the trigger onto a fixed cohort: listings from the 720 sellers active in January, threshold a 25 per cent fall on a single month's reading. That series read 2,480 in January and 1,612 in March, a fall of 35.0 per cent, so it would have fired in March, five months earlier. At ₹1.9 crore of burn a quarter, the five lost months cost ₹3.2 crore. A ratio trigger is a trigger on two quantities, and is silent whenever they move together.

9. Failure modes and their diagnostics

Scenarios without triggers. Early sign: the output is a document, not a budget line. Diagnostic: whose money moves, on whose signature, if scenario three happens? Caught late, the cost is the whole lead time — seven months of knowing and not acting.

Triggers on ratios. Early sign: the threshold is a per-something. Diagnostic: if numerator and denominator both halved, would this fire? Dhaaru's ₹3.2 crore is a modest instance; the same error in a capacity metric is not.

The base case smuggled in as a scenario. Early sign: one cell carries the budget's numbers. Diagnostic: does any scenario need a different hiring plan from the one approved? If not, the firm paid for scenario planning and bought a forecast.

Monitoring aimed at the wrong axis. Early sign: the budget was set before the information values were computed. Diagnostic: what is the ceiling on this driver under perfect knowledge, and is our spend inside it? Dakhini's was not — ₹3.60 crore over the horizon against a ₹1.20 crore one-off ceiling.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Should scenarios carry probabilities? The intuitive-logics position rests on observed behaviour, not theory: managers given four futures with numbers attached plan for the largest and treat the rest as courtesies, so the numbers destroy the widening the exercise exists to produce. It would be wrong if the widening survived them — and Dakhini is a case against it, since the ₹4.95 crore and ₹1.20 crore figures were the only reason anyone questioned the budget. The probabilistic position answers that a judgement you will not quantify cannot be audited or scored; it would be wrong if elicited probabilities were calibrated badly enough to mislead more than narrative.

Four scenarios, or ten thousand? Robust decision making holds that a handful of narratives is a sampling method with no coverage guarantee, and that a planner needs the boundary of the region where a strategy fails. Its evidence is computational: exploratory modelling in climate and water planning has found failure regions no workshop proposed. It would be wrong where the uncertainty is not parameterisable, or where nobody can act on a surface.

Does any of it improve decisions? Tetlock's challenge is that scenario work states nothing scorable, so the field has no record. The defence, steelmanned, is that the output is decision quality under conditions no forecast addresses, and the measurable product is the trigger: whether a firm acted earlier than one without. The field has largely not tested that.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the method starts from the environment and produces a 2×2. Someone who has internalised it starts from a decision with a deadline and a lead time, and often concludes it needs no scenarios at all. They price a driver before funding any watching of it. They write the action and the money into the trigger, not the review. They quote a lead-time assumption as a minimum and a payoff gap against the spread. They notice when a trigger is a ratio. And they retire axes, because most drivers flip nothing.

12. Two decisions, and three questions

Trehan took Stage to the board on 4 December: ₹11 crore for the ledger core, ₹24 crore held against the draft-rule signpost, the monitoring budget re-pointed to the policy desk. Her reasoning was not that Stage had the better expected value — it did not, by ₹0.72 crore — but that the means were tied at 0.025 of the spread while the worst cells differed by ₹11 crore, and the mandate axis was worth four times, on the independent table, the axis she was paying to watch.

Thaper placed 30,000 firm on 30 November with an option on 46,000 at ₹38, accepting a fee she would have called waste a year earlier: the fractile answer was best among firm orders and the most exposed, and ₹17.48 lakh bought the right to be right about the high scenario without being destroyed by the low one.

  1. Dharti's option nets 4.4 times its fee under the stated probabilities. At what probability on the low scenario does the firm order of 76,000 beat the option policy, and who should set that probability?
  2. Both protagonists bought flexibility from a counterparty. What is the equivalent instrument for a consumer product whose decisive driver is a platform's ranking policy, where nobody sells options?
  3. Dakhini's choice survives both an independent and a correlated joint distribution. Construct a payoff table for which it would not, and say what Dakhini would have to observe to know it was in that world.

13. Going deeper

The plan scenarios stress-test, and where its number is load-bearing.
Scenario and sensitivity modelling
Turns four cells into a surface and locates breakpoints.
Strategy under deep uncertainty
The robust-decision-making toolkit when probabilities are unavailable.
Strategy vs roadmap vs plan
Which of the three a scenario may change.
Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later
Later holds staged commitments; triggers give it dates.
The roadmap as communication
Showing a conditional plan without looking indecisive.
OKRs and goal setting
Where a trigger sits inside a key result.
Capacity planning
Whether the ₹24 crore release is staffable when it fires.
Dependency management
Lead time is mostly other people's lead time.
exp20v2-plan.scenario:
Scenario Planning

Delivery & Technology: Roadmapping, Planning & OKRs

1. A plan that assumed one future

On Monday 12 October 2026, Kuldip Sagoo, vice president of product at Coppice Freight Software, received a message from the chief financial officer, Kamaljot Sarao. Coppice, based in Gurugram, sells a transport management system (the software a freight forwarder uses to book, route and bill shipments) and expected ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue, or ARR: the the annualised run-rate of subscription revenue at a given date. The board would meet on Friday 6 November.

The draft annual plan assumed that 14 of Coppice's 62 engineers would spend 26 weeks from January 2027 building a module to issue the electronic invoices that a proposed tax rule might require of forwarders. "Might" was the difficulty. No draft rule had been published. Sarao wanted a single answer: build or do not.

Kirandeep Sohal, head of engineering, wanted the same answer for a different reason. If the rule arrived and Coppice was unready, rivals would take the forwarders who needed compliance. If it never arrived, ₹5.6 crore of engineering time would have produced a feature almost nobody bought, while two large customers waited for fraud alerts. Sagoo's problem was not that the future was unknown. It was that the plan had been written as if it were known.

2. The idea

Scenario planning is the practice of writing a few internally consistent stories about how the external world could turn out, choosing actions that hold up across them, and naming in advance the observable signal, called a trigger, that shows which story has begun. It was invented to cure a particular failure of forecasting: a single forecast, however careful, invites an organisation to arrange itself around one number.

Herman Kahn used scenarios for military planning at the RAND Corporation in the 1950s. Pierre Wack and colleagues in the planning group of Royal Dutch Shell adapted them for business in the early 1970s; Shell's managers, having rehearsed a supply shock, are reported to have responded faster than rivals when oil prices roughly quadrupled in late 1973. Peter Schwartz, who worked with Wack, popularised the method in The Art of the Long View (1991).

Sagoo could say in a meeting: "We are not predicting the rule; we are deciding now what we will do on the day it arrives, and what we must already have built to do it in time."

3. How it works

The method has seven steps, and the two that practitioners leave unspoken, the third and the seventh, matter most. First, fix the decision and its horizon: Sagoo's was the January build, judged on exit ARR in the financial year ending March 2028 (FY28). Second, list the external uncertainties. Third, discard those that are predetermined, such as the ageing of the installed base, because a scenario built on a certainty adds nothing. Fourth, choose two critical uncertainties: forces that are important to the decision, genuinely unknown, and independent of each other. Sagoo chose whether the rule takes effect and whether the market consolidates into a few large forwarders, treating them as independent because consolidation was already under way for funding reasons; a rule that forced mergers would break that assumption and the 60:40 split.

Fifth, cross the two axes to make four quadrants and give each a name and a plausible story. Sixth, test every candidate plan against every quadrant. Seventh, and usually omitted, attach to each uncertainty a trigger with an owner and a date, and check that the lead time between trigger and effect exceeds the time the response takes.

The matrix is not the product; the stories inside it are. Each quadrant needs a paragraph a sceptical colleague could read and say "that could happen". Sagoo's team wrote four, and noticed that S4 contradicted their instinct that consolidation always helps enterprise sales: merging buyers also cut the number of seats licensed.

4. A worked example

Sagoo's team compared three plans. Plan A commits all 14 engineers for 26 weeks, which is 364 engineer-weeks, or 7 engineer-years; at ₹80 lakh per fully loaded engineer-year that is ₹5.6 crore. Plan B builds the core for 14 weeks (196 engineer-weeks, about ₹3.0 crore), then pauses with 12 weeks of work remaining. Plan C holds. Table 1 shows each plan's net FY28 contribution in each scenario, in ₹ crore: Sagoo's team's judgement of ARR gained by March 2028, less the engineering cost and the value of the fraud-alert work the engineers would otherwise have shipped. The figures are judgements, not a subtraction of the cost lines above, which is why Plan B's partial core can lose less than Plan A's full module where the rule never comes.

Table 1. Net FY28 contribution, ₹ crore. Regret is the best outcome available in a scenario minus the plan's outcome. EV is the weighted sum across scenarios.

Two readings follow. Regret is how much a plan falls short of the best choice in hindsight. The best outcomes by scenario are 14, 10, 0 and 0, so Plan A's regrets are 0, 0, 5 and 5 (maximum 5), Plan B's are 4, 2, 1 and 2 (maximum 4), and Plan C's are 18, 13, 0 and 0 (maximum 18). Minimising the maximum regret selects B. Weighting by probability gives A: 0.3(14) + 0.2(10) + 0.3(-5) + 0.2(-5) = 3.7, and B: 3.0 + 1.6 - 0.3 - 0.4 = 3.9. B again leads, narrowly.

Now change one input. Suppose a draft rule is published and the probability of a rule rises from 50 to 75 per cent, keeping the 60:40 split. The weights become 0.45, 0.30, 0.15 and 0.10. A scores 6.3 + 3.0 - 0.75 - 0.5 = 8.05; B scores 4.5 + 2.4 - 0.15 - 0.2 = 6.55; C falls to -2.7. The top two swap. The crossover is the rule probability m at which 6.8m - 3.6 = 0, which is 52.9 per cent. The lesson is not the winner but the threshold: Sagoo now knew what belief would change his mind.

The same comparison can be read as insurance. Against A, Plan B gives up 4 in S1 and 2 in S2, a weighted premium of 0.3(4) + 0.2(2) = 1.6, and saves 4 in S3 and 3 in S4, a weighted protection of 0.3(4) + 0.2(3) = 1.8. The net of 0.2 is the gap between 3.9 and 3.7.

5. Nuances a learner must know

A scenario is not a forecast, and not a worst case

The common "best, base and worst" triple varies one dimension, and managers quietly treat the middle as the prediction. Scenarios differ in kind, not in degree, and none is the expected one.

The axes decide everything

Two uncertainties that move together, such as a rule and the regulator's budget, collapse the matrix into two real scenarios. Test independence by asking whether one axis could move while the other stays still.

A trigger must lead the response

If notice after a draft rule is 13 weeks and a full build takes 26, waiting for the trigger loses. Plan B's pre-build leaves 12 weeks, inside the notice, which is why it is worth its cost (Figure 3). The 13 weeks is an assumption, and the margin of one week holds only if the 14 engineers stay ring-fenced during the pause.

Probabilities are an addition, not the method

Many practitioners refuse to weight scenarios, because a weight invites the forecasting habit. Weights are useful for one thing, locating the threshold at which the choice flips, as the 52.9 per cent above did. Treat the point estimate as noise and the threshold as the finding.

It is not sensitivity analysis

Sensitivity analysis moves one input and holds the rest fixed. A scenario moves several together, in a coherent story, so that revenue, cost and customer behaviour change in ways a spreadsheet cell cannot capture.

What it cannot tell you

The method covers only futures someone imagined. A fifth quadrant, such as a competitor giving the module away, lies outside the matrix. Where outcomes cannot be listed at all, the next topic, strategy under deep uncertainty, takes over.

Link it to the plan, not beside it

Scenario planning builds on annual and quarterly planning: it stress-tests the plan already written. The useful output is a change to the quarterly objectives, such as a pre-build objective that exists only because one scenario is live, not a separate strategy document that sits beside the plan and never touches a sprint.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Who wrote the stories, and did anyone with a stake in a plan write the quadrant that favours it? Does each scenario imply a different action? A scenario that changes no decision is decoration.

6. How it differs by product and by stage

The mechanics are constant. What varies is which uncertainty dominates and how fast a trigger can fire.

SettingTypical critical uncertaintyTrigger speed
ConsumerPlatform or app-store policy; shifts in habitFast: daily metrics
B2BRegulation; customer consolidation; budget cyclesSlow: renewals, filings
MarketplaceSupply-side defection; rival subsidiesFast: weekly liquidity data
Early stageWhether funding arrives; product-market fitMonths of cash
Large companySeveral at once, across business unitsNeeds a standing owner

Table 2. Where the emphasis falls.

A start-up with ten months of cash cannot afford Plan B's 14 weeks of up-front spend; it needs scenarios mainly to decide what to cut first. In a marketplace, a rival's subsidy can erase a supply-side advantage within a quarter, so its triggers are built from weekly liquidity measures rather than annual events. A large company has the opposite difficulty: it can fund every plan, so the danger is that nobody owns the trigger.

7. Common mistakes

Three scenarios named high, medium and low

Symptom: the "medium" case appears in every budget. Misunderstanding: scenarios are being used as sensitivities. Diagnostic: ask whether the three differ in a story or only in a number.

Triggers written as moods

Symptom: "if the market looks soft" appears in the minutes, and nothing is done in the quarter it softens. Misunderstanding: a trigger is a conclusion rather than a measurable event. Diagnostic: could two people disagree about whether it fired?

A deck that is never reopened

Symptom: the matrix is dated, and nobody can name its owner. Misunderstanding: the work ends with the workshop. Diagnostic: find the last date a trigger was read.

A plan that wins every scenario

Symptom: the proposal is described as "no-regret" in all four quadrants. Misunderstanding: the author has compared a plan with a strawman, usually Plan C. Diagnostic: ask for the quadrant in which this plan loses, and its size in rupees.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Sagoo's decision has four marks. The plan sentence names the scenario it assumes and the one that would reverse it. The staged plan is priced, with its cost visible. Each trigger, such as publication of a draft rule in the official gazette, has an owner and a review date. And the board sees the threshold, 52.9 per cent, rather than a lone forecast. The directors' question becomes whether anyone holds a belief about the rule above or below that line.

9. Closing

On Friday 6 November, Sagoo asked the board for Plan B: 14 engineers for 14 weeks from January, then a pause. His reasoning rested on three facts. B had the lowest maximum regret, 4 against 5 and 18. It led at the current weights. And its remaining 12 weeks fit inside the 13 weeks of notice a draft rule would give. Sarao owned the trigger, a published draft; if it fired, Coppice would move to the full build at once, since 75 per cent clears 52.9. The next topic to read is scenario and sensitivity modelling, which turns this table into a spreadsheet that can be stressed, followed by strategy under deep uncertainty, for cases where the quadrants cannot be listed.

Two questions to sit with. Which decision in your own plan would look different if your single forecast were wrong in the most likely direction? And if your trigger fired tomorrow, how many weeks would your response take, and how many would you have?
exp40v2-plan.replanning:
Re-planning and change control

How a plan changes visibly when reality changes — and why the discipline fails most often on good news.

1. Two decisions, one kind of problem

On Wednesday 4 November 2026 the tax authority published a revised e-invoicing schema with two new document types. Gunvant Maniar, vice-president of product at Vantix Freight Cloud, a Pune company selling compliance software to large shippers, read it that afternoon. On Friday 6 November his engineering lead, Gowri Makwana, returned a re-estimate: the compliance workstream costed at 26 net engineer-weeks would now take 41. Twelve enterprise accounts, each on a ₹3.20 crore annual contract, ₹38.40 crore combined, warranted that Vantix would be compliant on the go-live date of Friday 1 January 2027. The quarter had opened on Monday 5 October with 108 net engineer-weeks of planning capacity, 92 committed and 16 in reserve. Five weeks were gone, and Gunvant had already been told of a resignation effective 20 November and a six-week medical leave from 9 November.

Gitanjali Mohta had the opposite problem. Velmora is a consumer AI study companion: 240,000 monthly active users, of whom 38,000 pay ₹299 a month, giving ₹113.62 lakh of monthly subscription revenue against ₹27.70 lakh of inference cost (38,000 paying users at ₹41 and 202,000 free users at ₹6) — a margin of ₹85.92 lakh of ₹113.62 lakh, or 75.6 per cent. Her eight-week cycle from Monday 9 November committed 34 of 40 net engineer-weeks, the largest handwriting grading at 16. On Thursday 5 November her model vendor shipped a capability that did most of it, and Goutham Meswani, her engineering head, re-estimated the item at 6. Ten engineer-weeks had appeared from nowhere, and nobody outside the team would ask her to account for them.

Gunvant's plan will be re-planned loudly, because the change cannot be hidden; Gitanjali's only if she chooses. That asymmetry is this page's subject.

2. The idea: a transition between two balanced states

Re-planning is replacing one plan of record with another, on a stated date, with a named owner and with the trade-off that paid for the change written down. Change control is what makes the replacement visible: a log of states, not of requests. The definition is deliberately narrow. A plan state is three quantities — capacity available, scope committed, reserve held — which must balance, and a re-plan is legitimate when the states before and after both balance and the arithmetic between them is written down. Silent drift is not slowness but the absence of a state transition: work moves, nothing is published, and the old state is still being quoted by people not in the room.

The machinery is old. Earned-value cost and schedule control criteria entered United States defence procurement in 1967 and brought the baseline: a frozen plan against which variance is measured, changed only through a configuration control board. It existed to stop contractors re-baselining away their overruns and reporting near-zero variance for years. The counter-tradition began from the observation that freezing a plan freezes the estimate too: Boehm's spiral model in 1988, Scrum in 1995 and Reinertsen's development-flow work of 1997 and 2009 all held that a plan is a forecast, to be re-derived rather than defended. Kahneman and Lovallo's 1993 outside view and Flyvbjerg's reference-class forecasting went further: the single date is the defect.

Four schools separate by what each will sign. The baseline school signs "variance is measured against the original commitment, and re-baselining destroys the only record of our forecasting error", and will not sign that a plan be re-derived each cycle. The rolling-wave school signs "the plan of record is whatever the latest cycle produced", and will not sign that last quarter's estimate has standing. The flow-economics school signs "re-plan when the value of acting on the news exceeds the churn cost", and will not sign a fixed threshold. The distribution school signs "publish a range and a confidence" and will not sign a single date as a commitment. None disagrees that an unlogged slip is a failure.

3. Mechanics: the three-quantity ledger, worked

Expert practice begins with a capacity build-down, because a plan starting from gross headcount cannot balance. Vantix ran twelve engineers over a twelve-week quarter: 144 gross engineer-weeks, less 16 for holidays and leave and 20 for the support rota, giving 108 net, levelled at 9.0 a week. Exhibit 1 is that quarter in three states; every figure below belongs to one.

Exhibit 1. Vantix Freight Cloud, Q3 FY27, net engineer-weeks by plan state. A is the plan of record of 28 September 2026, weeks 1–12; B the re-forecast of 6 November 2026, weeks 6–12, on actuals through week 5; C the plan of record of 9 November 2026, same weeks.
WorkstreamA: estimateSpent, wks 1–5 B: re-estimateB: remainingC: remaining

Weeks are working weeks, Monday to Friday, from 5 October 2026; week 5 closed on Friday 6 November, and spend of 45 is five weeks at 9.0. Capacity for weeks 6–12 is seven weeks at 9.0, or 63, less 11 lost to one resignation (weeks 8–12) and one medical leave (weeks 6–11): 52. Both losses are counted as net engineer-weeks at 1.0, neither person's lost weeks appearing in the 16 of planned leave or the 20 of rota, so nothing is counted twice; prorating them instead would give 54.75, so 52 is the conservative reading.

State A balances: 92 committed plus 16 reserve is 108. State B does not, and that is the whole content of a re-forecast. Remaining committed work of 68 plus reserve of 10 is 78 against 52 available — an overcommitment of 26 engineer-weeks, half the capacity remaining, decomposing exactly into 15 of scope growth (compliance from 26 to 41) plus 11 of capacity loss. State C balances again at 47 committed plus 5 reserve, paid for by deferring 21 engineer-weeks to Q4 (settlement phase two, 9; the shipper portal, 12) and releasing 5 from reserve; 21 plus 5 is 26.

The second mechanic is the trigger, usually left implicit. The natural rule is that a variance is absorbable without a re-plan if it is no larger than the reserve held against it. On Friday 30 October, before the schema news, the variance Gunvant could see was 11 engineer-weeks of capacity loss against a reserve of 12: 16 held at the start less 4 drawn through week 4. The rule said absorb, and he was about to. But absorbing 11 into 12 leaves 1 engineer-week of reserve against the 72 still to come (weeks 5–12 at 9.0), 1 of 72 or 1.4 per cent, where the same measure at the open was 16 of 108, or 14.8 per cent. A full-reserve trigger fires only once the buffer is gone, the last possible moment; set at half the reserve, a variance of 6, it would have fired on 30 October and bought five working days.

The third mechanic is pricing the alternatives in one currency. Missing 1 January 2027 triggers the warranty: one month of fees across the twelve accounts, ₹38.40 crore divided by twelve, or ₹3.20 crore. Deferring the shipper portal one quarter forgoes the support saving it was forecast to deliver from January: three months at ₹9.50 lakh, or ₹28.50 lakh, plus a restart penalty of 15 per cent of the 8 engineer-weeks already spent, or 1.2 engineer-weeks. Each as a one-off total, ₹320 lakh against ₹28.50 lakh is 11.2 to one. What made the decision easy was that the portal side was computable in rupees; the settlement deferral and the restart penalty were not.

4. When the discipline applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions state as tests. One: a published plan with a stated capacity and commitment. Vantix passes trivially, Velmora at 34 committed of 40. Two: the variance exceeds the reserve held against it. Vantix: 26 against 10, yes. Velmora: the variance is favourable, minus 10, and the reserve test is silent on favourable variance, which is the hole. Three: someone outside the team has decided something on the old plan. Vantix: twelve accounts and a warranty. Velmora: a campaign booked against the handwriting-grading launch. Four: the news survives another week of information. Vantix's schema is published regulation and will not move; Velmora's vendor capability was four days old and unmeasured on Hindi-medium scripts, which argues for releasing capacity into reserve rather than committing it.

The idea actively misleads in three situations. Where the plan is a forecast nobody committed to, formal change control teaches the team that an estimate is a promise, and estimates inflate until no variance appears. Where the work is discovery, the honest cadence of re-planning is shorter than any change-control cycle, so the log lags the truth and becomes fiction worse than no log. In incident response, a state transition per change costs speed.

5. Hard edges: seams, staircases and moving baselines

In the hard cases the cost of a slip is not proportional to its size. Vantix's scanner firmware needs a device-certification slot, and slots are booked monthly, so a one-week slip past a booking costs a month. Trimming a week off a staircase buys nothing, which is why Gunvant held firmware at its full 9 engineer-weeks in State C while cutting a smooth-curve workstream. In multi-product companies the cost of a re-plan is the cascade count: a platform date that moves obliges every dependent product to publish a new state, and teams stop publishing rather than trigger it. In a two-sided marketplace the supply side has signed contracts and the demand side has not, so the halves cannot be re-planned at one cadence. In regulated work the date is exogenous, collapsing a three-variable trade to two; because scope has a floor set by the regulation, the residual variable is quality, which is why compliance programmes overrun on defects rather than dates. For AI-native products the baseline moves under the plan: Velmora's largest single variance in November came from its supplier.

At a seam, a re-plan crossing a budget boundary stops being a product decision and moves at the finance calendar's speed. Mature companies say they run a change-control board. What they run is a weekly half-hour, a pre-authorised reserve at each seam, and a rule that anything inside the reserve needs no forum. The board ratifies, quarterly.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The re-plan is a state, not a document. Ask for the preceding state, with its date and three totals; an expert produces it at once, because it was published. The obvious reading, archiving, is wrong: the previous state makes the current one a decision.

Three quantities must balance in every state. Most published re-plans show capacity and scope and omit reserve, never accidentally: reserve absorbs the error. When a re-plan does not add up, the missing number is the reserve, and it is negative. The tell is a state with two numbers.

Levelled capacity hides calendar shape. Vantix's 9.0 engineer-weeks a week is a fiction in a quarter ending 25 December; the tell is a flat capacity line across a holiday cluster. The obvious correction, modelling each week, is wrong too: that precision invites arguments about single weeks. Level within a month, shape across them.

The reserve ratio should rise with uncertainty and almost always falls. Vantix went from 10 of 52 engineer-weeks, 19.2 per cent, to 5 of 52, 9.6 per cent, as its delivery risk rose. Reserve has no advocate in the room, so it pays for every settlement; the tell is a share quoted before a re-plan and never after.

Re-planning on good news is the rarer discipline. Ask when a team last published a state that released capacity; almost none has. The obvious reading is that nobody is harmed. It is wrong: a capacity figure only ever revised downwards is a bargaining position, not a capacity.

Drift is measured by the logging lag, not the slip. A six-week slip logged in week two is good practice; a three-week slip logged after the fact is not. The tell is a dashboard whose green count exceeds the number landing on time.

A trigger set at the reserve guarantees the latest possible re-plan. It reads as prudent and is structurally late, its condition being met only once the buffer is spent. Set it instead as a stated fraction of the reserve.

A re-plan that holds the date every time is a scope ratchet. At Valoris Mobility, below, the first four re-plans each held 16 March 2026 and removed 14 features between them; the vehicle still shipped 137 days late. The tell is a date surviving consecutive re-plans: ask which variable moved, and refuse "scope" twice running.

7. Product type and company stage

In consumer products the cycle is short and the plan is openly a forecast, so re-planning is cheap and visibility the only real problem: Velmora could change its mind weekly at no cost, which is why its changes went unlogged. In B2B and enterprise the plan is contractual, a re-plan is a customer communication first, and the real change-control board is the account team. On platforms and marketplaces the governing quantity is the cascade count, not the size of the change. In hardware the staircase means the re-plan must happen before the tooling or certification booking, months before the evidence is conclusive. In AI products much of the variance is supplier-side, so the plan needs an owner for supplier change, which almost no roadmap has.

By stage the differences are smaller than usually claimed. At seed there is often no plan of record to re-plan, and pretending otherwise is theatre. What matters is the first quarter in which the plan outlives the people who wrote it, usually past fifty engineers: that is when a published state stops being bureaucracy and becomes the only way two teams hold one belief. At scale a re-plan can cost more than the slip, and the answer is a larger reserve, not a bigger board.

8. Three worked examples

Vantix, November 2026: the discipline working. The 6 November re-forecast showed 78 required against 52 available. Three options were priced: accept a compliance miss at ₹3.20 crore; add contractors, rejected because the schema knowledge could not be acquired in seven weeks; or defer 21 engineer-weeks and release 5 of reserve. The third was published on 9 November, and Q4 inherited 21 engineer-weeks plus a 1.2-engineer-week portal restart penalty, 22.2 in all.

Velmora, November 2026: the favourable variance. Handwriting grading fell from 16 engineer-weeks to 6, releasing 10 of the 34 committed. Gitanjali Mohta could absorb it silently, commit all 10 to new scope, or publish a new state. She published, moving reserve from 6 of 40 engineer-weeks, 15.0 per cent, to 10 of 40, 25.0 per cent, and committing 6 to a free-tier rate limiter: 24 plus 6 committed and 10 reserve, balancing at 40. Her head of growth objected that publishing on good news invites finance to treat released capacity as permanent.

Valoris Mobility: the failure, and the recovery. Valoris builds electric two-wheelers: hardware and software on one date.

Exhibit 2. Valoris Mobility: six published re-plans of one vehicle launch. A re-plan is date-holding when the launch date after it equals the date before it.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Silent drift is the mode with the best evidence, because it can be measured. Exhibit 3 is Velmora's July-to-October cycle, the one that taught Gitanjali Mohta to publish; the five weeks between it and her November cycle are not shown.

Exhibit 3. Velmora: the four roadmap items that moved, of nine committed for the thirteen weeks from Monday 6 July to Sunday 4 October 2026. Weeks are numbered from 6 July; week 17 ended Sunday 1 November 2026. Slip is landed less committed week; logging lag is logged week less the week the slip became knowable.

Only the tutor-memory slip was logged before its committed week, so 1 of the 4 items that moved changed visibly, 25.0 per cent — the denominator is the four that moved, not the nine committed. Mean slip is 20 divided by 4, or 5.0 weeks; mean logging lag is 18 divided by 4, or 4.5 weeks, and 17 divided by 3, or 5.7 weeks, across the three logged late. The dashboard marked an item amber only when its owner changed the status, and three did so only after their committed week had passed, so at the end of week 8 it showed 8 of 9 items green, 88.9 per cent, while 5 of 9, or 55.6 per cent, went on to land in their committed week. The 33.3-point gap is what the dashboard concealed.

The diagnostic for drift is to ask when a slip became knowable and when it was logged; late, campaigns stay booked against dates nobody believes. Four more modes recur. The scope ratchet shows as a date surviving two consecutive re-plans; ask which variable moved last time. Valoris paid 137 days and 13 engineers. Reserve erosion shows as the reserve share falling while variance rises; ask for reserve as a share of remaining capacity, not of the original plan; late, the next variance has nowhere to land. Silent absorption shows as items finishing early with nothing published. Re-baselining shows as variance reports that all read near zero; ask against which baseline.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Against which baseline is variance measured? The baseline school at its strongest: an organisation that re-baselines freely has no record of its forecast error and cannot improve, and the 1967 criteria exist because that was observed at scale. It is wrong if the original estimates carried no information, in which case variance measures the estimator and punishing it produces padding. The rolling-wave reply is that the only forecast worth holding anyone to is the latest.

Threshold or economic calculation? The flow-economics position rests on the claim that delay cost and churn cost can differ by an order of magnitude — ₹320 lakh against ₹28.50 lakh, 11.2 to one, at Vantix. It is wrong wherever the two sides are not computable in one currency, which is most of the time; a threshold at least decides.

Should the reserve rise or fall after bad news? The two protagonists went opposite ways and neither is obviously wrong. Cutting it, as Vantix did from 19.2 to 9.6 per cent of remaining capacity, treats a published regulatory requirement as the lowest-variance item on the board and spends the buffer on what cannot slip. Raising it, as Velmora did from 15.0 to 25.0 per cent on good news, treats new information as evidence that more is coming. This is unresolved on purpose: it turns on whether the variance just absorbed came from the same distribution as the next, and nobody has shown it either way.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes a change-control process. Someone who has internalised it balances capacity, committed scope and reserve before arguing, because the arithmetic usually settles it; names the previous state and its date without looking; publishes re-plans that release capacity; and says which of the three variables moved, at the top — because a re-plan whose moving variable is unnamed will have moved scope, every time.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Gunvant Maniar published State C on Monday 9 November 2026: compliance intact at 31 engineer-weeks, settlement cut to a three-carrier phase one at 7, the shipper portal stopped at 0 with 12 deferred, firmware held at 9 for its certification slot, reserve cut to 5. He named the moving variable as scope, set the ₹3.20 crore exposure beside the ₹28.50 lakh forgone portal saving, and sent the note to the twelve accounts before his own team. Gitanjali Mohta published her state the same day: 30 committed, 10 in reserve, the moving variable named as reserve, and a line recording that the 10 engineer-weeks came from a supplier, not from the team.

1. Vantix cut its reserve from 19.2 to 9.6 per cent of remaining capacity as its delivery risk rose. Under what belief about the next variance is that right, and does the schema support it?

2. Velmora published a re-plan that released capacity. What would have to be true of its finance process for publishing to cost more than absorbing the 10 quietly?

3. Valoris re-planned six times, visibly, and shipped 137 days late. What must a re-plan contain beyond visibility, and would State C satisfy it?

13. Going deeper

  1. Milestones and release planning — the dates a re-plan moves; with none there is nothing to publish a change against.
  2. Strategy vs roadmap vs plan — which of the three a change touches, and how to stop strategy churn passing as re-planning.
  3. Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later — a horizon structure that makes most re-plans invisible by design.
  4. The roadmap as communication — the channel a state travels; a re-plan nobody reads is drift with paperwork.
  5. OKRs and goal setting — outcomes survive scope changes, so OKRs are what a re-plan is judged against.
  6. Annual and quarterly planning — sets the cadence of published states, and so the ceiling on drift.
  7. Capacity planning — the first of the three quantities; a re-plan is only as honest as its build-down.
exp20v2-plan.replanning:
Re-planning and Change Control

A case-style reading for product managers

1. A date promised in writing

On Monday 14 September 2026, Eklavi Lapsiwala, head of product at Tejora Pay, a Surat company selling a payments-and-ledger app to textile traders, opened an email from the maker of the ERP (enterprise resource planning) system most of her customers run. Its second-generation API, the interface through which other software reads its data, would not ship in mid-September. No new date was given.

Tejora had signed forty distributors on Monday 3 August, each paying ₹1.2 lakh a year, ₹48 lakh in all (40 × ₹1.2 lakh). Every contract was conditional on the Ledger Sync release going live by Friday 30 October; a distributor could walk away if the date passed without written agreement. Seven working weeks remained. Eight engineers at 0.75 productive weeks each, net of leave, holidays and support, gave 42 engineer-weeks, one engineer's productive week being the unit (8 × 7 × 0.75) against 36 committed, a reserve of 6. The email raised the connector from 14 to 20, and the reserve to zero. Lapsiwala could absorb the news quietly and hope. What that would cost is the subject of this page. If the date slid unannounced, the first signal would be a distributor's finance head asking on 30 October why nothing had arrived, with ₹48 lakh of annual revenue resting on the answer and Tejora's account of events weakened by weeks of silence.

2. The idea: a plan with a ledger

Change control means altering a plan only through a recorded decision. It keeps three things apart. The baseline is the version of the plan that outsiders were promised. The forecast is the team's current estimate of what will be true. The change record links them. Re-planning is producing a new baseline once forecast and baseline have drifted apart; change control is the rule about who may do it and what must be written down.

The practice descends from configuration management in United States defence engineering of the 1950s and 1960s, where one untracked alteration could invalidate another team's work. Project management adopted it as "integrated change control". Software teams, after the 2001 Agile Manifesto put responding to change above following a plan, kept the record and loosened the approval. The problem it solves is silent drift, a plan that is true in the tracker and false in everyone's head. The sentence Lapsiwala could repeat in a meeting: the plan may change every week, but never without a record of what moved, why, and who agreed. It builds directly on milestone planning: a re-plan is what you do when a milestone moves, and change control is what stops the move from being private.

3. How it works, step by step

Figure 3 shows seven steps. The first is to freeze a baseline: date, scope, the capacity assumption (eight engineers at 0.75), and the reserve. Most teams write down the first three and leave the reserve implicit, which is why it gets spent unseen. Writing the reserve down also fixes a second implicit item, the productivity factor: 0.75 says that a quarter of every engineer's week goes to leave, holidays and support, and anyone challenging the plan later can see what was assumed. The second is a tripwire, a condition agreed in advance that forces a decision. At Tejora it was that committed work plus the reserve must not exceed capacity.

The email set steps three onward running. Sizing is where practitioners cut corners: re-estimate everything sharing the same people, not only the item that moved, and total it in the baseline's own unit. Then frame options along three levers, date, scope and capacity, and name quality as a fourth that is easy to pull silently. One named person with authority to bind customers decides. The record captures the trigger, the options rejected and the new baseline. Finally, tell everyone who relied on the old plan, including people the tracker does not list, such as the sales representative who mentioned the date over lunch. Steps five to seven vanish first under pressure, because the plan feels finished once the arithmetic is done.

4. A worked example, and what changes when one input does

Capacity is 8 engineers × 7 weeks × 0.75 = 42 engineer-weeks, or 6 per week. The contract names three capabilities: the connector, reconciliation (8), and e-invoice export (7). Reminders (4) and a dashboard (3) are not named. The baseline commits 36, leaving 6, which is 14.3% of capacity (6 ÷ 42).

Engineer-weeks unless statedBaselineFirst passSecond pass
ERP connector142024
Other four items222222
Total committed364246
Capacity424242
Reserve (capacity − committed)60−4
Weeks needed with a reserve of 6789 (8.67)
Finish date30 Oct6 Nov13 Nov
Scope to cut instead0610

Table 1. Weeks needed = (committed + 6) ÷ 6, rounded up. Cut = committed − 36, the 36 being capacity less the reserve.

First pass: the connector costs 20, so committed is 42 and the reserve zero. To move the date, (42 + 6) ÷ 6 = 8 weeks, Friday 6 November. To cut scope, 42 − 36 = 6 must go; reminders and dashboard total 7, enough with one to spare, and neither is contracted.

Second pass, one input changed: the vendor's slip runs to January, forcing a manual mapping layer, and the connector costs 24. Committed is 46, reserve −4. Moving the date needs 52 ÷ 6 = 8.67, so nine weeks, Friday 13 November, two weeks late. Cutting needs 46 − 36 = 10, but reminders and dashboard give 7, so a contracted item must go as well; export, at 7, is the smaller. The method that made cutting painless now cuts the contract. Nothing in the procedure changed between the passes, only one estimate, which is why the tripwire matters more than the cleverness of the options.

5. Six nuances that separate users from understanders

Forecast is not baseline.

Teams that overwrite one with the other can never be wrong, because the plan always matches the latest guess. Keep both. The gap between them is the clearest measure of drift, and Figure 2 draws it. A weekly status that shows only the forecast cannot tell a reader whether the team is on plan or merely on its latest plan.

A reserve is not padding.

Padding hides inside each estimate and is consumed by it. A reserve belongs to the plan as a whole, appears as a number, and is spent only by recorded decisions. Tejora's six engineer-weeks of reserve were spent by a vendor's email, not by a choice, which is exactly why the number had to be visible. A reserve also has a purpose: it exists for shocks nobody can name in advance, and a plan that spends it on known work has none left for the unknown.

Control is proportional.

Figure 4 sorts changes by whether the reserve covers them and whether outsiders relied on the date. Covered changes, those leaving the reserve above its tripwire, are absorbed and logged; the rest escalate. A rule that sends every change for approval teaches people to stop reporting.

Three levers, and a hidden fourth.

Date, scope and capacity are visible. Quality is the one pulled silently: skipping a test cycle is a scope cut nobody recorded. Adding engineers late is slower than it looks, since newcomers consume the existing team's time; Fred Brooks made the point in 1975.

Re-planning cannot repair an estimate.

The 20 is a forecast, not a measurement, and the first estimate after a shock tends to anchor on the old number. State a range, say 18 to 24, and plan against the upper end for anything promised to a customer.

Ask before relying on it.

Who relied on the old date, and do they know? Who set the tripwire? Who may bind customers? Is the sizing in the baseline's unit? Nor is this anti-agile: reordering a backlog inside a sprint is not a baseline change, while moving a date a customer holds is.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; early and large

ProductWho relied on the dateWhat forces a re-plan
ConsumerMarketing, app-store slotReview delay against a fixed campaign
B2BContracted customers, as at TejoraVendor or integration delay
MarketplaceBoth sides of the marketA change that strands one side

Table 2. The same mechanics, with different people holding the promise.

Marketplaces are harder to control because a change for one side can break a promise to the other: delaying seller tools while buyer campaigns run leaves demand without supply. Early-stage companies need a one-page record and one decider, often the founder, and their failure is having no record at all. Large companies fail the opposite way, with boards so slow that teams stop reporting. Let the ceremony follow the number of outside parties who relied on the date.

7. Three common mistakes

Each mistake below shows itself outwardly before anyone inside admits it, which is why the diagnostics are phrased as questions an outsider could ask. All three come from treating the plan as a document to be kept current, not as a promise to be kept honest.

Symptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
A customer learns of a new date from a missed demoUpdating the tracker is communicatingAsk three people who relied on it which date they believe
Status stays green, then turns red overnightThe reserve is slack for each itemAsk for today's reserve as a number
Only the slipped item's date changesA change is localSum all remaining estimates against capacity

Table 3. Each diagnostic takes under ten minutes.

8. What good looks like

By the afternoon of the 14th, Emaad Lakhmani, the engineering lead, had re-estimated all five items, not only the connector, and found the other four unchanged at 22. Edhika Lehri, who ran customer success, listed the forty distributors and flagged the five largest by usage as needing a call, not a letter. The two of them also wrote down what had not been touched, the connector's 18 to 24 range included, so that nobody would later read the cut as a verdict on the team. The record read as follows.

FieldEntry
TriggerVendor API slip; connector 14 to 20
OptionsMove to 6 Nov; cut reminders and dashboard
Decision, ownerCut; Lapsiwala
ToldForty distributors, 16 Sep

Table 4. A change record that fits on one screen.

The target is not a perfect forecast. It is a plan in which the trigger was noticed on the day it arrived, the sizing covered every item, the options were compared in one unit, one person decided, and every holder of the old date heard it from Tejora rather than from a missed deliverable.

9. The decision, and what to carry forward

On Tuesday 15 September Lapsiwala held the date and cut reminders and the dashboard. Her reasoning: the contracts bound Tejora to a date and three capabilities, not to those two. Moving to 6 November would put at risk the ₹1.2 lakh a year of each of forty distributors; cutting two uncontracted items risked none. Committed work fell to 35, leaving a reserve of 7, which is 16.7% of 42. She set a new tripwire at a reserve of 3 or less. Had the connector reached 24, committed work would be 39 and the reserve 3, exactly the point to reopen export with the distributors. The letter went out on Wednesday 16 September, and the five largest distributors received a call before it arrived.

Learn next how outcome roadmaps carry dependencies and risks, because the vendor's API was a dependency no plan listed, and how OKRs tie the date to a purpose worth defending.

Two questions to sit with. Who today believes a date your tracker no longer shows, and what would it cost them? If your reserve were published as a number every Monday, which decisions would you take earlier?
exp20v2-plan.customer.roadmap:
Customer-Facing Roadmaps

What can we show customers without it becoming a contract?

1. The slide that came back as a clause

On Wednesday 9 September 2026, Meghal Vasani, head of product at Everline Software, read a clause she had not written. Everline, an Ahmedabad company, sells batch-tracking software to pharmaceutical distributors. Its annual recurring revenue (the fees customers have contracted to pay each year) stood at ₹1,800 lakh, or ₹18 crore. Harbourline Distribution, with fourteen warehouses, paid ₹240 lakh of it: 13.3 per cent. Its renewal was due on 30 September.

Harbourline's procurement head, Mahika Vagadia, had returned the draft contract with a new paragraph. On 12 May, Mayur Vithalani, Everline's head of enterprise sales, had emailed her a roadmap slide listing "Batch-recall alerts: Q4 2026". The paragraph turned that line into delivery by 31 December 2026, with a service credit of 2 per cent of the annual fee for each month of delay, capped at 10 per cent.

Vasani had three weeks, one engineering team and an uncomfortable fact: nobody had ever asked whether Q4 was a plan, a hope or a promise. Refusing the clause risked the renewal. Accepting it meant pricing a guess.

2. The idea

A customer-facing roadmap is a deliberately edited statement of where a product is heading, shown to the people who pay for it, in which every line carries an explicit level of confidence and none is worded as an undertaking unless the company has chosen to make one. It exists because salespeople answer "will you build this?" with whatever closes the deal, customers file the answer as a commitment, and engineering hears of it later. Saying nothing fails as well: enterprise buyers must plan their own systems around yours and will conclude you have no direction.

The format most teams start from, Now-Next-Later, spread through the product community in the early 2010s as a reaction to dated Gantt-style plans; it replaces dates with horizons. The legal half of the idea is older: a forecast, a statement of intention and a binding undertaking are different things, and the skill lies in keeping them visibly different. Vasani's sentence for the meeting: "We tell you what we intend and how sure we are, and we promise only what we have chosen to be accountable for."

3. How it works

Step one sorts each candidate item by what the company knows. Vasani used three states. Building: engineers are working on it, and a date range can be defended. Scoped: the problem is understood and sized but not staffed. Exploring: the problem matters and no solution exists yet. Only the first state may carry calendar language at all.

Step two restates each item as an outcome rather than a feature: not "recall alerts" but "a distributor learns within an hour that a batch it shipped is recalled". An outcome survives a change of design; a feature name invites the customer to hold you to the feature. Step three assigns horizons, Now, Next and Later. Exhibit 2 shows the board, and the contract line below it: the boundary beyond which nothing is promised unless a signed order form says so.

Three steps are usually left implicit. First, reconcile the board against every signed commitment, since a deal may already promise something the board omits. Second, stamp each version with a date and an audience, because an undated slide outlives the quarter it described. Third, log who was shown which version; without a log nobody could say, as Vasani could not, what Harbourline had actually been told.

4. A worked example

Vasani began with Everline's own record. Exhibit 3 covers the 20 dated items shown to customers between January 2025 and December 2025, all since shipped; the denominator is those 20 items, not every feature shipped. It records when each shipped relative to the quarter quoted.

Only 9 of 20 met the quoted quarter. Harbourline's clause charges 2 per cent of the ₹240 lakh fee, ₹4.8 lakh, per month of delay, capped at 10 per cent, ₹24 lakh. To keep the arithmetic cautious, a late item is charged as if it shipped on the last day of its quarter: one quarter after the promise is three months late (₹14.4 lakh), two quarters is six months (₹28.8 lakh, capped at ₹24 lakh), and "later" is assumed to hit the cap. Hold the engineering fixed: read the cumulative column as the chance the item is done by 31 December (45%), 31 March (80%), 30 June (95%) or later. Expected credit is probability times credit. For a 31 December promise: 0.35 × 14.4 + 0.15 × 24 + 0.05 × 24 = 5.04 + 3.60 + 1.20 = ₹9.84 lakh.

Second pass, changing one input. The Harbourline item must read recall notices from Harbourline's own warehouse system, and engineering judged it harder than the typical item: 30 per cent by 31 December, 60 by 31 March, 90 by 30 June, with 10 per cent later. The same promise now costs 0.30 × 14.4 + 0.30 × 24 + 0.10 × 24 = 4.32 + 7.20 + 2.40 = ₹13.92 lakh.

The comparison that matters is with the benefit. To a first approximation, a date is worth giving only if it raises the chance of renewal by at least the expected credit as a share of the fee (taking one year's fee as the prize): 4.1 points at 31 December on Everline's record, 5.8 on the harder item. Moving the promise to 30 June lowers those hurdles to 0.5 and 1.0 points. The table ignores the cost of lost trust, which no credit clause measures. The first pass also shows that the promised date, not the feature, set the price: identical work cost ₹9.84 lakh at one date and ₹1.20 lakh at another.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A forecast, a plan and a promise differ. A forecast says what is likely, a plan says what the team has resourced, and a promise says what the company will answer for. Customers hear all three as the third. Everline's Q4 line was a forecast when typed and a promise when copied into a clause; the words never changed, only the reader.

Wording carries the weight. Exhibit 5 sorts common phrases by what a buyer hears. The ladder matters more than any disclaimer.

A quarter is a date. "Q4" feels vague to its author and is read as 31 December by a procurement team. Use a Now-Next-Later label instead, and a date range only for items that are Building.

The audience, not the artefact, decides. One slide can be a sales exhibit, an email attachment and a contract schedule. Everline's outside counsel advised that the risk is not only the signed clause: a statement a buyer visibly relies on can be pulled into a dispute, which is why an entire-agreement clause (one saying the written contract is the whole deal) matters. This page is not legal advice.

Outcomes protect you more than features. A feature name is easy to check and easy to breach; an outcome leaves room to change the design. Vasani's recall alerts could arrive by email, text message or in-app banner; the outcome, an hour, was the real requirement.

It is not a release note or a service level. Release notes describe what shipped. A service level (an agreed performance measure) is a contract term by design. The internal roadmap may hold items the customer version never shows.

It cannot tell you whether the estimate is right. It communicates confidence; it does not create it. Only a record like Exhibit 3 does. Nor can it say whether customers will value the item once it exists; that needs discovery work done elsewhere.

Questions to ask before relying on it. Does the contract contain an entire-agreement clause? Who may speak for the company? What is the hit rate behind each horizon? Would you be comfortable if the customer's lawyer read the line aloud?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and late

Consumer teams publish themes rather than dates, since nobody signs anything and the damage is to trust. In B2B the roadmap becomes a negotiated artefact, so a deal desk (the group that reviews non-standard terms) matters. In a marketplace, sellers plan stock and cash around features such as settlement timing, so a slipped date can cost them money with no contract at all. Early-stage companies often sell the roadmap itself and lack the history to price it; large ones have the history and reviewers, and their risk is how many people can send a slide.

7. Common mistakes

All three share a root: the company treats the roadmap as a document, when it is a behaviour that leaves the building through many hands.

8. What good looks like

The good version of Vasani's decision has a board with three horizons, each Now item carrying a date range and a review stamp. Recall alerts sit under Next as an outcome. A cover line says intention, not undertaking, and product and legal both approved it. The deal desk reconciles the board with every order form, the hit rate is printed internally, and any dated commitment is written into the order form and priced like the figures in Exhibit 4. The slide that began the trouble would carry a version, an audience and a confidence label, and the sales head would hold a one-page guide to what he may say.

9. Closing

Vasani declined the 31 December clause. She offered Harbourline the board with recall alerts under Next, described as an outcome, and one dated commitment on a smaller item already in testing: a recall-notice export by 30 November 2026. If Vagadia still required a date for the alerts, it would be 30 June 2027 with the same credit terms, an expected cost of ₹2.4 lakh, 1.0 per cent of the fee, on the harder estimate. Vithalani objected that a rival had offered Harbourline a date. Vasani replied that a date is not a capability, and that Everline should lose a negotiation rather than fund a credit it expected to be large. She set that fallback date because it sat where Everline's own evidence, not its enthusiasm, put it.

Learn next how deal commitments constrain what a board may show, because Harbourline's clause arrived through a negotiation rather than a presentation, and the same reconciliation applies to every order form. Then learn how outcome roadmaps and OKRs (objectives and key results, a goal-setting method) tie horizons to strategy, so that Now, Next and Later answer to something other than the loudest customer.

Two questions to sit with. Which sentence in your own sales material would a buyer quote back to you? And what would your last twenty dated items say about the confidence you project?
exp40v2-plan.customer.roadmap:
Customer-facing roadmaps

What can be shown to a customer before it becomes a contract — and how two product leaders priced the answer in October 2026.

1. Two decisions, both live

On 14 October 2026 Nitya Yaghela, vice-president of product at Girnar Systems, published the quarterly customer roadmap for its logistics execution platform. Girnar closed FY26 with 141 paying accounts; after nine non-renewals and sixteen new contracts it now has 148 accounts and ₹59.2 crore of recurring revenue — a mean of ₹40.00 lakh an account (₹5,920 lakh ÷ 148). The roadmap carried seven items, two in a customer's contract.

That customer was Gandak Agro Logistics, Girnar's largest, on a one-year term from April 2026 at ₹2.40 crore — 4.1 per cent of recurring revenue (₹240 lakh ÷ ₹5,920 lakh). Its Exhibit C named e-invoice reconciliation by 31 March 2027 and driver-app localisation by 28 February 2027, both with service credits. Gandak owes thirty days' notice of non-renewal, so the renewal decision lands by 1 March 2027 — thirty days before the later date falls due.

Nirav Yarolia of Gomti Instruments had less room. Gomti sells cold-chain monitoring — loggers, gateways, a cloud console — with 3,450 loggers and 620 gateways across 48 pharmaceutical and dairy distributors. On 18 September 2026 a sales deck told a prospect that multi-site alarm routing would arrive in the first half of 2027. It needs the G4 gateway, which needs a cellular module ordered on 12 August 2026 against a 34-week lead time.

Both were doing the same arithmetic from opposite ends: Yaghela had too much specificity in the wrong channel, Yarolia a horizon honest in words and dishonest in margin. A customer-facing roadmap is an exposure problem. Specificity buys trust and sells optionality, and both must be priced over the same contract, period and population.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define a customer-facing roadmap as any artefact that tells a customer what the product will do before it does, and that the customer could reasonably act upon. The definition is channel-blind: it catches the public page, the review slide, the proposal annexe and the contract exhibit alike, because a customer who reorganises a depot around a February date has relied on it whichever it came from. Reliance, not publication, converts direction into obligation.

The word arrived from manufacturing. Motorola's technology roadmapping, documented by Willyard and McClees in Research Management in 1987, aligned long-lead semiconductor investment with product windows; Galvin generalised it in Science in 1998, and Cambridge's T-Plan work of Phaal, Farrukh and Probert in 2001 made it a method. Those roadmaps faced inward, at a supply chain. The promise problem appeared when software firms gave the artefact to buyers.

Three schools divide the field cleanly if you ask what each would sign. The disclosure-minimalist school signs “no date in front of a customer except in a contract amendment” and refuses “a date under a safe-harbour statement creates no expectation”. The outcome school, whose Now / Next / Later notation spread from ProdPad in the early 2010s and whose case was argued in Product Roadmaps Relaunched (2017), signs “we will name the problem we intend to solve in the next two quarters” and refuses “the feature”.

The third is under-read. The deliberate-commitment school signs “we will date three things a year and treat those dates as contractual”, refusing both “date everything” and “date nothing”. Its claim is empirical: vagueness reads as evasion, not humility, so a firm refusing all specificity pays in deal velocity what it saves in exposure. The schools disagree not about law but about whether a buyer can tell a confidence band from a hedge.

3. Mechanics: scoring specificity, then pricing it

Expert practice refuses to treat an item as one thing. Score each on three axes, 0 to 3. Time T: no horizon, a half-year band, a named quarter, a named date. Scope S: a problem, a capability area, a named feature, acceptance criteria. Attribution A: all customers, one account's review, a proposal, a contract exhibit with a remedy. Commitment weight W is the sum.

Exhibit 1 — Girnar's roadmap, 14 Oct 2026. W = T + S + A.
Item as publishedTSAW
Dock-wait variance, no horizon0000
Carrier-rate benchmarking, H1 FY281102
Scheduling API, Q1 FY282204
Multi-leg tendering, Q4 FY27, Gandak review2215
Yard-slot optimisation, Q3 FY27, Gopath proposal2226
Driver-app localisation, 28 Feb 2027, Exhibit C3238
E-invoice reconciliation, 31 Mar 2027, Exhibit C3339
Total, 7 items (mean W 4.86)1312934

34 ÷ 7 = 4.86; 13 + 12 + 9 = 34.

Define a class, then test every member. Call an item a hard commitment when W is 7 or more and A is 2 or more. Localisation (W 8, A 3) qualifies; e-invoice reconciliation (W 9, A 3) qualifies; yard-slot optimisation is in a signed proposal (A 2) but reaches only W 6 and fails; multi-leg tendering reaches W 5; three items have A 0. The count is two of seven, carrying 17 of 34 weight points — exactly half.

Specificity must be set against the probability it proves wrong, which is measurable. Girnar logged every item whose named quarter fell in the eight quarters of FY25 and FY26: 112 items, of which 71 shipped in the quarter named, 29 one or two quarters late and 12 were dropped. Pooled, 71 of 112 landed on time, 63.4 per cent. By horizon it is a decay curve, not a rate.

Exhibit 2 — Girnar items whose named quarter fell in April 2024–March 2026, by horizon at publication.
