The curve carries the formal rule. Exposure is commitment weight times the contract value behind it, and the heuristic is to hold the product of miss probability and exposure flat across horizons rather than specificity. Girnar's miss rate — not shipping in the quarter named — is 3 of 34, 8.8 per cent, this quarter and 12 of 15, 80.0 per cent, three or more out: a factor of 9.1 (0.8000 ÷ 0.0882). Twelve-month specificity should be about a ninth of three-month specificity.

Girnar's standard clause pays 5 per cent of the quarterly fee for each full quarter an Exhibit C item is late, capped at 20 per cent of the annual fee. On Gandak the quarterly fee is ₹240 lakh ÷ 4 = ₹60 lakh, so one quarter of delay costs ₹3.00 lakh and the cap ₹48.00 lakh. The implicit steps make it honest: a version number and expiry, an owner for every date, a reconciliation of shown against shipped, and a clock for when the customer learns.

4. The conditions, stated as tests

Five conditions make publication worthwhile, each testable. One: the buying committee's planning horizon exceeds your release cadence. Two: you hold a measured slip distribution by horizon. Three: you control every channel in Figure 2. Four: a slip's cost is bounded and priced on the contract that bears it. Five: disclosure gains more than it telegraphs.

Girnar passes one, two and four and fails three: its roadmap governs the public page while Exhibit C is drafted by a deal desk. Gomti passes three — a forty-person firm has one deck — and fails two: 620 gateways and one hardware generation give it no slip distribution, and its sample for “did the gateway arrive when we said” is one. It fails five too, since a gateway specification is copyable.

The idea turns actively misleading in three situations. Pre-product-market fit, a roadmap is a hypothesis list, and publishing it converts learning into breach. Where capability is purchased rather than built — AI-native products waiting on a vendor's releases — arrival is non-monotonic, and a dated roadmap misrepresents a distribution as a schedule. And where it has become the discovery mechanism, customers answer “when” because nobody asked “what”.

5. Hard edges and organisational seams

In multi-product firms the roadmap is published per product and read per customer. A buyer of three modules reads the union of three sets of dates and holds the vendor to the earliest, so aggregate commitment weight is super-additive in a way no product team sees. The mature answer is an account-level commitment register; the usual one is a spreadsheet nobody owns.

Two-sided businesses face a second problem: a supply-side item is a demand-side pricing signal. Telling installers that instant payouts arrive in Q2 tells buyers take rates will move, and the audiences talk. Regulated products invert the doctrine: where India's DPDP framework or a GST e-invoicing threshold sets a date, a statute has already given the customer that date.

Hardware plus software is where honesty gets expensive. Gomti's chain from module order to customer-ready gateway is 34 weeks of lead time plus 9 weeks of build and certification: 43 weeks, 301 days, of which 238 — 79.1 per cent — sit with a supplier. AI-native products invert it: the shippable unit is an accuracy level, so roadmaps there commit to evaluation thresholds on named datasets.

What mature companies do differs from what they say. The stated policy is almost always “we do not commit to dates”; the reality is a dated side-channel in the deal desk, used a few times a year, with an approval threshold and a priced remedy. Firms that handle it well have not abolished it; they have made it the only one, given it a budget, and published their slip record.

6. Eight distinctions an expert makes

Specificity is three variables. The competent practitioner argues about dates; the expert sees that scope and attribution move exposure as much as time. The tell is a roadmap with no dates and acceptance criteria in a contract exhibit — W of 6 with T of 0. An undated item can be the most binding thing on the page: the customer's engineers have already built against the endpoint.

The renewal clock runs ahead of the delivery clock. Gandak decides by 1 March 2027 on a commitment due 31 March 2027. The expert asks when the customer will learn, not when the item is due, because the signal arrives the quarter the release notes stop mentioning it. The tell is a team that learns of slips from the customer.

A contract does not change physics. The obvious reading is that contractualising a date concentrates the mind. Girnar's FY26 record says otherwise, and the expert treats a remedy clause as a price list, not an incentive. The tell is a firm that has tightened penalties twice without measuring whether its slip rate moved.

Cost and base must share a scope. A Girnar memo set two quarters of Gandak credits, ₹6.00 lakh, against recurring revenue of ₹5,920 lakh and called the commitment cheap at 0.10 per cent. On the contract that bears it the same ₹6.00 lakh is 2.50 per cent of ₹240 lakh, and the renewal it endangers is ₹240 lakh — forty times the credit, one period later. The tell is an exposure figure whose numerator and denominator come from different exhibits.

Dropping is a disclosure event, almost never treated as one. Of Girnar's 12 dropped items, 4 were announced and 8 never mentioned again: a notification rate of 4 ÷ 12, 33.3 per cent. Silent drops teach customers that the roadmap is marketing. The tell is a changelog with no vocabulary for removals.

Horizon bands relocate expectation rather than removing it. Now / Next / Later reads as this quarter, next quarter and this year to a procurement officer, that being the only mapping available. The tell is a customer quoting your “Next” column back with a month attached: the band was decoded, not accepted.

A hardware date is a commitment about someone else's factory. When 79.1 per cent of a chain sits with a supplier, the vendor's confidence is the supplier's, and the customer gets a second-hand estimate. The tell is a roadmap date defended with engineering detail and no mention of a purchase order.

The small sample is the usual condition. Most firms have a few dozen dated items and a handful of affected accounts: enough to price a decision, not to establish a rate. The expert states both in one breath. The tell of the merely competent is a confident percentage on a denominator under twenty.

7. How it varies — and where it does not

The legal mechanics do not differ between consumer and enterprise at all; what differs is whether anyone with standing is reading. A consumer roadmap creates reputational but almost no contractual exposure: no consumer reorganises a warehouse around it. Calling consumer roadmaps “lower risk” is imprecise: the same expectation risk runs through a channel with no remedy, which changes who bears the cost.

B2B and enterprise is where the schools collide, because one buyer can make a date a condition of signature. Platforms add the signalling problem above and an irreversibility: a published API deprecation date cannot be softened without stranding the developers who obeyed it.

Stage matters more than most of this. A seed-stage firm with twenty customers has no slip distribution, so it should commit narrowly and verbally, where being wrong costs an apology rather than a credit. Girnar at 148 accounts can publish Exhibit 2's curve, and has enough concentration — one account at 4.1 per cent of revenue — that one Exhibit C moves firm-level exposure.

Above that scale the problem inverts. A firm with thousands of accounts cannot negotiate per contract, so it standardises: one public roadmap, a commitment budget, a deal-desk exception process with a hard annual count. That rigidity is what keeps the union in Figure 2 inside what delivery can carry.

8. Three worked examples

Forward pricing at Girnar. The e-invoice commitment, published 14 October 2026 and due 31 March 2027, sits 5.5 months out, so Exhibit 2's next-quarter row applies: 12 of 38 items missed, 31.6 per cent. Assume one quarter of delay. Expected credit is 0.316 × ₹3.00 lakh = ₹0.95 lakh; expected renewal loss is 0.316 × 0.281 × ₹240 lakh = ₹21.3 lakh, with 0.281 the incremental non-renewal rate derived below.

Both share the 0.316 factor, so the ratio is (0.281 × ₹240 lakh) ÷ ₹3.00 lakh = ₹67.4 lakh ÷ ₹3.00 lakh = 22.5. The clause prices a twenty-second of what the commitment risks on that contract. At two quarters of delay the credit doubles to ₹6.00 lakh and the ratio falls to 11.2: the conclusion survives the assumption, the magnitude does not.

Gomti's honest-but-indefensible half-year. The module ordered on 12 August 2026 against 34 weeks arrives on 7 April 2027, day 238; 9 weeks of build and certification put customer-ready gateways at 9 June 2027, day 301. H1 2027 ends on 30 June, day 322. The margin is 21 days on a 301-day chain, 7.0 per cent. A second problem: the feature needs a G4, and G4s ship only from 9 June 2027. On a five-year replacement cycle the 620 installed gateways turn over at 124 a year, so in the 21 days to 30 June about 7 can carry it (124 × 21 ÷ 365 = 7.134) — 1.2 per cent of 620, not the half-year's 62. How many customers that is, the gateway count cannot say.

The failure: Girnar's FY26 Exhibit C programme. Nine contracts in force through FY26 carried an Exhibit C, 23 dated items between them, drawn from the same roadmap as the other 89 of the 112. Eight of the 23 slipped or were dropped, falling in six of the nine contracts. Those six had FY26 fees of ₹9.00 crore and took ₹37.50 lakh of credits — 4.17 per cent of that ₹9.00 crore, a mean of ₹6.25 lakh a contract, under clauses that varied by deal and are not the current standard.

Two of the six did not renew. Their FY26 fees were ₹3.60 crore, so FY27 revenue forgone at flat pricing is 40.0 per cent of the same ₹9.00 crore base on which credits were 4.17 per cent: a ratio of 9.6, one period later, same six contracts. Of the 135 other accounts renewing at the end of FY26, 7 lapsed, 5.2 per cent; two of six is 33.3 per cent, an increment of 28.1 points, and the exact one-tailed probability of two or more lapses in six at 5.2 per cent is 0.035 — suggestive, not settled.

The sharper finding is the one that is not a finding. Exhibit C items slipped at 8 of 23, 34.8 per cent; the 89 never contractualised at 33 of 89, 37.1 per cent. The 2.3-point gap sits against a standard error of 10.0 points on 23 items (√(0.366 × 0.634 ÷ 23)) — 0.23 of a standard error. On an unmatched-horizon comparison the clause bought nothing measurable. Recovery was structural in new business: Exhibit C capped at two items a contract, the standard clause adopted, the rest converted to outcomes, Exhibit 2 published. In FY27 to date 16 new contracts carry 6 Exhibit C items across 4 of them — a mean of 1.50 where any, against FY26's 23 ÷ 9 = 2.56.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Roadmap capture. One account's priorities colonise the published roadmap. The early warning is a rising share of dated items traceable to one logo; in Exhibit 1 four of seven items trace to two accounts, Gandak and Gopath, three to Gandak alone. The diagnostic is “which account would notice if this item vanished”, and a one-name answer is the signal. Caught late, it costs the other 146 accounts a roadmap they are not on.

Date laundering. “Targeting Q2” becomes “Q2” by the third deck and a day in Q2 by the fifth. The warning is divergence between the deck's version and the roadmap's; the diagnostic is to read the last deck actually sent. Caught late, the laundered date is what a reliance claim rests on, and a deck's version number is the only trace.

The expiring roadmap nobody expires and the silent drop are one failure in two channels: an artefact with no expiry keeps making claims after its assumptions die, and a removal with no notice teaches the customer to discount everything. Girnar's 4-of-12 notification rate is the measure; the diagnostic is to ask what the customer was told the week an item left the plan. The answer is usually nothing, and the cost falls at renewal.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is about what creates obligation. The channel-and-consideration position holds that only a contract binds, citing the safe-harbour language courts routinely accept in forward-looking statements. The reliance position holds that promissory estoppel attaches to detrimental reliance regardless of channel, citing buyers who can document the depot they rebuilt. For the first to hold, a sophisticated buyer could not show reliance on a document marked non-binding; for the second, disclaimers would be systematically ineffective.

The second is whether vagueness costs deals. The deliberate-commitment school cites win-rate gaps between dated and undated proposals. The difficulty is selection: the deals a firm chooses to date are disproportionately the ones it is already losing, so the gap is confounded by construction, and the effect needs the win rate of comparable deals it declined to date — a counterfactual almost nobody constructs. The direction is contested and the magnitude unmeasured, which is not the school being wrong.

The third is tractable. Does horizon banding reduce expectation or relocate it? The outcome school says customers stop asking for dates; sceptics say they stop asking and start assuming, which is worse because the assumption is invisible. Ask customers what month “Next” means and the question settles; few firms have.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this argues about whether to show dates. Someone who has internalised it keeps a commitment budget — the hard commitments the firm will make in a year — and spends it like capital, knowing the balance without looking. They state their slip rate by horizon from memory and volunteer it, because a discounted date beats a hedged one.

The deeper mark is scope discipline. The expert will not let a cost and a base come from different contracts, periods or populations, and names the contract a figure belongs to. They treat a removal as an announcement, the renewal calendar rather than the delivery calendar as the clock, and a sample of six as worth a decision and not a rate.

12. What they decided

Yaghela kept the e-invoice commitment and cut localisation to a quarter and a capability area (T 2, S 1, A 3, W 6), which fails the hard-commitment test, reasoning that one hard commitment at W 9 is a budget she can afford on a ₹240 lakh contract and two is not, and that the 1 March notice date meant Gandak would renew on a signal she could still control. She also moved the Gandak review slide to the published roadmap, closing the channel gap.

Yarolia did the opposite of what the margin suggested. He replaced “first half of 2027” with “available on G4 gateways shipped after June 2027”, cutting time precision by nothing and scope precision to the hardware boundary, and sent the correction to every prospect who saw the 18 September deck. His view: 7.0 per cent of margin was survivable, 1.2 per cent of the installed base not.

Three questions. First: if a remedy clause buys no delivery improvement, what is Girnar buying when it signs one, and who inside the firm is the buyer? Second: Yarolia's revision kept the date and narrowed the population — when is that more honest than narrowing the date, and when is it a sharper trap? Third: what does a competitor do with Exhibit 2?

13. Going deeper

  • The roadmap as communication — the parent idea: audience sets the risk, and unlocks channel design.
  • Roadmap commitments in deals — what priced Exhibit C; unlocks the commitment budget.
  • Strategy vs roadmap vs plan — separates artefacts a customer conflates; unlocks what may change unannounced.
  • Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later — the notation section 10 contests; unlocks the decoding experiment.
  • OKRs and goal setting — the link that lets an outcome roadmap be audited.
  • Annual and quarterly planning — the cadence fixing how often a horizon is revised, so how specific it may be.
  • Capacity planning — where Exhibit 2's distribution comes from; without it a date is an opinion.
  • Dependency management — Gomti's 79.1 per cent supplier share: date only what you own.
exp20v2-plan.outcome.roadmap:
Outcome roadmaps in practice

Delivery & Technology: Roadmapping, Planning & OKRs

1. A list with dates on it

At 9:40 on Monday 12 October 2026, Charuvi Jakhotia, head of product at Rivaaj Workflow in Ahmedabad, opened a spreadsheet from Chiraag Jajodia, the head of sales. Rivaaj sells invoicing and payment-collection software to wholesale distributors. It had 410 paying accounts, averaging ₹2.4 lakh a year each, an annual recurring revenue of ₹984 lakh (₹9.84 crore). The spreadsheet listed five features, each with a delivery date, and each attached to one of three prospects whose contracts totalled ₹39 lakh a year: ₹18 lakh, ₹12 lakh and ₹9 lakh.

Jakhotia had until Friday 16 October to present the plan for November to March to the chief executive. Her engineering lead, Chetali Jethani, had 30 engineer-weeks of discretionary capacity between Monday 2 November 2026 and Friday 26 March 2027, once maintenance was deducted. The spreadsheet alone would consume all of it.

Her own draft was different. It named a single result: raise the share of invoices that customers' buyers pay within 30 days from 52 per cent to 64 per cent. Distributors lived on that number, and Rivaaj's chief executive believed renewals did too. The draft had no feature names and no dates.

If she handed over the list, the company would build whatever the loudest deal demanded and learn nothing about collections. If she handed over only the outcome, sales would conclude product had stopped listening, and ₹30 lakh of the pipeline might walk. This page is about the third thing she could do.

2. The idea

An outcome is a change in the behaviour of customers or users that can be measured and that the business wants. An output is something the team ships. An outcome roadmap orders the outcomes the company intends to pursue, and beneath each outcome it holds bets: candidate pieces of work, each with an estimated effect and a stated uncertainty. A feature roadmap states what will be built by when. An outcome roadmap states what must become true, and treats each feature as a hypothesis about how.

The lineage is composite. Andy Grove developed objectives and key results at Intel in the 1970s, and John Doerr carried the method to Google in 1999. Janna Bastow proposed the Now / Next / Later layout around 2012, replacing dated columns with horizons of confidence. Josh Seiden's Outcomes Over Output (2019) gave the outcome vocabulary its current form. The problem all of it solves is one Jakhotia knew: dated feature lists promise precision that nobody has, and teams that deliver them on time can still change nothing.

The sentence she could repeat in any meeting was this: we commit to the result and to the evidence, and we hold the features loosely until the evidence arrives.

3. How it works

Jakhotia began by fixing the denominator. Between 1 June and 31 August 2026 active accounts raised 61,500 invoices through Rivaaj, of which 31,980 were paid within 30 days: 52.0 per cent. She used that window because invoices raised on 31 August reached day 30 on 30 September, so every invoice was settled one way or the other by the time she looked. The target of 64 per cent equals 39,360 invoices on the same volume, a gain of 12 points. Each point is 615 invoices.

Figure 1 shows the structure. The outcome sits above everything, with its denominator printed beside it. Beneath it, bets are arranged by how firmly the team believes in them, not by calendar. Now holds work that starts first, Next holds work that is funded but has not begun, and Later holds ideas the team will revisit. A bet in Later has no date and no promise attached.

Two steps are usually left implicit. First, every bet carries a cost in the same unit as the capacity, here engineer-weeks, because without that no ordering is possible. Second, requests with dates in them are not rejected; they are sorted. A date that a customer contract actually requires goes into the commitment lane with a named owner. A date that is merely a salesperson's estimate goes back into discovery.

4. A worked example

Jethani and Jakhotia scored four candidates and one commitment. "Points if it works" is the gain in the 30-day share if the bet succeeds. "Confidence" is the team's judgement that it will. Expected points is the product of the two, and points per week divides that by cost. The Tally export, sales's request, does not move the outcome; it is funded from the reserve.

BetWeeksPoints if it worksConfidenceExpected pointsPoints per week
B: UPI pay link5470%2.80.56
A: WhatsApp reminders6560%3.00.50
E: Dispute workflow9450%2.00.22
C: Credit-limit alerts8340%1.20.15
Total / average (pooled), B + A + E207.80.39

The arithmetic runs line by line. B is 4 × 0.70 = 2.8 points, over 5 weeks, which is 0.56. A is 5 × 0.60 = 3.0, over 6 weeks, 0.50. E is 4 × 0.50 = 2.0, over 9 weeks, 0.22. C is 3 × 0.40 = 1.2, over 8 weeks, 0.15. With 6 of 30 weeks reserved for commitments, 24 weeks remain. B, A and E together cost 20 weeks; adding C would cost 28, over the limit, and no other combination of 24 or fewer weeks beats 7.8 expected points. The total row's 0.39 is pooled: 7.8 over 20 weeks, not an average of the rates.

The plan therefore forecasts at most 52.0 + 7.8 = 59.8 per cent, against a 64 per cent target. At 615 invoices a point, on a quarter's 61,500 invoices, the shortfall is at least 4.2 points, 2,583 invoices. This assumes B, A and E ship before 1 January; a bet that ships in March adds almost nothing to the January to March cohort. Jakhotia decided to show that gap, not hide it.

Now change one input. Suppose Jajodia argues, reasonably, that three features are needed, and the reserve grows from 6 weeks to 12.

With 18 weeks, E no longer fits beside the other two (20 weeks), and B plus A at 11 weeks is the best available set. The extra six weeks for sales cost 7.8 − 5.8 = 2.0 expected points, or 1,230 invoices. That is the real price of the larger list, a price Jajodia can negotiate with rather than a refusal he can resent.

5. What a learner must become aware of

An outcome is not a goal in disguise

"Improve collections" is a wish. "Raise the 30-day paid share from 52 to 64 per cent among invoices raised by active accounts" names a population, a clock and a number. If a sceptic cannot say what would count as failure, the sentence is not yet an outcome.

Confidence falls with distance

Now, Next and Later are not size categories. They record how much the team knows. A bet in Now has a design and an owner; a bet in Later is a question. Moving items between columns is the roadmap working, not slipping.

Expected points do not simply add

The table sums 2.8, 3.0 and 2.0, but reminders and pay links both chase the same late payers. Where two bets reach the same invoices, their combined effect is less than the sum. Treat 7.8 as an upper reading, and say so.

The measurement lags the work

An invoice raised in March is only settled in April. A bet shipped in February can barely register by 31 March. The outcome date and the reading date are different things, and the roadmap should print both, as Figure 1 does. The baseline is June to August and the target is January to March, so season alone can move the share; measure January to March 2026 as a control before crediting any bet.

Confidence is a judgement, not a probability

Seventy per cent here means a few experienced people agreed. It is not a calibrated frequency. The remedy is to test the cheapest part of the riskiest bet early and revise the number, which is what makes the exercise honest.

It is not the same as OKRs, though it uses them

A key result is the measurable outcome; the bets are not key results. Teams that write "ship the UPI link" as a key result have rebuilt a feature roadmap inside an OKR template. The outcome roadmap is the link between that key result and the work.

Dependencies and risks belong beside the bets

Converting a feature list into an outcome roadmap means recording what each bet needs and what could stop it. The UPI pay link depends on a sponsor bank approving Rivaaj's collection flow, which the team does not control. That dependency is why its confidence is 70 per cent and not 90, and why the first two weeks of the bet should buy the approval before any screen is built.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products; small and large companies

In a consumer product, traffic is large and cheap to experiment on, so confidence updates weekly and Now moves fast; dates matter little. In B2B, as at Rivaaj, there are few accounts, some contracts name dates, and a commitment lane is essential. In a marketplace the outcome must name a side: raising buyers' repeat rate and sellers' fill rate pull in different directions, and a single blended number hides which side moved.

An early-stage company usually needs just one outcome, because runway makes a second one a distraction. A large company nests outcomes across teams, so that one team's bet becomes another team's dependency; the roadmap then has to show who is waiting on whom. In every setting the discipline is the same: name the outcome, price the bets, and keep customer dates in a visible lane.

7. Common mistakes

Features renamed as outcomes

Symptom: an outcome such as "better accounting integration". Misunderstanding: that an outcome is a nicer name for a deliverable. Diagnostic: ask whether the statement could be true while the number stays flat. If so, it is an output.

Dates removed entirely

Symptom: sales keeps a private spreadsheet of promises. Misunderstanding: no date may be given. Diagnostic: ask sales for their list of customer commitments; if the roadmap holds none of them, a shadow roadmap exists.

Confidence never revisited

Symptom: Later looks identical in March and in October. Misunderstanding: that the roadmap is a plan rather than a belief. Diagnostic: count how many bets changed confidence in the last four weeks. Zero suggests nobody is learning.

8. What good looks like

On Friday 16 October, Jakhotia brings one page: the outcome with its denominator, four bets with costs, and a commitment lane. Jajodia has seen it on Thursday and has already corrected one date. The chief executive sees a ceiling of 59.8 per cent and a named gap, and asks what would close it. Nobody has promised a feature the team has not sized, and nobody has been told the sales requests are unwelcome.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Jakhotia keeps the outcome, funds B, A and E, and puts the Tally export in a dated commitment lane for 30 November, because the ₹18 lakh and ₹12 lakh prospects who need it account for ₹30 lakh of the ₹39 lakh. The third prospect's mobile app is returned to discovery, with a request to Jajodia for the problem behind it. She chooses this because the lane protects the one date a contract genuinely requires, while the outcome keeps the other 24 weeks pointed at something measurable.

To go further, study how outcomes are decomposed into opportunities and bets, and how OKR scoring is run at quarter end; both test whether your confidence numbers deserve belief.

Two questions to sit with. Which date in your own roadmap would you defend in front of a customer, and which only exists because someone once asked? If your best-scoring bet failed in March, what would you have learned by then, and could you have learned it in November?
exp40v2-plan.outcome.roadmap:
Outcome roadmaps in practice

A roadmap of outcomes with candidate bets underneath is easy to draw and hard to keep alive. The pressure that kills it is not intellectual: it is a revenue officer with a kickoff date and a procurement officer with a clause. What follows is what expert practitioners do with the arithmetic, the lags and the seams.

1Two decisions, four days apart

On Thursday 15 January 2026, Devayani Khetan, VP Product at Svastha Freight Cloud, a transport-management platform sold to mid-market shippers, had three weeks until the FY27 sales kickoff on Wednesday 4 February. Her roadmap held one outcome: cut the share of shipment legs needing a manual exception touch from the 15.00 per cent recorded in Q3 FY26 — 186,000 touched legs of 1,240,000, across 318 paying accounts, October to December 2025 — to 10.50 per cent in Q2 FY27, July to September 2026, measured the same way.

Four candidate bets sat underneath. Dipannita Khimani, her analytics lead, had just priced them, and the honest total fell short. Dayal Kilachand, the chief revenue officer, wanted a dated feature list for the kickoff deck. Four accounts in his book carried contractual feature commitments: 1.3 per cent of 318 accounts, but ₹31.36 crore of Svastha's ₹196 crore ARR — 16.0 per cent — averaging ₹7.84 crore each against ₹0.52 crore for the remaining 314.

On Monday 19 January, Deepti Khatau, head of product at Setuka Care, a two-sided marketplace matching patients to home-physiotherapy clinicians, faced the same problem in another shape. Her founder, Dinanath Kanabar, wanted course completion on the quarterly roadmap. Completion is measured 90 days after a patient's first visit; the cohort she was about to discuss had first visits between 1 July and 30 September 2025, and its last 90-day window closed on 29 December 2025. Any outcome she set for the coming quarter would not be readable until the quarter after next.

2The idea, and who refuses to sign it

An outcome roadmap is a plan whose top-level rows are changes in measured behaviour — a rate, a share, a duration, a cost per unit — each with a baseline, a target, a measurement window and a named owner; whose second-level rows are candidate bets: work believed to move it, held as hypotheses with expected effects, costs and a stop rule. A feature roadmap names what will be built. An outcome roadmap names what must become true, and treats what gets built as replaceable.

The lineage runs from Peter Drucker's management by objectives (1954) through Andrew Grove's objectives-and-key-results discipline at Intel in the 1970s, carried outward by John Doerr, to the product literature's attack on the feature backlog after roughly 2010 — Marty Cagan's outcome-based roadmaps, Melissa Perri's build trap. The problem is specific: a feature roadmap commits on the dimension where the team has most information (what it can build) and none on the dimension where the business has a stake (whether anything changes).

Three schools disagree about propositions, not emphasis. The outcome school signs: no dated feature commitment belongs on the roadmap at all. It will not sign that enterprise procurement is a legitimate exception. The commitment school signs: where buyers run multi-year RFPs the roadmap is a sales instrument, and a vendor who cannot commit cannot sell. It will not sign that most committed features fail to move the metric they were sold on. The Goodhart school signs: any measure made a target is gamed, so an outcome roadmap merely moves the dishonesty from feature theatre to baseline theatre. It will not sign that feature roadmaps are therefore preferable.

3Mechanics: pricing the bets, and why they do not add up

The step most teams skip is the one Khimani did first. Before pricing any bet she wrote the measurement definition: numerator, touched legs; denominator, all legs billed in the quarter for accounts paying the full quarter; owner of the number, finance analytics, not product. Only then did she size each bet's addressable set — the subset of the 186,000 touched legs it could remove — and attach a kill rate from pilot evidence.

Two deductions separate a forecast from a wish. The first is overlap: Svastha's convention deducts the whole shared set at the lower of the two kill rates: 14,880 × 0.60 = 8,928 legs, or 0.72 points, leaving 5.88. A less conservative convention — independence, so the expected double-kill is 14,880 × 0.64 × 0.60 = 5,714 legs, or 0.46 points — leaves 6.14. The second is the firm's historical landing rate: across Q3 FY25 to Q2 FY26 Svastha's roadmap forecast 12.50 points of movement on this metric family and realised 7.25, a landing rate of 58.0 per cent. Applied to 5.88 points that gives 3.41, so 15.00 − 3.41 = 11.59 per cent. Under the independence convention, 6.14 × 0.58 = 3.56, giving 11.44 per cent. Either way Svastha misses 10.50.

The second-order effect is the one Kilachand will feel. Because the outcome is a rate it is volume-neutral: Svastha expects 1,560,000 legs over about 360 qualifying accounts in Q2 FY27, 25.8 per cent more legs than the baseline quarter. At 10.50 per cent that is 163,800 touched legs; at 11.59 per cent, 180,804 — a 1.09-point gap worth 17,004 legs of manual work, which is the form a staffing conversation can act on.

4When it applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions can be stated as testable claims. (i) Readability: on a one-quarter planning horizon, the outcome can be measured at least twice. (ii) Control: the team owns enough of the causal path that a plausible bet portfolio can move it. (iii) Freedom: commitments the business has already sold do not fix the feature set.

Neither clears the bar, and both will ship an outcome roadmap anyway, which tells you the conditions are not a gate but a map of where the work will be. Each failure prescribes a repair: a readability failure forces a leading indicator; a control failure forces a bet you do not own onto your roadmap; a freedom failure forces a dated commitment lane alongside the outcomes.

The idea is actively misleading in two situations. The first is an obligation: a statutory filing, a security remediation, a certification renewal. These have dates fixed elsewhere and no interesting metric; dressing them as outcomes ("improve compliance posture") buries a hard date in soft language. The second is a bet-the-company platform rewrite, where the measurable effect is zero for three quarters and then discontinuous. An outcome roadmap applied to it produces either a fake intermediate metric or a row that looks like failure for a year.

5Hard edges and organisational seams

In multi-product companies the fight is whether an outcome belongs to a product or a portfolio. A portfolio outcome — "reduce blended support contacts per active account" — is movable by six teams and owned by none; the settlement is per-product addressable sets under one portfolio outcome, Exhibit 1's structure one level up.

In two-sided markets the outcome has two populations and you must say which. Setuka's completion rate is a patient-side measure whose dominant driver is clinician continuity, a routing property. Setuka put continuity on the product roadmap as a bet it does not own, with the supply-operations lead named as owner — an arrangement most companies describe as cross-functional and run as a request queue.

In regulated markets the outcome and obligation lanes must be visibly separate, or the first audit converts the roadmap into a dated list. In hardware-plus-software the two lanes are forced by physics: tooling, certification and channel stocking run twelve to eighteen months ahead, while firmware and cloud do not. In AI-native products the subtler problem is baseline drift — swap the model and the denominator's composition changes, so the only stable comparison is a frozen evaluation set alongside the live metric.

The seam that breaks most often is definitional. Product owns the roadmap; finance or analytics owns the number; the two define "active account" differently, and the discrepancy surfaces in the quarter the target is missed. Mature companies name a single owner of each definition and date every change to it. What they say they run is one roadmap. What they run is two lanes and a reconciliation meeting.

6Eight nuances

Dates move, they do not disappear. The tell is that an expert's outcome roadmap carries more dates than the one it replaced: a commitment date, a readout date per bet, a cohort-close date. The obvious reading — outcomes are the undated alternative — inverts the practice: undatedness is what made the old roadmap safe to ignore.

Read lag, not build time, sets the cadence. The tell is that an expert asks "when can we read it?" before "when can we ship it?" Setuka's 90-day window means a bet shipped in July is judged in January. The obvious reading is that faster shipping fixes this; it does not: the constraint is measurement, and the repair is a leading indicator with a published conversion assumption.

Sales wants safety, not features. The tell is that the expert offers a dated commitment on a narrow slice rather than refusing dates. A revenue officer is punished for promises broken, not promises absent. The obvious reading — that sales is attached to feature lists — mistakes a risk position for a preference.

Overlapping bets cannot be summed. The tell is a forecast below the sum of its parts, with the deduction named: Svastha's 6.60 becomes 5.88. The obvious reading is that summing is conservative because kill rates are guesses. It is not: overlap bias and estimate error run in different directions and do not cancel.

The denominator moves while you work. The tell is an expert quoting the outcome twice — on the fixed baseline cohort and on the live population. Svastha's leg volume grows 25.8 per cent between two windows that are also different quarters of the year, with unknown mix. The obvious reading, that a rate is comparable across periods by construction, is the commonest source of a roadmap result nobody believes.

The biggest lever often sits outside product. The tell is an ops or pricing bet on the product roadmap with someone else's name against it. Setuka's 30.9-point continuity gap is a routing property, not a screen. The obvious reading calls this scope creep. The alternative is worse: an outcome you own and cannot move.

Sequence by information value, not expected effect. The tell is a small bet with a wide interval and a cheap read scheduled ahead of a large bet with a narrow one. The obvious reading ranks by expected movement. That holds only if every estimate is equally trustworthy — precisely what the first quarter of an outcome roadmap exists to discover.

An outcome you cannot lose is not an outcome. The tell is that the expert can state, unprompted, the number that would make them stop a named bet. The obvious reading calls stop rules pessimism. They are the only thing separating a bet from a commitment with better vocabulary, and their absence turns a roadmap of outcomes into a roadmap of features in four quarters.

7How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products outcomes are readable in days and the discipline is almost free; the failure is proliferation — twelve outcomes, no portfolio. In B2B and enterprise the outcomes are readable but the freedom condition bites, and the live question is whether a dated commitment lane is a concession or part of the design. Svastha's 16.0 per cent of ARR keeps the question live.

On platforms and marketplaces the outcome must name a side, and the cross-side effect is usually the dominant term. For hardware and physical goods the difference is lead time, not philosophy: an outcome roadmap works well on the firmware and cloud layers of a product whose tooling runs on a dated plan. For AI products much of what is called distinctive is not — the bets are still bets with addressable sets — but baseline drift is new, and a frozen evaluation set is the only honest denominator when the model underneath changes mid-quarter.

Stage matters more than type. Pre-product-market-fit, outcome roadmaps are ceremony: the baseline is too noisy and the horizon too short, and a list of the next four things to learn is better. From roughly Series B it starts paying: there are now enough teams for "which of you is moving this?" to be a real question. At scale it survives only if somebody owns each metric definition; otherwise it decays into a dashboard with a roadmap stapled to it.

8Three worked examples

Svastha: the gap you publish

Khetan's arithmetic is Exhibit 1 and the waterfall. The expert move is not finding a fifth bet in three weeks; it is publishing 11.59 per cent beside the 10.50 per cent target, so the 1.09-point gap — 17,004 legs at Q2 FY27 volume — becomes a resourcing question now, not a credibility question in October.

Setuka: decomposing a lagging outcome

Of 24,800 patients with a first visit in Q2 FY26, 13,392 attended a third visit within 21 days (54.0 per cent) and 8,184 completed their course within 90 days (33.0 per cent overall, and 61.1 per cent of the visit-3 group, every completer having attended visit 3). A 42.0 per cent completion target therefore needs visit-3 attendance at 68.7 per cent if the 61.1 per cent conditional holds, or the conditional at 77.8 per cent if attendance does not move. Split by clinician continuity, the 11,160 patients who saw one clinician throughout completed at 50.0 per cent (5,580) against 19.1 per cent (2,604 of 13,640) for the rest.

Saritya Instruments: where it failed

Saritya, a connected water-quality instrument maker, replaced its dated roadmap with three outcomes in April 2025. Seven of eleven channel partners asked for a dated commitment letter; four cut forward orders. The order book for the October 2025–March 2026 half, ₹14.00 crore as committed on 31 March 2025, stood at ₹10.64 crore by 31 July 2025 — down ₹3.36 crore, or 24.0 per cent. It failed because an outcome roadmap presumes the firm can reallocate work once it learns, and tooling and stocking commitments had spent that freedom. The recovery, from September 2025, was the two-clock structure: outcomes kept for firmware and cloud, dated milestones restored for the instrument. On the like-for-like measure — the order book for the October 2026–March 2027 half, valued on 31 March 2026 — the book stood at ₹13.44 crore, 96.0 per cent of the ₹14.00 crore the October 2025–March 2026 half held on 31 March 2025. Not full recovery.

9Failure modes and their early signs

The unmovable outcome. Early sign: two quarters in, it has no bet underneath with a priced addressable set. Diagnostic: "what would we have to observe next month to know this is moving?" Caught late, it costs a year of planning cycles re-wording the same row.

The feature in outcome clothing. Early sign: exactly one bet per outcome, and the outcome's wording names the bet. Diagnostic: "if this bet fails, what else would we try?" If there is no answer, it is a commitment. Caught late, it is shipped, the metric does not move, and the method takes the blame.

The shadow roadmap. Early sign: account teams quoting delivery dates product never gave. Diagnostic: "show me the last three decks sent to prospects." Caught late, the cost is a renewal lost on a promise nobody in product knew existed — Saritya in slower motion.

Baseline laundering. Early sign: the baseline is restated in the same review that reports the result. Diagnostic: "what was this number when we set the target, and who approved the change?" Caught late, the series becomes uninterpretable and no outcome can ever be shown to have failed.

The summed forecast. Early sign: the portfolio forecast exactly equals the sum of its bets. Diagnostic: "which two of these act on the same users?" Caught late, the shortfall arrives as a surprise in October rather than as a known 1.09 points in January.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

The outcome purists' strongest form is empirical: in most portfolios a minority of shipped features move their target metric, so a roadmap committing to features commits to a distribution it knows to be bad, and every dated exception sets the precedent for the next. Svastha's own 58.0 per cent landing rate is evidence that forecasts overshoot, which is half their case. They are wrong if the commitment itself has value independent of the feature. Svastha's four clause-holding accounts, at ₹7.84 crore of ARR each, are where that question has money on it.

The commitment realists' strongest form is institutional: in enterprise and hardware the buyer's planning cycle requires dates, and a vendor offering only outcomes transfers planning risk to a customer who cannot carry it. Saritya's ₹3.36 crore is their exhibit. They are wrong if narrow dated slices can satisfy procurement without fixing the rest of the portfolio — the two-clock claim, whose evidence is thin: 96.0 per cent recovery, one company, one year.

The Goodhart sceptics' strongest form is that every mechanism above is a gaming surface: targets sandbagged, baselines laundered, denominators quietly redefined, while a feature roadmap at least fails visibly. They are wrong if definitional ownership and dated definition changes hold under pressure. Nobody has shown that at scale, and the honest position is that this is an open question, not a settled practice.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces outcome-shaped rows and defends them on principle. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They write the measurement definition before the bet, and know who owns it. They quote a forecast below the sum of its parts and say what they deducted and why. They publish the gap between forecast and target while it is still a resourcing question. And they give the commercial organisation a narrow dated promise instead of a lecture, because the request was never about features.

The behavioural tell is how they talk about failure. A studier reports that a bet did not land and proposes another. A master reports which prior belief the result falsified, what the stop rule said, and what the landing rate now is — to them the roadmap is an instrument for improving the firm's forecasting, and the quarter's metric only its output.

12Closing: what each of them did

Khetan went to the 4 February kickoff with the outcome unchanged at 10.50 per cent, the forecast printed beside it at 11.59, and a dated commitment — 29 May 2026 — for Bet A, scoped to the four accounts holding contractual clauses and nothing else. Her reasoning: Kilachand needed one promise he could keep, not a list, and a published gap in January is cheaper than a missed target in October.

Khatau kept completion as Setuka's annual outcome and put visit-3-within-21-days at 68.7 per cent on the quarterly roadmap, with the 61.1 per cent conditional written down as an assumption to retest each cohort, and clinician continuity listed as a bet owned by supply operations, not by her.

  1. Svastha's 58.0 per cent landing rate came from four quarters and a family of metrics. On what grounds would you apply it to a single metric for a single quarter — and what would you do instead?
  2. Khatau's quarterly target rests on a conditional rate she cannot hold fixed. Which of her two routes to 42.0 per cent is the safer commitment, and what evidence would settle it?
  3. Saritya recovered to 96.0 per cent. Is the two-clock roadmap a solution or a managed defeat, and what result would change your answer?

13Going deeper

  1. Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later — the horizon grammar these outcomes sit inside; it unlocks expressing confidence without dates.
  2. OKRs and goal setting — outcomes are OKR-shaped, and the key-result mechanics are where baselines and targets get written properly.
  3. Strategy vs roadmap vs plan — tells you which document owes the dates, and stops the roadmap absorbing both other jobs.
  4. The roadmap as communication — the artefact Kilachand consumes; it unlocks the audience-specific cut that prevents shadow roadmaps.
  5. Annual and quarterly planning — the cadence that decides whether your read lag fits the horizon at all.
  6. Capacity planning — converts a 1.09-point gap into people and quarters, the only form a resourcing debate can take.
  7. Dependency management — the overlap arithmetic in Exhibit 1 is a dependency problem in disguise; it unlocks sequencing by information value.
  8. Milestones and release planning — how the commitment clock is run, and what a narrow dated promise costs to keep.
exp20v2-plan.commitment.levels:
Commitment Levels and Confidence Language

Which items on this roadmap are we actually committed to?

1. A letter due on Thursday

On Monday 12 October 2026, Karan Sojitra, head of product at Corbel Cloud, an Ahmedabad company that sells dispatch and invoicing software to road-freight operators, opened a draft renewal letter from Kartik Suthar, the head of sales. The customer, a Surat textile-logistics group paying ₹84 lakh a year, would sign by Friday 30 October if the letter listed five features with a delivery date of Friday 18 December: e-way bill auto-fill, customer portal invoices, rate-card import, driver app offline mode and Tally export. Kartik's draft used one verb for all five: "will deliver".

The customer's own contract draft added a credit of 5 per cent of the annual fee for every month a listed item ran late, which is ₹4.20 lakh a month. Karan's roadmap had a row for each feature, plus a sixth, a route optimisation pilot, and beside every row it said "Q4". Nothing on it told Kartik which rows were promises and which were hopes. That morning the CTO, Kalpen Sodhani, had called two of the five "probably fine, or probably not."

The letter was due out on Thursday 15 October. Promise all five and miss two, and Corbel would pay credits and teach a customer that "will" meant "might". Promise too little, and the renewal could drift to a rival. Karan's question was the one this page answers: which of these are we actually committed to?

2. The idea

A commitment level is a named grade attached to a roadmap item, stating how far the company has bound itself to deliver it. Confidence language is the controlled vocabulary that maps each grade to the words anyone may use about the item outside the product team. Together they solve a specific problem: a roadmap puts promises, forecasts and hopes in one identical format, and its readers treat every date as a promise.

Nobody owns the idea outright. One thread comes from intelligence analysis. In 1964 Sherman Kent proposed "words of estimative probability", fixing "almost certain" at about 93 per cent give or take 6, and "probable" at about 75 give or take 12, because readers of the same word put wildly different numbers on it. The other thread is product roadmapping. Around 2012 Janna Bastow's Now-Next-Later format replaced calendar dates with horizons so roadmaps would stop being read as schedules. Commitment levels refine that for the places where some dates must be firm.

Karan's sentence for the meeting was: "A promise is an item we have already decided what to give up in order to keep; everything else is a forecast, and we say so with a number behind the word."

3. How it works

The mechanics have six steps, and steps four to six are the ones practitioners usually leave implicit. First, define each level by an entry test rather than by enthusiasm: Figure 2 gives Karan's. Second, estimate each item's effort in person-weeks and its probability of landing by the date a customer would see. Third, compute capacity: Corbel had 8 engineers for a window of about ten weeks, so 80 person-weeks, less 25 per cent held for support and defects, leaving 60 plannable.

Fourth, apply the buffer rule: committed effort may fill no more than two-thirds of plannable capacity, here 40 person-weeks. The remaining third absorbs the overruns that every estimate eventually produces. Without this step a "committed" label is only a mood.

Fifth, and implicitly, decide who may upgrade an item (Karan and Kalpen together, never sales alone) and which dimension is promised, the date or the scope. Sixth, write the downgrade rule, which says what the customer is told on the day an item's probability falls below 0.90, and attach the permitted verb to every outbound sentence, so that the grade survives the journey from roadmap to letter.

4. A worked example

Table 1 is Karan's view on Monday 12 October. The first three items qualify as committed (0.90 or above, 34 person-weeks together, under the 40 ceiling with 6 spare). The next two are planned. The pilot stays exploring and consumes no delivery capacity: its 20 weeks are what building it would cost, not a scheduled amount. Committed plus planned is 62 against 60 plannable, Adding any planned item breaks the ceiling (34 + 10 = 44 against 40), and both are under 0.90, which is why they cannot be promised.

ItemEffort (person-weeks)P(on time by 18 Dec)Level
E-way bill auto-fill140.95Committed
Customer portal invoices120.90Committed
Rate-card import80.90Committed
Driver app offline mode180.70Planned
Tally export100.60Planned
Route optimisation pilot200.30Exploring
Total82–34 + 28 + 20

Now the cost of Kartik's draft. Assume, as a simplification, that the items succeed or fail independently. Promising all five as "will" then succeeds in full with probability 0.95 × 0.90 × 0.90 × 0.70 × 0.60 = 0.323, about 32 per cent. Promising only the committed three gives 0.95 × 0.90 × 0.90 = 0.7695, about 77 per cent. As a credit, driver offline mode alone costs 0.30 × ₹4.20 lakh = ₹1.26 lakh in expectation, if a miss means one month's delay.

Second pass. On Wednesday 14 October the e-way bill estimate rises from 14 to 22 person-weeks after a tax-portal interface change; the team judges its probability unchanged at 0.95. Committed effort becomes 22 + 12 + 8 = 42, over the 40 ceiling by 2. The rule demands a demotion, and the rate-card import, the smallest, drops to planned (0.90, but held out by the 40-week ceiling). Committed effort returns to 22 + 12 = 34, and the joint probability rises to 0.95 × 0.90 = 0.855, about 86 per cent. One changed input moved one item, and the promise got safer only because it got smaller.

5. Nuances to learn

Confidence is not commitment

Confidence is a belief about the world; commitment is a decision about consequences. An item can be 95 per cent likely and uncommitted, because nobody has agreed what to sacrifice if it slips, and a legally fixed deadline can bind the company at 60 per cent odds, which is a signal to add capacity rather than to relabel the item. Grade the decision as well as the odds.

Odds compound

Each of the three committed items looks safe alone. Together they are not, as Figure 4 shows, and a customer letter is judged on the bundle.

Name the fixed dimension

Time, scope and capacity cannot all be fixed. A real commitment says which one is promised: "this feature by 18 December" fixes both date and scope, and only the order of other work can flex. If the customer cares about the date, promise a smaller scope.

Horizon is not grade

Now-Next-Later says when the team expects to work on something; it says nothing about how bound the company is. An item in "Now" can be exploring, and an item in "Later" can be committed, because a contract fixed it.

Grades expire

Uncertainty shrinks as work proceeds, a pattern associated with Barry Boehm's 1981 estimating work and often called the cone of uncertainty. A grade assigned on 12 October is a measurement taken on 12 October; Corbel re-grades every Monday and on any estimate change.

Calibration decides whether the words mean anything

Of 20 items that sales had promised customers by a date in the previous four quarters, 17 shipped by that date, or 85 per cent; this is not a like-for-like test, since those promises were never graded 0.90. With 20 trials the standard error around a 0.90 rate is √(0.90 × 0.10 / 20) = 0.067, so 85 per cent neither confirms nor contradicts the 0.90 line. It does mean the threshold deserves evidence before anyone trusts it.

What it cannot tell you

Grades say how bound an item is, not whether it deserves building, nor whether its estimate is honest. A newcomer should ask who assigned the probability, what history backs it, who may upgrade it, and what the company gives up on a miss.

6. Across products and stages

In a consumer product the audience for a promise is the public, a store reviewer or a regulator, dates are rarely published, and a miss costs reputation across millions at once, so the grade mostly governs what marketing may announce. In B2B the promise lives in a contract, a security questionnaire or an email from sales, each customer sees a different slice, and credit clauses put a price on a miss, as at Corbel.

A marketplace promises to two sides at once. A committed seller tool can change what buyers see, so a commitment to one side needs a check on the other, and promises to suppliers often carry incentive payments. An early-stage company can run on one person's judgement, a founder who alone upgrades items, but a large one needs a shared register and notices that probabilities multiply across teams.

7. Common mistakes

Grade inflation. The symptom is a roadmap on which most items read "committed". The misunderstanding is treating the grade as a reward for importance rather than a claim on capacity. The cheapest diagnostic: add committed effort and compare it with the buffered ceiling, 40 person-weeks at Corbel.

The grade stripped in transit. The symptom is a customer quoting "Q4" back to your support desk in an escalation. The misunderstanding is that the grade lives on the internal roadmap rather than in the sentence. The diagnostic: ask the account manager to read aloud the sentence the customer saw, and find its verb in the vocabulary.

Frozen grades. The symptom is an item reported "committed" at three consecutive monthly reviews while its date moved twice. The misunderstanding is treating a grade as a label rather than a current estimate. The diagnostic: list every item whose date has moved since it was graded, and require a re-grade or a defence in the same meeting.

8. What good looks like

The same decision handled well produces a letter in three parts, each with its own verb. Committed items carry "will", the date of 18 December and the credit clause. Planned items carry "we expect to", the same target and a written status notice if their probability moves, but no credit. Exploring items appear as "we are investigating", with no date at all.

Behind the letter stand a one-page vocabulary table that sales can read in a minute, the capacity arithmetic and a Monday re-grade. The customer receives fewer promises, and the ones it receives are backed by something it can see. When committed effort falls back to 32 person-weeks or less, Karan can upgrade rate-card import in writing.

9. What Karan decides

On Thursday 15 October Karan sends the three-part letter. The letter names six items in all, two of them committed, and Kartik negotiates the credit clause so that it applies to the committed pair only. Karan's reasoning follows his own table: after the 14 October re-estimate, two items fit under the ceiling, and the pair together carries 0.855 odds, a number he can defend aloud. He accepts a smaller headline in exchange for a letter Corbel can keep. Kartik loses the word "will" on three features, but keeps the right to say, truthfully, that all three have a named owner and are tracked weekly. The ₹84 lakh is better protected by a letter that survives the first missed date.

To learn next, read “Roadmap commitments in deals”, since the contract is where grades turn into money, and then “The roadmap as communication”, which explains why grades must travel with the item.

Two questions to sit with. First, with 17 of 20 on time in the record, what evidence would make you set the committed line at 0.90 rather than lower, and who in your company would have to agree? Second, if a customer refuses any letter containing the word "expect", what would you trade, the date, the scope or the price, and who may make that trade?
exp40v2-plan.commitment.levels:
Commitment Levels and Confidence Language

Which items on this roadmap are we actually committed to?

1. Two letters and a mould

On Monday 19 October 2026, Laxita Thakrar, vice-president of product at Dhruvam Systems, a Pune company whose claims-adjudication platform runs behind four Indian health insurers, read the renewal letter her chief revenue officer meant to send that Thursday. Lavit Tulsiyan had lifted five items off the roadmap and used one verb for all five: Dhruvam will deliver, by Thursday 31 December 2026. The customer, a Chennai insurer paying ₹3.40 crore a year, would sign on Friday 30 October. Its draft attached a credit of 4 per cent of the annual fee — ₹13.6 lakh — for every listed item a month late.

Laxita's roadmap carried a probability against every item. Three of Lavit's five sat above 0.90, one at 0.78 and one at 0.62. Nothing in his draft separated them. Her question was not which items would land, but which Dhruvam could call a promise.

Three days later, on Thursday 22 October, Lakhan Taparia met the same question in a form that would not wait. He ran product at Dvaita Devices, a Bengaluru firm selling a cold-chain temperature logger and app to dairy and vaccine distributors. The Rev-C tooling order had to reach the Hosur contract manufacturer by Friday 20 November to hold a first shipment of Friday 30 April 2027. Six of the fifteen Rev-C items depended on the mould.

Each of those six would carry its label for 161 days with no way to revise it, while the nine app items could be re-graded until the branch cut on Friday 2 April. One ladder; two meanings of committed.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A commitment level is a named grade on a roadmap item stating what the organisation has given up to keep it. Confidence language is the controlled vocabulary mapping each grade to the words anyone may use about it outside the product team. The two are useless apart: a grade with no mandated sentence never reaches the customer; a vocabulary with no entry test is etiquette.

The problem predates software. In 1964 Sherman Kent, who ran the United States Office of National Estimates, published a note on words of estimative probability, having found colleagues read “serious possibility” in a 1951 estimate as anything from 20 to 80 per cent. His remedy was a fixed table: “probable” near 75 per cent, “almost certain” near 93 per cent. Software came late: Barry Boehm's 1981 funnel of narrowing estimate ranges, later renamed the cone of uncertainty, and the 2011 Scrum Guide replacing commitment with forecast.

Three schools now disagree. The calibrationists hold a grade is a probability and must be audited; they will sign “a tier whose measured hit rate is 0.74 may not be called committed” and will not sign “drop dates, because dates get read as promises”. The horizon school, following Now–Next–Later, holds the date is the defect; it will sign “an item more than a quarter out carries no date” and not “a probability makes a distant date safe”. The contract school holds that only money grades anything; it will sign “there are two levels, contractually committed and everything else”, and not that any middle grade survives a sales compensation plan.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice runs in six steps, of which four to six are usually implicit. First, define each tier by an entry test, not enthusiasm. Dhruvam's committed test has three clauses, all of which must hold (Figure 1): p at or above 0.90 by the published date, the named engineers staffed to that date, and the item inside a capped share of plannable capacity. Second, estimate effort and probability item by item.

Exhibit 1. Dhruvam's quarter, graded 19 October. The letter listed items 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7.

* Item 5's 0.97 assumes a contractor extension unapproved on 19 October, so it fails the staffing clause and any date quoted for it must carry that condition.

Third, build capacity down to a cap (Exhibit 2). Fourth, the first implicit step, hold the reserve against defects rather than spend it: a committed label on unreserved capacity is a mood. Fifth, make upgrade and downgrade asymmetric: an upgrade needs Laxita and the engineering director, Lohini Thobhani, together, while either may downgrade alone. Sixth, attach the permitted sentence.

Exhibit 2. The capacity build-down behind the cap.

Now the classification. Three items clear the probability clause: 1 at 0.94, 3 at 0.95 and 5 at 0.97. Only two clear the definition, because item 5's staffing fails, dropping it to PLANNED despite the highest p on the page. Their effort is 14 plus 9, line E, well inside the cap of 54.6; capacity is not what binds. The roadmap also asks 105.0 person-weeks of an 81.9 plannable quarter, 23.1 more, or 28.2 per cent over, so something below the committed tier will not happen.

The treatment that matters is the joint probability of a multi-item promise. Lavit's five items carry 0.94, 0.78, 0.95, 0.97 and 0.62; under independence the chance all five land by 31 December is their product, 0.419. But one squad builds all five, so a shock moves them together. Dependence need not be assumed: the five sum to 4.26, so the chance of all five cannot fall below 4.26 − 4, that is 0.26, nor rise above the smallest, 0.62. The honest sentence for Lavit is “between 0.26 and 0.62, not the 0.419 that independence would give, and the shared squad argues for the upper half of that range”. Run it on the two that pass the test, 0.94 and 0.95: they sum to 1.89, so the floor is 0.89 and the ceiling 0.94. Cutting five to two does not merely raise the odds; it collapses the range they can lie in.

Step seven, in companies that have done this a while: audit the tiers.

Exhibit 3. Dhruvam's record, the four quarters to Wednesday 30 September 2026.
