34/46 = 73.9 per cent; 17/31 = 54.8 per cent. The 51 delivered are 51 of the 77 dated items, 66.2 per cent.

Two readings of Exhibit 3 differ in strength. The committed tier's 34 of 46 is 73.9 per cent against a claimed 0.90. At a true 0.90, 46 items yield 41.4 on average, with standard deviation the square root of 46 × 0.9 × 0.1, or 2.03; so 34 sits 7.4 low, 3.6 standard deviations. A finding. The planned tier's 17 of 31 is 54.8 per cent, inside its band but at the bottom; against that band's rough midpoint of 0.70 it expects 21.7 with standard deviation 2.55, so 17 is 1.8 standard deviations low. That is a suspicion, and the distinction is the discipline.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

The method earns its cost under three conditions, each testable.

First, some audience must act differently on “will” than on “we expect to”. At Dhruvam it does: the difference is ₹13.6 lakh a month per item. At Dvaita it half does: the contract manufacturer acts on the grade, since tooling is ordered against it, but the distributors never see a roadmap.

Second, outcomes must be observable fast enough to recalibrate. Dhruvam graded 94 items in four quarters, enough for a numeric band. Dvaita has graded only 19 hardware items, across three revisions in about three years, and 12 of the 19 landed on time, a hit rate of 0.63. A normal-approximation 95 per cent interval around it is 1.96 × the square root of 0.63 × 0.37 ÷ 19, or ±0.22, so 0.41 to 0.85; had two of the seven misses landed on time, 14 of 19 would put 0.90 inside it. A tier that cannot distinguish 0.63 from 0.85 cannot be said to run at 0.90, and a number nobody can audit within the publisher's tenure is decoration.

Third, somebody must be able to refuse an upgrade. Dhruvam encodes this in its two-signature rule; Dvaita gets it from physics: after 20 November the mould exists and no seniority re-grades it.

The idea is actively misleading in one configuration, which Daksheya Labs discovered expensively: when the grade attaches to shipping while the customer buys an outcome. A ladder measuring the wrong event looks calibrated and still breaks promises it appears to be keeping.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In a multi-product company two roadmaps' grades are not independent when one platform team serves both, yet they are published as though they were and nobody owns the joint statement; mature firms cap committed effort per shared team, not per product. On a marketplace the supply-side commitment is deliverable and the demand-side consequence is not: shipping a seller-onboarding flow is a promise you can keep; the liquidity that seller was told to expect is not. Experts grade the artefact, forecast the outcome.

In a regulated product the date arrives from outside, as Dhruvam's NHCX claim-status API did, its go-live fixed by a deadline the insurer had filed with its board. Here probability does not set the grade; the grade sets the staffing. An externally fixed date the team puts at 0.94 is a resourcing instruction, not a forecast.

Hardware plus software defeats single ladders: one word carries a 161-day lock on one side of a product and 28 days on the other (Figure 3). AI-native products add an axis — what is in doubt is not whether code ships but whether a measured threshold holds, which can move as inputs drift.

At the seams, practice is less tidy than publication: grades leak upward, because a quota-carrying seller reads PLANNED as committed. Large firms keep two roadmaps, a graded internal one and a shorter external one holding only the committed tier, with that tier's audited hit rate printed on it.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A grade is a statement about sacrifice, not confidence. The tell is the answer to “what did we cut to protect this?” If nothing was, it is a forecast in promise's clothes. The obvious reading, that high probability earns the top tier, is wrong: probability is an output of staffing, not an input.

Correlation helps a promise and hurts a portfolio. Items built by one squad move together, which pushes the five-item chance from the independent 0.419 toward the 0.62 ceiling rather than below it. The tell is one squad's name against every committed row. The obvious reading, that shared teams make promises riskier, is wrong for the promise, right for the quarter.

Expected penalty and kept word are different quantities. The ₹10.06 lakh exposure computed below depends only on the five marginal probabilities; the chance of keeping the whole letter depends on how they co-move. The tell is finance and the account team quoting different risks off one list, both rightly.

A tier is named by its worst quarter, not its mean. An average hides the quarter a reorganisation emptied the reserve, and Exhibit 3 shows only a pooled rate. Experts ask for the minimum first.

Upgrades must cost more than downgrades. Dhruvam's rule is asymmetric because a symmetric one ratchets upward: upgrade pressure is continuous, downgrade pressure arrives once and late. The tell is a quarter with upgrades and no downgrades — not stability but an un-audited ladder.

The grade must attach to the event the customer is buying. The tell is an on-time rate far above the acceptance rate. The obvious reading, that delivery discipline is working, is wrong: the ladder measures a milestone the customer does not value, and the gap surfaces as a dispute.

Confidence language dies at the handoff. Grades live in the roadmap tool; promises live in renewal letters and release notes. The tell is a customer document with dates and none of the permitted verbs, so an expert audits outbound documents, not the roadmap.

A low-probability item still commits money. EXPLORING publishes no date and promises nothing, yet item 6 consumes 25 of Exhibit 1's 105 person-weeks. The tell is a reserve raided for discovery. The obvious reading, that exploratory work carries no commitment, confuses a promise to a customer with one to the quarter.

7. How this changes by product type and company stage

The arithmetic does not change across product types, and claiming it does is the usual mistake. What changes is the lag between label and feedback, and who reads it. In consumer products almost nobody outside reads a roadmap, so the ladder is internal arbitration and a small committed tier breaks nothing. In B2B, and especially enterprise software, the grade becomes contractual language, as at Dhruvam, and inflation costs cash. On platforms third-party developers commit on top of the grade, so a downgrade propagates, which is why mature platform teams give deprecation dates extra notice. The marketplace, hardware and AI differences are those above: differences in what the grade attaches to, not in how it is computed.

By stage the difference is real but simpler than it looks. A seed-stage company has no calibration data, so numeric bands are theatre and two levels — promised, not promised — are all its evidence supports. From Series A to Series C the ladder earns its keep, because there is a sales motion generating promises and enough history to audit them. At scale the constraint becomes disclosure, since a committed external date interacts with investor communication and, for a listed Indian company, with SEBI's materiality obligations.

8. Three worked examples

Dhruvam's letter. Treat a missed item as costing one month's credit of ₹13.6 lakh, which makes every figure here a floor, since real slips run longer. Listing all five, expected credit is the sum of their miss probabilities, 0.06 + 0.22 + 0.05 + 0.03 + 0.38 = 0.74, times ₹13.6 lakh, or ₹10.06 lakh. For a letter whose credit clause covers only items 1 and 3, the miss probabilities sum to 0.11 and expected credit is ₹1.50 lakh, 6.7 times smaller. Neither figure depends on how the items co-move, because expectations add whatever the dependence; only the all-five probability of 0.26 to 0.62 does.

Dvaita's freeze. One Rev-C feature, a second probe port, needs board area and a connector. Committing it in the mould risks a retool of ₹18 lakh and 11 weeks if the spec changes, which the supplier review put at 0.35: expected cash cost ₹6.3 lakh. Hedging — building the port in but grading the feature PLANNED and shipping it dark — costs ₹41 a unit on a 60,000-unit first build, ₹24.6 lakh, with no schedule risk. The hedge costs ₹18.3 lakh more, but the delay comes only with the spec change, so it avoids 0.35 × 11 = 3.85 expected weeks and pays only if a week is worth more than ₹18.3 ÷ 3.85 = ₹4.75 lakh. Laveena Tejani's model puts a week of deferred first shipment at ₹3.1 lakh of gross margin, averaged over the first twenty weeks and a floor; that is 0.65 of break-even, so the hedge clears it only if the true value is 1.5 times her floor.

Daksheya Labs, where it failed. Daksheya sells AI document extraction to lenders. In the quarter to Tuesday 30 June 2026 it graded 12 items COMMITTED and 11 of the 12 shipped on time, 92 per cent. Yet five were rejected at acceptance, because field-level extraction accuracy landed at 0.88 against the 0.95 the contracts named, so only seven of the twelve cleared. Milestones were equal at ₹10 lakh, so of ₹1.20 crore invoiced, ₹50 lakh was held. The ladder was sound and aimed at the wrong event. The recovery, in the quarter to Wednesday 30 September 2026, was an accuracy clause in the entry test: the threshold must be met on a held-out sample before the grade is given. Committed items fell from 12 to 4, and all four cleared. Lavendra Thanki's summary: the company had not become slower, it had stopped selling a date in place of a result.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Grade inflation. Warning sign: the committed share of plannable capacity rises two quarters running. Diagnostic: “what did we cut to protect this?” Caught late it costs credits and a renewal priced on a promise never held.

Unmeasured calibration. Warning sign: nobody can state last quarter's hit rate. Diagnostic: “of the items we called committed, how many landed on the published date?” Caught late the word is spent, and rebuilding it takes as long as debasing it did.

Loss of the sentence at the handoff. Warning sign: an outbound document carrying dates and no graded verbs, like Lavit's draft. Diagnostic: “show me the last three customer documents quoting a date.” Caught late, the roadmap is immaculate and the customer heard a promise.

Grading the ship rather than the outcome. Warning sign: on-time and acceptance rates diverging, as at Daksheya. Diagnostic: “what must the customer be able to do for this to count?” Caught late, the cost is held invoices, not a slip.

Reserve erosion. Warning sign: discovery work booked against line B of Exhibit 2. Diagnostic: “what was the reserve at the start of the quarter, and what is it now?” Caught late, the committed tier loses its buffer silently.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The calibrationist case is that words without numbers drift, as Kent showed in 1964 and Exhibit 3 shows again: against a floor of 0.90, a tier ran at 0.739 for a year, 16 points low, unnoticed. It would be wrong if published probabilities changed behaviour perversely — if a stated 0.90 licensed a seller to round up, or estimators learned to quote 0.90 because that is the tier rewarded. Both are measurable; neither usually is.

The horizon case is that a date is read as a date whatever decoration surrounds it, so the robust fix is to withhold dates beyond the near term; its evidence is that the costly failures are all distant-date failures. It would be wrong wherever a counterparty needs a date — Dvaita's manufacturer and Dhruvam's insurer both do — and there it has no answer except to let sales invent one.

The contract case is that any ladder with more than two rungs is read upward by whoever benefits, so middle grades launder optimism; its evidence is how reliably PLANNED becomes committed in a quota conversation. It would be wrong if the intermediate tier demonstrably changed external language — testable by auditing outbound documents, and almost never tested.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this builds the ladder, publishes the definitions and feels finished. Someone who has internalised it spends little time on labels and most on three things: the reserve, the audit and the outbound sentence. They state last quarter's hit rate per tier from memory and volunteer it unasked. They refuse upgrades in public, so the refusal is seen to cost something. Asked for a probability they give a range and say what would narrow it. And they are relaxed about a small committed tier, having noticed that the promises a company keeps are a better figure than those it makes.

12. The decisions, and questions for discussion

1. Dhruvam's committed tier delivered 34 of 46 on time. Is the repair to tighten the entry test or rename the tier to match its measured rate? What does each cost the people who read the word, and which would Lavit Tulsiyan prefer?

2. Lakhan must grade six hardware items 161 days out on the evidence of 19 past items. What is the most granular scheme that evidence supports, and what should he tell the manufacturer?

3. Expected credit depends only on the marginal probabilities; keeping the whole letter depends on how they move together. Which should set how many items a letter may list, and who should own that rule?

Laxita sent a letter naming two items with “will”, three with “we expect to, and here is the probability”, the credit clause confined to the two, plus one new sentence: Dhruvam's committed items landed on their published date 34 times out of 46 last year, and the test was being tightened. Her reasoning: the two-item promise spans 0.89 to 0.94 whatever the dependence, a width of 0.05, while the five-item version spans 0.26 to 0.62, a width of 0.36, more than seven times as wide; and a buyer told the hit rate can price it, while one surprised by it repudiates the vocabulary.

Lakhan built the probe port into the mould and graded the feature PLANNED, accepting ₹24.6 lakh of dark hardware as insurance against an 11-week schedule exposure. He also split the ladder: hardware graded once, at the freeze, stamped “locked 20 November”; app items weekly until the branch cut. Both ended with fewer promises, and expected to keep more of them.

13. Going deeper

The roadmap as communication is the parent idea: grades exist because a roadmap is read by people who were not in the room. Roadmap commitments in deals is where the grade meets money, which makes the vocabulary enforceable. Strategy vs roadmap vs plan separates the documents a grade can sit on, so teams stop grading strategy. Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later is the horizon school's format, the alternative to grading dates. OKRs and goal setting supplies the outcomes a grade should attach to. Annual and quarterly planning sets the cadence for resetting and auditing grades. Capacity planning produces the reserve and cap that make a committed label mean anything. Dependency management exposes the shared squads that decide whether your probabilities are independent.
exp40v2-plan.multi.year:
Multi-year product planning

Planning three years out for hardware, platforms and regulated products, where lead times outrun knowledge, without faking precision.

1. Two boards, one week

On Thursday 15 October 2026 the board of Pavaka Instruments met in Pune to approve an irreversible capital release. Pavaka builds a benchtop immunoassay analyser and the single-use cartridges it reads; the cartridges carry the business. Bhoomika Idariya, who runs product, had been asked for a three-year plan and had brought a one-page schedule of dates instead. The binding date was 1 December 2026, by which the company had to release ₹ 7.00 crore against five long-lead items for Model P2: a cartridge mould set, an imported optical bench, a CDSCO Class C licence with its clinical performance study, an antibody supply agreement, and a firmware and cloud rebuild. The longest lead time was nineteen months, and three further months carried the first instrument to a customer: first revenue would arrive in October 2028, twenty-two months from the binding date, in a plan whose horizon ends 31 March 2029.

On Friday 16 October, in Bengaluru, Bhavana Ikhera faced the mirror image. Pushkala Networks adjudicates health-insurance claims for Indian insurers using models it trains itself, against IRDAI's turnaround norms. A new investor wanted three years. Her difficulty was not a shortage of facts but that the chief one would not hold still: the inference cost of a claim on the platform had fallen from ₹ 3.40 in October 2024 to ₹ 0.86 in October 2026. She believed she had no long-lead commitments; nothing her teams had built took more than a quarter. What she could not say was what a three-year plan was for.

The two cases bracket the subject. Idariya must plan three years out because her decisions bind before she learns anything; Ikhera is told to although hers bind for ninety days. The discipline serving both separates decision dates from delivery dates.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define the practice narrowly: identifying, dating and pricing the decisions whose consequences reach beyond the next annual cycle, and committing only those that must be committed now. It is not a three-year feature list. Its test is not whether it predicts year three but whether it identifies what must be decided in month one.

Three intellectual sources still argue. Alfred Chandler's Strategy and Structure (1962) and Igor Ansoff's Corporate Strategy (1965) established the long-range tradition: when plant and tooling take years to build, the plan is the schedule of commitments. Shell's planners in the early 1970s, whose practice Pierre Wack described in 1985, broke the assumption that a plan needs one future, substituting scenarios with options bought against each. Henry Mintzberg's The Rise and Fall of Strategic Planning (1994) attacked the apparatus: planning departments produce documents, not strategy, and extrapolation past the point of knowledge is theatre. Rita McGrath and Ian MacMillan's discovery-driven planning (1995) and the real-options literature, Dixit and Pindyck's Investment under Uncertainty (1994), offered the reconciliation most practitioners use unnamed: plan the assumptions and their test dates, not the outcomes.

The schools diverge on single propositions. The commitment school will sign "a three-year plan is a dated ladder of irreversible choices and must be written"; it will not sign "the plan should forecast demand in year three." The emergent school signs "beyond about four quarters, specificity is negatively correlated with accuracy"; it will not sign "therefore do not plan." The scenario school signs "buy the option, not the path"; it will not sign "all futures are equally likely."

3. Mechanics: lead time, float and the price of waiting

Expert practice begins with an inventory that looks nothing like a roadmap: for each long-lead item, its lead time, the cash released at commitment, and the share recoverable on cancellation. The fourth quantity, usually left implicit and the one doing the work, is float: how long the item can be deferred before it, rather than the critical path, delays first revenue.

Define a class and test it, because the count matters. Call a line item committed when cash leaves before any market signal returns and under half of it is recoverable. Four of the five rows pass: licence, firmware, mould set, optical bench. The antibody agreement does not — its recoverable share is exactly one half, not less — so it fails the definition as written. Those four carry ₹ 574 lakh of the ₹ 700 lakh released, a share of 82.0 per cent. Count all five and the definition does no work.

Float then prices the option to wait. Idariya's choice was whether to hold the mould set until the clinical study's interim read, due six months later on 1 June 2027. Because the mould set carries five months of float, waiting six months delays first revenue by one month, not six: the second-order effect the naive calculation misses. Pavaka plans 210 Model P2 placements in the six months from 1 October 2028 to 31 March 2029 — 35 a month. Each placement earns over its first twelve months ₹ 1.50 lakh of instrument contribution (price ₹ 4.80 lakh less variable cost ₹ 3.30 lakh, a 31.25 per cent margin) plus 1,100 cartridges at ₹ 62 of contribution each, or ₹ 0.682 lakh: ₹ 2.182 lakh in all. A month of deferral therefore costs 35 × 2.182 = ₹ 76.37 lakh. Waiting buys the chance not to scrap the tool: ₹ 210 lakh at 10 per cent recoverable puts ₹ 189 lakh at risk, so waiting pays only if the study fails with probability above 76.37 ÷ 189 = 40.4 per cent. Pavaka's regulatory lead, Bhanurekha Itaria, put it at 18 per cent: an expected saving of 0.18 × 189 = ₹ 34.02 lakh against a cost of ₹ 76.37 lakh, 2.24 to one against waiting. Commit the tool.

4. When the discipline applies, and when it misleads

State the conditions as checkable claims. First: the horizon is forced only if some decision's lead time plus delivery tail exceeds the annual cycle. Pavaka: yes, 22 months. Pushkala: nothing on her list as it stood, though section 12 turns up one. Second: the plan is worth writing only if at least one forced decision has low recoverability; otherwise decide late and cheaply. Pavaka: yes, ₹ 565.25 lakh of the ₹ 700 lakh released does not come back. Pushkala: largely no. Third: multi-year quantification is defensible only where the planning unit is stable. Pavaka's cartridge consumption per analyser has moved little; Pushkala's cost per claim fell by a factor of 3.40 ÷ 0.86 = 3.95 in two years.

Where the idea actively misleads is Pushkala's case. Asked for three years of numbers on an unstable unit, a competent team produces them, and they are used — for hiring, pricing floors, board commitments — as though they were the Pavaka kind. The failure is not optimism but that a projection built on a quantity falling by half a year acquires, by being tabulated, the authority of a quantity that is not moving.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product portfolios break the single critical path: two products sharing a mould shop have interdependent floats, and deferring the lower-priority tool consumes the other's slack. Two-sided marketplaces are subtler: the long-lead commitment is usually supply-side capacity whose payoff depends on demand nobody will commit to for three years, so the plan is written in ratios, not volumes. Regulated products convert lead time into a queue: Pavaka's 19 months is an expected wait in a system with variance and no overtime, and a plan treating it as a duration will be late in a way no engineering recovers.

Hardware-plus-software is where the seam shows. Pavaka's firmware rebuild carries three months of float, so it can in principle start a quarter late; in practice the firmware team reports to engineering, which plans in quarters, while the tool release belongs to operations, which plans in years. The float is real and nobody owns it. AI-native products invert the problem: the capability frontier moves faster than any commitment, so the multi-year object is a data and evaluation asset: Pushkala's labelled adjudication corpus.

What mature companies do, as against what their templates say, is run two documents: a public three-year roadmap, revised annually, a communication device; and a short list of dated commitments with cash and recoverability against each, often held by finance rather than product. Pavaka's board paper on 15 October was the second.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert

Lead time forces the horizon; float is what the plan can act on.
The tell is which question comes first: a competent planner asks when launch is, an expert how long each item can wait before launch moves. The longest lead time looks like the horizon, but says nothing about which other decisions can be deferred, which is what a plan can actually change.
A multi-year plan schedules decisions, not deliverables.
The tell is a year-three page thinner than year one while the decision list is not. If every dated item is a shipment, the document is a forecast in plan's clothes. Dates on which someone must choose are falsifiable; dates on which something appears are not.
Reversibility is priced in cash recoverable, not in effort.
The tell is a team calling a decision reversible because the code can be deleted. Pavaka's firmware rebuild is 0 per cent recoverable though nothing physical is bought: sixteen months of calendar are not refundable. Effort measures what was spent, recoverability what comes back.
The rungs are not independent.
The tell is a cancellation discussed one line at a time. Dropping Pavaka's optical bench would not merely release ₹ 145 lakh at 35 per cent recovery; it would re-specify the cartridge optical window and re-open a mould set in cut. Float belongs to the network, not the row.
Precision should coarsen with distance, not merely shrink.
The tell is a year-three column carrying two decimal places. The expert changes the unit: bands, ratios and ranked order far out, absolute figures only near in. Shading the far numbers fails, since a tabulated number reads as a number whatever surrounds it.
Regulatory time is a queue with variance, not a duration.
The tell is a single regulatory date with no buffer. A 19-month expectation with a long tail is not the planning object a 19-month build is. The expert plans the resubmission, and asks what else the delay blocks: how a zero-float item becomes the whole plan.
A falling cost curve is a band with a stated multiplier.
The tell is one projected unit cost in year three. Ikhera's curve shows why: the same starting point at −30 and −60 per cent a year lands 5.4 times apart. A point estimate is not conservative or aggressive; it is a different kind of claim from what the evidence supports.
Year two is where the lying happens.
The tell is that year two reads as specifically as year one. Year three is obviously uncertain and readers discount it; year one is close enough to check. Year two invites detail and holds nobody to it, so it absorbs whatever the plan needs true.

7. How the practice changes by product type and stage

The real differences are differences in what has float. In consumer software almost everything has float, so the multi-year object is brand and platform position rather than features. In B2B and enterprise the float belongs to the customer: a bank's core-system window opens once, and missing it costs three years, not three quarters. On platforms and marketplaces the long-lead item is usually trust or a supply contract, and the plan is written in coverage ratios. In hardware the ladder in Exhibit 1 is the plan, and the discipline is almost entirely recoverability. In AI products the position is contested; section 10 takes it up.

Where the difference is asserted and is not real: planning cadence. Most types review on a roughly quarterly rhythm because that is how finance works, not the product. Stage matters less than people claim in one direction and more in another. A seed-stage company cannot plan three years of product — but if it builds hardware it must still commit tooling on a 14-month lead, and its answer is to buy the option through a contract manufacturer at a worse unit cost, not to pretend the decision is absent. Scale changes the option's price, not its existence.

8. Three worked cases

Pavaka, the forced ladder. Against the three-year FY2027–FY2029 research-and-capital envelope of ₹ 11.4 + ₹ 13.2 + ₹ 14.0 crore = ₹ 38.6 crore, the ₹ 7.00 crore release is 18.1 per cent; against FY2027 alone it is 61.4 per cent. Both are labelled, but only 61.4 per cent is like-for-like: the whole ₹ 7.00 crore leaves inside FY2027, and spreading a one-date release over three years' budget understates its weight where it lands. Clearing the unrecoverable ₹ 565.25 lakh takes 565.25 ÷ 2.182 = 259.1, so 260 placements' first-year contribution; the horizon places only 210, and most of their first year falls after 31 March 2029 — at least fifty short. Its payback is not inside it.

Pushkala, the unstable unit. The measured fall, ₹ 3.40 to ₹ 0.86 over twenty-four months, is 2.54 ÷ 3.40 = 74.7 per cent. Halving that to 37.4 per cent a year is wrong: the compounded annual factor is √(0.86 ÷ 3.40) = 0.5029, a fall of 49.7 per cent a year, putting October 2025 at ₹ 1.71. It put 3.60 crore claims through in the twelve months to 30 September 2026 at a volume-weighted blended ₹ 1.18 (below the ₹ 1.21 geometric mean, because volume grew through the window), for ₹ 4.248 crore of inference cost. The central factor gives 0.86 × 0.5029³ = ₹ 0.109 by October 2029, but the honest statement is the band, ₹ 0.055 (0.86 × 0.40³) to ₹ 0.295 (0.86 × 0.70³): 0.295 ÷ 0.055 = 5.4 times. Her ARR of ₹ 46.0 crore at 30 September 2026 sits over 23 paying insurers, ₹ 2.00 crore each; four more run unpaid pilots and sit outside that denominator, since 46.0 ÷ 27 gives ₹ 1.70 crore.

Prakhar Energy Systems, where it failed. In March 2023 Prakhar committed a three-year FY2024–FY2026 storage roadmap around a pack cost of ₹ 9,400 per kWh, including ₹ 14.2 crore of tooling specific to that chemistry. By September 2025 the market pack cost was ₹ 6,300 per kWh — a fall of 3,100 ÷ 9,400 = 33.0 per cent — and the cheaper chemistry would not fit the enclosure. FY2026 gross margin on the line was 11.4 per cent against a plan of 26.0, a miss of 14.6 percentage points. The error was not the forecast but that Bhuvanesh Ijariya's team committed a tool specific to one assumption when a two-chemistry enclosure cost ₹ 4.6 crore more: it bought the cheaper plan, not the cheaper option. Recovery, from July 2025, re-specified the enclosure for both; on matched halves the half-year to 30 September 2025 ran at 9.6 per cent and that to 30 September 2026 at 19.8, a gain of 10.2 points.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The feature list with years on it. Early sign: the three columns hold the same kind of object. Diagnostic: which cell is a decision somebody must make on a date? Caught late it costs an annual cycle: nothing trackable could have failed.

Committing the specific instead of the general. Prakhar's failure. Early sign: a tool, schema or contract whose specification contains an assumption rather than a requirement. Diagnostic: if it moved 30 per cent, what would we re-buy? Caught late it costs the tool, ₹ 14.2 crore here, plus the window.

Spending float without noticing. Early sign: a deferred start nobody logged as consuming slack. Diagnostic: what is this item's float today against last quarter? Caught late, a zero-float item appears unannounced, usually three months before a regulatory date.

Mismatching the window. Early sign: a one-year flow divided by a multi-year base, or the reverse. Diagnostic: name the numerator's window and the denominator's aloud. Caught late it distorts the budget conversation rather than the product, which is why it survives.

Treating a moving unit as fixed. Pushkala's exposure. Early sign: a projected unit cost with no band. Diagnostic: what multiplier separates the optimistic and pessimistic paths at the horizon? Caught late the damage is pricing: floors set against a cost already fallen past them.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The live disagreement is whether a fast-moving capability frontier makes long planning more necessary or impossible. Both positions are strong. The option-buying position holds that volatility raises the value of waiting, so the response to Ikhera's band is to commit almost nothing: rent capacity, keep model interfaces swappable, treat the plan as options with strike dates. Its evidence is the real-options result that option value rises with variance; Prakhar is its cautionary case. It fails where the options are not available at a fair price: Pavaka cannot rent a CDSCO licence.

The compounding-asset position holds the opposite: when unit costs fall predictably, durable advantage lies in an asset that takes years to build, so a volatile frontier makes multi-year commitment more important, not less. Its evidence is that falling costs commoditise the capability and leave proprietary data, distribution and regulatory position as the scarce goods; Pushkala's corpus is worth more precisely because inference is cheap. It fails if the asset is not durable: were a general model trained on public claims data to match it, the corpus would be a stranded cost, and nobody can rule that out.

A narrower dispute sits underneath: whether floats should be published and managed as a shared resource, or kept close because a published float is immediately spent, every team treating slack as licence. The second camp's evidence is behavioural and strong, and durable counter-examples in large organisations are hard to find.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in a planning meeting's first ten minutes: they ask for recoverability and lead times before scope, and will not accept effort as a proxy for either. They refuse a year-three number in the same unit as a year-one number, and say why rather than apologising. They treat every deferral as a withdrawal from a float account and can state the balance. They know which figures in the plan are load-bearing, usually two or three, with a test date against each. And asked for a three-year plan for something with no long leads, they say so plainly instead of producing one, which is the behaviour that separates command of the subject from fluency in its vocabulary.

12. The decisions, and questions for discussion

  1. Pavaka's four committed rows carry 82.0 per cent of the cash released. If Idariya could convert exactly one into a deferrable option, which row, and on what measure — cash, float or recoverability?
  2. Exhibit 2 reports a blended inference-cost share of 4.51 per cent and a mean of annual shares of 5.10 per cent. Which belongs in a board pack, and what does the gap say about the three years?
  3. Pavaka's unrecoverable ₹ 565.25 lakh is not repaid inside its own three-year horizon. Is that a defect in the plan, in the horizon, or in neither?

Idariya approved the whole ₹ 7.00 crore release for 1 December 2026, mould set included, on the section 3 calculation: a one-month slip cost more than twice the expected saving from waiting. Her board paper carried no year-three revenue line — only five dates, five recoverability figures, and 1 June 2027, the first point at which the plan could be falsified.

Ikhera declined the plan in the form requested, giving her investor Exhibit 2 instead: volumes on one declared path, cost as a band with its multiplier stated, and one committed item — an eighteen-month corpus build, the only thing on her list with a lead time beyond a year. Bodhan Ilolia, her finance head, noted that this made the plan harder to compare with a competitor's. She agreed.

13. Going deeper

  1. Annual and quarterly planning — the same discipline where estimates can be checked; this one inherits its cadence.
  2. Strategic bets and reversibility — supplies the recoverability column, and the vocabulary for one-way doors.
  3. Strategy vs roadmap vs plan — separates the documents mature companies keep apart, so a roadmap is not read as a commitment.
  4. Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later — the standard way to coarsen precision with distance.
  5. The roadmap as communication — why the public three-year document survives even when nobody plans from it.
  6. OKRs and goal setting — the link from a multi-year commitment to the quarter advancing it: where the two cadences meet.
  7. Capacity planning — makes float measurable, since slack is spent in people as often as calendar.
  8. Dependency management — the network view that makes floats recomputable after every change.
exp20v2-plan.multi.year:
Multi-year product planning

How do we plan three years out without pretending we know?

A date the board wanted

On Tuesday 3 March 2026, Ankur Hariyani carried one slide into the boardroom at Nirmal Medtech's Vadodara headquarters that he did not want to show. Hariyani, the chief product officer, had been asked for a launch date for Nirmal Flow, a wearable insulin pump that the company, a maker of diabetes-care devices, meant to sell in India and later in Europe. The board had set a funding envelope of ₹66 crore and wanted one date to hold him to.

Alpesh Hundiwala, the head of sales, had already told three distributors to expect stock in the first quarter of 2029. If the date held, the distributors would be ready. If it slipped a year, Nirmal would pay for idle service teams while the envelope ran dry with the pump still unsold.

The difficulty was structural. A pump is a regulated medical device: it needs a design that has passed verification testing, a clinical study, and a licence from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), India's national drug and device regulator, before one unit is sold. Each step has a long lead time and an outcome partly controlled by outsiders. The engineers could give a date for every stage. Every one of those dates would be wrong, and their sum was the date the board wanted.

The idea

Multi-year product planning is the practice of committing to different kinds of things at different distances. Close to today, a team commits to scope and dates. Further out it commits to outcomes and ranges of dates. Furthest out it commits only to options: choices deliberately kept open, with the evidence that would close them. It exists because a single-date plan three years long is fiction, while a plan that names no date cannot release money or sign a distributor.

The ingredients predate the name. The United States Navy's Polaris missile programme produced PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique) in 1958, which estimates each task with three numbers, a low, a most likely and a high, rather than one. Robert Cooper's Stage-Gate process, from the 1980s, divides development into stages separated by gates, the meetings at which money is released or withheld. Rolling-wave planning, from project management, plans the near term in detail and the far term coarsely. Multi-year planning joins the three.

Hariyani's sentence for the board was this: "We will commit to the destination and the next gate, publish a range for everything between, and say in advance what would change our mind."

How it works

His team took six steps, two of which usually stay implicit. First, state the outcome rather than a feature list: a licensed pump, in distributors' warehouses, available to patients. Second, and rarely written down, find the long-lead items, the stages whose duration cannot be bought down by adding people. At Nirmal these were the clinical study and the regulator's review, neither of which responds to extra engineers.

Third, estimate each long-lead stage as a range. Engineers resist giving a high number, so the useful question is what would have to go wrong for this stage to take longest. Fourth, give each horizon a commitment level, as Figure 1 shows: firm for the next gate, a range for the next band, an option beyond. Fifth, define the gates: each has a named decision, named evidence, a named decider and an amount of money released. Money follows gates, not calendar years.

Sixth, and also implicit, fix when the plan will be redrawn: a standing quarterly review, plus triggers such as a regulator's letter. Ranges narrow as gates pass. The plan is therefore a sequence of plans, each more precise than the last, and the board should expect to see the number change.

A worked example

Hariyani's team assumed four stages in sequence, starting 1 April 2026. For each, the expected duration is (low + 4 × most likely + high) ÷ 6, which is the PERT mean. Spread is measured by the variance, ((high − low) ÷ 6)², where variance is the average squared distance from the mean. All durations are in months.

Means add to 36.0 months, variances to 10.0. The standard deviation, the usual measure of spread, is the square root of the variance: √10 = 3.16 months. Treating the total as roughly bell-shaped, a date with one chance in ten of being beaten, and another with one chance in ten of being missed (the 10th and 90th percentiles), sit 1.28 standard deviations either side of the mean: 36.0 ± 1.28 × 3.16 = 36.0 ± 4.05, or 32.0 to 40.0 months. From 1 April 2026 that is 1 December 2028 to 1 August 2029, with the mean on 1 April 2029.

The most likely column sums to 34 months, 1 February 2029, which is the date a sales team would hear. It is two months earlier than the mean because stages B and C each have a longer tail than head. At a flat ₹1.8 crore a month, the mean costs 36 × 1.8 = ₹64.8 crore. The ₹66 crore envelope lasts 66 ÷ 1.8 = 36.7 months, leaving ₹1.2 crore of slack at the mean, though on this model the envelope is overrun about four times in ten.

Now change one input. Suppose the regulator signals that it may extend its review, lifting stage C's high estimate from 17 months to 29. Everything else stays. Stage C becomes (5 + 4 × 8 + 29) ÷ 6 = 11.0 months with variance ((29 − 5) ÷ 6)² = 16.0.

The mean moves two months. The 90th-percentile date moves four, and the 10th is unchanged at one decimal place. One piece of regulatory news widened the window from 8.0 to 12.0 months (40.0 − 32.0 and 44.0 − 32.0) and pushed the cost at the 90th percentile ₹7.2 crore higher, to ₹79.2 crore. It also takes the mean past the envelope: ₹68.4 crore against ₹66 crore. In this plan, bad news lengthens the tail more than the middle, which is why a single date hides exactly what the board most needs.

Nuances

Plan, forecast and commitment differ. A forecast says what is likely; a commitment says what the company will do whatever happens; a plan relates the two. Quoting the most likely outcome as a commitment, as the sales team did, transfers risk to distributors who never saw the range.

Mean and most likely are not the same. The most likely outcome is the single most probable one. The mean averages all outcomes, including the long tail. When delays are skewed, as here, the mean is later, and budgets should be built on it.

The arithmetic assumes independence. Adding variances assumes stage durations are unrelated, and that stages run strictly in sequence. If a weak design causes both a poor study and a hard review, the true spread is wider than 3.16 months. Overlapping stages would shorten the total.

A range is a statement about learning. Width tells you how much remains to be found out. It narrows when a gate passes, not when someone is asked to be more confident.

It applies where lead times are long. The conditions are irreversible spend, outside gatekeepers and long lead times. A web feature shipped weekly gains little from three-year ranges; confusing this with a long annual plan, or with a vision roadmap that has no dates at all, loses the discipline.

Ranges are not buffers. Padding each estimate and quoting the total hides which stage carries the risk. A range keeps the risk attached to its stage so that someone can own it.

It cannot tell you what you have not imagined. The ranges cover known risks. A supplier failure, a rival's licence or a change in reimbursement is outside them, and nothing here says whether patients will want the pump. Ask who produced the ranges, whether past estimates were checked against outcomes, and what the plan assumes about the regulator.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace; early and large

In consumer products, build lead times are usually short, so multi-year ranges attach to adoption, brand and platform bets, or to hardware with factory commitments. In B2B, the customer's procurement and integration cycle sets the clock, and the multi-year roadmap is partly a sales document: ranges must be honest enough to survive a contract review. In marketplaces the long-lead item is liquidity, the density of buyers and sellers at which the product works, and the range is time to reach that density city by city.

Company size changes the purpose. An early-stage firm's horizon is its runway: with eighteen months of cash, a three-year plan is a hypothesis about the next round, and gates should be set to cash. A large firm's problem is coordination across teams, so the plan's main function is to expose dependencies. Nirmal, mid-sized with one regulated product, sat between them.

Common mistakes

One date, no range. From outside, you see successive quarters promising the same launch quarter, then slipping together. The misunderstanding is that a precise number is a firm one. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask for the low and high of the longest stage; if nobody can give them, the date was asserted.

Equal detail for every year. Year three shows feature lists, year one shows themes. The misunderstanding is that more detail means more rigour. Count the commitments in each year: they should shrink outward.

A plan frozen at approval. The symptom is a roadmap whose date has not moved in a year while the regulator's correspondence has. The misunderstanding is that changing the plan signals failure. Check the date of the last revision against the date of the last gate.

What good looks like

Handled well, Hariyani's slide carries four things: a destination, a window of 32.0 to 40.0 months with the mean at 36.0, the next gate and what it releases, and the inputs, stage C's high estimate among them, whose change would move the window. Sales hears a quarter range, not a day. The board sees the envelope lasting 36.7 months and knows which news would exhaust it.

What Hariyani decided

He told the board that Nirmal would not promise a date. It would release money to the end of the verification gate, publish the 32.0 to 40.0 month window, and tell distributors "between December 2028 and August 2029" (eight chances in ten), with a firm date to follow once the licence application was accepted. The reasoning was that the board's real need was not a date but a trigger: the moment when the envelope and the window stopped agreeing.

To learn next, study the strategic bets that sit above such a plan, how reversible each stage's spend is, and how objectives and key results link the plan to strategy.

Two questions to sit with. Which commitments in your own plan are firm because you have evidence, and which are firm only because someone asked for a date? And what is the one input in your plan whose change would move the tail twice as far as the middle?
exp20v2-plan.annual:
Annual and Quarterly Planning at Akhand Supply Cloud

1. Six of fourteen

On Monday 12 October 2026, Indresh Popat opened a blank spreadsheet and typed two numbers. The first was 14, the initiatives Akhand Supply Cloud had committed in April to deliver by the end of September. The second was 6, the number that had shipped. Popat, the Ahmedabad company's vice-president of product, could see that six of fourteen is 43 per cent (the 14 being every initiative committed in April for the first half, the 6 those shipped by 30 September), and he knew the chief executive, Ishwarlal Panchal, could see it too.

Akhand sells software that lets textile and chemical distributors manage orders, dealer credit and warehouses. Its annual recurring revenue (ARR, the yearly value of subscriptions in force) stood at ₹48 crore. The board would meet on Thursday 19 November to approve the plan for the financial year beginning 1 April 2027; in India that year runs April to March. Engineering wanted five more engineers, and finance had hinted that the budget might cover fewer.

Two stakes were concrete. Two anchor customers, together paying ₹6 crore of ARR (12.5 per cent of ₹48 crore), would renew on 30 June 2027 only if Akhand held an audit-trail certification. And every product leader had asked for more than the team could build. If Popat repeated April's method, adding good ideas until the room stopped objecting, he would produce a plan believed on 19 November and disbelieved by May. His problem was not which ideas were good. It was how to produce commitments that the people delivering them would believe.

2. The idea

Annual and quarterly planning is the routine by which an organisation turns strategy, a budget and a team's real capacity into a short list of funded bets and a shorter list of promises. A bet is a named piece of work with an expected outcome, a size and an owner. It exists to solve a mismatch. Budgets, which large firms formalised in the early twentieth century, are set once a year and fix money and headcount. Strategy moves faster, and engineering work is uncertain, so a plan that merely copies the budget breaks by spring.

Objectives and key results (OKRs), a goal method Andy Grove practised at Intel in the 1970s and John Doerr later carried to Google, supply the link by stating which outcome the year must move. A roadmap says roughly when work will arrive. Planning is where these meet the budget.

Two cadences do different jobs. The annual cycle sets themes, headcount and the largest bets, and may be approximate. The quarterly cycle turns the nearest slice into commitments. Popat's sentence for the meeting: “We will promise only what we have sized against the people we actually have, and label everything else as intent.”

3. How it works

The cycle has seven steps, and practitioners usually leave the last three implicit. First, gather inputs: strategy, OKRs, customer obligations, technical debt and last year's delivery record. Second, write each candidate as a bet. Third, compute capacity, the engineer-weeks genuinely available after leave, upkeep and slack. Fourth, allocate: obligations first, then the rest by expected return per engineer-week, skipping any bet that no longer fits.

The implicit steps matter more. Fifth, grade promises by distance, as Exhibit 2 shows: promise the coming quarter, state intent for the next, offer only themes beyond. Sixth, test the result with the leaders who own dependencies and risks. Seventh, write down the cut line, the order in which bets drop if capacity shrinks, and the trigger for re-planning. Without the seventh, every change of circumstance becomes a negotiation from scratch. Popat's April plan dated September deliveries as firmly as June ones, and nothing told readers which dates were firm.

The fourth and sixth steps are where politics enters. Each leader arrives with a favourite bet and an estimate of its payoff, and the allocation rule, obligations first and then return per engineer-week, is what lets Popat say no without making it personal. The test with dependency owners is equally practical: a bet that needs the data team in May is not a Q1 commitment until the data team has agreed, in writing, to that May.

4. A worked example

Popat's first pass covers Q1 of FY2027-28, thirteen weeks from April to June 2027. He assumes the five requisitions are approved, so 25 engineers are in seat. Exhibit 3 shows the subtraction. Gross capacity is 25 × 13 = 325 engineer-weeks. Leave and holidays take two weeks each, 50, leaving 275. Keeping the lights on (support, defects, security work) takes 20 per cent of 275, which is 55, leaving 220. A slack reserve of 10 per cent of 220 is 22. Commitment capacity is 198 engineer-weeks, 60.9 per cent of gross (198 ÷ 325).

BetSize (engineer-weeks)Expected ARR (₹ lakh)₹ lakh per engineer-weekDecision at 198
B. Audit-trail certification60901.50Commit (obligation)
C. Mobile order capture801602.00Commit
A. Dealer credit limits901501.67Does not fit
E. Self-serve onboarding40601.50Commit
D. Warehouse analytics50400.80Does not fit

Expected ARR is leadership's estimate of revenue added or protected within twelve months of release. Certification’s 90 is deliberately a fraction, 15 per cent of the ₹600 lakh at risk, because only that share is attributed to the certification work itself. The fourth column divides it by size. Requests total 320 engineer-weeks against 198, so at least 122 must go; lumpiness makes it 140. Certification guards ₹6 crore of renewals, so it enters first, at 60. Mobile ordering has the best ratio, 160 ÷ 80 = 2.00, and takes 80, reaching 140. Dealer credit limits rank next at 150 ÷ 90 = 1.67 but need 90 when 58 remain. Onboarding needs 40 and fits, reaching 180 and leaving 18 unallocated. Committed expected ARR is 90 + 160 + 60 = ₹310 lakh. Warehouse analytics, at 0.80, fits under neither funding case; its place on the list is a reminder that a request is not a plan.

Now change one input: finance funds only the existing 20 engineers. Gross is 20 × 13 = 260; less 40 of leave is 220; less 20 per cent, 44, is 176; less 10 per cent, 17.6, is 158.4. Five of 25 engineers is a 20 per cent cut, and capacity falls by 20 per cent (39.6 of 198). Commitments, however, fall from 180 to 140, because bets are lumpy: certification and mobile ordering still fit, onboarding does not, and committed expected ARR drops to ₹250 lakh.

5. Nuances

A commitment is not a target.

A target, as in an OKR, is deliberately ambitious and may be scored partly met. A commitment is a promise whose miss demands an explanation. A team that scores 70 per cent on a stretch target has succeeded; a team that delivers 70 per cent of its commitments has not. Mixed together, teams sandbag the targets or leaders disbelieve the promises.

Capacity is not headcount.

Twenty-five engineers yielded 325 engineer-weeks but only 198 promisable ones. The other 127 engineer-weeks went to leave, upkeep and slack. Calibrate each deduction against last quarter’s actuals, not hope, because an optimistic deduction is how a plan arrives already broken.

A ratio sorts; it does not decide.

The ₹ lakh figures come from the people who want the bets. A difference between 1.67 and 1.50 sits inside the error of such estimates, and obligations override rank anyway.

Bets are lumpy.

Capacity shrinks smoothly; bets leave whole. Splitting dealer credit limits into a first milestone helps only if that milestone delivers value alone, for instance a credit limit that works for one customer segment. A half-built module earns nothing and still consumes the weeks.

Dependencies sit outside the number.

The 198 counts Akhand’s 25 engineers. A bet needing the platform team, or a customer’s IT staff, borrows capacity nobody counted. List each such dependency beside the bet, with a named owner and a date, or the plan inherits delays it cannot see.

New hires are not capacity on day one.

The first pass treated five hires as productive from 1 April. Recruits spend weeks being trained by the engineers already counted, so treat their arrival as a risk, not an input, and let their first quarter appear as slack until the evidence says otherwise.

What it cannot tell you.

Planning tests feasibility, not wisdom. It cannot say whether certification is worth ₹6 crore or whether the strategy is right, and it says nothing about estimates that are all biased in the same direction. Before relying on a plan, ask who estimated, when, and against what record.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; small and large

The mechanics hold everywhere; the proportions do not. In consumer products, outcomes arrive through experiments, so plans reserve a fixed share of capacity for tests not yet defined, and the quarter’s promise is to learn rather than to ship. In B2B products such as Akhand’s, contracts create dated obligations, and the first allocation goes to them. In marketplaces, capacity must be planned on two sides: a bet adding demand without matching supply disappoints buyers, so bets are paired and sized together. Exhibit 4 sets the contrasts side by side.

Scale changes the process too. A fifteen-person start-up has little use for an annual plan: its commitment horizon is six weeks. A large firm’s budget locks headcount months before quarters begin, so dependencies across many teams, and the cut line, become the real work. The question to ask in any setting is what will be allowed to claim capacity first.

7. Common mistakes

Planning to one hundred per cent.

Symptom: the same items slip each quarter and teams dismiss the plan by week five; Akhand’s 6 of 14 shows the cost. Misunderstanding: capacity treated as headcount times calendar. Diagnostic: compare the plan with the engineer-weeks delivered last quarter; if the plan is larger, it is wrong before it starts.

Calling features outcomes.

Symptom: nobody can say what would count as failure. Misunderstanding: output mistaken for result. Diagnostic: for each bet ask which number moves, by how much, by when.

Promising the distant quarter.

Symptom: third- and fourth-quarter items quietly vanish at review. Misunderstanding: precision mistaken for certainty. Diagnostic: count commit-tier items beyond the next quarter; the answer should be zero.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Popat’s 19 November pack is two pages. Page one shows capacity as subtraction, 25 engineers becoming 198 engineer-weeks, then three bets totalling 180, one conditional, ₹310 lakh expected, 18 weeks unallocated, Q2 marked intent and Q3 and Q4 marked themes. Page two states the cut line: if only 20 engineers are funded, onboarding falls out, leaving 140 weeks and ₹250 lakh. The board sees that the five requisitions are worth ₹60 lakh of expected ARR, and each owner has already said, before the meeting, that they will be held to their number. At the end of June the same two pages are reopened, and the gap between 180 weeks committed and what shipped becomes the first input to the next cycle.

9. Closing

Popat decides to submit the 25-engineer plan but to commit unconditionally only certification and mobile ordering, 140 engineer-weeks that fit under both funding cases. Onboarding is listed as conditional on the requisitions being approved. His reasoning is that a commitment should survive the more pessimistic budget the board might plausibly pass, and a conditional label costs less credibility than a miss in June. In effect he trades a larger headline for a number that will still be true when the renewals fall due.

To go further, read scenario planning, which generalises the one-input change above; investment themes and allocation, which sets the Q3 and Q4 shares; and multi-year product planning, which asks what survives beyond one fiscal year.

Two questions to sit with. Which input in Popat’s capacity subtraction would you measure first, and from what record? And which commitment in a plan you know would you reclassify as intent today, and how would people behave differently?
exp40v2-plan.annual:
Annual and quarterly planning: the arithmetic of a promise

Turning strategy, a budget and a finite number of engineer-weeks into commitments that survive the quarter — and why two firms with one planning calendar face different problems.

1. Two firms, two Octobers

On Tuesday 20 October 2026 Jaanvi Rughani had four bets on one page and room for about two. Rughani runs product at Barrowfield Systems, which sells claims-adjudication software to mid-sized commercial insurers. Its fiscal year opens on 1 January, and the plan she owed the board covered the thirteen weeks from Monday 4 January 2027. Her chief financial officer, Joyita Ranka, wanted dates in the annual plan: three renewals worth a combined eighteen per cent of recurring revenue were being negotiated against a roadmap. Her own record argued against dates. Across the four quarters to September 2026 Barrowfield's plans promised 2,520 engineer-weeks of new work and delivered 1,739 inside the quarter promised; the other 781 slipped, were descoped or quietly died. Nobody had been fired; nobody believed the plan either.

Five days earlier, on Thursday 15 October 2026, Jayvir Ratanpura was looking at a different page. He is head of product at Brightkiln, which makes connected commercial ovens for bakery chains and sells a subscription on top. Brightkiln's 2027 engineering plan came to $12.5 million, and one line carried a date no agility could move: the purchase order for tooling and non-recurring engineering on a new control board had to be placed by Friday 12 March 2027 to hold a 13 August production start, because the board's lead time is twenty-two weeks. The pilot that would tell him whether the new board was the right board reports on Friday 23 April; waiting for it moved production to 24 September.

Both are planning problems; they are not the same problem. Rughani's question is how much to promise; Ratanpura's is when a promise stops being reversible. Most of what goes wrong in planning comes from answering one with machinery built for the other.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A planning cycle is the recurring procedure by which a firm turns strategy and a budget into a bounded set of commitments, each with an owner, a capacity cost and a review point. Three things it is not: a strategy, a choice about where to compete; a roadmap, intent with no capacity attached; and a forecast, a belief rather than a promise. The annual plan is the roadmap put through a budget cycle: the passage where intent acquires a price.

The machinery is a century old: Alfred Sloan and Donaldson Brown built it at General Motors in the 1920s to make a multi-divisional firm legible to its centre. Robert Anthony's 1965 framework split strategic planning from management control and operational control; his middle layer is what firms still call annual planning. Programme budgeting, introduced in the US Defense Department from 1961, added the claim that money buys outcomes, not line items. Peter Pyhrr's zero-based budgeting at Texas Instruments in 1970 attacked the base; Andy Grove's management by objectives at Intel, in High Output Management in 1983 and at Google as OKRs from 1999, attacked its content; Jeremy Hope and Robin Fraser's Beyond Budgeting work, from 1998, attacked the cycle itself.

Three live schools inherit that argument, told apart by the sentence each signs and the one each refuses. The commitment school signs a plan with no commitment in it is a forecast with ambition and refuses re-cut the plan whenever the evidence changes. The adaptive school signs separate the target, the forecast and the resource decision, because one number cannot honestly be all three and refuses the annual number is the team's goal. The bet-portfolio school signs fund teams against outcomes and gate the bets and refuses a date on a roadmap is a promise to a customer. Ranka is commitment-school, Rughani's engineers bet-portfolio by instinct; they argue about which failure is cheaper.

3. Mechanics: the build-down and the discount

Expert practice opens with a build-down most plans skip, and it is arithmetic, not judgement. Ninety-six engineers over thirteen weeks give 1,248 engineer-weeks of gross capacity, less four deductions, none optional.

The second step is where planning becomes empirical. Available calendar capacity is not commitment capacity: a plan's historic yield is a measurable property of the firm. Barrowfield delivered 1,739 of 2,520 promised engineer-weeks inside the quarter promised, a delivery ratio of 0.690. It is delivered over promised, and transfers to capacity because those four plans averaged 630 engineer-weeks a quarter (2,520 ÷ 4) against the 646 available. Applying it, 646 × 0.690 = 445.7, rounded to 446 engineer-weeks of commitment capacity. The gap — 646 − 446 = 200 engineer-weeks, or 31.0 per cent of available calendar capacity — is not waste but the buffer the record says will go to slipped promises and to work nobody has thought of yet. The quarter ending Wednesday 30 September 2026 consumed 206 engineer-weeks on escalations, an unplanned patch programme and an acquisition integration — unplanned work alone, six more than the whole new buffer.

Now the bets enter: four, asking 634 engineer-weeks together. That fits the calendar — 646 − 634 = 12 engineer-weeks spare — which is why plans built on calendar capacity feel achievable. Against commitment capacity the same ask is 188 engineer-weeks over, or 42.2 per cent above the 446 Barrowfield can promise. The two figures rest on different denominators deliberately: the 12 spare against 646 engineer-weeks of calendar time, the 42.2 per cent against 446 of promisable capacity. Conflating them is an easy way for a planning deck to mislead.

Three second-order effects follow. First, the ratio is endogenous: publish it and teams inflate their asks to survive the discount, so it must be computed from the record, not negotiated. Second, the plan should carry commitment levels, not confidence percentages: Barrowfield's 446 splits into 306 engineer-weeks committed (bets A and C), 120 contingent and 20 unallocated, and 306 + 120 + 20 = 446 exactly. Third, a contingent bet needs a real gate. Bet D funds fifteen engineers for eight weeks — the 120 engineer-weeks — to Sunday 28 February 2027, and its gate is extraction accuracy of 85 per cent on the 1,400-document benchmark set, against which today's model reads 1,000 documents correctly, or 71.4 per cent. If the gate holds, D's remaining 60 engineer-weeks become a Q2 commitment, not a mid-quarter raid.

4. When the cycle applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are testable: applied to a firm, they can come back false. Claim one: the cycle is shorter than the time its principal uncertainty needs. Barrowfield passes — extraction accuracy resolves in eight weeks inside a thirteen-week quarter. Brightkiln fails structurally: the pilot reports on 23 April and the tooling gate closes on 12 March, so the uncertainty resolves after the decision. A firm there cannot fix it by planning more often; it must buy information earlier or buy reversibility.

Claim two: a commitment is worth making only where the cost of breaking it exceeds the cost of the buffer that protects it. Barrowfield's renewals make that true for A and C and false for D, which is why D is contingent. Claim three: the resource the plan allocates is the resource that bounds output. This condition is the most assumed and least tested, and where it fails the apparatus turns actively misleading: a well-built capacity plan produces confident, specific, wrong targets for a firm bounded by anything but engineering effort. Two further misleading cases: a firm bound by cash runway, where the plan is a financing decision in a product costume; and a team whose interrupt load exceeds half its calendar capacity, where the planning problem is an unmade staffing decision.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature firms actually do

In multi-product firms the seam is ownership: one line's commitment consumes capacity held by a shared platform team, which is the mechanism behind the 230 engineer-weeks of sold deliverables already in Barrowfield's deductions. The plan that works names that capacity once and makes the lines bid for it. In two-sided marketplaces the binding side can change between planning and delivery, so the plan's first line must name which side binds and what would show it had moved. In regulated businesses statutory work has a date set outside the firm and is not a bet: Barrowfield's 104 engineer-weeks of compliance belong in the deductions, and a firm that lets them compete with revenue bets loses expensively. Hardware plus software runs two clocks at different speeds, joined at a tooling date. AI-native products carry uncertainty in model capability, which does not resolve on a schedule; the mature response funds two architectures to a gate rather than forecasting a capability date.

Mature firms say they run an annual plan reviewed quarterly. What they run is that plan plus an unpublished monthly reallocation meeting, where the decisions happen. The published plan is the contract with the outside, the reallocation meeting the contract with the inside; trouble starts when the two drift so far apart that nobody can say which is measured.

6. Eight distinctions that separate experts from competent planners

One: capacity is a distribution, not a number. The tell is a plan holding "about twenty per cent buffer" that cannot say what last quarter's unplanned work cost. A buffer looks like prudence; it is a measurement, and a firm that has measured 206 engineer-weeks need not argue about twenty per cent.

Two: the delivery ratio is a property of the planning process, not the engineers. The tell is a ratio that would stay near 0.69 across two reorganisations and a new engineering leader. The obvious reading, that estimation improves or decays with the team, may be wrong: the ratio could instead measure how much the firm commits before it knows, which section 10 leaves open.

Three: commitment levels beat confidence percentages. The tell is a roadmap item labelled "70 per cent confidence", on which nobody can act. Committed, contingent and unfunded are three different conversations with sales; a probability feels like more information and is less actionable.

Four: oversubscription is information, not failure. An experienced planner reads Barrowfield's 42.2 per cent oversubscription of commitment capacity as healthy and five per cent as alarming, because a nearly-fitting ask means teams censored their proposals before the meeting. The obvious reading is that a plan which fits is well made.

Five: the irreversibility date, not the fiscal date, sets the cycle. The tell is an expert's first question: when is the last reversible moment? Brightkiln's planning year turns on 12 March, not 1 January, and a firm that gates on the fiscal calendar reaches its irreversible dates unprepared.

Six: what is not in the plan is its most load-bearing sentence. The tell is a written, dated deferred list — Barrowfield's bet B, funded at nothing, with a Q2 re-entry. Naming what you dropped looks like inviting argument; it ends it, because unlisted work does not disappear, it returns as an interrupt.

Seven: capacity released by a kill is not capacity gained. The tell is a plan that re-promises a killed bet's weeks inside the same quarter. Those weeks already sat inside the buffer the delivery ratio created, so spending them twice turns an honest kill into a second broken promise.

Eight: the constraint must be re-derived each cycle, not inherited. The tell is the same build-down, in the same spreadsheet, applied to a year in which the binding resource moved. Consistency in the template is rigour; consistency in the constraint is an assumption nobody re-tested.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

Section 5 covered the seams; the cycle differences are shorter. In consumer products demand rather than supply usually binds, so the annual plan is mostly a budget and the quarterly plan does the work. In B2B and enterprise the question is how much to pre-sell, because contracts consume capacity before any bet is weighed. On platforms and marketplaces the plan must name the binding side. In hardware the irreversible date dominates. In AI products the plan carries gates where other plans carry dates. Where the difference is not real, say so: the build-down in Exhibit 1 is identical across all five once the bounding resource is named, as is the need for a written deferred list.

Stage changes the cycle more than product type does. Below roughly fifteen engineers a quarterly ceremony is theatre: the plan is the runway and the founder the reallocation meeting. In growth-stage firms the cycle becomes real before the delivery ratio exists; the honest move is to borrow a figure in the 0.65 to 0.75 range, say so out loud, and replace it after two quarters. At scale the binding problem becomes cross-team dependency, and the cycle's output shifts from bets to hand-offs.

8. Three worked examples

Barrowfield, Q1 2027 — the plan as built. Exhibits 1 and 3 are the example, and the figure to watch is the covering note's comparison of the 200-engineer-week buffer with the 206 engineer-weeks of unplanned work in the quarter to September 2026 — different quarters, different headcount, and different measures, which is why she labelled it indicative, not a forecast.

Brightkiln, 2027 — a freeze smaller than the firm believed. Ratanpura's planning deck asserted that $7.4 million of the $12.5 million plan, or 59.2 per cent, was frozen by the tooling decision. He then wrote the definition down — an item is annually irreversible if reversing it after the gate costs more than twenty per cent of its own budget — and tested every line.

The correction changed the decision: whether to hold the order open six weeks for the pilot. Brightkiln plans 14,000 ovens for 2027 at 350 a week, 70 a day on a five-day line, over forty production weeks: twenty on the existing board, which then stops, and twenty on the new one from 13 August. Weeks lost at the new-board start are therefore weeks in which nothing ships: six of them are 2,100 ovens, 15.0 per cent of the year's 14,000, worth 2,100 × $1,900 = $3.99 million of contribution at $1,900 an oven. That is an upper bound, not an estimate: the plant can run ten Saturday shifts at 70 ovens each, recovering 700 and leaving 1,400 net, or 1,400 × $1,900 = $2.66 million. Against it, the expected saving from waiting is the chance the pilot reverses the board choice — Ratanpura's team put it at thirty per cent, a judgement, not a measurement — times the $1.15 million cost of re-cutting tooling: 0.30 × $1.15m = $0.345 million. Even on the recovered basis, waiting costs 2.660 ÷ 0.345 = 7.7 times its expected saving.

Bluefern, 2025 — the plan that failed, and the recovery. Bluefern runs a home-services marketplace. Its 2025 plan committed to lifting completed jobs from 1.26 million to 2.10 million, a rise of 0.84 million or 66.7 per cent, and the quarterly plans sent almost all new engineering capacity to demand. Nobody tested the supply arithmetic. At the end of 2024 Bluefern had 42,000 active providers, so on the convention it used throughout — jobs divided by providers active at year-end — each completed 30.0 jobs. Delivering 2.10 million jobs at 30.0 jobs needed 70,000 providers, an increase of 28,000 — the same 66.7 per cent, and 2.43 times the 11,500 providers added in 2024, the firm's best year. Nobody had asked the recruiting team. The year closed at 1.54 million jobs, 73.3 per cent of target, with 51,800 providers each completing 29.7 jobs: the constraint held where the arithmetic said it would.

The recovery, built by Jaimini Rachh in November 2025, put supply on the plan's first line. Bluefern's twenty-five recruiters had added 11,500 providers in 2024, or 460 each, and 9,800 in 2025, or 392 each — a fall of 14.8 per cent as recruiting moved into thinner metros. Rachh planned on 392 rather than 460, and on thirty recruiters: 30 × 392 = 11,760 providers added, giving 51,800 + 11,760 = 63,560 providers, and 63,560 × 30 = 1.91 million jobs, which became the 2026 commitment. Through September 2026 Bluefern had completed 1.39 million jobs, 72.8 per cent of the 1.91 million plan, with its strongest quarter still to run.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Five failure modes recur, each announcing itself early. The diagnostic column matters more than the warning: a sign tells you to look, a question tells you where.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first position holds that annual commitments are the only mechanism that reliably forces trade-offs, on organisational rather than statistical evidence: firms that abolish the annual contract stop killing things, because nothing makes them choose. For it to be wrong you would need firms sustaining reallocation discipline without one, and its advocates offer the Beyond Budgeting literature's banking exemplars as exactly that.

The second holds that the annual cycle is a tax rarely costed — weeks of senior time producing a document the reallocation meeting overrides by March. For it to be wrong, commitments to customers, regulators or capital markets would have to genuinely require annual horizons, which in Barrowfield's renewals and Brightkiln's tooling they do.

The third is sharpest, and it attacks this page's arithmetic. It holds that capacity-based planning is false precision: a firm whose delivery ratio is 0.690 does not have a capacity model but a 31 per cent error bar, and the honest response is to fund durable teams against outcomes. For it to be wrong, the ratio would have to be improvable by better planning rather than fixed by the work. Nobody has that measurement, because no firm runs both regimes on comparable work at once, and this page does not resolve it: the build-down above is a decision aid, not a forecast.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied planning cycles produces a better document. Someone who has internalised them behaves differently in four ways. They ask what is irreversible before what is important, so their gates fall on supplier dates rather than fiscal quarters. They state a denominator before a rate, out loud, in meetings, which is why their plans survive finance review. They treat the deferred list as the plan's most quoted page and keep it dated. And they are relaxed about an oversubscribed intake and uneasy about a tidy one, knowing which hides a decision already made alone.

12. What each of them decided, and three questions

Rughani committed 306 engineer-weeks to bets A and C with dates attached, funded bet D's 120 to a 28 February gate with no external date, left 20 unallocated, and sent Ranka an annexe putting dates only against the 306. The renewals were sold on it. Ratanpura placed the tooling order on 12 March rather than waiting for the April pilot, on the arithmetic that waiting cost 7.7 times its expected saving, and moved Brightkiln's optionality into the firmware line Exhibit 4 puts outside the freeze.

  1. Barrowfield's delivery ratio of 0.690 comes from four quarters of its own record. What would have to change about how it plans for that ratio to become the wrong number to plan with?
  2. Brightkiln's reversibility test turns on a twenty per cent threshold that Ratanpura chose. Who in a firm should own that threshold, and what evidence would justify moving it?
  3. All three firms planned on single point estimates: capacity at Barrowfield, line rate at Brightkiln, recruiter throughput at Bluefern. What would a planning cycle look like if each were stated as a range, and what would that cost in commitments the firm could no longer make?

13. Going deeper

  • Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later — the artefact the plan prices.
  • Budgeting and headcount planning — sets the build-down's gross capacity line.
  • Strategy vs roadmap vs plan — the distinction section 2 assumes.
  • OKRs and goal setting — the link from strategy to bets.
  • Capacity planning — Exhibit 1's deductions, done rather than assumed.
  • Dependency management — what binds instead of capacity at scale.
  • Milestones and release planning — how a committed bet becomes dates.
  • Scenario planning — question three's subject.
  • Investment themes and allocation — how firms stop re-litigating bets.
  • Multi-year product planning — where Brightkiln's problem is normal.
  • The roadmap as communication — why Rughani's annexe, not her plan, is what the market reads.
